book: How to Win Friends and Influence People

questions.unitTitle: Preface
questions.q: According to the Preface, how many copies were printed in the first edition of How to Win Friends and Influence People in 1937?
options: Five thousand copies
Fifty thousand copies
Five hundred copies
One million copies
questions.explain: The Preface says the book first came out in an edition of only five thousand copies, and neither Carnegie nor Simon and Schuster expected more than this modest sale. The book then became an overnight sensation.

questions.unitTitle: Preface
questions.q: True or false: According to the Preface, Dale Carnegie and his publishers expected from the start that the book would become a huge best-seller.
questions.explain: The Preface says the opposite: neither Carnegie nor Simon and Schuster anticipated more than a modest sale, and the book's success came to their amazement.

questions.unitTitle: Preface
questions.q: In the Preface, Dorothy Carnegie recalls that Dale Carnegie used to say it was easier to make a million dollars than to put a ____ into the English language.
questions.explain: Carnegie's saying was that making a million dollars was easier than adding a phrase to the language, and the book's title became exactly such a phrase, quoted, paraphrased and parodied.

questions.unitTitle: Preface
questions.q: In the Preface, what was How to Win Friends and Influence People originally written to be used as?
options: A memoir of Carnegie's early career
A guide for salesmen at Simon and Schuster
A textbook for his courses in Effective Speaking and Human Relations
A companion to his book on effective speaking
questions.explain: The Preface says the book was written as a textbook for Carnegie's courses in Effective Speaking and Human Relations, and is still used in those courses. His separate book on effective speaking is mentioned only as something he updated several times.

questions.unitTitle: Preface
questions.q: Which of these does the Preface give as reasons for revising the book?
options: Carnegie himself was a tireless reviser who would have updated it had he lived longer
Many prominent people named in the book are no longer recognized by today's readers
Some examples and phrases now seem quaint and dated
The original principles had been shown to be wrong
Readers had complained that Carnegie's style was too colloquial
questions.explain: The Preface justifies the revision by Carnegie's own habit of revising and by dated names, examples and phrases that weaken the message. It insists the content was not tampered with and that the breezy, colloquial style was deliberately kept intact.

questions.unitTitle: Preface
questions.q: Sort these according to what the 1981 revision described in the Preface did.

items.t: A few excisions were made
A few more contemporary examples were added
The brash, breezy Carnegie style
The thirties slang
The book's content and principles

questions.explain: The Preface says the revisers only made a few excisions and added some contemporary examples, aiming to clarify and strengthen the book “without tampering with the content.” Carnegie's style, slang included, was left intact.

questions.unitTitle: Preface
questions.q: Match each item from the Preface with what the Preface says about it.
pairs: Year the book was first published
Year Dorothy Carnegie signed the Preface to the revision
questions.explain: The Preface dates the first edition to 1937 and Carnegie's death to 1955, names Simon and Schuster as publishers, and is signed by Dorothy Carnegie in 1981.

questions.unitTitle: Preface
questions.q: Put the front matter of How to Win Friends and Influence People in the order it appears before Part One.
items: Preface
How This Book Was Written—and Why
Nine Suggestions on How to Get the Most Out of This Book
Fundamental Techniques in Handling People
questions.explain: The Preface by Dorothy Carnegie comes first, explaining the revised edition, then Carnegie's own account of how the book was written, then his nine suggestions for using it, and only then Part One's techniques.

questions.unitTitle: Preface
questions.q: According to the Preface, why did Dorothy Carnegie think it was right to revise a book that was still selling well, and what did the revision try to do?
questions.a: Dale Carnegie was himself a tireless reviser who kept improving his course and his speaking book, and had he lived longer he would have revised this book to reflect changes since the thirties. Dated names, examples and phrases weakened the book's message for modern readers. So the revision aimed to clarify and strengthen the book for a modern reader “without tampering with the content,” making only a few excisions and adding some contemporary examples.

questions.unitTitle: Preface
questions.q: In the Preface, what evidence does Dorothy Carnegie give that the book met a lasting human need rather than being a passing fad, and what image does she use for the revision?
questions.a: The book became an overnight sensation, then kept selling without interruption into the eighties, almost half a century later, and was translated into almost every written language. Its title became a phrase quoted, paraphrased and parodied, and each generation found it relevant. She offers the revision in the spirit of the “honing and polishing of a finely made tool.”

questions.unitTitle: How This Book Was Written—and Why
questions.q: In the introduction to How to Win Friends and Influence People, an engineer with the best technical knowledge in her firm keeps being passed over for higher-paid roles. Which explanation fits the research Carnegie cites?
options: Engineering firms pay mainly for years of service, not for knowledge
About 85 percent of financial success comes from skill in dealing with and leading people
About 85 percent of financial success comes from technical knowledge kept up to date
Technical ability matters only in accountancy and architecture, not in engineering
questions.explain: The Carnegie Foundation research, confirmed at the Carnegie Institute of Technology, found that even in engineering only about 15 percent of financial success comes from technical knowledge. The other 85 percent comes from skill in human engineering, that is, personality and the ability to lead people.

questions.unitTitle: How This Book Was Written—and Why
questions.q: In the introduction, Carnegie reports research finding that even in engineering, about 85 percent of one’s financial success is due to skill in ____ engineering.
questions.explain: He calls the people skill “human engineering” and links it to personality and the ability to lead people. Technical knowledge accounts for only about 15 percent.

questions.unitTitle: How This Book Was Written—and Why
questions.q: True or false: In the introduction, Carnegie says the Meriden survey found that people, meaning how to understand and get along with them, was the prime interest of adults.
questions.explain: The survey found that health was the prime interest of adults. People, and how to get along with them, came second.

questions.unitTitle: How This Book Was Written—and Why
questions.q: In the introduction, what did the University of Chicago and United Y.M.C.A. Schools survey reveal about what adults want to study?
options: Their first interest is making money, and their second is health
Their first interest is people, and their second is public speaking
Their first interest is public speaking, and their second is people
Their first interest is health, and their second is people
questions.explain: The survey found that health was the prime interest of adults, and people came second: how to understand and get along with them, make them like you and win them to your way of thinking.

questions.unitTitle: How This Book Was Written—and Why
questions.q: In the introduction, the adult-education survey ended in a Connecticut town chosen as a typical American town, where every adult was asked 156 questions. That town was ____.
questions.explain: The last part of the survey was made in Meriden, Connecticut, chosen as a typical American town. Every adult there was interviewed and asked 156 questions.

questions.unitTitle: How This Book Was Written—and Why
questions.q: In the introduction, when the Meriden survey committee asked a leading authority on adult education for a suitable textbook on getting along with people, what did he answer?
options: That several good books existed but were too academic for adults
That adults learn better from lectures than from textbooks
That he knew what the adults wanted, but the book they needed had never been written
That the course should be built from the writings of the old philosophers
questions.explain: He replied that he knew what those adults wanted, but “the book they need has never been written.” Carnegie says his own years of searching for a practical handbook on human relations confirmed this.

questions.unitTitle: How This Book Was Written—and Why
questions.q: In the introduction to How to Win Friends and Influence People, why does Carnegie say he wrote the book?
questions.a: Since 1912 he had run courses for business and professional adults in New York, at first in public speaking only. He came to see that these adults needed training in getting along with people even more than in speaking, and he needed it himself. The Meriden survey showed adults wanted such a course, yet no practical textbook existed, so he wrote one for use in his own courses.

questions.unitTitle: How This Book Was Written—and Why
questions.q: In the introduction, Carnegie describes how the printed material for his course grew over the years. Put the stages in order, from first to last.
items: A set of rules on a card no larger than a postcard
A larger card
A leaflet
A series of booklets
This book
questions.explain: Each season the material expanded in size and scope: from a postcard-sized card, to a larger card, a leaflet and a series of booklets. The book came after fifteen years of experiment and research.

questions.unitTitle: How This Book Was Written—and Why
questions.q: In the introduction, Carnegie describes how his talk on human relations developed. Put these steps in order, from first to last.
items: He prepared a short talk from all his research material
The talk expanded into a lecture of an hour and a half
He urged listeners to test the ideas in their business and social contacts
Listeners came back to class to speak about their results
questions.explain: The short talk, called How to Win Friends and Influence People, grew into a ninety-minute lecture. Listeners were then sent out to test it and report their experiences back in class, which made the course a laboratory.

questions.unitTitle: How This Book Was Written—and Why
questions.q: In the introduction, Carnegie lists famous people he interviewed about human relations. Match each person to the group Carnegie puts them in.
questions.explain: Carnegie names inventors like Marconi and Edison, political leaders like Franklin D. Roosevelt and James Farley, the business leader Owen D. Young, movie stars like Clark Gable and Mary Pickford, and the explorer Martin Johnson.

questions.unitTitle: How This Book Was Written—and Why
questions.q: In the introduction, Carnegie quotes several people. Match each person to the idea Carnegie quotes from them.
pairs: He would pay more for the ability to deal with people than for any other
Compared to what we ought to be, we are only half awake
Education is the ability to meet life’s situations
The great aim of education is not knowledge but action
questions.explain: Rockefeller called dealing with people a purchasable commodity like sugar or coffee; William James said we use only a small part of our resources; Hibben defined education as meeting life’s situations; Spencer said its aim is action, which leads Carnegie to call this an action book.

questions.unitTitle: How This Book Was Written—and Why
questions.q: In the introduction, Carnegie gives examples of course members changed by his principles. Match each person to what happened.
pairs: His employees became his friends and even the janitor used his first name
He was saved from demotion and promoted with increased pay
He was so stirred that he could not sleep for two nights and a day
He learned more in fourteen weeks than in four years of college
questions.explain: The employer turned 314 enemies into 314 friends, the belligerent gas works executive was promoted instead of demoted, the art dealer was too shaken to sleep, and the carpet factory owner made his fourteen-weeks claim at the Yale Club.

questions.unitTitle: How This Book Was Written—and Why
questions.q: In the introduction, Carnegie says his course members were fascinated by working in a new kind of ____, the first and only one of human relationships for adults that had ever existed.
questions.explain: Course members tested the principles in daily life and reported back, so Carnegie calls the course “the first and only laboratory of human relationships for adults that had ever existed.”

questions.unitTitle: How This Book Was Written—and Why
questions.q: In the introduction, Carnegie says the book was not written in the usual sense of the word. What does he mean?
options: It was dictated from his lectures by a stenographer and lightly edited
It grew like a child, out of the experiences of thousands of adults in his courses
It was compiled mainly from the biographies of great leaders
It was written by his trained researcher and only revised by him
questions.explain: He says the book “grew as a child grows,” developing out of the laboratory of his courses and the experiences of thousands of adults. Reading and interviews supplied material, but the book took shape through testing in class.

questions.unitTitle: How This Book Was Written—and Why
questions.q: In the closing line of the introduction, Carnegie sums up his book by calling it an ____ book.
questions.explain: After quoting Herbert Spencer that the great aim of education is not knowledge but action, Carnegie ends: “And this is an action book.”

questions.unitTitle: How This Book Was Written—and Why
questions.q: Which of these does Carnegie say, in the introduction, that he and his researcher read in preparing the book?
options: Newspaper columns and magazine articles
Records of the family courts
Minutes of company board meetings
Over one hundred biographies of Theodore Roosevelt
Government census tables
questions.explain: Carnegie read everything he could find, from newspaper columns and magazine articles to family court records and the writings of philosophers and psychologists, and his team read over a hundred biographies of Theodore Roosevelt alone. Board minutes and census tables are not mentioned.

questions.unitTitle: How This Book Was Written—and Why
questions.q: Which of these results of applying the principles does Carnegie report in the introduction?
options: Salespeople sharply increased their sales and opened new accounts
Executives were given increased authority and pay
Spouses said their homes had become much happier
Students raised their examination grades
Employers cut their workforce and saved costs
questions.explain: Carnegie reports higher sales and new accounts for salespeople, more authority and pay for executives, and happier homes according to spouses at the end-of-course banquet. He mentions nothing about exam grades or job cuts.

questions.unitTitle: How This Book Was Written—and Why
questions.q: Which of these abilities does Carnegie say, in the introduction, a person needs on top of technical knowledge to be headed for higher earning power?
options: The ability to express ideas
The ability to assume leadership
The ability to arouse enthusiasm among people
A degree from a leading university
Willingness to work longer hours than others
questions.explain: Carnegie says mere technical ability can be hired at nominal salaries, but the person who adds the ability to express ideas, assume leadership and arouse enthusiasm is headed for higher earning power. Degrees and long hours are not part of his claim.

questions.unitTitle: How This Book Was Written—and Why
questions.q: In the introduction, sort each fact into the Meriden adult-education survey or Carnegie’s own research for the book.

items.t: Cost $25,000 and took two years
Asked every adult 156 questions
Run by the University of Chicago and the United Y.M.C.A. Schools
Found health to be the first interest of adults
A trained researcher spent a year and a half in libraries
Read over one hundred biographies of Theodore Roosevelt
Interviewed Marconi and Edison
Fifteen years of experiment in courses

questions.explain: The survey was an outside study of what adults want to study, and it showed the need for a book. The library research, biographies, interviews and years of course experiment were Carnegie’s own work to meet that need.

questions.unitTitle: How This Book Was Written—and Why
questions.q: In the introduction, sort each detail about the employer with 314 employees into before or after he studied Carnegie’s principles.

items.t: He drove, criticized and condemned his employees
No one greeted him as he walked through
Employees looked the other way when he approached
His organization showed new loyalty and teamwork
Even the janitor called him by his first name
He found more profit, leisure and happiness

questions.explain: Before, kindness and appreciation were alien to his lips and his staff avoided him. After changing his philosophy, 314 enemies became 314 friends, and he gained profit, leisure and, most importantly, happiness.

questions.unitTitle: How This Book Was Written—and Why
questions.q: In the introduction, why does Carnegie stress that the man who could not sleep after a talk was a sophisticated art dealer who spoke three languages and had two European degrees?
options: To show the principles moved even a worldly, educated man, not just a naïve person
To show that the principles work best for people who speak several languages
To show that his courses attracted mainly wealthy and well-travelled students
To show that European universities fail to teach human relations
questions.explain: Carnegie asks whether the man was a naïve person ready to gush over any new theory and answers no: he was a sophisticated, blasé man about town. The point is that the effect was not gullibility.

questions.unitTitle: How This Book Was Written—and Why
questions.q: In the introduction, Carnegie quotes William James saying people habitually fail to use many of their powers. What does Carnegie say follows for his book?
options: Its main aim is to teach the latest findings of psychology
Its main aim is to teach better public speaking
Its sole purpose is to help readers discover, develop and profit by those unused assets
Its sole purpose is to show how great leaders of the past behaved
questions.explain: Picking up James’s phrase, Carnegie says the sole purpose of the book is to help readers discover, develop and profit by those dormant and unused assets. Leaders’ biographies were research material, not the purpose.

questions.unitTitle: How This Book Was Written—and Why
questions.q: In the introduction, Carnegie sets a test for his book. By what point does he say that, if you are not better equipped to meet life’s situations, he will count the book a total failure for you?
options: After you finish the first three chapters
After you finish the whole book
After you complete fourteen weeks of his course
After you review the book each month for a year
questions.explain: Carnegie says that if you are not a little better equipped to meet life’s situations by the time you have finished the first three chapters, he will consider the book a total failure as far as you are concerned.

questions.unitTitle: How This Book Was Written—and Why
questions.q: In How to Win Friends and Influence People, the introduction comes between the Preface and the Nine Suggestions on How to Get the Most Out of This Book. What job does the introduction do in that sequence?
options: It explains how Dorothy Carnegie revised the book for modern readers
It gives the study method: read each chapter twice and underscore ideas
It begins the techniques with the rule against criticizing people
It argues why the book was needed and why it is worth reading
questions.explain: The introduction opens by asking why Carnegie wrote another book and why anyone should read it, and answers with the need for it and its results. The revision story belongs to the Preface, and the study method follows in the Nine Suggestions.

questions.unitTitle: How This Book Was Written—and Why
questions.q: In the introduction to How to Win Friends and Influence People, what does the research on engineers suggest about technical skill and success, and how do Carnegie’s engineering classes support it?
questions.a: The Carnegie Foundation research found that even in engineering only about 15 percent of financial success comes from technical knowledge and about 85 percent from skill in human engineering, meaning personality and the ability to lead people. Over fifteen hundred engineers came to his classes because they had seen that the highest-paid engineers are often not those who know the most engineering. Technical ability can be hired cheaply; adding the ability to express ideas, lead and arouse enthusiasm brings higher earning power.

questions.unitTitle: How This Book Was Written—and Why
questions.q: In the introduction to How to Win Friends and Influence People, what does Carnegie mean when he calls his course a laboratory of human relationships, and how did it shape the book?
questions.a: Carnegie gave his talk and then asked adults to go out and test the ideas in their business and social contacts, and come back to class to report their experiences and results. This testing in real life made the course a kind of laboratory. The book grew out of it, from a postcard-sized set of rules through cards, a leaflet and booklets, after fifteen years of experiment and research, so the rules are not mere theory or guesswork.

questions.unitTitle: How This Book Was Written—and Why
questions.q: The introduction to How to Win Friends and Influence People ends by calling it an action book. How does this ending prepare the reader for the Nine Suggestions that follow?
questions.a: Carnegie closes with Herbert Spencer’s line that the great aim of education is not knowledge but action, and says the book should leave you better able to meet life’s situations. The Nine Suggestions then turn this into a method: build a deep desire to learn, stop to ask how to apply each suggestion, and apply the principles at every opportunity. So the introduction sets the goal of action and the suggestions show how to reach it.

questions.unitTitle: How This Book Was Written—and Why
questions.q: Why does Carnegie open the introduction to How to Win Friends and Influence People with figures about publishing, such as one publisher losing money on seven out of every eight books?
questions.a: He points out that most books printed in America were deadly dull and many were financial failures. This sets up two fair questions: why he dared write yet another book, and why the reader should bother to read it. The rest of the introduction answers them by showing the need for a practical handbook on human relations and the results it has produced.

questions.unitTitle: How This Book Was Written—and Why
questions.q: In the introduction to How to Win Friends and Influence People, how does Carnegie use William James’s idea that we are only half awake to state the purpose of his book?
questions.a: James said that compared with what we ought to be, we use only a small part of our physical and mental resources and live far within our limits. Carnegie takes up the powers we “habitually fail to use” and says the sole purpose of the book is to help the reader discover, develop and profit by those dormant and unused assets.

questions.unitTitle: How This Book Was Written—and Why
questions.q: True or false: In the introduction, Carnegie quotes John D. Rockefeller as saying he would pay more for the ability to deal with people than for any other ability under the sun.
questions.explain: Rockefeller called the ability to deal with people as purchasable a commodity as sugar or coffee and said he would pay more for it than for any other. Carnegie then wonders why colleges do not teach this highest-priced ability.

questions.unitTitle: How This Book Was Written—and Why
questions.q: True or false: In the introduction, Carnegie says he hired a trained researcher to spend three years in libraries reading everything he had missed.
questions.explain: The researcher spent one and a half years in libraries, reading psychology, magazine articles and biographies to find how great leaders dealt with people.

questions.unitTitle: How This Book Was Written—and Why
questions.q: In the introduction, Carnegie says that when he began his New York courses in 1912, they were courses in public ____ only.
questions.explain: At first he taught public speaking only, to help adults think on their feet and express ideas. He gradually saw they needed training in getting along with people even more.

questions.unitTitle: How This Book Was Written—and Why
questions.q: Put these parts of the front of How to Win Friends and Influence People in the order they appear in the book.
items: Preface
How This Book Was Written—and Why
Nine Suggestions on How to Get the Most Out of This Book
Part One: Fundamental Techniques in Handling People
questions.explain: Dorothy Carnegie’s Preface comes first, then Carnegie’s introduction on why the book exists, then the Nine Suggestions on how to study it, and only then Part One with the techniques themselves.

questions.unitTitle: Nine Suggestions on How to Get the Most Out of This Book
questions.q: In Carnegie's first suggestion, what is the one indispensable requirement for getting the most out of the book?
options: A system of careful note-taking on every chapter
A deep, driving desire to learn and determination to deal better with people
A willingness to read the whole book in one sitting
A teacher or class to explain the principles
questions.explain: Carnegie calls it “a deep, driving desire to learn, a vigorous determination to increase your ability to deal with people.” Study rules and techniques, he says, matter far less than this.

questions.unitTitle: Nine Suggestions on How to Get the Most Out of This Book
questions.q: According to Carnegie's first suggestion, how can a reader develop the urge to learn the book's principles?
options: By memorising each principle word for word
By reading the book quickly several times in a row
By constantly reminding yourself how important the principles are to you
By promising a friend to finish the book
questions.explain: He says to keep reminding yourself how important the principles are and to picture how mastering them will make life richer and happier. Memorising or rereading quickly is not his method for building desire.

questions.unitTitle: Nine Suggestions on How to Get the Most Out of This Book
questions.q: In Carnegie's second suggestion, why should a reader go back and reread each chapter thoroughly after a rapid first reading?
options: In the long run it saves time and gets results
It makes the book more entertaining
It lets the reader skip the later review
It is required to understand the stories
questions.explain: Carnegie says rereading thoroughly will, in the long run, mean saving time and getting results. Rushing on is only fine if you read merely for entertainment.

questions.unitTitle: Nine Suggestions on How to Get the Most Out of This Book
questions.q: Why did the insurance office manager in Carnegie's fifth suggestion read all her company's contracts every month?
options: Her employer required a monthly audit
She was looking for errors made by clerks
She was training new staff to read contracts
It was the only way she could keep their provisions clearly in mind
questions.explain: Experience had taught her that rereading was the only way to keep the provisions clearly in mind. Carnegie uses her to show how quickly we forget.

questions.unitTitle: Nine Suggestions on How to Get the Most Out of This Book
questions.q: What point does Carnegie draw from Bernard Shaw's remark that if you teach a man anything, he will never learn?
options: Books are a poor substitute for teachers
Learning is an active process; we learn by doing
Adults cannot change their habits
People resent being given advice
questions.explain: Carnegie agrees with Shaw and concludes that learning is active: we learn by doing, so the rules must be applied at every opportunity. Only knowledge that is used sticks.

questions.unitTitle: Nine Suggestions on How to Get the Most Out of This Book
questions.q: In Carnegie's sixth suggestion, what should you do when facing a specific problem such as satisfying an irritated customer?
options: Hesitate to do the natural, impulsive thing and review the paragraphs you underscored
Act at once on your first instinct before the moment passes
Ask the other person what principle they would like you to use
Wait until your weekly review to decide what to do
questions.explain: He says the natural, impulsive thing is usually wrong; instead turn to the book and review your underscored paragraphs, then try the new ways. Acting on instinct is exactly what he warns against.

questions.unitTitle: Nine Suggestions on How to Get the Most Out of This Book
questions.q: What did the Wall Street bank president in Carnegie's eighth suggestion do on Saturday evenings?
options: Read biographies of great financiers
Met with his family to plan the coming week
Taught a class on human relations
Went through his engagement book and reviewed the week's interviews and meetings
questions.explain: He went off by himself after dinner, opened his engagement book and thought over all the week's interviews, discussions and meetings. His family made no plans for him on Saturday nights for this reason.

questions.unitTitle: Nine Suggestions on How to Get the Most Out of This Book
questions.q: Why does the chapter Nine Suggestions on How to Get the Most Out of This Book come before Part One, Fundamental Techniques in Handling People?
options: It summarises every principle in the four Parts
It tells the story of how Carnegie came to write the book
It sets out how to study and apply the principles that the following Parts present
It lists the people interviewed for the book
questions.explain: The chapter is about method: desire, rereading, marking, review and practice, so that the principles which follow become habits. The story of how the book was written belongs to the preceding introduction.

questions.unitTitle: Nine Suggestions on How to Get the Most Out of This Book
questions.q: True or false: Carnegie says that, because he wrote the book, he found it easy to apply everything he advocated.
questions.explain: He says the opposite: even though he wrote the book, he frequently found it difficult to apply everything he advocated. He uses this to warn the reader that forming new habits takes persistence.

questions.unitTitle: Nine Suggestions on How to Get the Most Out of This Book
questions.q: True or false: In Carnegie's seventh suggestion, you offer a friend a dime or a dollar each time you catch the friend violating one of the principles.
questions.explain: The payment goes the other way: you pay the friend, spouse, child or associate each time he or she catches you violating a principle. The aim is to make a lively game of mastering the rules.

questions.unitTitle: Nine Suggestions on How to Get the Most Out of This Book
questions.q: True or false: Nine Suggestions on How to Get the Most Out of This Book comes after How This Book Was Written—and Why and before Part One.
questions.explain: In the book's order it is the last piece of front matter, following the preface and the introduction and leading into Part One, Fundamental Techniques in Handling People.

questions.unitTitle: Nine Suggestions on How to Get the Most Out of This Book
questions.q: Carnegie's sixth suggestion, drawing on Bernard Shaw, says: Learning is an ____ process.
questions.explain: Carnegie writes that learning is active and “We learn by doing.” That is why he urges applying the rules at every opportunity.

questions.unitTitle: Nine Suggestions on How to Get the Most Out of This Book
questions.q: Carnegie asks readers to regard the book as a working ____ on human relations.
questions.explain: He wants it consulted whenever a specific problem arises, such as handling a child or an irritated customer, rather than read once and shelved.

questions.unitTitle: Nine Suggestions on How to Get the Most Out of This Book
questions.q: Carnegie's second suggestion: read each chapter rapidly at first to get a ____ view of it.
questions.explain: A quick first reading gives an overview; then the reader should go back and reread the chapter thoroughly.

questions.unitTitle: Nine Suggestions on How to Get the Most Out of This Book
questions.q: Carnegie's ninth suggestion asks readers to use the blank pages at the end of the book to record their ____ in applying the principles.
questions.explain: He asks for specific entries with names, dates and results, saying such a record will inspire greater efforts.

questions.unitTitle: Nine Suggestions on How to Get the Most Out of This Book
questions.q: Carnegie tells readers that they are not merely trying to acquire information; they are attempting to form new ____.
questions.explain: He adds that this is a new way of life, which requires time, persistence and daily application.

questions.unitTitle: Nine Suggestions on How to Get the Most Out of This Book
questions.q: Which of these does Carnegie give as examples of how much easier the natural reaction is than applying his advice?
options: It is easier to criticize and condemn than to understand the other person's viewpoint
It is easier to listen than to talk about yourself
It is frequently easier to find fault than to find praise
It is more natural to talk about what you want than about what the other person wants
It is easier to admit a mistake than to defend it
questions.explain: Carnegie lists criticizing over understanding, finding fault over praise, and talking about your own wants. He does not claim listening or admitting mistakes comes naturally.

questions.unitTitle: Nine Suggestions on How to Get the Most Out of This Book
questions.q: Which of these questions did the Wall Street bank president in Carnegie's eighth suggestion ask himself in his weekly review?
options: Who owes me a favour this week?
What mistakes did I make that time?
What did I do that was right, and how could I have improved?
How much money did my bank earn this week?
What lessons can I learn from that experience?
questions.explain: His three questions were about mistakes, what he did right and how to improve, and lessons to learn. Favours and earnings were not part of his self-examination.

questions.unitTitle: Nine Suggestions on How to Get the Most Out of This Book
questions.q: Which of these does Carnegie say will result if you use a weekly check-up system like the banker's?
options: You will be engaged in an educational process that is intriguing and priceless
You will never make the same mistake twice
Your ability to meet and deal with people will grow enormously
You will become an important financier
questions.explain: Carnegie names exactly two results: an intriguing, priceless educational process, and an enormous growth in your ability to deal with people. He promises neither perfection nor wealth.

questions.unitTitle: Nine Suggestions on How to Get the Most Out of This Book
questions.q: Put these points from Carnegie's closing summary list in the order he gives them.
items: Develop a deep, driving desire to master the principles
Read each chapter twice before going on
Stop frequently to ask how you can apply each suggestion
Underscore each important idea
Review this book each month
Apply these principles at every opportunity
questions.explain: The summary list follows the order of the numbered suggestions: desire first, then rereading, reflecting, marking, monthly review and application.

questions.unitTitle: Nine Suggestions on How to Get the Most Out of This Book
questions.q: Put the steps of the Wall Street bank president's Saturday evening routine in order.
items: Have dinner
Go off by himself
Open his engagement book
Think over the week's interviews, discussions and meetings
Ask himself what mistakes he made and what lessons to learn
questions.explain: After dinner he went off alone, opened his engagement book, thought over the week's meetings, and then questioned himself about mistakes, improvements and lessons.

questions.unitTitle: Nine Suggestions on How to Get the Most Out of This Book
questions.q: Match each person in Nine Suggestions on How to Get the Most Out of This Book to the point Carnegie uses them to make.
pairs: Rereading regularly is the only way to keep details clearly in mind
Being taught is not enough; we learn by doing
A weekly self-examination improves your dealings with people
Even an author forgets what he wrote without going back over it
questions.explain: Each example supports a suggestion: the manager and Carnegie's own book show how fast we forget, Shaw shows learning is active, and the banker models weekly review.

questions.unitTitle: Nine Suggestions on How to Get the Most Out of This Book
questions.q: Match each of Carnegie's suggestions to the purpose he gives for it.
pairs: Read with a pencil or highlighter in hand
Makes the book more interesting and easier to review rapidly
Pay a dime or a dollar when caught violating a principle
Makes a lively game out of mastering the rules
Record your triumphs on the blank pages
Keeps you from forgetting and builds the principles into habits
questions.explain: Carnegie attaches a reason to each habit: marking aids review, the dime game adds fun, the record inspires effort, and monthly review fights rapid forgetting.

questions.unitTitle: Nine Suggestions on How to Get the Most Out of This Book
questions.q: Sort these reading habits into what Carnegie recommends and what he warns against.

items.t: Rereading each chapter thoroughly after a quick first pass
Rushing on to the next chapter after one quick reading
Reviewing the book for a few hours every month
Skimming through the book once and putting it away
Keeping the book on your desk and glancing through it often
Doing the natural, impulsive thing when a problem arises

questions.explain: Carnegie wants thorough rereading, monthly review and constant reference; he warns that one skim will not suffice and that the impulsive reaction is usually wrong.

questions.unitTitle: Nine Suggestions on How to Get the Most Out of This Book
questions.q: Sort these suggestions by whether they concern studying the book itself or checking your practice of the principles with people.

items.t: Read each chapter twice
Underscore each important idea
Review the book each month
Pay a friend who catches you violating a principle
Review each week's mistakes and lessons
Note when and how you applied the principles

questions.explain: Rereading, underscoring and monthly review are about absorbing the text; the dime game, the weekly check-up and the record of triumphs track how you actually use the principles.

questions.unitTitle: Nine Suggestions on How to Get the Most Out of This Book
questions.q: What does Carnegie call the one indispensable requirement for getting the most out of the book, and how does he say a reader can develop it?
questions.a: Carnegie says the essential requirement, more important than any rule of study, is a deep, driving desire to learn and a vigorous determination to increase your ability to deal with people. You develop it by constantly reminding yourself how important the principles are and picturing how mastering them will give you a richer, happier life. He suggests repeating that your popularity, happiness and sense of worth depend largely on your skill in dealing with people.

questions.unitTitle: Nine Suggestions on How to Get the Most Out of This Book
questions.q: Why does Carnegie insist that skimming the book once will not give lasting benefit, and what does he recommend instead?
questions.a: Carnegie says “The rapidity with which we forget is astonishing,” citing the office manager who reread her firm's contracts monthly and his own need to reread his public-speaking book. So after reading thoroughly, the reader should review the book for a few hours every month, keep it on the desk and glance through it often. The principles become habitual only through a constant, vigorous campaign of review and application.

questions.unitTitle: Nine Suggestions on How to Get the Most Out of This Book
questions.q: Explain what Carnegie means when he says the reader is not merely acquiring information but attempting a new way of life.
questions.a: Carnegie says the principles cut against natural reactions: it is easier to criticize than to understand, to find fault than to praise, and to talk about what you want than about what others want. So reading is about forming new habits, which takes time, persistence and daily application. That is why he urges applying the rules at every opportunity and using the book as a working handbook when real problems arise.

questions.unitTitle: Nine Suggestions on How to Get the Most Out of This Book
questions.q: Describe the Wall Street bank president's system of self-improvement and why Carnegie recommends something similar.
questions.a: Every Saturday evening the banker went through his engagement book, reviewed the week's interviews and meetings, and asked what mistakes he made, what he did right and how he could improve, and what lessons he could learn. Over the years his blunders grew less frequent, and he said the system improved his decisions and his contacts with people more than anything else. Carnegie suggests a similar weekly check-up on applying the book's principles, which he says will be an intriguing, priceless education and will greatly increase your ability to deal with people.

questions.unitTitle: Nine Suggestions on How to Get the Most Out of This Book
questions.q: How does Nine Suggestions on How to Get the Most Out of This Book prepare the reader for the four Parts of principles that follow it?
questions.a: The chapter teaches no principle of human relations itself; it sets out a method for learning the principles in Parts One to Four. It asks the reader to bring a strong desire to learn, read each chapter twice, mark and review it, and above all apply the rules daily, checking progress weekly. In this way the later chapters are meant to be used as a working handbook and turned into habits rather than read once for information.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: In the letter “Two Gun” Crowley wrote while police fired into his apartment, how did he describe himself?
options: As having a weary but kind heart that would harm nobody
As a desperate man who regretted killing the policeman
As a public benefactor who gave people lighter pleasures
As a hunted man who only wanted a fair trial
questions.explain: Crowley wrote that under his coat was “a weary heart, but a kind one” even though he had just gunned down a policeman. The public benefactor claim belongs to Al Capone, not Crowley.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: When “Two Gun” Crowley arrived at the death house in Sing Sing, what did he say, according to Carnegie?
options: That this was what he got for killing people
That the police had framed him for the shooting
That this was what he got for defending himself
That he would gladly die to protect his sweetheart
questions.explain: Crowley said it was what he got for defending himself, not for killing people. Carnegie uses this to show that Crowley blamed himself for nothing.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: How did Al Capone regard himself, according to Carnegie?
options: As a criminal who deserved his punishment
As an unappreciated and misunderstood public benefactor
As a victim of corrupt Chicago police
As a businessman forced into crime by poverty
questions.explain: Capone complained that he had spent his best years giving people the lighter pleasures and received only abuse. Carnegie says he saw himself as a misunderstood public benefactor rather than condemning himself.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: What did Lewis Lawes, warden of Sing Sing, tell Carnegie about the prisoners there?
options: Most of them admitted their guilt once they were sentenced
Most of them blamed alcohol and bad company for their crimes
Most of them were hardened men with no feelings at all
Few of them regarded themselves as bad men
questions.explain: Lawes said that “few of the criminals in Sing Sing regard themselves as bad men,” and that they reason their way to justifying their acts even to themselves.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: What did John Wanamaker say he had learned thirty years earlier?
options: That firm discipline makes the best employees
That praise should be saved for exceptional work
That it is foolish to scold
That people improve fastest when shown their errors
questions.explain: Wanamaker confessed he had learned “that it is foolish to scold,” since he had enough trouble with his own limitations. The other ideas run against the chapter's point.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Why does Carnegie call criticism futile?
options: It puts a person on the defensive and makes him strive to justify himself
It is usually based on incomplete facts about the other person
It takes too much time compared with simply giving orders
It teaches the other person to criticize in return
questions.explain: Carnegie says criticism is futile because it puts a person on the defensive and usually makes him justify himself. Wounding pride and arousing resentment are what make it dangerous, a separate point.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: What did B. F. Skinner's experiments show, as Carnegie reports them?
options: Punished animals avoid mistakes better than rewarded ones
An animal rewarded for good behavior learns faster and retains more than one punished for bad behavior
Animals learn equally well from reward and punishment if both are consistent
Rewards work only for animals, while humans need correction
questions.explain: Skinner found that rewarded animals learn more rapidly and retain what they learn far more effectively than punished ones, and Carnegie adds that later studies found the same for humans.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: A warehouse supervisor finds workers again not wearing their safety gloves. Following George B. Johnston’s experience with hard hats, which approach would Carnegie expect to work best?
options: Quote the regulation with authority and insist they comply
Report the workers to management so the rule is enforced
Post warning signs and say nothing to the workers directly
Ask if the gloves are uncomfortable and pleasantly remind them they protect against injury
questions.explain: Johnston's authoritative orders got sullen acceptance and hats came off once he left. Asking whether the hats were uncomfortable and reminding the men pleasantly of their purpose brought more compliance with no resentment.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: In the election that followed the quarrel between Theodore Roosevelt and President Taft, how many states did Taft and the Republican party carry?
options: Only one
Only five
Only two
Only ten
questions.explain: Taft and the Republicans carried only Vermont and Utah, which Carnegie calls the most disastrous defeat the party had ever known.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: What point does Carnegie draw from the quarrel between Theodore Roosevelt and President Taft?
options: Roosevelt’s criticism did not persuade Taft he was wrong; it only made him justify himself
Roosevelt was right to criticize Taft because Taft had betrayed him
Taft lost because he refused to answer Roosevelt’s criticism publicly
Public quarrels between leaders always end with one side admitting fault
questions.explain: Carnegie says he does not know or care who was to blame; the point is that all the criticism merely made Taft strive to justify himself, tearfully repeating that he could not have done differently.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.section: Principle: Don’t criticize, condemn or complain
questions.q: Which saying of Dr. Johnson does Carnegie quote near the end of the chapter, before stating the principle?
options: To know all is to forgive all
God himself, sir, does not propose to judge man until the end of his days
Any fool can criticize, condemn and complain
A great man shows his greatness by the way he treats little men
questions.explain: Carnegie quotes Dr. Johnson on God not judging man until the end of his days and then asks why we should. The line about how a great man treats little men is Carlyle's.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: How did Mrs. Fall react when Herbert Hoover hinted that a friend had betrayed President Harding?
options: She admitted her husband had made a terrible mistake
She refused to comment and left the room
She blamed Harding’s other advisers for the scandal
She insisted her husband had never betrayed anyone and had himself been betrayed
questions.explain: Mrs. Fall wept and screamed that her husband never betrayed anyone and was the one who had been betrayed. Carnegie calls this human nature in action: wrongdoers blaming everybody but themselves.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Why did Abraham Lincoln choose cavalry broadswords for his duel with James Shields?
options: He was a trained swordsman from West Point
Shields was known to be an excellent shot
He had very long arms
Pistols were banned in Illinois
questions.explain: Lincoln was given the choice of weapons and, since he had very long arms, chose broadswords and took lessons from a West Point graduate.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: What lasting lesson did Lincoln take from the near-duel with James Shields?
options: Never again did he write an insulting letter or ridicule anyone
He resolved to write only anonymous criticism in future
He decided to settle all disputes in court rather than in public
He learned to hide his feelings by never writing letters at all
questions.explain: Carnegie says the episode taught Lincoln an invaluable lesson: he never again wrote an insulting letter or ridiculed anyone, and almost never criticized anybody. He still wrote letters, as the unsent Meade letter shows.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: When Mrs. Lincoln and others spoke harshly of the southern people, what did Lincoln reply?
options: That the South would be punished after the war
Not to criticize them, since they were just what we would be under similar circumstances
That only their leaders, not the people, deserved blame
That harsh words would only lengthen the war
questions.explain: Lincoln said, “Don’t criticize them; they are just what we would be under similar circumstances.” He did not blame the leaders instead, nor argue from the length of the war.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: What happened to the stern letter Lincoln wrote to General Meade after Lee escaped across the Potomac?
options: Meade read it and resigned from the army
Meade received it and attacked Lee south of the river
Lincoln read it aloud to his cabinet
Lincoln never mailed it, and it was found among his papers after his death
questions.explain: Meade never saw the letter, because Lincoln never mailed it; it was found among his papers after he died. Resignation was only one of the harms Lincoln feared the letter might cause.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Why did Mark Twain’s stinging letters do no real harm, according to Carnegie?
options: Twain always apologized the next day
The people he wrote to found them funny
His wife secretly lifted them out of the mail
He wrote them under a pen name
questions.explain: Writing the letters let Twain blow off steam, and they did no harm because his wife secretly removed them from the mail, so they were never sent.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: You have drafted a sharp email to a colleague whose mistake cost your team a week. Following Lincoln’s handling of his letter to Meade, what would Carnegie suggest?
options: Send it at once so the colleague knows how serious the mistake was
Put it aside unsent and imagine how things looked from the colleague’s position
Soften a few words and copy in your manager
Send it but add praise at the end to balance the criticism
questions.explain: Lincoln wrote his rebuke, then imagined Meade's circumstances and set the letter aside, knowing sending it would relieve his feelings but make Meade justify himself and condemn him.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: What did test pilot Bob Hoover do when he met the mechanic who had filled his plane with the wrong fuel?
options: He had the mechanic reported and dismissed
He explained calmly how dangerous the error had been
He asked the mechanic to write a report of what went wrong
He put an arm around him and asked him to service his F-51 the next day
questions.explain: Instead of scolding, Hoover said, “To show you I’m sure that you’ll never do this again, I want you to service my F-51 tomorrow.” He did not even criticize the young man.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: What does the chapter’s title, about gathering honey without kicking over the beehive, signal in light of its argument?
options: That hard work matters more than kindness in dealing with people
That people should be left alone when they are angry
That criticism stirs up resentment that ruins any chance of getting what we want from people
That it is wise to avoid all contact with difficult people
questions.explain: The chapter argues that criticism wounds pride and arouses resentment, so the hive kicked over stands for the reaction criticism provokes, and the honey for the cooperation we lose by it.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: In “Father Forgets”, what brings the father to his sudden remorse?
options: His son ran in and kissed him good night even after he had snapped at him
His wife told him he had been too hard on the boy
He found a note from his son asking why he was always angry
He saw his son crying alone in his room
questions.explain: After being snapped at, the boy ran across the room, hugged and kissed his father, and left; shortly afterwards the father's paper slipped from his hands as he asked what habit had been doing to him.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Which principle does Carnegie give in the chapter that follows this one, The Big Secret of Dealing with People?
options: Arouse in the other person an eager want
Give honest and sincere appreciation
Become genuinely interested in other people
Let the other person save face
questions.explain: Part One's three principles run from not criticizing, to giving honest and sincere appreciation in chapter 1.2, to arousing an eager want in chapter 1.3.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: True or false: This chapter’s principle is repeated as the first of three principles in the In a Nutshell summary of Fundamental Techniques in Handling People.
questions.explain: The summary at the end of Part One lists not criticizing, condemning or complaining as Principle 1, followed by honest appreciation and arousing an eager want.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: True or false: Dutch Schultz admitted in a newspaper interview that he was a public enemy who deserved to be punished.
questions.explain: Schultz said in a newspaper interview that he was a public benefactor, and Carnegie adds that he believed it.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: True or false: Carnegie says it took him a third of a century to begin to see that people almost never criticize themselves, however wrong they are.
questions.explain: Unlike Wanamaker, who learned early, Carnegie says he had to blunder through the world for a third of a century before this began to dawn on him.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: True or false: The psychologist Hans Selye said that as much as we thirst for approval, we dread condemnation.
questions.explain: Carnegie quotes Selye: “As much as we thirst for approval, we dread condemnation.”

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: True or false: According to Carnegie, bitter criticism drove the novelist Thomas Hardy to suicide.
questions.explain: Bitter criticism made Thomas Hardy give up writing fiction forever; it was the poet Thomas Chatterton whom criticism drove to suicide.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: True or false: This chapter opens Part Two of the book, Six Ways to Make People Like You.
questions.explain: It is the first chapter of Part One, Fundamental Techniques in Handling People; Part Two begins later with Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: True or false: “Father Forgets” first appeared in the Reader’s Digest.
questions.explain: It first appeared as an editorial in the People’s Home Journal; Carnegie reprints the version condensed in the Reader’s Digest.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.section: Principle: Don’t criticize, condemn or complain
questions.q: True or false: Carnegie says that trying to understand why people do what they do breeds sympathy, tolerance and kindness.
questions.explain: Instead of condemning people, Carnegie urges us to understand them, which he says is more profitable than criticism and “breeds sympathy, tolerance and kindness.”

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Carnegie warns that criticisms are like ____ pigeons: they always return home.
questions.explain: He says criticisms always return home, because the person we condemn will probably justify himself and condemn us in return.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: This chapter is the first chapter of Part One, titled Fundamental Techniques in ____ People.
questions.explain: Part One is Fundamental Techniques in Handling People, and its first technique is this chapter's principle.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Police Commissioner Mulrooney said that “Two Gun” Crowley would kill at the drop of a ____.
questions.explain: Mulrooney called Crowley one of the most dangerous criminals in New York's history, a man who would kill at the slightest pretext.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Albert B. Fall’s handling of the oil reserves at Elk Hill led to the ____ scandal.
questions.explain: Fall leased the Navy's oil reserves at Elk Hill and Teapot Dome to his friend Doheny without competitive bidding, and the resulting scandal sent Fall to prison.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Carnegie studied Lincoln for ten years and wrote a book about him titled Lincoln the ____.
questions.explain: He says he spent three years writing and rewriting Lincoln the Unknown and made a special study of Lincoln's way of dealing with people.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: One of Lincoln’s favorite quotations was: Judge not, that ye be not ____.
questions.explain: Carnegie gives this as one of Lincoln's favorite quotations, fitting his silence while half the nation condemned his generals.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: After Gettysburg, Lincoln ordered General ____ to attack Lee at once, but he called a council of war instead.
questions.explain: Meade disobeyed, hesitated and refused to attack, and Lee escaped over the Potomac when the waters receded.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Carnegie reminds us that in dealing with people we are not dealing with creatures of logic but with creatures of ____.
questions.explain: He describes people as “creatures bristling with prejudices and motivated by pride and vanity,” which is why criticism wounds rather than persuades.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Confucius advised: don’t complain about the snow on your neighbor’s ____ when your own doorstep is unclean.
questions.explain: Carnegie uses the saying to argue that improving ourselves is more profitable and less dangerous than trying to improve others.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Carlyle said that a great man shows his greatness by the way he treats ____ men.
questions.explain: Carnegie quotes Carlyle right after saying that being understanding and forgiving takes character and self-control.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: The author of “Father Forgets” is W. Livingston ____.
questions.explain: Larned wrote that the piece had been reproduced in hundreds of magazines and newspapers and in many foreign languages.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: In “Father Forgets”, the father vows to keep saying, as if it were a ritual: He is nothing but a ____.
questions.explain: The father realises he has been treating his son as a man and promises to remind himself the child is “nothing but a boy—a little boy!”

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.section: Principle: Don’t criticize, condemn or complain
questions.q: Principle 1 of the book is: Don’t criticize, condemn or ____.
questions.explain: The chapter closes with the principle in full: Don’t criticize, condemn or complain.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Which of these men does Carnegie cite as criminals who did not blame themselves for anything?
options: “Two Gun” Crowley
John Wilkes Booth
Al Capone
Edward L. Doheny
Dutch Schultz
questions.explain: Carnegie names Crowley, Capone and Schultz as criminals who justified themselves. Booth appears only as Lincoln's assassin and Doheny as Fall's friend in the Teapot Dome story.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Which of these does Carnegie give as reasons criticism is dangerous?
options: It wounds a person’s precious pride
It makes the critic look foolish to onlookers
It hurts a person’s sense of importance
It arouses resentment
It spreads quickly as gossip
questions.explain: Criticism is dangerous, Carnegie says, because it wounds pride, hurts the sense of importance and arouses resentment. The other ideas are not in the chapter.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Which of these generals does Carnegie list among those who blundered while commanding the Army of the Potomac?
options: Lee
McClellan
Stanton
Pope
Hooker
questions.explain: Carnegie lists McClellan, Pope, Burnside, Hooker and Meade. Lee led the opposing army, and Stanton was Secretary of War.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: In Carnegie’s guess at Lincoln’s thoughts, which of these did Lincoln fear sending his letter to Meade would do?
options: Make Meade try to justify himself
Make Meade attack Lee recklessly
Make Meade condemn Lincoln
Perhaps force Meade to resign from the army
Turn Congress against Lincoln
questions.explain: Lincoln imagines the letter would relieve his feelings but make Meade justify himself, condemn Lincoln, arouse hard feelings and perhaps force him to resign.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Which of these does Carnegie say were results of the Teapot Dome scandal?
options: It ruined the Harding Administration
It led Theodore Roosevelt to form the Bull Moose party
It put Albert B. Fall behind prison bars
It threatened to wreck the Republican party
It forced the Navy to give up its oil reserves
questions.explain: Carnegie says the scandal ruined the Harding Administration, threatened to wreck the Republican party and put Fall in prison. The Bull Moose party belongs to the Roosevelt–Taft quarrel.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Which of these people wrote angry letters that were never sent?
options: Abraham Lincoln
Richard Harding Davis
Mark Twain
Dale Carnegie
Albert B. Fall
questions.explain: Lincoln never mailed his rebuke to Meade, and Twain's wife lifted his stinging letters out of the mail. Davis did send his rebuke back to Carnegie.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Which of these did George B. Johnston do in his second, more successful approach to workers without hard hats?
options: Asked whether the hats were uncomfortable
Told them firmly that the regulation required compliance
Asked whether the hats fitted properly
Reminded them pleasantly that the hat protected them from injury
Warned that he would report them
questions.explain: His new approach asked about comfort and fit and pleasantly reminded the men of the hat's purpose. Stating the regulation with authority was the old approach that brought sullen acceptance.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Which of these does the father in “Father Forgets” remember scolding his son for?
options: Giving his face merely a dab with a towel
Losing his schoolbooks
Not cleaning his shoes
Putting his elbows on the table
Fighting with his friends
questions.explain: The father recalls faulting the boy for the quick dab with the towel, unclean shoes and elbows on the table, among other things. Lost books and fighting are not mentioned.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Which of these does the father in “Father Forgets” promise to do tomorrow?
options: Chum with his son
Buy him new stockings
Bite his tongue when impatient words come
Laugh when his son laughs
Explain his mistakes to the boy over breakfast
questions.explain: He promises to be a real daddy: to chum with the boy, suffer and laugh with him, and bite his tongue. He says the boy would not understand these things if told them while awake.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Put the events of the “Two Gun” Crowley story in the order they happened.
items: Crowley shoots a policeman who asks for his license on Long Island
Police besiege his top-floor hideaway on West End Avenue
Bleeding, he writes a letter addressed to whom it may concern
He is sentenced to the electric chair
At the Sing Sing death house he says it is what he gets for defending himself
questions.explain: The shooting came a short time before the siege; he wrote his letter during the siege, and after capture he was sentenced and sent to Sing Sing.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Put the stages of the quarrel between Theodore Roosevelt and President Taft in order.
items: Roosevelt leaves the White House and supports Taft
Roosevelt goes to Africa to shoot lions
On his return, Roosevelt denounces Taft’s conservatism
Roosevelt forms the Bull Moose party
Taft and the Republicans carry only Vermont and Utah
questions.explain: Roosevelt backed Taft in 1908, went to Africa, then exploded on his return, formed the Bull Moose party and split the vote, leaving Taft with two states.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Put the events of the Teapot Dome scandal in order, as Carnegie tells them.
items: Fall is entrusted with leasing the Navy’s oil reserves
Fall hands the contract to his friend Doheny without competitive bidding
Doheny gives Fall a one hundred thousand dollar loan
Fall sends Marines to drive off neighboring competitors
The competitors go to court and expose the scandal
questions.explain: The contract came first, then Doheny's so-called loan, then the Marines, and finally the competitors' court case that blew the lid off the scandal.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Put the events after the Battle of Gettysburg in order.
items: Lee retreats southward on the night of July 4
Lincoln orders Meade to attack Lee immediately
Meade calls a council of war against orders
The waters recede and Lee escapes over the Potomac
Lincoln writes a stern letter to Meade and never sends it
questions.explain: Lee was trapped by a swollen river; Lincoln ordered an attack, Meade delayed, Lee escaped, and only then did Lincoln write the unsent letter.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Put the father’s actions in “Father Forgets” in the order of the day he describes.
items: Scolds the boy while he dresses for school
Finds fault with him at breakfast
Answers his goodbye wave with Hold your shoulders back
Marches him home from playing marbles
Snaps What is it you want at him in the library
Kneels at his bedside, ashamed
questions.explain: The father moves from morning dressing, to breakfast, to the goodbye, to the late-afternoon marbles, to the evening in the library, and finally to the bedside.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Put the stages of Lincoln’s life with regard to criticism in order, as Carnegie traces them.
items: Drops ridiculing letters on country roads in Pigeon Creek Valley
Attacks opponents in newspaper letters as a Springfield lawyer
Lampoons James Shields and is challenged to a duel
Holds his peace while half the nation condemns his Civil War generals
questions.explain: Lincoln criticized as a youth and as a young lawyer until the Shields duel taught him a lesson; by the Civil War he almost never criticized anybody.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Put the three principles of Part One, Fundamental Techniques in Handling People, in the book’s order.
items: Don’t criticize, condemn or complain
Give honest and sincere appreciation
Arouse in the other person an eager want
questions.explain: This chapter supplies Principle 1; chapter 1.2 gives honest appreciation and chapter 1.3 arousing an eager want.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Match each wrongdoer to how he (or his wife) justified him.
pairs: Said he was being punished for defending himself
Gave people the lighter pleasures and got only abuse
Told a newspaper he was a public benefactor
Called by his wife the one betrayed and led to the slaughter
questions.explain: Each example shows Carnegie's point that wrongdoers blame everybody but themselves, even the worst criminals.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Match each person to the saying Carnegie quotes from him.
pairs: We thirst for approval and dread condemnation
Don’t complain about the snow on your neighbor’s roof
Greatness shows in how a great man treats little men
Speak ill of no man and all the good I know of everybody
questions.explain: All five sayings support the chapter's case against criticism and for understanding.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Match each person to his role in the chapter.
pairs: Safety coordinator for an engineering company
Police Commissioner who called Crowley very dangerous
Friend who received the oil reserve contract
Test pilot whose plane was given the wrong fuel
questions.explain: These figures supply the evidence and examples Carnegie uses, from prisons and police to safety work and aviation.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Match each story to the point Carnegie draws from it.
pairs: Criticism only made the target justify himself
A stinging remark can rankle for decades
Trust instead of scolding after a mistake
Blow off steam, but never send the letter
questions.explain: Each story illustrates a different side of the same lesson: criticism breeds defensiveness and resentment, while understanding works better.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Match each stage of Lincoln’s life to how he behaved.
pairs: Dropped ridiculing letters where they would be found
Attacked opponents openly in newspaper letters
Lampooned James Shields in an anonymous letter
Held his peace about his blundering generals
questions.explain: The Shields duel was the turning point; afterwards Lincoln never again ridiculed anyone and almost never criticized.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Match each writer to what Carnegie says about him.
pairs: Gave up writing fiction after bitter criticism
Wrote stinging letters his wife kept from the mail
Returned young Carnegie’s letter with a scribbled rebuke
questions.explain: Hardy and Chatterton show criticism's damage; Twain shows a harmless outlet; Davis shows how a rebuke breeds lasting resentment.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Match each item to its link with “Father Forgets”.
pairs: Where it first appeared as an editorial
Source of the condensed version Carnegie reprints
Readers Carnegie urges to read it first
questions.explain: Carnegie introduces the piece for parents tempted to criticize their children, reprinting Larned's editorial as condensed in the Reader's Digest.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Sort these approaches by how they turned out in the chapter.

items.t: Johnston asking if the hard hats fitted
Hoover asking the mechanic to service his F-51
Franklin speaking ill of no man
Johnston quoting the regulation with authority
Roosevelt denouncing Taft
Lincoln lampooning James Shields
Davis returning Carnegie’s letter with a rebuke

questions.explain: The criticisms provoked defiance, self-justification, a duel challenge and decades of resentment; the understanding approaches brought compliance and goodwill.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Sort these people by their role in the chapter.
groups: Person who chose not to criticize

items.t: “Two Gun” Crowley
Al Capone
Albert B. Fall
Dutch Schultz
Bob Hoover
John Wanamaker
Lincoln during the Civil War

questions.explain: The criminals and Fall show that wrongdoers rarely blame themselves; Hoover, Wanamaker and the mature Lincoln show the restraint Carnegie recommends.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Sort these actions by when Lincoln did them, relative to the Shields duel.

items.t: Dropping ridiculing letters on country roads
Attacking opponents in Springfield newspapers
An anonymous letter in the Springfield Journal
Holding his peace about his generals
Telling Mrs. Lincoln not to criticize southerners
Leaving his letter to Meade unsent

questions.explain: Carnegie says that after the duel Lincoln never again wrote an insulting letter or ridiculed anyone, and almost never criticized anybody.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.section: Principle: Don’t criticize, condemn or complain
questions.q: Sort these effects by whether Carnegie links them to criticizing people or to understanding them.

items.t: Puts a person on the defensive
Arouses resentment
Returns home like a homing pigeon
Breeds sympathy
Breeds tolerance and kindness
Is more profitable and intriguing

questions.explain: Carnegie closes by contrasting the futility and danger of criticism with understanding, which is more profitable and breeds sympathy, tolerance and kindness.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Sort these details from “Father Forgets”.
groups: Something the father found fault with
A sign of the boy’s good heart

items.t: Spreading butter too thick
Holes in his stockings
Throwing things on the floor
Turning to wave and call goodbye
Rushing in to kiss his father good night
Affection that even neglect could not wither

questions.explain: The father's list of petty faults is set against the boy's warm, spontaneous affection, which shows him how much was good and fine in his son.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Sort these details by the story they belong to.

items.t: Oil reserves at Elk Hill
Marines driving off competitors
A one hundred thousand dollar loan
A trip to Africa to shoot lions
The Bull Moose party
Only Vermont and Utah carried

questions.explain: Both stories end the same way in Carnegie's telling: the criticized man, Taft or Fall, never accepts the blame.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Why does Carnegie open the chapter with “Two Gun” Crowley, Al Capone and Dutch Schultz?
questions.a: They are among the most notorious criminals of their time, yet none of them blamed himself; each saw himself as kind, misunderstood or even a public benefactor. Carnegie reasons that if such men do not blame themselves, the ordinary people we deal with will not either. This sets up his claim that people almost never criticize themselves, no matter how wrong they are.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
