questions.q: Explain Carnegie’s two reasons why criticism is both futile and dangerous.
questions.a: Criticism is futile because it puts a person on the defensive and usually makes him strive to justify himself, so it does not change him. It is dangerous because it wounds a person’s precious pride, hurts his sense of importance and arouses resentment. So it fails to correct the fault and makes an enemy as well.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: What did Skinner’s experiments show, and what does Carnegie conclude from them about criticism?
questions.a: Skinner found that an animal rewarded for good behavior learns faster and remembers better than one punished for bad behavior, and later studies found the same for humans. Carnegie concludes that by criticizing we do not make lasting changes and often incur resentment. The resentment can demoralize employees, family and friends without correcting the situation.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Describe George B. Johnston’s two approaches to workers without hard hats and why the second worked better.
questions.a: At first he told the workers with authority about the regulation and that they must comply, which brought sullen acceptance, and they often took the hats off once he left. Later he asked whether the hats were uncomfortable or did not fit, then pleasantly reminded the men that the hat protected them from injury. This avoided putting them on the defensive, so compliance rose with no resentment or emotional upset.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: What does the Roosevelt–Taft quarrel show, according to Carnegie, and why does he refuse to say who was to blame?
questions.a: Roosevelt's criticism of Taft split the Republican party and changed history, yet it never persuaded Taft he was wrong; it only made him justify himself and say tearfully that he could not have done differently. Carnegie says he does not know or care who was to blame, because his point is not about fault. It is that criticism makes the target defend himself rather than change.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: How did the near-duel with James Shields change the way Lincoln dealt with people?
questions.a: As a young man Lincoln ridiculed people in letters and poems and attacked opponents in the newspapers, until his anonymous lampoon of Shields led to a challenge and a duel stopped only at the last minute. The episode taught him an invaluable lesson. He never again wrote an insulting letter or ridiculed anyone, and from then on he almost never criticized anybody for anything.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: According to Carnegie’s guess, why did Lincoln put aside his letter to General Meade?
questions.a: Carnegie imagines Lincoln reflecting that it was easy to order an attack from the quiet of the White House, and that had he seen Meade's bloodshed or had his timid temperament he might have done the same. He also saw that sending the letter would relieve his own feelings but make Meade justify himself, condemn Lincoln, and perhaps resign. Lincoln had learned that sharp criticisms and rebukes almost always end in futility.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Your teenage child has scraped the family car and you are tempted to give them a severe dressing-down. How would Carnegie suggest you handle it, drawing on Bob Hoover’s story?
questions.a: Hoover had every reason to be angry at the mechanic whose fuel error wrecked his plane and nearly killed three people, yet he did not even criticize him. Instead he showed trust by asking him to service his F-51 the next day. Carnegie would suggest the same: the child already feels the mistake, so show understanding and confidence rather than condemnation, which would only arouse resentment.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: What does Carnegie’s own experience with Richard Harding Davis show about criticism?
questions.a: Wanting to look important, the young Carnegie ended a letter to Davis with Dictated but not read, and Davis sent it back with a cutting remark about his bad manners. Carnegie admits he deserved the rebuke, but he resented it so sharply that ten years later, when Davis died, the hurt was what he still remembered. A little stinging criticism, however justified, can stir up a resentment that lasts for decades.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: What does Carnegie mean when he says we are dealing with creatures of emotion, not creatures of logic?
questions.a: People do not weigh criticism coolly on its merits; they are “creatures bristling with prejudices and motivated by pride and vanity.” Criticism therefore hits their pride and provokes defensiveness and resentment instead of reasoned change. Carnegie points to Thomas Hardy giving up fiction and Chatterton's suicide as examples of how deeply criticism can wound.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: A coworker keeps complaining to you about how sloppy a teammate is and wants to tell them off. Using Carnegie’s advice and the saying of Confucius, how might you respond?
questions.a: Carnegie says he is all in favor of improving people, but suggests beginning on yourself, since that is more profitable and far less dangerous than trying to improve others. Confucius warned against complaining about the snow on a neighbor’s roof while your own doorstep is unclean. You might encourage the coworker to look at their own habits first and to understand why the teammate works as they do instead of criticizing.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: What does Carnegie say about the difference between a fool and a person of character in dealing with others’ faults, and how does Benjamin Franklin illustrate it?
questions.a: Carnegie says any fool can criticize, condemn and complain, and most fools do, but it takes character and self-control to be understanding and forgiving. Franklin, tactless in his youth, became so diplomatic and skilled at handling people that he was made American Ambassador to France. His secret was to speak ill of no man and speak all the good he knew of everybody.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: In “Father Forgets”, what does the father realise about his habit of finding fault?
questions.a: He sees that the habit of finding fault and reprimanding had become his reward to his son for being a boy. It was not that he did not love him; he expected too much of youth and was “measuring you by the yardstick of my own years.” He resolves to remember that the child is nothing but a little boy and to be a real daddy.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.section: Principle: Don’t criticize, condemn or complain
questions.q: What does Carnegie urge us to do instead of condemning people, and why?
questions.a: He urges us to try to understand people and figure out why they do what they do. This is more profitable and intriguing than criticism, and it breeds sympathy, tolerance and kindness, since to know all is to forgive all. He closes with Dr. Johnson's remark that God himself does not judge man until the end of his days, asking why we should.

questions.unitTitle: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
questions.q: Why is it fitting that the book’s first principle for handling people is Don’t criticize, condemn or complain?
questions.a: It opens Part One, Fundamental Techniques in Handling People, by clearing away the most common and most damaging habit before any positive technique is offered. Criticism puts people on the defensive and breeds resentment, so it would undo any later attempt to win cooperation. The next chapters then build on this foundation with honest and sincere appreciation and arousing an eager want, the honey gathered once the hive is left alone.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: According to Carnegie at the start of The Big Secret of Dealing with People, what is the only way to get anybody to do anything?
options: Make the other person want to do it
Threaten them with a penalty they fear
Explain your reasons logically
Offer a fair trade of favours
questions.explain: Carnegie insists there is just one way: making the other person want to do it. Threats work only until your back is turned and carry “sharply undesirable repercussions.”

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: In The Big Secret of Dealing with People, which phrase does Carnegie attribute to John Dewey as the deepest urge in human nature?
options: The desire to be great
The desire to be important
The craving to be appreciated
The urge for self-preservation
questions.explain: Dewey called it the desire to be important, and Carnegie tells readers to remember the phrase because it recurs through the book. The desire to be great is Freud's wording; the craving to be appreciated is William James's.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: Of the eight things Carnegie lists that most people want, which one does he say is seldom gratified?
options: Sleep
Money and the things money will buy
A feeling of importance
The well-being of our children
questions.explain: Almost all the wants are usually gratified except one: the longing Freud calls the desire to be great and Dewey the desire to be important, which is the feeling of importance.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: Why does Carnegie tell the story of his father's blue ribbons from Missouri livestock shows?
options: It shows that hard work on a farm is always rewarded by prizes
It shows that pedigree animals are more valuable than ordinary ones
It shows that his father taught him to value modesty above success
The hogs cared nothing for the ribbons, but his father did, showing the human need for importance
questions.explain: The ribbons meant nothing to the hogs but gave his father a feeling of importance, which Carnegie calls one of the chief differences between mankind and the animals.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: In The Big Secret of Dealing with People, what does Carnegie call the one significant difference between Dillinger and Rockefeller?
options: How they got their feeling of importance
How much money each of them amassed
How they were brought up as children
How much schooling each received
questions.explain: Rockefeller got his feeling of importance by funding a hospital in Peking; Dillinger got his by being a bandit. Carnegie says how a person gets this feeling determines his character.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: According to E. P. Mulrooney, as quoted by Carnegie, what is the average young criminal's first request after arrest?
options: A lawyer to argue that he is innocent
The lurid newspapers that make him out a hero
A visit from his family
A chance to make a statement to the police
questions.explain: Mulrooney said young criminals are filled with ego and first ask for the newspapers that make them heroes; the prospect of prison seems remote while they gloat over their pictures.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.section: Principle: Give honest and sincere appreciation
questions.q: A friend reads The Big Secret of Dealing with People and says praise is just flattery and never works with intelligent people. What is Carnegie's reply?
options: He says flattery works on everyone if it is laid on thick enough
He says intelligent people are the only ones who respond to praise
He agrees flattery fails with discerning people, but he is urging sincere appreciation, not flattery
He says one should praise only people who have earned a title
questions.explain: Carnegie grants that flattery is shallow, selfish and insincere and usually fails. He insists he is not suggesting flattery at all but “a new way of life” of honest appreciation.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: In The Big Secret of Dealing with People, what does the head physician say about his patient who believes she is Lady Smith?
options: He hopes a new treatment will soon restore her sanity
He believes her illness was caused by damage to her brain cells
He thinks she is pretending in order to escape her husband
He would not restore her sanity even if he could, because she is happier as she is
questions.explain: The physician told Carnegie: “If I could stretch out my hand and restore her sanity, I wouldn’t do it. She’s much happier as she is.”

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: Why, according to Charles Schwab, did Andrew Carnegie pay him a million dollars a year?
options: Largely because of his ability to deal with people
Because he was a genius at business strategy
Because he knew more about making steel than anyone else
Because he worked longer hours than any other executive
questions.explain: Schwab admitted many of his men knew more about steel than he did. He said he was paid largely for his ability to deal with people, above all to arouse enthusiasm through appreciation.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: In The Big Secret of Dealing with People, what does Charles Schwab say most kills the ambitions of a person?
options: Low wages and long hours
Criticisms from superiors
Lack of training and skill
Competition from colleagues
questions.explain: Schwab said, “There is nothing else that so kills the ambitions of a person as criticisms from superiors,” and so he never criticized anyone.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: When Edward T. Bedford lost a million dollars on a bad buy in South America, how did John D. Rockefeller respond?
options: He criticized Bedford privately but not in public
He asked Bedford to repay part of the loss
He congratulated Bedford for saving 60 percent of the money invested
He said nothing and moved Bedford to another post
questions.explain: Knowing Bedford had done his best, Rockefeller found something to praise: saving 60 percent. “That’s splendid,” he said.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: What did Andrew Carnegie's self-written epitaph praise, according to The Big Secret of Dealing with People?
options: His success in building the largest steel company
His generosity in giving away his fortune
His own skill in the manufacture of steel
His knack for gathering around him men cleverer than himself
questions.explain: Carnegie wanted to praise his assistants even on his tombstone: “Here lies one who knew how to get around him men who were cleverer than himself.”

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: According to a study Carnegie cites in The Big Secret of Dealing with People, what was the main reason wives ran away?
options: Lack of appreciation
Lack of money
Quarrels with in-laws
Boredom with rural life
questions.explain: The study found the main reason was lack of appreciation, and Carnegie bets a study of runaway husbands would find the same, because we take spouses for granted.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: When his wife asked him to list six things she could do to become a better wife, what did the class member in The Big Secret of Dealing with People do?
options: Wrote six gentle suggestions and gave them to her that evening
Sent her six red roses with a note saying he loved her as she was
Asked her to list six things he should change first
Told her the question was too difficult to answer
questions.explain: Instead of criticizing, he sent six roses with a note that he could not think of six things to change. Her tearful welcome taught him the power of appreciation.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: What point does Carnegie make with his story of fasting for six days?
options: Fasting is a healthy habit that sharpens the mind
Hunger for food grows stronger the longer one goes without it
People who would never starve their families for six days let them go years without the appreciation they crave
Physical needs must always be met before emotional ones
questions.explain: He compares the two hungers: we feed bodies faithfully but leave people six weeks or sixty years without the hearty appreciation they crave almost as much as food.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.section: Principle: Give honest and sincere appreciation
questions.q: A café regular keeps telling a barista she is the best in town, mainly so he will get free refills. In Carnegie's terms, what is he offering?
options: Honest appreciation, because it is warm and frequent
Encouragement, because it gives her an incentive to work
Approbation, because it names her good points
Flattery, because it is insincere and selfish
questions.explain: Carnegie defines the difference simply: appreciation is sincere and unselfish, flattery insincere and selfish. Praise given to get something comes “from the teeth out.”

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.section: Principle: Give honest and sincere appreciation
questions.q: Why does Carnegie say readers should not copy Disraeli, who flattered Queen Victoria heavily?
options: Disraeli was a rare genius, and what worked for him would not necessarily work for others
Queen Victoria saw through the flattery and dismissed him
Flattering royalty was against the law in Britain
Disraeli later admitted that his flattery never worked
questions.explain: Carnegie calls Disraeli one of the most adroit men who ever ruled the Empire. What worked for him might not work for us, and in the long run flattery does more harm than good.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.section: Principle: Give honest and sincere appreciation
questions.q: A supervisor manages a cleaner whose poor work makes co-workers jeer at him, and nothing she tries helps. Following Pamela Dunham's example, what should she do?
options: Write him a firm warning and copy it to the whole team
Watch for his occasional good work and praise it in front of the others
Ignore his work entirely until he improves on his own
Ask the co-workers to tell him what he does wrong
questions.explain: Pam praised the janitor publicly for the good pieces of work she noticed, and he improved until he did an excellent job. Honest appreciation succeeded where criticism and ridicule failed.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: What does the title The Big Secret of Dealing with People turn out to refer to?
options: Avoiding all criticism, condemnation and complaint
Arousing in the other person an eager want
Giving honest and sincere appreciation to satisfy people's desire to feel important
Remembering people's names and using them often
questions.explain: The chapter builds from the universal desire to feel important to its Principle 2: give honest and sincere appreciation. Avoiding criticism is the principle of the previous chapter, and arousing an eager want belongs to the next.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: How does The Big Secret of Dealing with People relate to the chapter before it, If You Want to Gather Honey, Don't Kick Over the Beehive?
options: It contradicts the earlier chapter by allowing criticism of superiors
It repeats the earlier chapter's principle using new examples
It moves on from handling people to making a good first impression
It supplies the positive counterpart: after warning against criticism, it urges sincere appreciation
questions.explain: The earlier chapter's principle is not to criticize, condemn or complain. This chapter adds what to do instead, echoed in Schwab's words: “I never criticize anyone.”

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: True or false: Carnegie reports that Freud said everything we do springs from two motives, the sex urge and the desire to be great.
questions.explain: Carnegie opens his answer to the question of what people want with Freud's two motives, then gives Dewey's similar phrase, the desire to be important.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: True or false: Carnegie stresses that William James spoke of the wish to be appreciated.
questions.explain: Carnegie points out that James did not say the wish, desire or longing, but the craving: “The deepest principle in human nature is the craving to be appreciated.”

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: True or false: Andrew Carnegie picked Charles Schwab to be the first president of the newly formed United States Steel Company when Schwab was only thirty-eight.
questions.explain: The chapter says Schwab was chosen at thirty-eight and was one of the first people in American business paid over a million dollars a year.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: True or false: Carnegie presents the story of the farm woman who served her menfolk a pile of hay as a true event he witnessed.
questions.explain: He calls it a silly story that he knows never happened, but repeats it because it illustrates a truth: people want to know their work is noticed.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: True or false: Florenz Ziegfeld raised the salary of chorus girls from thirty dollars a week to as high as one hundred and seventy-five.
questions.explain: Carnegie calls Ziegfeld practical as well as chivalrous: besides raising salaries, he sent telegrams to the stars and roses to every chorus girl on opening night.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.section: Principle: Give honest and sincere appreciation
questions.q: True or false: Carnegie says flattery usually works well with discerning people as long as it is delivered smoothly.
questions.explain: He says the opposite: “Of course flattery seldom works with discerning people.” It is shallow, selfish and insincere, and it ought to fail.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.section: Principle: Give honest and sincere appreciation
questions.q: True or false: The words carved below General Obregon's bust warn that enemies who attack you are more dangerous than friends who flatter you.
questions.explain: The carving reverses this: “Don’t be afraid of enemies who attack you. Be afraid of the friends who flatter you.”

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: True or false: Give honest and sincere appreciation is the second of three principles in Part One, Fundamental Techniques in Handling People.
questions.explain: Part One's principles are: do not criticize, condemn or complain; give honest and sincere appreciation; and arouse in the other person an eager want.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: John Dewey, quoted by Carnegie, said the deepest urge in human nature is the desire to be ____.
questions.explain: Carnegie tells readers to remember Dewey's phrase, the desire to be important, because they will hear much about it in the book.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: Carnegie notes that William James did not speak of the wish or desire to be appreciated but of the ____ to be appreciated.
questions.explain: Carnegie stresses James's stronger word, craving, to show how deep and insistent this hunger is.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: Carnegie says that how you get your feeling of importance tells what you are; it determines your ____.
questions.explain: He writes that the source of a person's feeling of importance “determines your character” and is the most significant thing about them, as Rockefeller and Dillinger show.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: Charles Schwab said the way to develop the best in a person is by appreciation and ____.
questions.explain: Schwab named his ability to arouse enthusiasm his greatest asset and said it is developed through appreciation and encouragement.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: Charles Schwab described himself as anxious to praise but loath to find ____.
questions.explain: Schwab said he never criticizes anyone; he believes in giving a person incentive to work and is hearty in approbation and lavish in praise.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.section: Principle: Give honest and sincere appreciation
questions.q: Disraeli confessed that in flattering Queen Victoria he spread it on with a ____.
questions.explain: Disraeli put the flattery on thick, but Carnegie warns that what worked for such a genius would not necessarily work for us.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.section: Principle: Give honest and sincere appreciation
questions.q: Carnegie says appreciation comes from the heart out, while flattery comes from the ____ out.
questions.explain: This is one of Carnegie's contrasts: appreciation is sincere and unselfish, flattery insincere and selfish.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.section: Principle: Give honest and sincere appreciation
questions.q: After quoting a maxim of King George V, Carnegie says that all flattery is is cheap ____.
questions.explain: The maxim asked to neither proffer nor receive cheap praise, and Carnegie equates flattery with exactly that.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.section: Principle: Give honest and sincere appreciation
questions.q: Carnegie says that when not thinking about a definite problem, we spend about 95 percent of our time thinking about ____.
questions.explain: If we stop thinking about ourselves and think of the other person's good points, he says, we will not need to resort to cheap, false flattery.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.section: Principle: Give honest and sincere appreciation
questions.q: Emerson, quoted by Carnegie, said that every man he met was his ____ in some way, and in that he learned of him.
questions.explain: Carnegie uses Emerson's humility to urge readers to look for other people's good points and appreciate them honestly.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.section: Principle: Give honest and sincere appreciation
questions.q: Carnegie calls appreciation the legal ____ that all souls enjoy.
questions.explain: He reminds readers that all associates are human beings who hunger for appreciation, which he likens to money every soul accepts.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: The actor Alfred Lunt said there was nothing he needed so much as nourishment for his ____.
questions.explain: Carnegie uses Lunt's remark to argue that we feed people's bodies but seldom nourish their self-esteem with kind words.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: Which of these appear on Carnegie's list of things most people want?
options: Sleep
Fame in the newspapers
The well-being of our children
A feeling of importance
Revenge on rivals
questions.explain: Carnegie's eight wants include health, food, sleep, money, life in the hereafter, sexual gratification, the well-being of our children and a feeling of importance. Fame and revenge are not on the list.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: Which of these achievements does Carnegie say were inspired by the desire for a feeling of importance?
options: Lincoln studying law books found in a barrel
Dickens writing his novels
Schwab learning the steel trade
Wren designing his buildings
Disraeli's rise to prime minister
questions.explain: Carnegie names Lincoln, Dickens and Christopher Wren's symphonies in stone as products of this desire. He says Schwab was not paid for steel knowledge, and he uses Disraeli only as a flatterer.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: Which of these does Carnegie give as examples of famous people struggling for a feeling of importance through titles or honours?
options: George Washington wanting to be called His Mightiness
Columbus pleading for the title Admiral of the Ocean
Florenz Ziegfeld sending roses to chorus girls
Victor Hugo hoping Paris would be renamed for him
Emerson's motto about learning from every man
questions.explain: Washington, Columbus and Victor Hugo all appear among history's amusing examples of the craving for importance. Ziegfeld and Emerson illustrate giving appreciation, not seeking it.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: Which of these does Carnegie say average people do, in contrast to Charles Schwab?
options: Bawl out subordinates when they dislike something
Praise their associates publicly
Say nothing when they like something
Look for something to praise in a failure
questions.explain: Carnegie says average people do the exact opposite of Schwab: they scold when displeased and stay silent when pleased. Public praise and finding something to praise describe Andrew Carnegie and Rockefeller.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: Which of these are examples Carnegie gives of people who turned to illness, physical or mental, to gain a feeling of importance?
options: Mrs. McKinley keeping the President at her bedside
The young woman Mary Roberts Rinehart described
Catherine the Great refusing unaddressed letters
The patient who insists on being called Lady Smith
Mrs. Lincoln scolding Mrs. Grant
questions.explain: Mrs. McKinley and Rinehart's young woman became invalids, and the Lady Smith patient found importance in insanity. Catherine the Great and Mrs. Lincoln sought importance through rank, not illness.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.section: Principle: Give honest and sincere appreciation
questions.q: Which of these words or phrases does Carnegie use to describe flattery?
options: Counterfeit
Cheap praise
From the heart out
Shallow
Universally admired
questions.explain: Carnegie calls flattery shallow, selfish and insincere, likens it to counterfeit money and equates it with cheap praise. Coming from the heart and being universally admired describe appreciation.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.section: Principle: Give honest and sincere appreciation
questions.q: Which of these everyday acts does Carnegie recommend as ways of showing appreciation?
options: Sending word to the chef that a meal was excellently prepared
Pointing out a waiter's mistakes so he can improve
Mentioning a tired salesperson's unusual courtesy
Praising a child who brings home a good report card
Praising only those who have earned praise many times
questions.explain: Carnegie urges thanking the chef, noting a salesperson's courtesy and praising children's report cards and first cakes. Pointing out mistakes is the criticism he warns against.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: Which of these did Florenz Ziegfeld do, according to The Big Secret of Dealing with People?
options: Raised chorus girls' salaries sharply
Hired only famous stage beauties
Sent telegrams to the stars on opening night
Criticized his cast to push them harder
Deluged every chorus girl with roses
questions.explain: Ziegfeld made plain women feel beautiful through gallantry and consideration: he raised salaries, sent telegrams to the stars and roses to every chorus girl. He took drab unknowns, not famous beauties.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: Put these in the order Carnegie presents them as he answers the question of what people want.
items: Freud's two motives, the sex urge and the desire to be great
Dewey's desire to be important
A list of eight things most people want
William James's craving to be appreciated
questions.explain: Carnegie moves from Freud to Dewey, then lists eight common wants, picks out the one seldom gratified, and backs it with Lincoln and William James.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: Put the events of Mary Roberts Rinehart's story about the young invalid in order.
items: She faced something hard, perhaps her age
She took to her bed
For ten years her mother carried trays to her
Her weary mother died
She got up and resumed living
questions.explain: Rinehart's story shows illness used to get attention and importance: once the mother who served her died, the invalid got up and lived again.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: Put the events of the class member's six-roses story in order.
items: His wife asked for six things she could change
He said he would answer in the morning
He had six red roses sent with a note
His wife greeted him almost in tears
Women from her church called it most considerate
questions.explain: Instead of listing faults, he sent roses saying he loved her as she was. The reactions at home and at church showed him the power of appreciation.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.section: Principle: Give honest and sincere appreciation
questions.q: Put the events of Pamela Dunham's experience with the janitor in order.
items: Co-workers jeered at the janitor's poor work
Pam tried various ways to motivate him without success
She noticed he occasionally did a good piece of work
She praised him for it in front of others
His work improved until it was excellent
questions.explain: Carnegie's conclusion is that honest appreciation got results where criticism and ridicule failed.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: Put the events of Paul Harvey's story about Stevie Morris in order.
items: A Detroit teacher asked Stevie to help find a lost mouse
Stevie was shown appreciation for his remarkable ears for the first time
He developed his gift of hearing
He became the singer Stevie Wonder
questions.explain: Harvey told the story to show how sincere appreciation can change a life; Stevie later called that act the beginning of a new life.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: Put the stages of the argument in The Big Secret of Dealing with People in order.
items: The only way to get people to act is to make them want to
The want seldom gratified is a feeling of importance
Some people even go insane to find importance
Schwab, Carnegie and Rockefeller succeeded through appreciation
Appreciation is distinguished from flattery
Principle 2: give honest and sincere appreciation
questions.explain: The chapter moves from what people want, to how desperately they want importance, to proof that appreciation works, then separates it from flattery before stating the principle.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: Match each person to the words Carnegie quotes or attributes to them about human desire.
questions.explain: Carnegie lines up these voices to show that thinkers agree on one deep hunger: to feel important and appreciated.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: Match each person to how, according to Carnegie, they got a feeling of importance.
pairs: Funding a hospital in Peking for people he would never see
Being a bandit, bank robber and killer
Showing off his blue ribbons on a sheet of muslin
Making the President neglect affairs of state to soothe her
questions.explain: Carnegie says the way a person gets this feeling reveals their character, as the contrast between Rockefeller and Dillinger shows.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: Match each historical figure to the honour Carnegie says they sought.
pairs: To be called His Mightiness, the President of the United States
The title Admiral of the Ocean and Viceroy of India
Letters addressed to Her Imperial Majesty
The city of Paris renamed in his honor
A coat of arms for his family
questions.explain: Carnegie offers these as amusing examples from history of famous people struggling for a feeling of importance.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.section: Principle: Give honest and sincere appreciation
questions.q: Match each person to the words Carnegie quotes from them about praise or flattery.
pairs: Be afraid of the friends who flatter you
Teach me neither to proffer nor receive cheap praise
He spread it on with a trowel
You can never say anything but what you are
questions.explain: Carnegie uses these sayings to separate cheap, insincere flattery from the honest appreciation he recommends.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: Match each leader to the act of appreciation Carnegie credits to them.
pairs: Being hearty in approbation and lavish in praise
Praising his assistants even in his own epitaph
Congratulating a partner for saving 60 percent of a loss
Deluging every chorus girl with roses on opening night
questions.explain: Each example shows appreciation as a practical secret of success in handling people.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: Match each chapter of Part One to its principle.
pairs: If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive
The Big Secret of Dealing with People
He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him
Arouse in the other person an eager want
questions.explain: Part One, Fundamental Techniques in Handling People, moves from what to stop doing, to giving appreciation, to arousing an eager want.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.section: Principle: Give honest and sincere appreciation
questions.q: Sort each description into appreciation or flattery, as Carnegie contrasts them.

items.t: Sincere
Comes from the heart out
Unselfish
Universally admired
Insincere
Comes from the teeth out
Selfish
Universally condemned

questions.explain: Carnegie says the difference is simple: one is sincere, heartfelt, unselfish and admired; the other insincere, from the teeth, selfish and condemned.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: Sort these into the crude methods Carnegie rejects and the way he says actually gets people to act.

items.t: A revolver in someone's ribs
Threatening to fire employees
A whip or a threat to a child
Making the other person want to do it
Giving people what they want
Honest appreciation

questions.explain: Carnegie says crude methods have sharply undesirable repercussions; the only way to get someone to act is to make them want to, by giving them what they want.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: Sort these into Charles Schwab's way of handling people and what Carnegie says average people do.

items.t: Anxious to praise, loath to find fault
Never criticizes anyone
Lavish in praise for what he likes
Bawl out subordinates for what they dislike
Say nothing when they like something

questions.explain: Carnegie says average people do the exact opposite of Schwab, as in the couplet about hearing ever of the bad and never of the good.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: Sort these by whether Carnegie says the want is usually gratified or seldom gratified.

items.t: Food
Sleep
Health and the preservation of life
Money and the things money will buy
What Freud calls the desire to be great
What Dewey calls the desire to be important

questions.explain: Almost all the wants are usually met except one longing, almost as deep as hunger, which Freud and Dewey each named in their own words.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: Sort these by what Carnegie says we usually give the people around us and what we usually neglect.

items.t: Food for their bodies
Roast beef and potatoes for energy
Nourishment for their self-esteem
Kind words of appreciation
Praise for a child's good report card

questions.explain: We nourish bodies but seldom self-esteem, Carnegie says, and we neglect to praise children's report cards and first successes.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: Sort these examples by whether the person sought a feeling of importance in a way that helped others or harmed others or themselves.

items.t: Rockefeller funding a hospital in Peking
Dickens writing his novels
Lincoln studying law books
Dillinger robbing banks
Young people joining criminal gangs
Rinehart's young woman taking to her bed

questions.explain: Carnegie shows the same desire producing both civilization's achievements and crime or invalidism; which path a person takes reveals their character.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: Why does Carnegie reject threats and force as ways of getting people to do things, and what does he propose instead?
questions.a: Carnegie admits a revolver, a threat to fire or a whip can produce compliance, but only until your back is turned, and such crude methods have sharply undesirable repercussions. The only real way is to make the other person want to do it, which means giving people what they want.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: Explain how Carnegie uses his father's blue ribbons to show what separates people from animals.
questions.a: His father's prize hogs did not care about the ribbons they won, but his father proudly displayed them on a sheet of muslin to visitors. The ribbons gave him a feeling of importance, and Carnegie calls this desire one of the chief differences between mankind and the animals.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: How can the same desire for a feeling of importance produce both civilization and crime, according to Carnegie?
questions.a: Carnegie says without this flaming urge civilization would have been impossible: it drove Lincoln to study law, Dickens to write and Wren to build. Yet the same desire lures young people into gangs and made Dillinger proud to be Public Enemy Number One. How a person gets this feeling determines their character.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: What conclusion does Carnegie draw from people who become invalids or even go insane to find a feeling of importance?
questions.a: Carnegie argues that if some people are so hungry for importance that they will take to their beds or find it in the dreamland of insanity, the hunger must be enormous. He concludes we can achieve miracles by giving people honest appreciation “this side of insanity.”

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: What was Charles Schwab's secret for dealing with people, and why does Carnegie value it so highly?
questions.a: Schwab said his greatest asset was his ability to arouse enthusiasm, and that the best in a person is developed by appreciation and encouragement, never by criticism from superiors. He was anxious to praise and loath to find fault. Carnegie says these words ought to be cast in bronze and memorized by children, because Schwab's people skills, not his steel knowledge, earned his million-dollar salary.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: What does Rockefeller's response to Edward T. Bedford's million-dollar loss teach about handling a failure?
questions.a: Rockefeller knew Bedford had done his best, so instead of criticizing he found something to praise: Bedford had saved 60 percent of the money invested. Carnegie presents this as sincere appreciation, one of the secrets of Rockefeller's success in handling men.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: What truth does Carnegie draw from the farm woman's pile of hay and the study of runaway wives?
questions.a: The hay story, which Carnegie admits never happened, shows that people want to know their daily work is noticed. The runaway wives study found lack of appreciation was the main cause. Both show that we take those closest to us for granted and never let them know we appreciate them.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: A parent makes sure the children are well fed and clothed but rarely comments on their efforts. How would Carnegie's fasting comparison apply?
questions.a: Carnegie notes that people who would feel criminal letting their families go six days without food will let them go years without the hearty appreciation they crave almost as much. The parent is nourishing the children's bodies but neglecting their self-esteem, and should praise things like a good report card or a first cake.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.section: Principle: Give honest and sincere appreciation
questions.q: How does Carnegie distinguish appreciation from flattery, and why does he warn against flattery?
questions.a: Appreciation is sincere, unselfish and from the heart; flattery is insincere, selfish and from the teeth out. Flattery is cheap praise and counterfeit, and like counterfeit money it will eventually get you into trouble. It seldom works with discerning people and in the long run does more harm than good.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.section: Principle: Give honest and sincere appreciation
questions.q: You want to praise a quiet colleague but worry it will sound like flattery. Using Carnegie's advice, how should you go about it?
questions.a: Carnegie says we spend about 95 percent of our time thinking about ourselves; if we stop and think of the other person's good points, we will not need cheap flattery. Like Emerson, assume the colleague is your superior in some way, find that real good point and praise it honestly, being hearty in approbation and lavish in praise.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.section: Principle: Give honest and sincere appreciation
questions.q: Recite Principle 2 of Part One from memory, and say briefly what it asks.
questions.a: Principle 2: Give honest and sincere appreciation. It asks us to stop thinking of our own wants, find the other person's good points and praise them sincerely rather than flatter.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: Why might Carnegie call the idea in this chapter the big secret of dealing with people?
questions.a: Carnegie argues the only way to get people to do anything is to give them what they want, and the one want seldom gratified is a feeling of importance. Since this hunger is nearly universal and rarely fed, whoever honestly satisfies it will hold people in the palm of his hand. That makes honest appreciation the master key to handling people.

questions.unitTitle: The Big Secret of Dealing with People
questions.q: How does The Big Secret of Dealing with People connect with the chapters on either side of it in Part One?
questions.a: The previous chapter warns against criticizing, condemning or complaining, and this chapter gives the positive alternative, honest appreciation, as Schwab's refusal to criticize shows. Its opening claim that you must make people want to act prepares for the next chapter's principle, arousing in the other person an eager want.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: In Carnegie's fishing story from Maine, why did he bait his hook with worms rather than strawberries and cream?
options: He thought about what the fish wanted, not about what he liked himself
Worms were cheaper and easier to carry on a fishing trip
Strawberries and cream would have spoiled in the summer heat
A local guide told him that fish in Maine bite only on worms
questions.explain: Carnegie loves strawberries and cream, but fish prefer worms, so he thought about what they wanted. He then asks why we do not use the same common sense when fishing for people.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: Lloyd George said that if his staying in power could be put down to any one thing, it was learning that it was necessary to bait the hook to suit the ____.
questions.explain: Lloyd George, Britain's Prime Minister during World War I, applied the same lesson as Carnegie's fishing story: offer what the other party wants.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: True or false: Carnegie says Lloyd George stayed in power after the other wartime leaders Wilson, Orlando and Clemenceau had been forgotten.
questions.explain: Someone asked Lloyd George how he had stayed on top after those leaders were forgotten, and he credited learning to bait the hook to suit the fish.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: According to Carnegie, what is the only way on earth to influence other people?
options: Explain clearly and firmly what you want from them
Point out calmly where their present thinking is wrong
Talk about what they want and show them how to get it
Appeal to their sense of duty and their conscience
questions.explain: Carnegie says talking about what we want is childish, since only we are interested in it. The way to influence people is to talk about what they want and show them how to get it.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: A mother wants her son, a keen sprinter, to stay away from cigarettes. Following Carnegie's advice in Chapter 1.3, what should she do?
options: Tell him firmly how much she wants him not to smoke
Show him that smoking may keep him from winning his races
Preach to him about the moral failings of smokers
Forbid cigarettes and promise a punishment if he smokes
questions.explain: Carnegie advises parents not to preach or talk about what they want, but to show children that cigarettes may keep them from making the basketball team or winning the hundred-yard dash.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: In the story of Emerson and the calf, Carnegie says the Irish housemaid had more horse sense, or ____ sense, than Emerson had.
questions.explain: She could not write essays and books, but she thought of what the calf wanted, which Emerson and his son failed to do.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: How did the Irish housemaid get the calf into the barn when Emerson and his son could not?
options: She pushed from behind while Emerson pulled from the front
She tempted the calf forward with a bucket of fresh hay
She drove the calf in by waving her apron behind it
She let the calf suck her finger as she gently led it in
questions.explain: Emerson pushed and his son pulled, thinking only of what they wanted. The housemaid thought of what the calf wanted and put her maternal finger in its mouth as she led it.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: True or false: Carnegie says the calf refused to leave the pasture because it was frightened of the barn.
questions.explain: Carnegie says the calf was doing just what Emerson and his son were doing: thinking only of what it wanted, so it stiffened its legs and refused to move.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: What point does Carnegie make with the example of a large contribution to the Red Cross?
options: Truly generous acts are the one exception to self-interest
People give to charity mainly to impress their customers
Charitable giving shows that most people act from duty alone
Even a generous gift is made because the giver wanted something
questions.explain: Carnegie says the donation is no exception to the rule: you gave because you wanted the feeling of doing a beautiful, unselfish act more than you wanted the money.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: Which of these reasons does Carnegie give for why someone might have made a contribution to the Red Cross?
options: They wanted to lend a helping hand
They were ashamed to refuse
A customer asked them to give
The law required them to contribute
They hoped their name would be printed in the newspaper
questions.explain: Carnegie lists wanting to help, shame at refusing and a customer's request. Whatever the reason, he says, the giver made the contribution because they wanted something.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: Carnegie quotes Harry A. Overstreet's illuminating book Influencing Human ____.
questions.explain: Overstreet's book supplies the chapter's title and its principle: first, arouse in the other person an eager want.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: Overstreet, quoted by Carnegie, says that action springs out of what we fundamentally ____.
questions.explain: Overstreet's point is that action grows out of basic desire, so the best advice for would-be persuaders is first to arouse in the other person an eager want.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: Put the events of Andrew Carnegie's wager about his nephews at Yale in order.
items: His sister-in-law worries that her sons never write home
He offers to bet a hundred dollars he can get a reply
He writes a chatty letter promising each boy five dollars
He leaves the money out of the envelope
Replies arrive by return mail thanking Dear Uncle Andrew
questions.explain: Carnegie won the bet without asking for a reply. The postscript about a five-dollar bill gave the nephews a reason of their own to write back.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: True or false: Carnegie says Andrew Carnegie attended school for only four years, yet learned how to handle people.
questions.explain: Andrew Carnegie started work at two cents an hour and later gave away $365 million. He learned early that the only way to influence people is to talk in terms of what they want.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: Match each person to how Carnegie describes them in Chapter 1.3.
pairs: Great Britain’s Prime Minister during World War I
Poor Scottish lad who began at two cents an hour and gave away $365 million
Sales manager of A. Zerega’s Sons, Inc.
Telephone engineer whose three-year-old daughter would not eat breakfast food
Noted lawyer and one of America’s great business leaders
questions.explain: Each figure appears in the chapter as an example or authority for the idea of talking in terms of what the other person wants.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: When his son Tim refused to start kindergarten, what question did Stan Novak ask himself instead of sending the boy to his room?
options: How can I make Tim see that he has no choice in the matter?
If I were Tim, why would I be excited about going to kindergarten?
What punishment will make Tim change his mind by morning?
Why is Tim behaving so badly about such a small change?
questions.explain: Stan saw that banishing Tim would not help him start school in the best frame of mind, so he looked at kindergarten from Tim's point of view and listed the fun things he would do there.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: Put the events of the Novak family's kindergarten story in order.
items: Tim kicks and screams that he will not go to kindergarten
His parents list the fun things he will do there
The family finger-paints together at the kitchen table
Tim begs to join and is told he must go to kindergarten first
Next morning Tim is found asleep in a chair, waiting to go
questions.explain: Stan Novak says the family's enthusiasm aroused in Tim an eager want that no amount of discussion or threat could have achieved.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: To win over his son Tim, Stan Novak, his wife and his other son started ____ on the kitchen table.
questions.explain: Finger painting was on their list of fun things Tim would do at kindergarten. When Tim asked to join, he was told he had to go to kindergarten first to learn how.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: Which of these fun things did Stan Novak and his wife list for their son Tim to look forward to at kindergarten?
options: Finger painting
Singing songs
Making new friends
Riding the school bus
Playing football at break time
questions.explain: The Novaks listed the things Tim himself would enjoy, then acted them out with the whole family, starting with finger painting at the kitchen table.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: Why did Stan Novak's approach get his son Tim eager for kindergarten when his usual reaction would not have?
questions.a: His normal reaction was to send Tim to his room and tell him he had no choice, which would not help Tim start school in the right frame of mind. Instead Stan asked why Tim himself would be excited about kindergarten, listed the fun things he would do there and acted them out with the family. Their enthusiasm aroused in Tim an eager want that, as Stan put it, no discussion or threat could have produced.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: What is Carnegie's point in the fishing story and the remark of Lloyd George that open Chapter 1.3?
questions.a: Carnegie likes strawberries and cream, but he baits his hook with worms because that is what the fish want. Lloyd George likewise said he stayed in power by learning to bait the hook to suit the fish. The lesson is to use the same common sense with people: stop talking about what we want, since nobody else is interested in it, and talk about what the other person wants.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: Using the Red Cross example, explain Carnegie's claim that every act you have ever performed was performed because you wanted something.
questions.a: Carnegie says even a generous donation is no exception. You gave because you wanted to lend a helping hand and do a beautiful, unselfish act, and you wanted that feeling more than your money; or perhaps you were ashamed to refuse or a customer asked you. Either way you gave because you wanted something, which is why persuasion must start from what people want.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: Put the events of Carnegie's dispute over the hotel ballroom rent in order.
items: He learns the rent will nearly triple after tickets are printed
He visits the manager and says he does not blame him
He lists advantages and disadvantages to the hotel on a letterhead
He hands the sheet over and asks for a final decision
A letter next day raises the rent only 50 percent
questions.explain: Carnegie got the reduction without saying a word about what he wanted; he talked all the time about what the manager wanted and how he could get it.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: How did Carnegie open his meeting with the hotel manager who had nearly tripled the ballroom rent?
options: He protested that the tickets were printed and he could not pay the increase
He threatened to tell his large audiences how badly the hotel treated him
He said he did not blame him, since a manager's duty is to make all the profit possible
He asked the manager to honour the old rent out of goodwill and fairness
questions.explain: Carnegie said that in the manager's position he would probably have written a similar letter, and that a manager who failed to make all the profit possible ought to be fired.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: Sort each point on Carnegie's sheet for the hotel manager into Advantages or Disadvantages of insisting on the rent increase.

items.t: The ballroom would be free to rent for dances and conventions
Those affairs would pay more than a lecture series
Carnegie's rent income would be wiped out, not increased
Crowds of educated and cultured people would stop visiting
Advertising worth more than five thousand dollars would be lost

questions.explain: Carnegie granted the hotel a real advantage, a free ballroom, then showed that the increase would cost it his whole rent and the advertising value of his lecture audiences.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: True or false: After reading Carnegie's list of advantages and disadvantages, the hotel manager raised the rent by only 50 percent instead of 300 percent.
questions.explain: Carnegie received a letter the next day with the smaller increase. He stresses that he got it without saying a word about what he wanted.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: What does Carnegie say would have happened if he had stormed into the hotel manager's office protesting the rent increase?
options: An argument would start, and the manager's pride would make it hard for him to give in
The manager would have backed down at once to avoid losing a good customer
The manager would have offered a smaller increase but asked for a longer contract
The hotel would have cancelled the lectures and kept the money for the tickets
questions.explain: Carnegie says the human, natural thing is to protest, but an argument would boil up, and even if he convinced the manager he was wrong, pride would make it difficult to back down.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: In the hotel rent story, sort each line by whether Carnegie actually said it or only imagined saying it if he had stormed in.
groups: What he imagined storming in to say

items.t: I don’t blame you at all
Your duty is to make all the profit possible
Let’s write down the advantages and the disadvantages
Three hundred percent! Ridiculous! Absurd!
I won’t pay it!
What do you mean by raising my rent?

questions.explain: Carnegie's real words all concerned the manager's interests. The angry lines are what he calls the human, natural thing, which would only have started an argument.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: How did Carnegie persuade the hotel manager to cut the rent increase, and what was notable about what he said?
questions.a: He began by saying he did not blame the manager, whose duty was to make all the profit possible. He then wrote down the advantages and disadvantages to the hotel: a free ballroom on one side, and on the other the loss of his rent and of the advertising his cultured audiences brought. The increase fell from 300 to 50 percent, and he got it without saying a word about what he wanted.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: Your landlord announces a big rent rise for the shop you rent. Using Carnegie's hotel ballroom approach, how would you handle it?
questions.a: Rather than protesting about what you want, you would meet the landlord, say you understand that his job is to make a profit, and then set out the advantages and disadvantages of the rise from his side. You would grant any real advantage he gains, then show what he stands to lose, such as your rent entirely if you must move and any other value your presence brings. Carnegie's point is to talk only about what the other person wants and how he can get it.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: Henry Ford, quoted by Carnegie, said that if there is any one secret of success, it lies in the ability to get the other person's point of ____.
questions.explain: Ford added that one should see things from that person's angle as well as from one's own. Carnegie liked the advice so much that he quoted it twice.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: How widely does Carnegie say Henry Ford's advice about seeing the other person's point of view is ignored?
options: By 90 percent of people 90 percent of the time
By half of all people most of the time
By nearly everyone except salespeople
By 90 percent of business letters only
questions.explain: Carnegie says the advice is so simple and obvious that anyone should see its truth, “yet 90 percent of the people on this earth ignore it 90 percent of the time.”

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: Match each person quoted in Chapter 1.3 to the idea of their words.
pairs: Success lies in getting the other person’s point of view
First arouse in the other person an eager want
Those who understand others’ minds need not fear the future
Self-expression is the dominant necessity of human nature
It is necessary to bait the hook to suit the fish
questions.explain: Carnegie gathers these voices behind one idea: influence comes from understanding and serving what the other person wants.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: In Carnegie's bracketed reactions to the radio advertising agency's letter, which of these worries does the station manager have on his mind?
options: The bank is foreclosing the mortgage on his house
Bugs are destroying the hollyhocks
He missed the eight-fifteen that morning
His best announcer has just resigned
His car broke down on the way to work
questions.explain: Carnegie lists the manager's own troubles, including the mortgage, the hollyhocks, the stock market and the missed train, to show that the reader cares about his problems, not the agency's desires.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: In the radio agency's letter, which part does Carnegie say finally mentioned something that might help the station manager?
options: The opening line about the agency's leadership in the radio field
The request to be put on the station's preferred list
The postscript offering a reprint from the Blankville Journal to broadcast
The closing promise that a reply would be mutually helpful
questions.explain: Carnegie's reaction to the postscript is that at last the writer mentions something that may help him solve one of his problems, and asks why the letter did not begin with it.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: In Carnegie's bracketed reactions to the radio agency's letter, what does he say about its claim that a reply would be “mutually helpful”?
options: It is the only honest and useful sentence anywhere in the letter
At last the writer sees his viewpoint, but is vague about how it would benefit him
It shows the agency has carefully studied the station's needs
It makes up for the letter's boasting about the agency's size
questions.explain: Carnegie says the phrase shows the writer has at last begun to see the reader's viewpoint, but he never explains how the arrangement would be to the reader's advantage.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: The radio agency's letter asks the local station manager to put the company on his ____ list for weekly station information.
questions.explain: Carnegie's reaction is that the writer makes him feel insignificant with talk of the agency's size and then asks to be preferred without even saying please.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: What lesson does Carnegie draw from the radio advertising agency's letter to local station managers?
questions.a: The letter talks only about what the agency desires and how big it is, while the reader is worried about his own problems, such as his mortgage and his health. It asks favours without saying please and leaves its one useful offer to the postscript. Carnegie's point is that if people who pose as experts in influencing others write such letters, we can expect little better from the butcher, the baker or the auto mechanic unless we learn to see the other person's point of view.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: Match each part of the radio agency's letter to Carnegie's bracketed reaction.
pairs: Its wish to keep its leadership in radio
Who cares what your company desires? I have my own problems
Its boast of being at the top year after year
I am interested in how big I am, not how big you are
Its request to be on a preferred list
You don’t even say please when you ask
Its request for a prompt acknowledgment
You send a form letter yet expect a personal reply
Its postscript offering a newspaper reprint
Finally, something that may help me with a problem
questions.explain: Each reaction makes the same point from the reader's side: the letter is about the sender's wants until the very end.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: What effect did the freight terminal superintendent's first letter have on Edward Vermylen, according to his comment?
options: It persuaded him at once to send his trucks in the morning
It confused him, because the request was buried in figures
It had no effect, because he never got round to reading it
It had the reverse effect, raising antagonism rather than cooperation
questions.explain: Vermylen said the letter opened with the terminal's difficulties, asked for cooperation without thinking of his convenience and mentioned his own benefit last, so the whole effect was “one of raising a spirit of antagonism rather than of cooperation.”

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: Put the contents of the freight terminal superintendent's original letter to Mr. Vermylen in the order they appeared.
items: The terminal’s congestion and overtime problems
The late lot of 510 pieces received on November 10
A request to deliver earlier or partly in the morning
The advantage to the customer of faster unloading
questions.explain: Vermylen's complaint was about exactly this order: what his company cared about most came last.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: Which of these features appear in Carnegie's revised version of the freight terminal letter to Mr. Vermylen?
options: Thanks for fourteen years as a good customer
A picture of the workers going home early to enjoy the customer's macaroni and noodles
A note that he is busy and need not trouble to answer
A warning that late deliveries will be charged extra
A detailed account of the terminal's overtime costs
questions.explain: The revision starts with the customer, explains how morning deliveries help his own trucks and freight, and ends by sparing him the trouble of replying.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: Carnegie's revised freight terminal letter ends by telling Mr. Vermylen that he is busy and need not trouble to ____ the note.
questions.explain: This closing contrasts with the radio agency's letter, which demanded a prompt personal reply from busy readers.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: True or false: In Carnegie's revised freight letter, the terminal's workers are pictured getting home early to enjoy the macaroni and noodles that Mr. Vermylen's company manufactures.
questions.explain: The revision ties the terminal's wish for morning deliveries to things the customer cares about, ending even the workers' benefit with a compliment to his product.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: Sort each feature by whether it belongs to the freight terminal's original letter or to Carnegie's revision.

items.t: Opens with the terminal’s congestion and overtime
Asks for cooperation without thought of inconvenience
Mentions the customer’s benefit only at the end
Opens by thanking a customer of fourteen years
Says morning deliveries keep the customer’s trucks moving
Tells the reader not to trouble to answer

questions.explain: Carnegie rewrote the letter on Henry Ford's advice: stop talking about our problems and start from the other person's point of view.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: What result did Barbara Anderson get from the letter she sent to twelve banks in Phoenix?
options: Two of the twelve banks replied, and one offered her a job
Half of the banks asked her to send references first
None replied until she telephoned each bank in person
Eleven of the twelve banks invited her to be interviewed
questions.explain: She had her choice of offers, because she did not state what she wanted but wrote about how she could help the banks.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: True or false: Barbara Anderson wanted to move from New York to Phoenix because she had been passed over for promotion.
questions.explain: She wanted to move to Phoenix because of the health of her son. Her letter, however, said nothing of her own needs and focused on what she could do for the banks.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: Why did Barbara Anderson's letter to the Phoenix banks succeed so well?
questions.a: Instead of saying that she needed a job in Phoenix, she wrote about how her ten years of banking experience could contribute to the growth and profit of a rapidly growing bank. Carnegie says she focused on their wants, not her own. Eleven of the twelve banks invited her to an interview, and she could choose which offer to accept.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: Why does Carnegie say thousands of salespeople are tired, discouraged and underpaid?
options: They are not given enough training in their products
They are always thinking only of what they want
They visit too few customers in a working day
They give up too easily when a customer says no
questions.explain: Carnegie says salespeople fail because they think of their own wants. If they showed customers how their goods would solve the customers' problems, they would not need to sell; people would buy.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: Carnegie says customers like to feel that they are buying, not being ____.
questions.explain: He argues that nobody wants to buy anything as such; we want to solve our problems, and we buy when someone shows us how a product helps.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: Which of these does Carnegie say salespeople fail to realize about customers?
options: Neither you nor I want to buy anything as such
We are eternally interested in solving our own problems
Customers like to feel they are buying, not being sold
Customers respond best to steady pressure and persistence
Price is the only thing most customers really care about
questions.explain: Carnegie says that if salespeople show us how their goods solve our problems, they will not need to sell us; we will buy.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: Why, according to Carnegie, do so many salespeople fail, and what should they do instead?
questions.a: They think only of what they want, while customers do not want to buy anything as such but are eternally interested in solving their problems. If salespeople show how their goods or services will solve those problems, they will not need to sell; the customer will buy. Customers like to feel they are buying, not being sold.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: Carnegie asked a Forest Hills real-estate man whether his stucco house was built with metal lath or hollow ____.
questions.explain: The man could have found out with a sixty-second phone call. Instead he told Carnegie to phone the Forest Hills Garden Association and asked to handle his insurance.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: Match each person to what they did in Carnegie's examples of selling and asking.
pairs: Told Carnegie to phone for the answer and asked for his insurance
Casually mentioned a new policy and said he would get back later
Excitedly urged the managers to sign applications the same day
Wrote how her banking experience could help the banks grow
questions.explain: Carnegie contrasts those who think only of themselves, like the real-estate man and Carl, with those who arouse an eager want in the other person.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: In J. Howard Lucas's story of two insurance agents, why did John make the sales that Carl could have had?
options: He offered a lower price than Carl's company could match
He waited until he had every detail of the policy in writing
