His enthusiasm aroused an eager want for the policy even before details were available
He had known the company's managers for many years
questions.explain: Both agents had the same new policy. Lucas says John's enthusiasm aroused in them an eager want, while Carl made no effort to arouse any desire for the policies.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: True or false: In J. Howard Lucas's story, Carl made the sales because he waited until he had full details of the new policy.
questions.explain: John made the sales. He not only sold each manager a policy but later doubled their coverage; Carl made no effort to arouse any desire.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: Contrast how Carl and John handled the same new insurance policy in J. Howard Lucas's story, and what Carnegie draws from it.
questions.a: Carl casually mentioned the policy, said the company might be interested later and that he would get back to them. John stopped the managers on the sidewalk, told them excitedly about the policy introduced that very day and got the applications signed while an expert came to explain it. His enthusiasm aroused an eager want; he sold each of them a policy and later doubled their coverage, while Carl, Lucas says, made no effort to arouse any desire.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: In which of these examples from Chapter 1.3 does the persuader's own enthusiasm arouse an eager want?
options: John's pitch for the new executive life insurance policy
The Novak family's finger painting for Tim
Carl's mention of the new insurance policy
The Forest Hills real-estate man's letter
questions.explain: Lucas says John's enthusiasm aroused an eager want for the policy, and Stan Novak says his family's enthusiasm did the same for Tim. Carl and the real-estate man made no effort to arouse any desire.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: Match each figure to the number Carnegie gives for it in Chapter 1.3.
pairs: Nights Carnegie rented the hotel ballroom each season
The rent increase the hotel finally asked
Banks that invited Barbara Anderson to interview
Andrew Carnegie’s wager on his nephews’ replies
Years Zerega’s Sons had been the terminal’s customer
questions.explain: These details anchor the chapter's examples; in each, the result came from addressing the other side's interests.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: Match each participant in Carnegie's course to the place Carnegie gives for them.
pairs: Moving from a New York bank to Phoenix, Arizona
questions.explain: Carnegie draws many of the chapter's examples from ordinary people who used the principle after taking his course.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: Sort these attempts at persuasion from Chapter 1.3 by whether they worked or failed.

items.t: Andrew Carnegie’s postscript about five-dollar bills
Barbara Anderson’s letter to the Phoenix banks
John’s enthusiastic pitch for the new policy
The freight terminal’s original letter
The Forest Hills real-estate man’s letter
Carl’s casual mention of the new policy

questions.explain: The successful attempts all spoke to what the other person wanted; the failures spoke of what the writer or speaker wanted.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: Which of these details does Carnegie give about Andrew Carnegie in Chapter 1.3?
options: He started work at two cents an hour
He finally gave away $365 million
He attended school only four years
He studied at Yale with his nephews
He served in Parliament before going into business
questions.explain: Carnegie presents him as a poverty-stricken Scotch lad with little schooling who still learned that the way to influence people is to talk in terms of what they want. It was his nephews, not he, who were at Yale.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.section: Principle: Arouse in the other person an eager want
questions.q: Carnegie advises that before you speak to persuade someone, you pause and ask yourself: How can I make this person ____ to do it?
questions.explain: Carnegie says this question will stop us from rushing into a situation heedlessly with futile chatter about our own desires.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.section: Principle: Arouse in the other person an eager want
questions.q: According to Carnegie, what does asking “How can I make this person want to do it?” stop us from doing?
options: Rushing in heedlessly with futile chatter about our own desires
Giving up too soon when the other person first says no
Promising more than we can afford to give in return
Criticizing the other person before we know the facts
questions.explain: Carnegie says the question will stop us from rushing into a situation heedlessly, with futile chatter about our desires.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.section: Principle: Arouse in the other person an eager want
questions.q: Which of these questions do people in Chapter 1.3 ask themselves as they turn their thinking to the other person's wants?
options: How can I make this person want to do it?
How can I tie up what I want to what he wants?
If I were Tim, why would I be excited about going to kindergarten?
How can I make him admit that he is wrong?
What is the least I can offer and still get my way?
questions.explain: Carnegie recommends the first question to every reader; the father of the underweight boy and Stan Novak asked versions of it. None of the chapter's examples aim to prove the other person wrong.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.section: Principle: Arouse in the other person an eager want
questions.q: Carnegie says the rare individual who unselfishly tries to serve others has an enormous advantage, because he has little ____.
questions.explain: Carnegie says the world is full of grabbing, self-seeking people, which is why the person who tries to serve others stands out.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.section: Principle: Arouse in the other person an eager want
questions.q: Owen D. Young, quoted by Carnegie, said that people who can put themselves in the place of others and understand their minds need never worry about what?
options: What the future has in store for them
Whether other people will like them
Losing an argument with a rival
Finding enough customers to buy
questions.explain: Young's words were that such people “need never worry about what the future has in store for them.”

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.section: Principle: Arouse in the other person an eager want
questions.q: What is the one thing Carnegie hopes readers will get out of the book, and why does he value it so highly?
questions.a: He hopes readers gain an increased tendency to think always in terms of the other person's point of view and see things from their angle. He says that if they get only that one thing from the book, it may easily prove to be one of the building blocks of their career. Because the world is full of self-seeking people, the person who serves others has little competition.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.section: Principle: Arouse in the other person an eager want
questions.q: A sales clerk uses Carnegie's principle to create an eager want in a customer for an expensive product the customer does not need and will regret buying. How does Carnegie's caveat apply?
options: It is acceptable, since anything that makes the customer want to buy counts as success
It is fine as long as the clerk truly believes in the product being sold
It is not what he means: arousing an eager want must not be manipulation to the other's detriment
It is the principle working as intended, because the customer bought willingly
questions.explain: Carnegie says arousing an eager want is not to be read as manipulating someone into doing something only for your benefit and his detriment. Each party should gain from the negotiation.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.section: Principle: Arouse in the other person an eager want
questions.q: Which of these examples does Carnegie cite when he says that both parties gained from arousing an eager want?
options: The letters to Mr. Vermylen
Barbara Anderson's letter to the banks
John's sale of insurance to Mr. Lucas
Emerson and the calf
The radio agency's letter to station managers
questions.explain: Carnegie says the sender and receiver of the freight letter both gained, the bank got a valuable employee and Mrs. Anderson a job, and John and Mr. Lucas both benefited.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.section: Principle: Arouse in the other person an eager want
questions.q: Why does Carnegie insist that arousing an eager want is not the same as manipulation?
questions.a: He says looking at the other person's point of view and arousing an eager want must not be construed as getting someone to do something only for your benefit and his detriment. Each party should gain from the negotiation. His examples show this: in the freight letters, Barbara Anderson's job letter and John's insurance sale, both sides came out ahead.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.section: Principle: Arouse in the other person an eager want
questions.q: Put the events of Michael Whidden's service station story in order.
items: A neglected station's sales decline badly
Mike's pleas and heart-to-heart talks have no effect
Mike invites the manager to see the newest Shell station
The station is cleaned up and sales rise
Mike reaches the Number One spot in his district
questions.explain: Carnegie says all Mike's talking had not helped, but showing the manager the modern station aroused an eager want, and both men benefited.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.section: Principle: Arouse in the other person an eager want
questions.q: What finally persuaded the older manager of a run-down service station to clean it up, in Michael Whidden's story?
options: A warning that Shell would replace him as manager
Visiting the newest Shell station in the territory
A promise of a bonus if his sales rose that year
Many patient heart-to-heart talks with Mike
questions.explain: The manager was so impressed by the new station's facilities that his own was cleaned up by Mike's next visit. The talks and exhortations had had no impact.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.section: Principle: Arouse in the other person an eager want
questions.q: True or false: In Michael Whidden's story, it was Mike's many heart-to-heart talks that finally persuaded the station manager to clean up his station.
questions.explain: Carnegie says all of Mike's talking and discussion had not helped. What worked was arousing an eager want by showing the manager the modern station.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.section: Principle: Arouse in the other person an eager want
questions.q: How does Michael Whidden's service station story illustrate both the principle of arousing an eager want and Carnegie's point that each party should gain?
questions.a: Mike's pleas and heart-to-heart talks failed, but when he took the manager to see the newest Shell station, the manager wanted a station like it and cleaned up his own. The station's sales rose, which helped the manager, and Mike reached the Number One spot in his district. Carnegie presents it as an example in which everybody gains.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.section: Principle: Arouse in the other person an eager want
questions.q: A colleague tells co-workers: I want you to join my lunchtime running group; I keep running alone and I hate it. Following Carnegie's comment on the basketball speech, what should he have said instead?
options: How lonely and disappointed he feels when nobody else turns up
How much the group means to him and how hard he has worked on it
How often he has invited them and how rarely they have come
How running would give them more energy, a keener appetite, a clearer head and fun
questions.explain: Carnegie says the basketball speaker talked only about what he wanted. He could have shown the others how to get things they want: more pep, a keener appetite, a clearer brain, fun and games.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.section: Principle: Arouse in the other person an eager want
questions.q: Carnegie says most people go through college and learn to read ____ and master the mysteries of calculus without discovering how their own minds function.
questions.explain: He introduces the basketball speech of a young Carrier Corporation graduate as an example of an educated person who did not understand how minds work.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.section: Principle: Arouse in the other person an eager want
questions.q: In the basketball example from Carnegie's Effective Speaking course, sort each item by whether the speaker talked about it or it was something he could have offered.

items.t: His own wish to play basketball
A gymnasium with too few people for a game
The black eye he got the other night
More pep
A keener edge to the appetite
A clearer brain, fun and games

questions.explain: Carnegie says the speaker talked about nothing his listeners wanted. Nobody wants an empty gym or a black eye, but everybody wants energy and fun.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.section: Principle: Arouse in the other person an eager want
questions.q: True or false: In the basketball example, the speaker won his listeners over by telling them he had recently got a black eye at the gym.
questions.explain: The black eye was part of a speech about what he wanted. Carnegie says listeners do not want a black eye; the speaker should have offered things they did want.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.section: Principle: Arouse in the other person an eager want
questions.q: When the father of the underweight boy finally saw his mistake, what did he ask himself?
options: How can I make the boy understand why good food matters?
Which foods can I hide in his meals so he eats them?
Why does the boy ignore everything his mother tells him?
What does that boy want? How can I tie up what I want to what he wants?
questions.explain: Carnegie says no one should expect a three-year-old to react to the viewpoint of a thirty-year-old father, as this father had done before he changed his approach.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.section: Principle: Arouse in the other person an eager want
questions.q: Put the events of the underweight boy's story in order.
items: His parents scold and nag him to eat
His father sees a three-year-old cannot share his viewpoint
His father notes a bully keeps taking the boy’s tricycle
His father promises that eating will make him big enough to beat the bully
The boy eats spinach, sauerkraut, salt mackerel, anything
questions.explain: Once the father tied what he wanted to what the boy wanted, there was no longer any problem of dietetics.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.section: Principle: Arouse in the other person an eager want
questions.q: True or false: Carnegie says the underweight boy was willing to eat anything once he believed it would make him big enough to beat the bully who took his tricycle.
questions.explain: Carnegie says the boy would have eaten spinach, sauerkraut, salt mackerel or anything else to be big enough to whip the bully who had humiliated him so often.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.section: Principle: Arouse in the other person an eager want
questions.q: Which of these does Carnegie name as the emotions that goaded the underweight boy to want revenge on the bully?
options: His pride
His anger
His desire for a feeling of importance
His fear of his father
His jealousy of his brother
questions.explain: Carnegie calls these all the strongest emotions in the boy's makeup. His father tied eating to them by promising the boy he could one day beat the bully.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.section: Principle: Arouse in the other person an eager want
questions.q: What two things did the little boy who wet his bed want, which his parents used to cure the habit?
options: To stay up late and to sleep with the light left on
To wear pajamas like Daddy and to have a bed of his own
To get a new tricycle and to beat the bully down the street
To sleep in his parents' room and to have a pet dog
questions.explain: Grandmother gladly offered to buy pajamas if he reformed, and nobody objected to his having his own bed, so both wants could be met.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.section: Principle: Arouse in the other person an eager want
questions.q: Put the events of the bed-wetting story in order.
items: Scolding, spanking and shaming fail to keep the bed dry
His mother takes him to a Brooklyn department store
The salesgirl asks the young man what she can show him
He chooses the bed his mother wanted him to buy
His father praises the bed and asks if he will wet it
The boy keeps his promise because his pride is involved
questions.explain: The bed was his, he had bought it himself and he wore pajamas like a man, so he wanted to act like a man.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.section: Principle: Arouse in the other person an eager want
questions.q: When the little boy showed off his new bed, his father obeyed Charles Schwab's injunction to be hearty in his approbation and lavish in his ____.
questions.explain: Carnegie links the bed story back to Schwab's advice on appreciation. The praise strengthened the boy's pride in a bed he alone had bought.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.section: Principle: Arouse in the other person an eager want
questions.q: Why did the little boy in Carnegie's story stop wetting his bed?
questions.a: Scolding, spanking and shaming had failed, so his parents asked how they could make him want to stop. He wanted pajamas like Daddy and a bed of his own, so he was given pajamas and allowed to buy his own bed, made to feel important by the salesgirl and praised by his father. His pride was involved: it was his bed, he alone had bought it, and he wanted to act like a man.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.section: Principle: Arouse in the other person an eager want
questions.q: The same little boy had two problems in Carnegie's story. Sort each detail by which problem it belongs to.

items.t: A bully kept pulling him off his tricycle
He was promised he could one day beat the bigger boy
He was told Mother wants you to eat this and that
He slept with his grandmother
He wanted pajamas like Daddy
He bought a bed for himself at a department store

questions.explain: In both cases the parents' pleas about what they wanted failed, and success came from finding what the boy wanted.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.section: Principle: Arouse in the other person an eager want
questions.q: Sort these methods from Carnegie's stories about children by whether they failed or worked.

items.t: Scolding and nagging the boy to eat
Spanking and shaming the boy over the wet bed
Pleading and coaxing the girl to eat cereal
Promising the boy he could beat the bully
Letting the boy buy his own bed
Letting the girl make the cereal herself

questions.explain: Every failed method talked about what the parents wanted; every successful one gave the child a want of his or her own.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.section: Principle: Arouse in the other person an eager want
questions.q: How did K. T. Dutschmann and his wife get their three-year-old daughter to eat her breakfast food?
options: They promised her a treat if she finished her bowl
They ate the cereal themselves and praised its taste
They let her stand on a chair and make the cereal herself
They let her choose a new cereal at the grocery store
questions.explain: The girl loved to imitate her mother and feel grown up. Having made the cereal, she ate two helpings without coaxing because she was interested in it.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.section: Principle: Arouse in the other person an eager want
questions.q: William Winter, quoted by Carnegie, remarked that self-____ is the dominant necessity of human nature.
questions.explain: Carnegie says the Dutschmann girl found in making the cereal an avenue of self-expression and a feeling of importance.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.section: Principle: Arouse in the other person an eager want
questions.q: A manager has an idea for improving her team's weekly schedule. Applying Carnegie's lesson from the cereal story, what should she do?
options: Let the team work out the idea themselves so they regard it as their own
Present it as her own brilliant idea so the team respects it
Announce it firmly as a rule so that no one argues about it
Ask her own boss to present it so it carries more weight
questions.explain: Carnegie suggests that instead of making others think a brilliant idea is ours, we let them cook and stir it themselves. They will then regard it as their own and like it.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.section: Principle: Arouse in the other person an eager want
questions.q: Match each person in Chapter 1.3 to the want that was used to persuade them.
pairs: The five dollars they believed was on its way
The fun of finger painting, songs and new friends
Growing big enough to beat the bully
Feeling grown up by making the cereal herself
A station as fine as the newest Shell station
questions.explain: In each case the persuader stopped talking about his or her own wishes and tied the request to something the other person already wanted.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.section: Principle: Arouse in the other person an eager want
questions.q: Why did the Dutschmann girl eat two helpings of cereal, and what lesson does Carnegie draw for business?
questions.a: Scolding, pleading and coaxing had failed, but when her parents let her make the cereal, she achieved a feeling of importance and found an avenue of self-expression. She ate because she was interested in it. Carnegie says that in business, instead of making others think a brilliant idea is ours, we should let them cook and stir the idea themselves, so they regard it as their own.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.section: Principle: Arouse in the other person an eager want
questions.q: Your teenager will not tidy his room, and nagging has failed. How would Carnegie's principle suggest handling it?
questions.a: Carnegie would have you stop talking about what you want and ask: How can I make him want to do it? You would look for something he already wants, such as a space he can be proud to show friends or a sense of being grown up, and tie the tidying to it. As with the boy who bought his own bed, a want of his own will work where scolding and pleading do not.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.section: Principle: Arouse in the other person an eager want
questions.q: Principle 3 of Part One reads: Arouse in the other person an eager ____.
questions.explain: The principle restates Overstreet's advice to would-be persuaders, which Carnegie repeats three times in the chapter.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.section: Principle: Arouse in the other person an eager want
questions.q: Recite Principle 3 of Part One and the words of Overstreet behind it from memory.
questions.a: Principle 3: Arouse in the other person an eager want. Overstreet's words, quoted by Carnegie: First, arouse in the other person an eager want. He who can do this has the whole world with him. He who cannot walks a lonely way.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: Where does Chapter 1.3 sit in the structure of How to Win Friends and Influence People?
options: It is the last chapter of Part One, Fundamental Techniques in Handling People
It is the first chapter of Part Two, Six Ways to Make People Like You
It is the middle chapter of Part One, between two chapters on criticism
It is the last chapter of Part Three, How to Win People to Your Way of Thinking
questions.explain: Chapter 1.3 completes Part One and is followed by the In a Nutshell summary of Part One's three principles; Part Two begins next.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: Put the three principles of Part One, Fundamental Techniques in Handling People, in the order the book gives them.
items: Don’t criticize, condemn or complain
Give honest and sincere appreciation
Arouse in the other person an eager want
questions.explain: The In a Nutshell summary at the end of Chapter 1.3 lists the three principles in this order, with arousing an eager want as Principle 3.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: Where does the title of Chapter 1.3 come from?
options: A remark Lloyd George made about staying in power
Henry Ford's statement about the secret of success
A passage in Harry A. Overstreet's book Influencing Human Behavior
A saying of Owen D. Young about understanding others
questions.explain: The title repeats the end of Overstreet's advice: first, arouse in the other person an eager want, for he who can do this has the whole world with him.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: Match each Part One chapter title to the principle it teaches.
pairs: “If You Want to Gather Honey, Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”
The Big Secret of Dealing with People
“He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
Arouse in the other person an eager want
questions.explain: The three chapters of Part One each end with one principle, and the In a Nutshell summary after Chapter 1.3 gathers them.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: True or false: The In a Nutshell summary at the end of Chapter 1.3 lists six ways to make people like you.
questions.explain: The summary covers Fundamental Techniques in Handling People and lists Part One's three principles. Six Ways to Make People Like You is the title of Part Two, which follows.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: How does the bed-wetting story in Chapter 1.3 connect back to the previous chapter, The Big Secret of Dealing with People?
questions.a: When the boy shows his new bed, his father obeys Charles Schwab's injunction to be hearty in his approbation and lavish in his praise, which comes from the chapter on giving honest and sincere appreciation. The boy is also driven by the desire for a feeling of importance, the desire that chapter calls central to human nature. So Chapter 1.3 builds on appreciation and importance to show how to arouse an eager want.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: Which of these links between Chapter 1.3 and the earlier chapters of Part One can be seen in the text?
options: The bed-wetting boy's father follows Charles Schwab's advice to be lavish in praise
The underweight boy is driven by the desire for a feeling of importance
Carnegie avoids arguing with the hotel manager because pride would stop him giving in
Carnegie retells the story of Lincoln's letter to General Meade
The Father Forgets reading is repeated as the chapter's ending
questions.explain: Schwab's praise and the feeling of importance come from The Big Secret of Dealing with People, and the danger of wounded pride echoes the first chapter's warning against criticism. The chapter ends with Principle 3 and the In a Nutshell summary, not with Father Forgets or the Lincoln letter.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: Why is Arouse in the other person an eager want a fitting principle to close Part One, Fundamental Techniques in Handling People?
questions.a: The first two principles teach what to stop doing and what to give: do not criticize, condemn or complain, and give honest and sincere appreciation. Chapter 1.3 adds the active step of getting people to act, by talking about what they want and showing them how to get it. Carnegie even calls an increased tendency to see things from the other person's angle the one thing worth taking from the whole book, so it rounds off the fundamental techniques before Part Two turns to making people like you.

questions.unitTitle: “He Who Can Do This Has the Whole World with Him. He Who Cannot Walks a Lonely Way”
questions.q: Which later chapter's opening develops the cereal-story lesson that people like ideas better when they think the ideas are their own?
options: You Can’t Win an Argument
How to Get Cooperation
A Drop of Honey
Give a Dog a Good Name
questions.explain: How to Get Cooperation opens by asking whether we do not have more faith in ideas we discover ourselves, which develops Carnegie's advice to let others cook and stir an idea themselves.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: At the start of Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere, whom does Carnegie name as the greatest winner of friends the world has ever known?
options: A dog, which shows affection with no ulterior motive
Theodore Roosevelt, who was loved even by his servants
Howard Thurston, who told himself he loved his audience
A salesman who greeted every clerk in a drugstore
questions.explain: He points to the dog that wags its tail as you approach and wants nothing from you: it does not want to sell you real estate or marry you. Roosevelt and Thurston come later as human examples of the same idea.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: In Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere, what did the New York Telephone Company study find to be the word used most often in telephone conversations?
options: The word you
The personal pronoun I
The word please
The pronoun we
questions.explain: The study found the personal pronoun I was used most often, which Carnegie uses to show that people are interested in themselves rather than in us.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: According to the New York Telephone Company study Carnegie cites, how many times was the word I used in 500 telephone conversations?
options: 500 times
1,200 times
3,900 times
9,000 times
questions.explain: Carnegie reports 3,900 uses of I in 500 conversations, almost eight per call, as evidence of how self-centred people are.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: Why does Carnegie bring in Napoleon’s last meeting with Josephine in Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere?
options: To show that a great leader can win loyalty through fear
To show that the famous make friends more easily than others
To show that marriage is the strongest of all friendships
To show that trying to impress people does not win true friends
questions.explain: Napoleon tried to impress people and ended saying Josephine was the only person he could rely on, and historians doubt he could rely even on her. Carnegie’s point is that real friends are not made by impressing others.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: In Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere, Carnegie quotes the Viennese psychologist Alfred Adler from which book?
options: What Life Should Mean to You
Theodore Roosevelt, Hero to His Valet
The Principles of Psychology
Hints to Self-Help
questions.explain: Carnegie quotes Adler’s book What Life Should Mean to You. Theodore Roosevelt, Hero to His Valet is the book by Roosevelt’s valet, James E. Amos.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: In Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere, what did the magazine editor tell Carnegie’s short-story class at New York University?
options: That a story succeeds mainly through a clever plot twist
That after a few paragraphs he could feel whether the author liked people
That writers should study psychology before writing fiction
That busy editors read only the first page of each story
questions.explain: The editor said he could tell within a few paragraphs whether an author liked people, and readers would not like the stories of an author who did not. Carnegie concludes this must be even truer of dealing with people face to face.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: In Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere, Howard Thurston gave Carnegie two reasons for his success as a magician. One was his showmanship. What was the other?
options: A superior knowledge of magic
A good formal education
A genuine interest in people
A set of secret, unpublished tricks
questions.explain: Thurston said scores of people knew as much about magic as he did and he had little schooling. What set him apart was showmanship plus a genuine interest in his audience.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: In Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere, how did George Dyke of North Warren, Pennsylvania, build a new life after he was forced to retire?
options: By becoming one of the finest fiddlers in the eastern United States
By opening a new service station beside the highway
By teaching music lessons to the young people of his town
By taking a sustained interest in the musicians he met
questions.explain: Dyke was not a great fiddler himself, but he took a humble, friendly interest in the background and interests of every musician he met, made many friends, and was enjoying life at seventy-two.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: In the story James E. Amos tells in Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere, why did Theodore Roosevelt telephone the Amos cottage?
options: To tell Mrs. Amos there was a bobwhite outside her window
To invite the Amos family to dinner at the main house
To thank James Amos for writing a book about him
To ask Mrs. Amos to bake corn bread for his guests
questions.explain: Mrs. Amos had asked Roosevelt about a bobwhite, a bird she had never seen, and he later phoned to tell her one was outside her window. The corn bread belongs to a different story, about Alice the White House kitchen maid.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: In Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere, what did Theodore Roosevelt do when he visited the White House while President and Mrs. Taft were away?
options: He inspected the new rooms and gave orders for changes
He greeted all the old servants by name, even the scullery maids
He spoke only with the senior staff and the head usher
He left a gift of money for each of the servants
questions.explain: Roosevelt greeted every old servant by name and asked Alice the kitchen maid about her corn bread. The head usher, Ike Hoover, called it the only happy day they had had in nearly two years.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: In Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere, why did the Hingham drugstore owner welcome sales representative Edward M. Sykes back and double his order?
options: Sykes returned with a lower price on Johnson and Johnson products
Sykes promised that his company would stop favouring discount stores
The soda clerk told the owner Sykes was one of the few who bothered to say hello to the staff
The owner realised he had run out of stock while Sykes was away
questions.explain: Sykes always chatted with the soda clerk and sales clerk before seeing the owner. The young clerk told the owner that if any salesperson deserved his business, it was Sykes.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: In Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere, how did Carnegie get busy authors such as Kathleen Norris and Ida Tarbell to come to his Brooklyn fiction course?
options: He offered each author a generous speaking fee
He asked a famous publisher to introduce him to them
He invited them to give a prepared lecture on writing
He sent letters of admiration signed by about 150 students, with questions about themselves to answer
questions.explain: The letters said the students admired their work and knew they were too busy to prepare a lecture, so they enclosed questions about the authors and their methods. Carnegie says the authors liked that, and asks who wouldn’t.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: In the story of the German Kaiser in Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere, what did the little boy do, and what followed?
options: He wrote the Kaiser a sincere letter of admiration, and the Kaiser later married the boy’s mother
He wrote the Kaiser a letter asking for money, and the Kaiser sent him a gift
He visited the Kaiser in Holland, and the Kaiser made him a royal servant
He defended the Kaiser in a newspaper, and the Kaiser returned to Germany
questions.explain: When the Kaiser was despised after World War I, one boy wrote that he would always love Wilhelm as his emperor. The Kaiser invited him to visit; the boy came with his mother, and the Kaiser married her.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: In Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere, where did Charles R. Walters get the stamps that won over the corporation president?
options: From his own childhood collection
From the foreign department of his bank, which collected stamps from letters
From the president’s secretary, who had saved them
From a stamp dealer recommended by his class
questions.explain: Walters remembered that the foreign department of his bank collected stamps from letters arriving from every continent. He brought some for the president’s twelve-year-old son, and the president then gave him every fact he needed.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.section: Principle: Become genuinely interested in other people
questions.q: In Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere, what finally led the chain-store executive to offer to buy fuel from C. M. Knaphle?
options: Knaphle publicly attacked chain stores until the company gave in
Knaphle offered a lower price than the out-of-town dealer
Knaphle asked the executive for help with a debate in which he was defending chain stores
Knaphle brought Carnegie along to make the sales pitch
questions.explain: Knaphle said he was not there to sell fuel but to ask a favour: facts for his debate. By becoming interested in the executive and his work, he made more headway in two hours than years of trying to sell had achieved.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.section: Principle: Become genuinely interested in other people
questions.q: What condition does Carnegie place on showing interest in other people in Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere?
options: It should be shown only to people who can help you
It works best if the other person does not notice it
It should be saved for important business contacts
It must be sincere and benefit both people
questions.explain: Carnegie says a show of interest must be sincere and must pay off for the person receiving the attention as well as the person showing it: “It is a two-way street—both parties benefit.”

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.section: Principle: Become genuinely interested in other people
questions.q: Priya has just moved to a new town and wants to make friends quickly. According to Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere, which approach will work best?
options: Telling new acquaintances about her travels and achievements so they find her interesting
Asking neighbours about their own lives and interests, and remembering what they tell her
Waiting until others show interest in her before she shows interest in them
Joining many clubs so that as many people as possible see her
questions.explain: Carnegie’s claim is that you make more friends in two months by becoming genuinely interested in others than in two years by trying to get them interested in you. Impressing people with one’s achievements is exactly what he says fails.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: What does the word This refer to in the chapter title Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere?
options: Become genuinely interested in other people
Smile at everyone you meet
Remember people’s names
Arouse in the other person an eager want
questions.explain: The chapter ends with Principle 1 of Part Two, become genuinely interested in other people, which is the thing that makes you welcome anywhere. Smiling and remembering names are the next principles; arousing an eager want ends Part One.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: True or false: In Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere, Carnegie says the dog is the only animal that doesn’t have to work for a living.
questions.explain: He contrasts the dog with the hen that lays eggs, the cow that gives milk and the canary that sings: the dog makes his living by giving nothing but love.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: True or false: In Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere, Carnegie’s boyhood dog Tippy was killed by a passing car.
questions.explain: Tippy was killed by lightning one night within ten feet of Carnegie’s head, which he calls the tragedy of his boyhood.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: True or false: In Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere, Howard Thurston told Carnegie that his success came mainly from knowing more about magic than other magicians.
questions.explain: Thurston said hundreds of books had been written on magic and scores of people knew as much as he did. His edge was showmanship and a genuine interest in people.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: True or false: In Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere, Carnegie says he learned his friends’ birthdays by asking whether they believed the date of birth affects character, even though he had no faith in astrology.
questions.explain: He used the astrology question as an opening to ask for the month and day, wrote them down, and sent a letter or telegram on the day, often as the only person who remembered.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.section: Principle: Become genuinely interested in other people
questions.q: True or false: In Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere, C. M. Knaphle asked the chain-store executive for ten minutes of his time.
questions.explain: Knaphle asked for precisely one minute, and the executive then talked to him for an hour and forty-seven minutes.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.section: Principle: Become genuinely interested in other people
questions.q: True or false: In Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere, Carnegie says the Roman poet Publilius Syrus lived about a hundred years after Christ.
questions.explain: Carnegie places Publilius Syrus a hundred years before Christ was born, to show that Knaphle had not discovered a new truth.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.section: Principle: Become genuinely interested in other people
questions.q: True or false: In Martin Ginsberg’s story in Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere, the student nurse was due off duty at 4 p.m. but stayed until almost 11 p.m.
questions.explain: She stayed on her own time, shared Thanksgiving dinner with the ten-year-old boy, played games and talked with him until he fell asleep.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: Carnegie says you can make more friends in two ____ by becoming genuinely interested in other people than you can in two years by trying to get other people interested in you.
questions.explain: He repeats the line for emphasis: two months of interest in others outdoes two years of trying to make others interested in you.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: In Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere, Carnegie’s little yellow-haired boyhood dog was named ____.
questions.explain: Tippy was his constant companion for five years and, Carnegie says, knew by instinct the secret of making friends.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: Alfred Adler, quoted by Carnegie, wrote that it is the individual who is not interested in his ____ who has the greatest difficulties in life and provides the greatest injury to others.
questions.explain: Carnegie thinks this so important that he repeats it in italics, adding Adler’s conclusion: “It is from among such individuals that all human failures spring.”

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: Before every show, the magician Howard Thurston said to himself over and over: I love my ____.
questions.explain: Unlike magicians who saw the audience as suckers to be fooled, Thurston told himself he was grateful to them and would give them his very best.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: After retiring from his service station, George Dyke became known to country music fans as Uncle George, the Fiddle ____ from Kinzua County.
questions.explain: He was not a great fiddler, but his friendly interest in other musicians made him widely known and liked.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: Theodore Roosevelt’s valet, James E. Amos, wrote a book about him entitled Theodore Roosevelt, Hero to His ____.
questions.explain: Carnegie uses Amos’s book to show that even Roosevelt’s servants loved him, because he took a real interest in them, as in the bobwhite story.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: Charles R. Walters turned a barren interview into a scoop by bringing the corporation president ____ for his twelve-year-old son.
questions.explain: The president had been vague and unhelpful, but after half an hour talking about the stamps and his boy, he gave Walters every fact he wanted.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.section: Principle: Become genuinely interested in other people
questions.q: For years C. M. Knaphle of Philadelphia tried without success to sell ____ to a large chain-store organization.
questions.explain: The company hauled its fuel from an out-of-town dealer right past his office until he stopped selling and took an interest in the executive’s work.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.section: Principle: Become genuinely interested in other people
questions.q: Carnegie tells Knaphle he did not discover a new truth, since the old Roman ____ Publilius Syrus said we are interested in others when they are interested in us.
questions.explain: Carnegie calls Publilius Syrus a famous old Roman poet who lived a hundred years before Christ.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.section: Principle: Become genuinely interested in other people
questions.q: Principle 1 of Part Two of How to Win Friends and Influence People is: Become genuinely ____ in other people.
questions.explain: The chapter closes with this principle, offered to anyone who wants others to like them and wants to help others while helping themselves.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.section: Principle: Become genuinely interested in other people
questions.q: Carnegie advises that when somebody calls you on the telephone, you should say Hello in tones that show how ____ you are to have the person call.
questions.explain: Greeting people with animation and enthusiasm is one way to show interest; he notes companies train operators to greet callers this way so callers feel the company cares.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: Which of these does Carnegie say Howard Thurston had that other magicians did not have?
options: The ability to put his personality across the footlights
A genuine interest in people
A superior knowledge of magic
Better schooling than most performers
More expensive stage equipment
questions.explain: Thurston was a master showman who knew human nature, and he genuinely cared for his audience. He had little schooling and said scores of people knew as much magic as he did.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: Which of these does Carnegie recommend in Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere as ways to make friends?
options: Doing things for others that take time, energy, unselfishness and thoughtfulness
Greeting people with animation and enthusiasm
Remembering people’s birthdays and sending a note on the day
Telling people about your successes so they find you interesting
Waiting for others to show interest in you first
questions.explain: Carnegie gives the Prince of Wales learning Spanish, his own birthday book and the enthusiastic telephone greeting as examples. Trying to get others interested in you is the approach he says does not work.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: Which of these prominent people does Carnegie say he persuaded to speak to his students by showing interest in them?
options: Leslie M. Shaw
William Jennings Bryan
Franklin D. Roosevelt
Alfred Adler
Howard Thurston
questions.explain: He lists Shaw, George W. Wickersham, Bryan and Franklin D. Roosevelt among those he persuaded. He quotes Adler’s book and visited Thurston’s dressing room, but neither is named as a speaker.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: Which of these authors did Carnegie invite to his fiction-writing course at the Brooklyn Institute of Arts and Sciences?
options: Ida Tarbell
Lowell Thomas
Fannie Hurst
James E. Amos
Rupert Hughes
questions.explain: The authors named are Kathleen Norris, Fannie Hurst, Ida Tarbell, Albert Payson Terhune and Rupert Hughes. Amos is Roosevelt’s valet who wrote a book about him.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: Which of these did the corporation president do for Charles R. Walters after Walters brought stamps for his son?
options: Spent half an hour talking stamps and showing a picture of his boy
Gave more than an hour of information without being asked
Called in his subordinates and questioned them for Walters
Asked Walters to come back after the next board meeting
Sent Walters to his secretary for the facts
questions.explain: The president loaded Walters with facts, figures, reports and correspondence, phoning associates and calling in subordinates, all without Walters suggesting it.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.section: Principle: Become genuinely interested in other people
questions.q: Which of these did the chain-store executive do after agreeing to give C. M. Knaphle one minute?
options: Talked to him for an hour and forty-seven minutes
Called in another executive who had written a book on chain stores
Told him to come back with a lower price for fuel
Refused to discuss the chain-store debate
questions.explain: The executive also wrote to the National Chain Store Association for a copy of a debate and, at the door, offered to place a fuel order in the spring, without Knaphle asking.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.section: Principle: Become genuinely interested in other people
questions.q: Which of these does Carnegie say about showing interest in other people?
options: It must be sincere
It must pay off for the person receiving the attention as well as the giver
It is a two-way street in which both parties benefit
It works best when combined with flattery
It benefits only the person who shows it
questions.explain: Carnegie says that, like every principle of human relations, a show of interest must be sincere and must benefit both sides: “It is a two-way street—both parties benefit.”

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: Put the events of Edward M. Sykes’s visit to the Hingham drugstore in order.
items: The owner says he will no longer buy Johnson and Johnson products
Sykes drives around town for several hours
Sykes returns and greets the clerks as usual
The owner gives him double the usual order
questions.explain: After being sent away, Sykes came back to explain his company’s position. In the meantime the soda clerk had praised him to the owner, so he was welcomed and given double his order.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: Put the events of Charles R. Walters’s visit to the corporation president in order.
items: A secretary says she has no stamps for the president that day
The president gives vague answers and the interview is brief
Walters remembers his bank’s foreign department collects stamps
Walters returns the next afternoon with stamps for the boy
The president gives him every fact he needs and more
questions.explain: Walters noticed the remark about stamps for the twelve-year-old son, used it to show interest in what mattered to the president, and turned a barren interview into a scoop.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.section: Principle: Become genuinely interested in other people
questions.q: Put the events of C. M. Knaphle’s story in order.
items: Knaphle condemns chain stores in a speech to Carnegie’s class
Knaphle takes the side defending chain stores in a class debate
Knaphle asks a chain-store executive for one minute of help
The executive talks to him for nearly two hours
The executive offers to place an order for fuel
questions.explain: At Carnegie’s suggestion Knaphle stopped attacking chain stores, took their side in a debate and asked the executive for facts. His interest in the man’s work won the order he had failed to get for years.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: Put the events of the story of the German Kaiser and the little boy in order.
items: The Kaiser flees to Holland, hated by millions
A little boy writes him a sincere letter of admiration
The Kaiser invites the boy to visit him
The boy comes to see him with his mother
The Kaiser marries the boy’s mother
questions.explain: Carnegie uses the story to show that all of us, even a king, like people who admire us; the boy knew instinctively how to win a friend.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: Put the steps of Carnegie’s method for remembering friends’ birthdays in order.
items: Ask whether they think the date of birth affects character
Ask for the month and day of their birth
Write down the name and date once their back is turned
Copy it into a birthday book
Schedule the dates in the calendar pad each year
Send a letter or telegram on the day
questions.explain: Carnegie repeated the date to himself until he could write it down, then moved it into a birthday book and his calendar so that the day came to his attention automatically.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: Put the six principles of Part Two, Six Ways to Make People Like You, in the order the book gives them.
items: Become genuinely interested in other people
Smile
Remember that a person’s name is to that person the sweetest sound
Be a good listener
Talk in terms of the other person’s interests
Make the other person feel important, and do it sincerely
questions.explain: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere gives Principle 1, which opens Part Two. Smiling, names, listening, talking about the other person’s interests and making them feel important follow in the next five chapters.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: Match each person in Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere to what they did.
pairs: Told himself before every show that he loved his audience
Made many friends among fiddlers after retiring
Always said hello to the drugstore clerks
Brought stamps for a company president’s son
Asked a chain-store executive for help with a debate
questions.explain: Each is an example of genuine interest in others paying off, whether in an audience’s affection, new friendships, a kept account, needed information or a new customer.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: Match each speaker in Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere to the idea Carnegie quotes from them.
pairs: Josephine was the only person in the world on whom he could rely
Human failures spring from those not interested in their fellow men
We are interested in others when they are interested in us
Roosevelt’s visit was the only happy day in nearly two years
If an author doesn’t like people, people won’t like the stories
questions.explain: Napoleon shows the failure of trying to impress; Adler and Publilius Syrus state the principle; Hoover and the editor show its effect in life and in fiction.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: Match each person to the way they showed interest in others in Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere.
pairs: Spent months learning Spanish before touring South America
Sent friends a letter or telegram on their birthdays
Greeted the old White House servants by name
Asked a depositor about her hospitalised mother
Shared Thanksgiving dinner with a lonely boy in hospital
questions.explain: Carnegie says that to make friends we must do things for others that require time, energy, unselfishness and thoughtfulness; each of these acts did.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: Match each example in Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere to the point Carnegie uses it to make.
pairs: Affection given with no ulterior motive wins friends
People are mainly interested in themselves
Trying to impress people does not win true friends
The boy who wrote to the Kaiser
Everyone, even a king, likes people who admire them
Interest in customers builds loyalty to a company
questions.explain: Each example supports one step in the argument that genuine interest in others, not efforts to impress them, is what makes people like you.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: Match each number to what it measures in Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere.
pairs: Uses of the word I in 500 telephone conversations
People who had paid to see Thurston’s show
Students who signed each letter to the busy authors
Time the chain-store executive talked to Knaphle
George Dyke’s age when Carnegie heard him
questions.explain: The figures come from the telephone study, the Thurston, Brooklyn course and Knaphle stories, and the account of Uncle George.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: Match each part of How to Win Friends and Influence People to its title.
pairs: Six Ways to Make People Like You
How to Win People to Your Way of Thinking
Be a Leader: How to Change People Without Giving Offense
questions.explain: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere is the first chapter of Part Two, which moves from handling people to making them like you.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: Sort each attitude into Howard Thurston’s attitude or the attitude of the many magicians he described.

items.t: I am grateful these people come to see me
I love my audience
I will give them the very best I can
There is a bunch of suckers out there
They are a bunch of hicks
I will fool them all right

questions.explain: Thurston said many magicians looked down on the audience as people to be fooled, while he went on stage grateful to them and determined to give them his best.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.section: Principle: Become genuinely interested in other people
questions.q: Sort each action into the approach Carnegie says wins friends or the approach he says fails.
groups: Trying to get others interested in you

items.t: Sending busy authors questions about their own methods
Bringing stamps for a client’s son
Asking a rival for facts about his own work
Telling everyone about your own achievements
Trying to wigwag people into noticing you
Trying to impress people with your importance

questions.explain: Carnegie says people are interested in themselves, so efforts to make them interested in us fail, while genuine interest in them wins friends, time and cooperation.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: Sort each example by what the show of interest mainly won, as Carnegie tells it.

items.t: Edward M. Sykes and the drugstore account
Charles R. Walters and the confidential report
C. M. Knaphle and the fuel order
Theodore Roosevelt and his servants
The little boy who wrote to the Kaiser
George Dyke and the fiddlers

questions.explain: Carnegie shows interest winning business and help at work as well as love and friendship in private and public life; it is a quality for a salesperson and, as Sykes says, for any person.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: Sort each principle into the part of How to Win Friends and Influence People where it appears.
groups: Part One: Fundamental Techniques in Handling People
Part Two: Six Ways to Make People Like You

items.t: Don’t criticize, condemn or complain
Give honest and sincere appreciation
Arouse in the other person an eager want
Become genuinely interested in other people
Smile
Be a good listener

questions.explain: Part One gives three principles for handling people; Part Two begins with Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere and its principle of genuine interest in others.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: Sort each fact into whether Carnegie tells it about George Dyke or about Theodore Roosevelt.

items.t: Retired after thirty years when a highway was built over his business
Became known as a fiddle scraper from Kinzua County
Was enjoying life at seventy-two
Phoned his valet’s wife about a bird outside her window
Asked the kitchen maid Alice about her corn bread
Was loved even by his servants

questions.explain: Both men show how sustained interest in other people, including humble or seemingly unimportant people, wins friends and affection.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: Why does Carnegie open Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere with the example of a dog?
questions.a: The dog is the greatest winner of friends because it shows affection with no ulterior motive and makes its living by giving nothing but love. Carnegie’s dog Tippy knew by instinct that you can make more friends in two months by becoming genuinely interested in others than in two years by trying to get them interested in you. The dog is a simple picture of the chapter’s whole principle.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: What do the telephone company study and the group photograph show in Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere, and why does this matter for making friends?
questions.a: The study found that I was the most used word, 3,900 times in 500 calls, and in a group photograph we look for ourselves first. They show that people are interested in themselves, not in us. So trying to impress people and make them interested in us will never win many true, sincere friends.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: Why does Carnegie think Alfred Adler’s statement is so significant that he repeats it in italics?
questions.a: Adler says that the person who is not interested in his fellow men has the greatest difficulties in life and does the greatest injury to others, and that all human failures spring from such people. Carnegie says one could read scores of psychology books without finding a statement more significant. It makes interest in others not just a social skill but a key to success and failure in life.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: What did Howard Thurston tell Carnegie was the secret of his success as a magician?
questions.a: It was not schooling, since he ran away as a boy, or superior knowledge of magic, since scores of people knew as much. He was a master showman who rehearsed every gesture, and he had a genuine interest in people. While other magicians thought of the audience as suckers to fool, he told himself he was grateful to them and said over and over: “I love my audience.”

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: What lesson did Edward M. Sykes draw from his experience at the Hingham drugstore?
questions.a: Sykes always spent a few minutes talking to the soda clerk and sales clerk before seeing the owner. When the owner dropped Johnson and Johnson, the young clerk told him Sykes was one of the few salespeople who even said hello to them, and the owner gave him double the order. Sykes learned that genuine interest in others, including seemingly unimportant people, is a most important quality for a salesperson and for anyone.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: How did Carnegie win the time and cooperation of busy, sought-after people for his courses?
questions.a: He became genuinely interested in them. For his Brooklyn fiction course he sent authors letters, signed by about 150 students, saying they admired their work and wanted their advice, and enclosing questions about the authors and their methods instead of asking for a lecture. The authors liked that and came; by the same method he brought cabinet members, William Jennings Bryan and Franklin D. Roosevelt to his public speaking classes.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: Explain how Charles R. Walters turned a barren interview into a scoop.
questions.a: The corporation president was vague and would not talk, but Walters had heard the secretary mention stamps for the president’s twelve-year-old son. He returned with stamps from his bank’s foreign department, and the president welcomed him warmly, talked about the stamps and his boy, and then gave over an hour of information unasked. Showing interest in what mattered to the president achieved what direct questions could not.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.section: Principle: Become genuinely interested in other people
questions.q: How did C. M. Knaphle finally win the chain-store account, and what does Carnegie say about his discovery?
questions.a: After years of failing and condemning chain stores, Knaphle took their side in a class debate and asked an executive for help, saying he was not there to sell fuel. Given one minute, the executive talked for nearly two hours, changed Knaphle’s view and offered to order fuel. Knaphle said he gained more in two hours by becoming interested in the man than in ten years of trying to interest him in his product; Carnegie notes that Publilius Syrus said the same long ago: “We are interested in others when they are interested in us.”

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.section: Principle: Become genuinely interested in other people
questions.q: Why does Carnegie insist that interest in other people must be sincere, and what does he mean by calling it a two-way street?
questions.a: Like every principle of human relations, a show of interest must be sincere, or it is only a technique to get something. It must pay off not only for the person showing it but also for the person receiving it. Calling it a two-way street means both parties benefit, which is why he says the principle helps others at the same time as it helps you.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.section: Principle: Become genuinely interested in other people
questions.q: What does Martin Ginsberg’s story of the student nurse illustrate in Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere?
questions.a: At ten, poor, alone and afraid before surgery on Thanksgiving Day, Ginsberg was crying under his covers. A student nurse wiped his tears, shared her own loneliness, ate Thanksgiving dinner with him and stayed hours past her shift until he slept. Her sincere interest made his ordeal bearable and he never forgot it, showing how genuine interest benefits the person who receives it, not only the giver.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.section: Principle: Become genuinely interested in other people
questions.q: A new team leader wants her team to like and cooperate with her. Using Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere, what should she do and avoid?
questions.a: She should become genuinely interested in each person: learn about their lives and interests, remember things such as birthdays, greet them with warmth and enthusiasm, and do things for them that take time and thoughtfulness, including people others overlook, as Roosevelt did with servants. She should avoid trying to impress them with her own importance, because people are interested in themselves. Her interest must be sincere, so that both she and the team benefit.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.section: Principle: Become genuinely interested in other people
questions.q: Recite Principle 1 of Part Two from memory, and say briefly what it asks of the reader.
questions.a: Become genuinely interested in other people. It asks the reader to stop trying to make people interested in them and instead to care sincerely about others, their lives, interests and concerns. Carnegie offers it to anyone who wants to be liked, develop real friendships and help others while helping themselves.

questions.unitTitle: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
questions.q: Why is Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere a fitting opening for Part Two, and how does it follow from Part One?
questions.a: Part One gave fundamental techniques for handling people and ended with arousing in the other person an eager want, which rests on seeing things from the other person’s side. Part Two, Six Ways to Make People Like You, starts from the same fact that people are interested in themselves, and makes genuine interest in them the first way to be liked. The later principles of Part Two, such as smiling, remembering names and listening, are specific ways of showing that interest.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: In Carnegie's story of the inherited-money guest at a New York dinner party, what had she neglected while trying to impress everyone?
options: Her sables, diamonds and pearls
The expression on her face
Her manners at the table
Her choice of conversation
questions.explain: She spent a modest fortune on furs and jewels but did nothing about her face, which “radiated sourness and selfishness.” Her finery was the very thing she had not neglected.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: How much did Charles Schwab tell Carnegie his smile had been worth?
options: A million dollars
A thousand dollars a year
More than his steel mills
Exactly nothing, he said
questions.explain: Schwab said his smile had been worth a million dollars, and Carnegie adds he was probably understating it, since his charm and captivating smile were central to his success.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: In veterinarian Stephen K. Sproul's story, what turned the bored, tense waiting room into a pleasant experience?
options: The vet came out and apologised for the long wait
A kitten began playing among the waiting clients
A nine-month-old baby smiled at a distraught gentleman
The receptionist told a joke to the whole room
questions.explain: The baby's big smile made the impatient man smile back; he began chatting with the mother, and soon the whole room joined in. The kitten was present but plays no part in the change.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: Why, according to psychologist James V. McConnell, is encouragement a more effective teaching device than punishment?
options: Because punishment is now forbidden in most schools
Because children forget punishments within a day
Because teachers who punish are disliked by parents
Because there is far more information in a smile than a frown
questions.explain: McConnell says people who smile manage, teach and sell more effectively, and that a smile carries far more information than a frown, which is why encouragement beats punishment.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: Whom did the employment manager of a large New York department store say she would rather hire as a sales clerk?
options: A doctor of philosophy who looked serious and capable
Someone who had not finished grade school but had a pleasant smile
Anyone with previous experience in a rival store
A graduate who spoke well on the telephone
questions.explain: She preferred a clerk without even a grade-school education, if he or she had a pleasant smile, to a Ph.D. with a somber face. Qualifications counted for less than the smile.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: Why did the Purdue graduate recruited by Robert Cryer choose Cryer's company over larger, better-known ones?
options: Cryer's voice on the phone sounded glad to hear from him
Cryer offered the highest salary of all the companies
Cryer's company was closest to his family home
Cryer promised him a quicker promotion
questions.explain: Other managers spoke in a cold, business-like way that made him feel like a mere transaction, while Cryer sounded as if he really wanted him. A smile, Carnegie notes, comes through in the voice.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: What did the chairman of one of the largest US rubber companies observe about success?
options: Hard work alone is the magic key to success
Success comes mainly from luck and good timing
People rarely succeed at anything unless they have fun doing it
Only people who avoid risk succeed for long
questions.explain: He put little faith in the old adage about hard work alone; he had seen people succeed while having a good time and then fail once the fun became work.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: A shop assistant feels gloomy before her shift and does not feel like smiling. Following the advice Carnegie draws from William James, what should she do?
options: Wait quietly until her mood improves on its own
Tell her customers honestly that she is having a bad day
Avoid customers until she genuinely feels cheerful
Act and speak as if she were already cheerful
questions.explain: James says action and feeling go together, and since action is under the will's direct control, regulating it indirectly regulates feeling. Waiting for the mood to change reverses this order.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: A friend is about to open a café. Which ancient Chinese proverb, quoted by Carnegie, fits the situation?
options: A journey of a thousand miles begins with one step
A man without a smiling face must not open a shop
A good name is better than great riches
The customer who smiles will always return
questions.explain: Carnegie says the proverb is worth pasting inside our hats: “A man without a smiling face must not open a shop.” The other sayings do not appear in the chapter.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.section: The Value of a Smile at Christmas
questions.q: Why did a New York department store publish The Value of a Smile at Christmas in its advertisements?
options: In recognition of the pressures its sales clerks were under during the Christmas rush
To announce a new training course in friendliness for its staff
To apologise for poor service during a previous holiday season
To promote a range of greeting cards on sale that December
questions.explain: Carnegie says the store offered this homely philosophy because its clerks were under pressure in the Christmas rush; it ends by asking tired shoppers to give a smile to tired staff.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: When Carnegie gives the principle Smile, which kind of smile does he mean?
options: A polite grin worn whenever a customer is watching
