A broad smile practised in front of a mirror
A smile saved for people who can help your career
A real, heartwarming smile that comes from within
questions.explain: He rejects the insincere grin because it fools nobody: we know it is mechanical and resent it. He means a real smile that comes from within.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: In Part Two, Six Ways to Make People Like You, which principle comes immediately before Smile?
options: Be a good listener
Make the other person feel important
Become genuinely interested in other people
Remember that a person’s name is the sweetest sound
questions.explain: Smile is Principle 2 of Part Two. It follows Principle 1, become genuinely interested in other people; the name principle comes next, as Principle 3.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: True or false: Carnegie says the expression one wears on one's face is far more important than the clothes one wears on one's back.
questions.explain: He draws this lesson from the dinner-party guest whose costly furs and jewels could not offset her sour expression.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: True or false: Carnegie asked thousands of business people to smile at someone every hour of the day for a month and then report the results in class.
questions.explain: The assignment lasted a week, not a month: smile at someone every hour of the day for a week, then come to class and talk about the results.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: True or false: Maria Gonzalez of Guadalajara waited for her co-workers to come to her, and after some weeks they approached her first.
questions.explain: She realised she could not expect them to come to her and had to go out and meet them; she began greeting people with her brightest smile, and the response was immediate.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.section: The Value of a Smile at Christmas
questions.q: True or false: The Value of a Smile at Christmas asks shoppers to complain to the manager if a salesperson is too tired to give them a smile.
questions.explain: It asks shoppers to leave one of their own smiles, because nobody needs a smile more than those who have none left to give.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: True or false: The chapter that follows A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression gives the principle about remembering a person's name.
questions.explain: The next chapter, If You Don't Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble, gives Principle 3: remember that a person's name is to that person the sweetest and most important sound.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: Telephone companies in the United States run a program for employees who sell by phone called “phone ____”, which suggests smiling while talking.
questions.explain: The phone power program teaches that your smile comes through in your voice, showing that a smile works even when it is unseen.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: Abe Lincoln remarked that most folks are about as happy as they make up their ____ to be.
questions.explain: Carnegie agrees with Lincoln and illustrates the point with the laughing boys on crutches climbing the Long Island Railroad station stairs.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: Carnegie quotes Shakespeare as saying there is nothing either good or bad, but ____ makes it so.
questions.explain: The quotation supports Carnegie's claim that happiness depends not on outward conditions but on what you think about them.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: Elbert Hubbard's advice, quoted by Carnegie, ends with the line: We are gods in the ____.
questions.explain: Hubbard's passage stresses that thought is supreme and that we become like that on which our hearts are fixed, closing with the image of gods in the chrysalis.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.section: The Value of a Smile at Christmas
questions.q: The Value of a Smile at Christmas opens by saying a smile costs ____, but creates much.
questions.explain: The ad's first line is “It costs nothing, but creates much.” It goes on to say a smile enriches the receiver without impoverishing the giver.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.section: The Value of a Smile at Christmas
questions.q: The Value of a Smile at Christmas says a smile cannot be bought, begged, borrowed or stolen, for it is no earthly good to anybody till it is ____ away.
questions.explain: A smile has value only when given away, which is why the ad can ask shoppers to give one to tired clerks.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: Principle 2 of Six Ways to Make People Like You is a single word: ____.
questions.explain: The chapter ends with the shortest principle in the book's list of six: Smile.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: Which of these did psychologist James V. McConnell say people who smile tend to do more effectively?
options: Manage
Sell
Invent
Negotiate contracts
Teach
questions.explain: McConnell said people who smile tend to manage, teach and sell more effectively, and to raise happier children. Inventing and negotiating are not mentioned.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: Which of these changes, besides smiling, did stockbroker William B. Steinhardt say he had made?
options: Eliminated criticism from his system
Stopped talking about what he wanted
Moved to a new brokerage firm
Took a long holiday from the Stock Exchange
Gave appreciation and praise instead of condemnation
questions.explain: Steinhardt also dropped criticism, gave appreciation and praise, stopped talking about what he wanted and tried to see the other person's viewpoint. He did not change firms or take a break.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: Which of these does Carnegie advise for someone who is alone and does not feel like smiling?
options: Force yourself to whistle, hum or sing
Wait until a cheerful feeling arrives
Act as if you were already happy
Force yourself to smile
Think about the people who have wronged you
questions.explain: Carnegie's two remedies are to force yourself to smile (or whistle, hum or sing when alone) and to act as if you were already happy, which tends to make you happy.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: Which of these does Elbert Hubbard advise in the passage Carnegie quotes?
options: Greet your friends with a smile and put soul into every handclasp
Study your enemies closely so you can outwit them
Draw the chin in and carry the crown of the head high
Picture the able, earnest, useful person you desire to be
Guard against being misunderstood at all costs
questions.explain: Hubbard tells readers not to fear being misunderstood and not to waste a minute thinking about enemies, so those options reverse his advice.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.section: The Value of a Smile at Christmas
questions.q: Which of these does The Value of a Smile at Christmas say a smile does?
options: Creates happiness in the home
Fosters good will in a business
Can be bought by those rich enough
Is the countersign of friends
Impoverishes those who give it
questions.explain: The ad says a smile creates happiness at home, fosters good will in business and is the countersign of friends; it cannot be bought and enriches without impoverishing the giver.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: Put the events of veterinarian Stephen K. Sproul's waiting-room story in order.
items: A young woman with a baby and a kitten sits beside an impatient gentleman
The baby gives him a great big smile
The gentleman smiles back at the baby
He chats with the mother about her baby and his grandchildren
The whole reception room joins the conversation
questions.explain: One baby's smile sets off a chain: a smile returned, a conversation, then the whole room, turning boredom and tension into an enjoyable experience.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: Put the steps of William B. Steinhardt's smile experiment in the order he describes them.
items: Resolves in front of the mirror to wipe the scowl off his face
Greets his wife at breakfast with a smile
His wife is bewildered and shocked
Smiles at the elevator operator, doorman and subway cashier
A clerk admits he had thought him a terrible grouch
questions.explain: Steinhardt starts at home, then carries the smile to everyone on his way to and at work, and finally learns how others had seen him before the change.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: Put the stages of Maria Gonzalez's story in order.
items: She works alone and envies the chatter of her co-workers
She shyly looks the other way when passing them in the hall
She tells herself she must go out and meet them
She smiles and greets each person at the water cooler
Acquaintanceships ripen into friendships
questions.explain: Her situation changed only when she stopped waiting and took the first step with a smile; the effect, Carnegie says, was immediate.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: Put these chapters of Part Two, Six Ways to Make People Like You, in the order they appear.
items: Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere
A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.explain: Smile is the second of the six ways, between becoming genuinely interested in others and remembering names, and before the chapter on listening.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: In A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression, match each person to the idea Carnegie quotes or reports from them.
pairs: His smile had been worth a million dollars
There is more information in a smile than a frown
Folks are as happy as they make up their minds to be
Nothing is good or bad but thinking makes it so
questions.explain: Carnegie gathers these voices to show the power of a smile and the dependence of happiness on attitude rather than circumstance.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: Match each person in the chapter to how Carnegie identifies them.
pairs: Psychologist at the University of Michigan
questions.explain: Carnegie draws his cases from ordinary working people and a psychologist, showing the smile working in many settings.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: Match each example in the chapter to the lesson Carnegie draws from it.
pairs: The dinner-party guest in sables and pearls
Your expression matters more than your clothes
Dogs that almost jump out of their skins
Those glad to see us make us glad to see them
A smile comes through in your voice
Peasants toiling happily in tropical heat
Happiness depends on mental attitude, not conditions
questions.explain: Each example supports a step in the argument: a smile signals gladness, works unseen, and flows from an attitude we can control.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.section: The Value of a Smile at Christmas
questions.q: In The Value of a Smile at Christmas, match each thing a smile is said to be with the people or problem it serves.
questions.explain: The ad lists a smile as rest to the weary, daylight to the discouraged, sunshine to the sad and Nature's best antidote for trouble.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: Sort each item by whether Carnegie says it decides whether you are happy.

items.t: What you have
Where you are
What you are doing
Who you are
What you think about it
Your mental attitude
Controlling your thoughts

questions.explain: Carnegie says happiness depends on inner, not outward, conditions: “It is what you think about it.” Two people with the same lot can be miserable and happy.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: Sort each description into the real smile Carnegie wants or the insincere grin he rejects.

items.t: Comes from within
Heartwarming
Brings a good price in the marketplace
Mechanical
Fools nobody
Resented by those who see it

questions.explain: Carnegie says an insincere grin fools nobody because we know it is mechanical and resent it; he means a real smile from within.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: In Robert Cryer's recruiting story, sort each description into the other companies or Cryer's company.

items.t: Many were larger and better known
Managers spoke in a cold, business-like way
Made him feel like just another transaction
A voice that sounded glad to hear from him
Seemed to really want him in the organization
Won the candidate

questions.explain: Size and reputation lost to warmth: the candidate chose Cryer because his voice sounded glad, and Cryer still answers his phone with a smile.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: What does veterinarian Stephen K. Sproul's waiting-room story show about the effect of a smile?
questions.a: A waiting room full of bored, silent, impatient clients was transformed when a baby smiled at a distraught gentleman. He smiled back, struck up a conversation with the mother, and soon the whole room joined in. The story shows that one genuine smile is returned and spreads, converting boredom and tension into a pleasant experience.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: Why does Carnegie say “You must have a good time meeting people if you expect them to have a good time meeting you,” and what observation supports it?
questions.a: The chairman of a large rubber company told Carnegie that people rarely succeed at anything unless they have fun doing it; he had seen people succeed while enjoying their business and fail once the fun became work. Carnegie applies this to meeting people: your own enjoyment shows in your face and is what makes others enjoy meeting you.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: Describe William B. Steinhardt's experiment with smiling and what it led to.
questions.a: Steinhardt, a self-described grouch who seldom smiled at his wife, tried smiling for a week: he greeted his wife with a smile each morning and smiled at the elevator operator, doorman, subway cashier and people at the Stock Exchange. Everybody smiled back, complaints were settled more easily, and he said smiles brought him dollars every day. Combined with dropping criticism and seeing others' viewpoints, it made him a happier man, richer in friendships and happiness.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: Using William James, explain how Carnegie says you can become cheerful when you do not feel like smiling.
questions.a: James argues that action seems to follow feeling, but really action and feeling go together. Action is under the more direct control of the will, so by regulating it we can indirectly regulate feeling. So when cheerfulness is lost, Carnegie says force yourself to smile and act and speak as if you were already happy, and that will tend to make you happy.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: What lesson did Carnegie draw from the boys on canes and crutches climbing the stairs of the Long Island Railroad station?
questions.a: Carnegie was astonished at their laughter and gaiety; a man in charge explained that once a boy got over the shock of being crippled for life, he usually resigned himself and became as happy as normal boys. This illustrated Lincoln's remark that most folks are about as happy as they make up their minds to be: happiness depends on inner conditions, not outward ones.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.section: The Value of a Smile at Christmas
questions.q: Explain the reasoning of The Value of a Smile at Christmas, including its closing request to shoppers.
questions.a: The ad says a smile costs nothing but creates much, enriches the receiver without impoverishing the giver, and is no earthly good to anybody until it is given away. So if tired salespeople in the Christmas rush have no smile to give, shoppers are asked to leave one of theirs, because “nobody needs a smile so much as those who have none left to give!”

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: Summarise Carnegie's case for the principle Smile.
questions.a: A smile says “I like you. You make me happy. I am glad to see you,” which is why people warm to it as they do to dogs and babies. A real smile from within, not a mechanical grin, helps people manage, sell and make friends, and works even unseen over the phone. Carnegie calls a smile a messenger of good will that brightens the lives of all who see it, especially those under pressure.

questions.unitTitle: A Simple Way to Make a Good First Impression
questions.q: How does this chapter's remark about dogs connect with the chapter before it, Do This and You’ll Be Welcome Anywhere?
questions.a: The previous chapter opened with Carnegie's dog Tippy as the greatest winner of friends, who won people by being genuinely interested in them. This chapter says dogs make such a hit because they are so glad to see us that we are glad to see them. A smile carries the same message of gladness, so Smile builds on genuine interest as the next way to make people like you.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: How did Jim Farley’s father die in Stony Point in 1898, according to Carnegie?
options: He caught a fever while working in a brickyard
He was kicked by a restless horse he was leading to the water trough
He froze in the snow walking home from a funeral
He was injured in an accident at a gypsum works
questions.explain: The horse, unexercised for days, wheeled playfully and kicked him as he was preparing to go to a neighbor child’s funeral, so the village had two funerals that week. The brickyard is where his ten-year-old son later went to work.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: When Carnegie said he understood Jim Farley could call ten thousand people by their first names, how did Farley reply?
options: He said the real secret was hard work, not names
He said the number was closer to five thousand
He said he could call fifty thousand people by their first names
He said he kept a card index of ten thousand voters
questions.explain: Farley corrected him upward: “I can call fifty thousand people by their first names.” Hard work was the joking answer he gave first, which Carnegie waved away.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: In Jim Farley’s simple system for remembering names, what did he find out whenever he met a new acquaintance?
options: The person’s complete name and facts about their family, business and political opinions
The person’s nickname and the name of the town they grew up in
The person’s first name and the name of their employer only
The person’s full name and how much they might donate to the party
questions.explain: Farley learned the complete name plus facts about family, business and political opinions and fixed them as part of a picture. That let him ask about the family and even the hollyhocks a year later.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: After his nineteen-day trip through twenty states for Roosevelt’s campaign, what did Jim Farley do once he was back East?
options: He telephoned the mayor of each town to thank the townspeople
He sent every town a printed thank-you card signed by Roosevelt
He published the names of his hosts in a campaign newspaper
He asked one person per town for a guest list and sent each guest a personal letter
questions.explain: He wrote to one person in each town for a list of everyone he had talked to, then sent each a personal letter opening with the guest’s first name and signed with his own. Carnegie calls this a subtle flattery.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: When Carnegie organized a public-speaking course in Paris and sent out form letters, who wrote him a scathing rebuke?
options: A French typist who had been blamed for the errors
The manager of a large American bank in Paris whose name was misspelled
An American diplomat who had not been invited to the course
A course member whose name had been left off the class list
questions.explain: French typists with little English made blunders filling in names, and the bank manager was angered that his name was misspelled. Carnegie uses it to show the cost of getting a name wrong.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: How did Nicodemus Papadoulos react when Sid Levy greeted him by his full name?
options: He laughed and told Levy to just call him Nick like everyone else
He corrected Levy’s pronunciation and then placed a large order
After a long silence he said, in tears, that no one had made that effort in fifteen years
He asked Levy who had told him his real name
questions.explain: Papadoulos was shocked, said nothing for what seemed minutes, then wept that “nobody has ever made the effort to call me by my right name” in his fifteen years in the country. Most people simply called him Nick.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: As a boy in Scotland, how did Andrew Carnegie get food for his nest of little rabbits?
options: He promised the neighborhood children he would name the bunnies after them if they gathered clover and dandelions
He sold some of the rabbits to buy feed for the rest
He paid other boys a penny for each basket of clover
He persuaded a local farmer to let the rabbits graze in his field
questions.explain: Carnegie offered to name the bunnies in honor of the children who pulled enough clover and dandelions. The plan worked like magic, and he later used the same psychology in business.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: What did Andrew Carnegie do when he wanted to sell steel rails to the Pennsylvania Railroad?
options: He offered J. Edgar Thomson a seat on his company’s board
He undercut every rival’s price on rails
He invited J. Edgar Thomson to name a new railroad car
He built a huge steel mill in Pittsburgh and named it the Edgar Thomson Steel Works
questions.explain: Thomson was the railroad’s president, so Carnegie named his new Pittsburgh mill after him. Carnegie’s riddle about where Thomson then bought rails implies the answer: from Carnegie.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: What did P. T. Barnum, disappointed that he had no sons to carry on his name, offer his grandson C. H. Seeley?
options: His circus, if the grandson ran it under the Barnum name
$25,000 if he would call himself “Barnum” Seeley
A share of his fortune if he named his first son Barnum
A museum wing named for him if he kept the Barnum shows going
questions.explain: Barnum offered $25,000 for the grandson to take the name “Barnum” Seeley. Carnegie cites it to show that people strive to perpetuate their names at any cost.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: According to Carnegie, what is the simple reason most people don’t remember names?
options: They have naturally poor memories for sounds
They meet too many people to keep track of
They don’t take the time and energy to concentrate, repeat and fix names in their minds
They think remembering names is a trick only politicians need
questions.explain: Carnegie says people fail to spend the effort to concentrate, repeat and fix names, then excuse themselves as too busy. He answers the excuse by noting that Franklin D. Roosevelt was busier and still remembered mechanics’ names.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: What does the chapter title “If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble” refer to?
options: Failing to smile when you meet people
Failing to listen when others talk about themselves
Failing to give honest and sincere appreciation
Failing to remember and use people’s names
questions.explain: The chapter’s principle is to remember that a person’s name is to them the sweetest and most important sound, and it warns that forgetting or misspelling a name puts you at a sharp disadvantage. Smiling is the previous chapter’s principle.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.section: Principle: A person’s name is the sweetest and most important sound
questions.q: Maya starts a new job and wants the building’s receptionist, whom most staff ignore, to feel valued. Which action best follows Carnegie’s principle about names?
options: Learn the receptionist’s name, check how to spell it, and greet her by it each day
Bring the receptionist a gift on her first week
Give the receptionist a friendly nickname that is easy to say
Praise the receptionist to her manager without speaking to her
questions.explain: Carnegie says that remembering a name and using it easily is a subtle and very effective compliment, as with Ken Nottingham and Eunice. Swapping in an easy nickname is exactly what people did to Nicodemus Papadoulos, and it left him feeling unseen.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: True or false: Jim Farley went to high school before he went into politics.
questions.explain: Farley went to work in a brickyard at ten and never saw the inside of a high school. Even so, four colleges later honored him with degrees.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: True or false: Andrew Carnegie, called the Steel King, himself knew little about the manufacture of steel.
questions.explain: Carnegie had hundreds of people who knew far more about steel than he did. What made him rich, the author says, was that he knew how to handle people.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: True or false: Andrew Carnegie boasted that while he was personally in charge, his steel mills had only a few short strikes.
questions.explain: He boasted that no strike ever disturbed his steel mills while he was personally in charge. He was also proud that he could call many of his factory workers by their first names.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: True or false: Karen Kirsch learned the names of passengers in her cabin while working as a flight attendant for Pan Am.
questions.explain: Karen Kirsch was a flight attendant for TWA, and one passenger wrote that he would fly nothing but TWA from then on because the airline felt personalized.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: True or false: Benton Love believed that the bigger a corporation gets, the colder it becomes, and that remembering names helps warm it up.
questions.explain: Love, chairman of Texas Commerce Bancshares, said an executive who cannot remember names is operating on quicksand, because names are a significant part of the business.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: When Pullman asked what the merged company would be called, Andrew Carnegie replied: the Pullman ____ Car Company.
questions.explain: Carnegie named the new company after his rival, and Pullman’s face brightened as he invited Carnegie to talk it over. Carnegie had again remembered “the lesson of the rabbits.”

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.section: Principle: A person’s name is the sweetest and most important sound
questions.q: Principle 3 of Part Two: Remember that a person’s name is to that person the sweetest and most important ____ in any language.
questions.explain: The principle calls a name the sweetest and most important sound in any language. It sums up every example in the chapter, from Farley to Eunice.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: One of the first lessons a politician learns, according to Carnegie: To recall a voter’s name is statesmanship. To forget it is ____.
questions.explain: The full saying is “To recall a voter’s name is statesmanship. To forget it is oblivion.” Carnegie adds that the skill is almost as important in business and social life.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: Carnegie admits that remembering names takes time, but quotes Emerson: Good manners are made up of petty ____.
questions.explain: After describing Napoleon the Third’s pains to remember names, Carnegie quotes Emerson that good manners “are made up of petty sacrifices.”

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: At the General Motors cafeteria, Ken Nottingham read the scowling server’s name tag and greeted her with: Hello, ____.
questions.explain: Once he greeted her by name, she forgot the scale, piled on the ham, gave three leaves of lettuce and heaped on chips. The day before he had felt “just another sandwich to her.”

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: According to Carnegie, if you remember a person’s name and call it easily, you have paid a subtle and very effective ____.
questions.explain: Carnegie says that remembering a name is a subtle, effective compliment, while forgetting or misspelling it puts you at a sharp disadvantage.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: By writing an important person’s name down, concentrating on it and tearing up the paper, Napoleon the Third gained an ____ impression of the name as well as an ear impression.
questions.explain: Hearing the name gave him an ear impression; seeing it written gave him an eye impression as well. He did this only for people of importance, when alone.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: Which of these were part of Napoleon the Third’s technique for remembering names?
options: Saying he hadn’t got the name clearly if he didn’t hear it distinctly
Keeping a notebook of names that he reread each morning
Asking how an unusual name was spelled
Having an aide whisper each guest’s name to him
Repeating the name during the conversation and linking it to the person’s features
questions.explain: He asked again if the name was unclear, asked for the spelling of unusual names, and repeated the name while associating it with the person’s features, expression and appearance. Writing it down was done once, then the paper was torn up, not kept.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: Which of these does Carnegie give as examples of people perpetuating their names?
options: The Astor and Lenox collections at the New York Public Library
Mayors renaming city streets after themselves
Stained-glass windows in churches commemorating donors
Explorers naming mountains after their own families
Benjamin Altman and J. P. Morgan at the Metropolitan Museum
questions.explain: Carnegie says libraries, museums and churches owe much to people who cannot bear their names to perish, naming these collections and windows, as well as donor-named university buildings. Streets and mountains are not among his examples.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: Which of these did Franklin D. Roosevelt do when W. F. Chamberlain delivered his special car to the White House?
options: He asked Chamberlain to stay for his meeting with the Federal Reserve Board
He called Chamberlain by name and made him feel comfortable
He sought out the shy mechanic before leaving, called him by name and thanked him
He offered the mechanic a job maintaining the White House cars
He later sent Chamberlain an autographed photograph and a note of thanks
questions.explain: Roosevelt used Chamberlain’s name, remembered the mechanic’s name after hearing it once, and wrote afterward. He mentioned keeping the Federal Reserve Board waiting thirty minutes as his reason to get back to work, not as an invitation.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: Which of these did Jim Farley do for Franklin D. Roosevelt’s presidential campaign?
options: He wrote hundreds of letters a day to people in the western and northwestern states
He gave a speech in every state capital
He covered twenty states and twelve thousand miles in nineteen days
He hired a staff to telephone voters in each town
He sent personal letters to the people he met, signed simply “Jim”
questions.explain: Farley wrote hundreds of letters daily, toured twenty states in nineteen days by buggy, train, car and boat, and followed up with personal letters signed “Jim.” He met people at meals for heart-to-heart talks rather than giving formal speeches.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.section: Principle: A person’s name is the sweetest and most important sound
questions.q: Which of these reasons does Carnegie give for the magic contained in a person’s name?
options: It is wholly and completely owned by that person and nobody else
It sets the individual apart and makes him or her unique
People value their titles far more than their names
A request takes on special importance when made with the person’s name
Names are easy to remember once you write them down
questions.explain: Carnegie writes, “The name sets the individual apart; it makes him or her unique among all others,” and says it belongs wholly to that person and lends special importance to what we say. He never ranks titles above names.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: Put these events in Jim Farley’s life in the order Carnegie tells them.
items: His father is killed by a horse
At ten he goes to work in a brickyard
As a gypsum salesman and town clerk he builds a system for names
He manages Roosevelt’s 1932 campaign
questions.explain: Farley’s father died in 1898, leaving the ten-year-old boy to work in a brickyard. His name system grew during his years as a salesman and town clerk, and it helped him put Roosevelt in the White House in 1932.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: Put these steps of the Carnegie and Pullman story in the order they happened.
items: Both companies slash prices for the Union Pacific business
Carnegie meets Pullman at the St. Nicholas Hotel
Carnegie proposes merging their interests
Pullman asks what the new company would be called
Carnegie answers: the Pullman Palace Car Company
questions.explain: The price war was destroying profit, so Carnegie proposed a merger. Pullman was not wholly convinced until Carnegie offered to name the company after him, after which Pullman invited him to talk it over.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: Put the steps of Napoleon the Third’s name technique in the order he used them.
items: Ask for the name again if not heard distinctly
Ask how an unusual name is spelled
Repeat the name and link it to the person’s face
When alone, write it down, study it, then tear up the paper
questions.explain: He first made sure he had the name and its spelling, then repeated it during the conversation. Only afterward, alone and only for important people, did he write it down to add an eye impression.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: Put these examples in the order they appear in the chapter on remembering names.
items: Jim Farley calls fifty thousand people by first name
Sid Levy greets Nicodemus Papadoulos
Andrew Carnegie names rabbits and a steel works
Roosevelt remembers the mechanic’s name
Napoleon the Third writes names down
Ken Nottingham greets Eunice
questions.explain: Carnegie opens with Farley, moves through Levy and Andrew Carnegie, then Roosevelt and Napoleon the Third, and closes with Nottingham to show the method works for ordinary people, not only kings and executives.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: Match each person to how they used names.
pairs: Sent personal letters signed with his first name
Named a steel works after a railroad president
Wrote important names down, then tore up the paper
Offered his grandson money to take his surname
Learned the names of passengers in her cabin
questions.explain: Each figure shows a different use of names: Farley’s letters, Carnegie’s business naming, Napoleon’s memory technique, Barnum’s wish to perpetuate his name, and Kirsch’s personal service on TWA.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: Match each person to their role in the chapter on remembering names.
pairs: Delivered a special Chrysler car to the White House
General Motors employee who ate at the company cafeteria
Salesman who learned a customer’s full name
questions.explain: Love warned that executives who forget names operate on quicksand; Chamberlain described Roosevelt; Nottingham greeted Eunice; Levy greeted Papadoulos; and Thomson had a steel works named after him.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: Match each name to where Carnegie says it was honored or perpetuated.
pairs: Collections at the New York Public Library
Benjamin Altman and J. P. Morgan
The Palace Car Company formed by merger
questions.explain: The library and museum names come from donors who wanted their names remembered, while Andrew Carnegie deliberately gave the Thomson and Pullman names to a mill and a company to win cooperation.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: Match each Part Two principle number to its wording.
pairs: Become genuinely interested in other people
Remember that a person’s name is the sweetest sound to them
Be a good listener and encourage others to talk about themselves
questions.explain: Remembering names is the third of the six ways to make people like you, following genuine interest and smiling and preceding good listening.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: Sort these episodes by whether a name was used well or got wrong or neglected.

items.t: Sid Levy greets Papadoulos by his full name
Ken Nottingham says hello to Eunice
Karen Kirsch uses passengers’ names
French typists misspell a bank manager’s name
Most people just call Papadoulos Nick
An executive says he can’t remember names

questions.explain: Using names won tears of gratitude, extra ham and loyal customers. Misspelling earned a scathing rebuke, the easy nickname left Papadoulos unrecognized for fifteen years, and Benton Love says the forgetful executive is on quicksand.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: Sort these details by whether they belong to Andrew Carnegie or to Jim Farley.

items.t: Named rabbits after neighborhood children
Proposed the Pullman Palace Car Company
Called many factory workers by first name
Worked in a brickyard from age ten
Asked about the hollyhocks in the backyard
Signed thousands of letters simply Jim

questions.explain: Carnegie used names to win cooperation in business, from rabbits to the Pullman merger. Farley built a memory system for names, family and opinions that let him ask after people’s families and gardens years later.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: Sort these details by whether they describe Franklin D. Roosevelt or Napoleon the Third.

items.t: Remembered a shy mechanic’s name after hearing it once
Told the porter George to care for the suitcases
Sent an autographed photograph afterward
Asked how an unusual name was spelled
Wrote names down, then tore up the paper
Boasted he remembered everyone he met despite royal duties

questions.explain: Roosevelt, despite his workload, remembered and used names, even a mechanic’s and the porter’s. Napoleon the Third, nephew of the great Napoleon, used a deliberate technique of asking, spelling, repeating and writing names.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.section: Principle: A person’s name is the sweetest and most important sound
questions.q: Recite Principle 3 of Part Two from memory.
questions.a: Remember that a person’s name is to that person the sweetest and most important sound in any language.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: Describe Jim Farley’s system for remembering names and explain how it paid off.
questions.a: Whenever Farley met someone new, he learned the complete name and some facts about the person’s family, business and political opinions, and fixed these in mind as part of a picture. Even a year later he could shake hands, ask after the family and mention the hollyhocks in the backyard, which built him a following. Carnegie says this ability helped Farley manage Roosevelt’s 1932 campaign and put him in the White House.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: How does Andrew Carnegie’s boyhood episode with the rabbits connect to his later business success?
questions.a: As a boy he got neighborhood children to gather clover and dandelions by promising to name the bunnies after them, learning how much people value their own names. Later he used the same psychology: he named a Pittsburgh steel mill after J. Edgar Thomson to sell rails to the Pennsylvania Railroad, and won Pullman over to a merger by calling it the Pullman Palace Car Company. Carnegie calls remembering and honoring names one of the secrets of his leadership.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: Why did Nicodemus Papadoulos react so strongly when Sid Levy greeted him, and what does Carnegie draw from the story?
questions.a: Most people avoided his hard name and just called him Nick, but Levy practised it beforehand and greeted him by his full name. Papadoulos wept that in fifteen years nobody had made the effort to call him by his right name. Carnegie’s point is that taking the trouble to learn a difficult name, instead of ignoring it or substituting a nickname, shows respect people deeply feel.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: What excuse does Carnegie say people give for not remembering names, and how does the story of Roosevelt and the mechanic answer it?
questions.a: Carnegie says people fail because they don’t spend the time and energy to concentrate, repeat and fix names, and they excuse themselves as too busy. Yet Franklin D. Roosevelt, surely busier, remembered the name of a shy mechanic he had heard only once, sought him out, called him by name and thanked him. Roosevelt knew that remembering names and making people feel important was one of the simplest ways of gaining good will.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: A new coach meets twenty players at the first practice and wants to know every name by the end of it. Using Napoleon the Third’s technique, what should the coach do?
questions.a: If a name is not heard clearly, the coach should ask for it again, and ask how any unusual name is spelled. During practice the coach should repeat each name several times and associate it with the player’s features, expression and appearance. Afterward, alone, the coach could write the names down, concentrate on them and then tear up the paper, gaining an eye impression as well as an ear impression.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.section: Principle: A person’s name is the sweetest and most important sound
questions.q: Why does Carnegie say there is magic in a person’s name, and where does he say it works?
questions.a: A name is wholly and completely owned by the person we are dealing with and nobody else. It sets the individual apart and makes him or her unique among all others. Whatever information or request we bring takes on special importance when we approach the person by name. Carnegie says it works with everyone, from the waitress to the senior executive.

questions.unitTitle: If You Don’t Do This, You Are Headed for Trouble
questions.q: How does the chapter on remembering names fit into Part Two, Six Ways to Make People Like You, and what links it to the chapters around it?
questions.a: It gives the third of the six ways, following genuine interest in others and smiling and preceding being a good listener. Remembering a name is a concrete way of showing the genuine interest of the first principle, and like the later principle of making the other person feel important, it pays a person a subtle and very effective compliment. Carnegie’s Roosevelt example ties the two ideas together: remembering names and making people feel important.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: At the bridge party in An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist, what did the woman who asked about Carnegie's travels really want?
options: Advice on which European cities to visit
An interested listener so she could tell about her own trip
An introduction to Lowell Thomas
A chance to hear about Carnegie's radio work
questions.explain: Once Carnegie asked about her trip to Africa, she talked for forty-five minutes and never again asked about his travels. All she wanted was an interested listener so she could expand her ego.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: Why does Carnegie find it surprising that the botanist at the New York dinner party called him a most interesting conversationalist?
options: He had argued with the botanist about indoor gardens
He had talked mostly about his own travels
He had said hardly anything and had simply listened intently
He had left the party early without saying good night
questions.explain: Carnegie knew almost nothing about botany and said hardly anything; he had listened intently because he was genuinely interested. He calls such listening one of the highest compliments we can pay anyone.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: According to former Harvard president Charles W. Eliot, as quoted by Carnegie, what is very important in successful business intercourse?
options: A carefully prepared sales argument
Knowing more about the product than the customer
A firm handshake and a confident manner
Exclusive attention to the person who is speaking to you
questions.explain: Eliot said there is no mystery about successful business intercourse: exclusive attention to the speaker is very important, and nothing else is so flattering.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: How did the novelist Henry James describe Charles W. Eliot's way of listening?
options: As a form of activity, not mere silence
As polite silence while waiting to reply
As a habit of taking careful written notes
As a stern, piercing gaze that unsettled speakers
questions.explain: James recalled that Eliot's listening “was not mere silence, but a form of activity.” He seemed to hear with his eyes as well as his ears, and speakers felt they had had their say.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: In the story of Mrs. Henrietta Douglas and the torn coat lining, what saved the Chicago department store from losing her as a customer?
options: A written apology from the store's owner
A department manager who listened to the whole story and offered to repair, replace or refund
A discount on her next purchase at a special sale
The sales clerk changing her mind after reading the sign again
questions.explain: The clerk refused even to listen, but the manager heard the whole story, examined the coat and explained that the no-return policy did not apply to damaged goods.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: In the story of Millie Esposito, how did her son Robert say he really knew his mother loved him?
options: She told him so every evening
She cooked his favourite meals
She stopped whatever she was doing and listened whenever he wanted to talk
She never criticized his decisions
questions.explain: Robert said he knew she loved him because whenever he wanted to talk she stopped what she was doing and listened. Carnegie uses this to show listening matters at home as much as in business.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: How many times did the New York Telephone Company troubleshooter interview the furious customer before closing the case?
options: Once
Twice
Three times
Four times
questions.explain: The troubleshooter listened for nearly three hours at the first visit and went back for more; the disputed point was not even raised until the fourth interview, when he closed the case completely.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: Why did Julian F. Detmer tell the angry customer that he would wipe the disputed charge off the books?
options: Because the customer was a careful man with one account, while Detmer's clerks had to look after thousands
Because the sum was too small to be worth collecting
Because the credit department had already admitted its mistake
Because the customer had threatened to sue the company
questions.explain: Detmer reasoned that a careful man with only one account was less likely to be wrong than clerks handling thousands. In fact Detmer believed the customer was wrong, but he let him talk himself out first.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: How, according to Carnegie, did Edward Bok get his start as a young Western Union office boy?
options: By taking night classes paid for by his employer
By writing to famous people and asking them to tell him more about their own lives
By publishing a magazine of his own at fourteen
By working his way up through the bakery where he washed windows
questions.explain: Bok read the lives of famous people in an encyclopedia of American biography and wrote asking about their childhoods. Carnegie says he was a good listener who asked famous people to tell him more about themselves.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: During the Civil War, what did Lincoln actually want from the old friend he called to the White House from Springfield?
options: Expert advice on the proclamation freeing the slaves
Help answering letters from newspaper critics
A friendly, sympathetic listener to whom he could unburden himself
A report on public opinion in Illinois
questions.explain: Lincoln talked for hours and sent his friend home without even asking his opinion. He had not wanted advice, only a sympathetic listener, which Carnegie says is what we all want when we are in trouble.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.section: Principle: Be a good listener. Encourage others to talk about themselves
questions.q: At a wedding you are seated beside a stranger who mentions she restores old clocks. Following Carnegie's advice for becoming a good conversationalist, what should you do?
options: Tell her about your own hobbies so she knows you are interesting
Change the subject to something everyone at the table knows
Correct anything she says that sounds doubtful
Ask questions she will enjoy answering and encourage her to talk about her work
questions.explain: Carnegie's advice is to be interested rather than try to be interesting: ask questions others will enjoy answering and encourage them to talk about themselves and their accomplishments.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.section: Principle: Be a good listener. Encourage others to talk about themselves
questions.q: What point is Carnegie making when he says a person's toothache means more to that person than a famine in China which kills a million people?
options: People are far more interested in themselves and their own problems than in you and yours
People are naturally cruel and indifferent to suffering
Small problems should be solved before large ones
Conversations should avoid serious world events
questions.explain: He uses the toothache and the boil on the neck to remind readers that the people they talk to are a hundred times more interested in themselves than in anyone else, so conversation should centre on them.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: What does the title An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist signal about the chapter's message?
options: Good conversation depends on a wide stock of interesting stories
The easy way to be thought a good talker is to be a good listener
Conversation is a talent some people are simply born with
Good conversationalists learn to steer talk toward their own expertise
questions.explain: The easy way turns out to be listening: Carnegie was thought a good conversationalist when in reality he had been merely a good listener who encouraged the other man to talk.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: Carnegie says the furious telephone customer really wanted a feeling of importance. Which earlier idea in the book does this echo?
options: The power of a smile from Chapter 2.2
The value of remembering names from Chapter 2.3
The deep human desire to be important from Chapter 1.2, The Big Secret of Dealing with People
Admitting your own mistakes from Chapter 3.3
questions.explain: Part One's chapter on the big secret of dealing with people stresses the desire for a feeling of importance. Here the kicker got that feeling by complaining, until a listener gave it to him instead.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: True or false: Carnegie says he knew no more about botany than he knew about the anatomy of a penguin.
questions.explain: He admits he could not have said anything about botany without changing the subject; his only contribution was listening intently.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: True or false: Mrs. Henrietta Douglas had bought her damaged coat at a department store in New York.
questions.explain: The store was in Chicago, and Mrs. Douglas had taken Carnegie's course there. She had bought the coat at a special sale.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: True or false: When the young Edward Bok wrote to General Grant about a certain battle, Grant drew him a map and invited him to dinner.
questions.explain: Grant drew a map for the fourteen-year-old and spent an evening talking with him, one of many famous people who answered Bok's questions about themselves.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: True or false: After talking for hours with his old Springfield neighbour, Lincoln finally asked for his opinion on freeing the slaves.
questions.explain: Lincoln sent his friend back to Illinois without even asking his opinion. He had done all the talking himself, and that seemed to clarify his mind.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: True or false: Isaac F. Marcosson reported that very important people told him they prefer good talkers to good listeners.
questions.explain: Marcosson said the reverse: important people prefer good listeners to good talkers, yet the ability to listen seems rarer than almost any other good trait.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: True or false: Be a good listener. Encourage others to talk about themselves is the fourth of the six ways to make people like you in Part Two.
questions.explain: It is Principle 4 of Part Two, coming after remembering names and before talking in terms of the other person's interests.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.section: Principle: Be a good listener. Encourage others to talk about themselves
questions.q: Carnegie's short rule for good conversation: to be interesting, be ____.
questions.explain: Carnegie tells the aspiring conversationalist to be an attentive listener, because interest in others is what makes us interesting to them.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: Jack Woodford, quoted by Carnegie, wrote that few human beings are proof against the implied flattery of rapt ____.
questions.explain: Carnegie quotes Strangers in Love to explain why the botanist was so pleased: “few human beings are proof against the implied flattery of rapt attention.”

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.section: Principle: Be a good listener. Encourage others to talk about themselves
questions.q: Dr. Nicholas Murray Butler of Columbia University said that those people who think only of themselves are hopelessly ____.
questions.explain: Butler added that such people are not educated no matter how instructed they may be. Carnegie links this to bores who talk only of themselves.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: Carnegie quotes the Reader's Digest: many persons call a doctor when all they want is an ____.
questions.explain: The quotation shows that ordinary people, not just celebrities, crave a good listener.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: The once-furious telephone customer started an organization he called the Telephone Subscribers' Protective ____.
questions.explain: The troubleshooter became a charter member of it during his visits, and believed he and its founder were its only members.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.section: Principle: Be a good listener. Encourage others to talk about themselves
questions.q: Principle 4 of Part Two reads: Be a good ____. Encourage others to talk about themselves.
questions.explain: The chapter closes on this principle after showing that Carnegie was thought a good conversationalist when he had merely been a good listener.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: Carnegie says the raging telephone customer, who saw himself as a holy crusader, really wanted a feeling of ____.
questions.explain: He got that feeling first by kicking and complaining; once a company representative gave it to him, his imagined grievances vanished.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: After leaving school at thirteen, Edward Bok became an office boy for ____.
questions.explain: Even as a Western Union messenger boy he refused to give up on education and began educating himself.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.section: Principle: Be a good listener. Encourage others to talk about themselves
questions.q: Which of these are part of Carnegie's recipe for making people shun you and laugh at you behind your back?
options: Never listen to anyone for long
Ask people too many questions
Talk incessantly about yourself
Interrupt in the middle of a sentence when you have an idea
Praise people too lavishly
questions.explain: The recipe is to never listen long, talk about yourself constantly and bust in mid-sentence. Asking questions and praising generously are what Carnegie recommends, not what he warns against.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: Which of these did the sales clerk do when Mrs. Henrietta Douglas tried to return her coat with a torn lining?
options: Refused even to listen to her complaint
Pointed to a sign saying all sales are final
Told her to sew up the lining herself
Offered to replace the lining
Called the department manager over
questions.explain: The clerk would not listen, pointed to the sign and told her to sew it herself. The offer to repair or replace came from the manager, who happened to arrive on her own.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: Which of these famous people does Carnegie name among those the young Edward Bok corresponded with?
options: Ralph Waldo Emerson
Louisa May Alcott
Mark Twain
Mrs. Abraham Lincoln
Thomas Edison
questions.explain: Carnegie lists Emerson, Oliver Wendell Holmes, Longfellow, Mrs. Abraham Lincoln, Louisa May Alcott, General Sherman and Jefferson Davis. Twain and Edison are not on his list.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: Which of these did Julian F. Detmer do after letting the angry customer talk himself out?
options: Thanked him for coming to Chicago to tell him about the problem
Insisted that the credit department was right
Wiped the charge off the books
Recommended some other woolen houses
Refused to see him again
questions.explain: Detmer thanked him, cancelled the charge and even recommended competitors. He did not defend his credit department, though he believed the customer was wrong.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: Which of these people does Carnegie say frequently want nothing more than a sympathetic listener, as Lincoln did?
options: The irritated customer
The dissatisfied employee
The hurt friend
The famous author on tour
The confident salesman
questions.explain: After the Lincoln story Carnegie says a sympathetic listener is what we all want in trouble, and frequently all the irritated customer, the dissatisfied employee or the hurt friend wants.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.section: Principle: Be a good listener. Encourage others to talk about themselves
questions.q: Which of these does Carnegie advise for anyone who aspires to be a good conversationalist?
options: Prepare a few good stories in advance
Ask questions that other persons will enjoy answering
Encourage others to talk about themselves and their accomplishments
Correct mistakes so the conversation stays accurate
Be an attentive listener
questions.explain: His advice is to be an attentive listener, ask questions others enjoy answering and get them talking about themselves. Preparing stories and correcting people keep the focus on yourself.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: Put these events at Carnegie's bridge party in the order they happened.
items: The woman asks Carnegie to tell her about his travels
She mentions a recent trip to Africa
Carnegie asks her to tell him about Africa
She talks for forty-five minutes without asking about his travels again
questions.explain: The woman began by asking about Carnegie's travels, but one question about her own trip turned the whole conversation to her.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: Put these stages of the New York Telephone Company story in order.
items: The customer curses, refuses to pay and files complaints and lawsuits
A troubleshooter listens to him rave for nearly three hours
The troubleshooter joins the customer's new subscribers' association
At the fourth interview the bills are paid and the complaints withdrawn
questions.explain: The troubleshooter did not even mention his errand on the first three visits; patient listening made the customer almost friendly, and the case closed on the fourth.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: Put these events of the Detmer Woolen Company story in order.
items: The customer travels to Chicago refusing to pay or ever buy again
Detmer lets him talk himself out
Detmer thanks him and cancels the charge
They have lunch and the customer places his largest order yet
The customer finds a mislaid bill and sends a check with apologies
questions.explain: Listening came first; only when the customer simmered down did Detmer speak, and the goodwill that followed led to a bigger order and a voluntary payment.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: Put these stages of Edward Bok's early life in the order Carnegie tells them.
items: Washing bakery windows and gathering coal from the gutter
Leaving school at thirteen to work for Western Union
Buying an encyclopedia of American biography
Writing to famous people about their lives
Visiting famous people as a welcome guest in their homes
questions.explain: Carnegie traces Bok from poverty to friendships with the famous, and says all of it came from the principles of this chapter.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: Match each person to the way of listening Carnegie describes.
pairs: Seemed to hear with his eyes as well as his ears
Mild, genial eyes and extraordinary concentrated attention
Talked for hours and wanted only a sympathetic listener
Stopped whatever she was doing when her son wanted to talk
questions.explain: Eliot and Freud are models of active, attentive listening; Lincoln shows what a troubled person wants; Mrs. Esposito shows listening at home.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: Match each source to the idea Carnegie quotes from it.
pairs: Few people can resist the implied flattery of rapt attention
People fail to impress because they think about what to say next
Those who think only of themselves are hopelessly uneducated
Many people call a doctor when they just want an audience
questions.explain: Each quotation supports one side of the chapter's case: that attentive listening flatters, and self-absorption repels.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: Match each story to its outcome.
pairs: Gave his son the middle name Detmer
Withdrew his complaints from the Public Service Commission
Was offered repair, replacement or her money back
The botanist at the dinner party
Praised Carnegie as a most interesting conversationalist
questions.explain: In every case it was being listened to, not argued with or talked at, that changed the other person's attitude.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: Match each number in Part Two, Six Ways to Make People Like You, to its principle.
pairs: Become genuinely interested in other people
Remember that a person's name is the sweetest sound to them
Be a good listener and encourage others to talk about themselves
Talk in terms of the other person's interests
questions.explain: Listening sits between remembering names and talking in terms of the other person's interests, all of them ways of turning attention toward the other person.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.section: Principle: Be a good listener. Encourage others to talk about themselves
questions.q: Sort each behaviour into what Carnegie presents as good listening or poor listening.

items.t: Giving exclusive attention to the speaker
Letting a complainer talk himself out
Asking questions the other person enjoys answering
Sympathizing with each point a critic makes
Interrupting in the middle of a sentence
Contradicting customers
Thinking about what to say next
Talking incessantly about yourself

questions.explain: Carnegie's examples of good listening all keep the focus on the speaker; the poor habits, from rude clerks to self-absorbed bores, keep it on oneself.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: Sort each action into the telephone company troubleshooter's story or Julian Detmer's story.

items.t: Listened for nearly three hours on the first visit
Became a charter member of the customer's association
Raised the disputed point only at the fourth interview
Thanked the customer for coming to Chicago
Cancelled the disputed charge
Invited the customer to lunch

questions.explain: Both men let an angry customer pour out his grievance before saying anything about the dispute, and both turned an enemy into a loyal customer.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: Sort these details of Edward Bok's life into his humble beginnings or what his listening brought him.

items.t: Washed bakery windows after school
Collected stray coal from the gutter
Had no more than six years of schooling
Corresponded with Emerson and Longfellow
Spent an evening with General Grant
Stayed as a welcome guest in famous homes

questions.explain: Carnegie contrasts Bok's poverty with the confidence, vision and ambition he gained by asking famous people to talk about themselves.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: Sort each action into what the sales clerk did or what the department manager did with Mrs. Henrietta Douglas.

items.t: Refused to listen to the complaint
Pointed to the all sales are final sign
Told her to sew up the lining herself
Listened attentively to the whole story
Examined the coat
Said the no-return policy did not cover damaged goods

questions.explain: The same store nearly lost and then kept a long-term customer, and the difference was whether anyone listened.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: Explain how Carnegie came to be called a most interesting conversationalist by the botanist, and what lesson he draws from it.
questions.a: Carnegie knew nothing about botany and said hardly anything; he simply listened intently all evening because he was genuinely interested, and praised the botanist sincerely. The botanist felt that attention and was pleased by it. Carnegie concludes that he was thought a good conversationalist when in reality he had been merely a good listener who encouraged the other man to talk.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: What does Henry James's description of Charles W. Eliot teach about what real listening involves?
questions.a: Eliot's listening was not mere silence but a form of activity. He sat still, faced the speaker, seemed to hear with his eyes as well as his ears, and considered what was said while it was being said. As a result, people who talked to him felt they had had their say.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: Why does Carnegie criticize department store owners who hire clerks who are poor listeners?
questions.a: Such owners spend heavily on space, goods, window displays and advertising, then hire clerks who interrupt, contradict and irritate customers until they all but drive them away. The Chicago store nearly lost a customer who spent thousands a year because a clerk would not listen, and only a manager who listened kept her.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: Why did the furious telephone customer's grievances vanish after the troubleshooter's visits?
questions.a: He saw himself as a crusader for public rights, but what he really wanted was a feeling of importance, which he had been getting by kicking and complaining. The troubleshooter listened for hours and sympathized with every point. Once he got his feeling of importance from a company representative, his imagined grievances vanished, he paid his bills and he withdrew his complaints.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: How did listening turn Julian Detmer's angry customer into a friend for life?
questions.a: Detmer resisted the urge to interrupt and let the man talk himself out, then thanked him for coming, cancelled the charge and said he would feel the same in his shoes. Disarmed, the customer accepted lunch, placed his largest order ever, later found and paid the mislaid bill, named his son after Detmer and stayed a customer until his death twenty-two years later.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: According to Carnegie, how did the principle of listening give Edward Bok his start?
questions.a: Bok, a poor boy with six years of schooling, bought an encyclopedia of American biography and wrote to famous people asking them to tell him more about themselves. They answered, and some, such as Grant, invited him in. Carnegie says these friendships gave him confidence, vision and ambition, all made possible by being a good listener.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: What does the story of Lincoln and his old Springfield friend show about what people in trouble want?
questions.a: Lincoln talked for hours about freeing the slaves and sent his friend home without asking his opinion; the talk clarified his mind and he felt easier. He did not want advice, only a friendly, sympathetic listener. Carnegie says this is what we all want in trouble, and often all an irritated customer, dissatisfied employee or hurt friend wants.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.section: Principle: Be a good listener. Encourage others to talk about themselves
questions.q: Why does Carnegie say that people who talk only of themselves fail as conversationalists, and what should you do instead?
questions.a: People who talk only of themselves think only of themselves; they are bores drunk with their own importance, and Butler called them hopelessly uneducated. Since others are a hundred times more interested in themselves than in you, Carnegie says to be interested rather than interesting: listen attentively, ask questions they enjoy answering and encourage them to talk about themselves and their accomplishments.

questions.unitTitle: An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist
questions.q: How does this chapter on listening fit among the other ways to make people like you in Part Two?
questions.a: It is Principle 4, following genuine interest in others, smiling and remembering names, and preceding talking in terms of the other person's interests. Listening puts the earlier principle of genuine interest into practice in conversation. It also draws on Part One's idea that people crave a feeling of importance, which a good listener gives them.

questions.unitTitle: How to Interest People
questions.q: In How to Interest People, how did Theodore Roosevelt manage to know what to say to every kind of visitor, from cowboys to diplomats?
options: He asked each guest to talk about themselves at length
He kept a card index of every guest’s family details
He sat up late the night before reading up on the guest’s favourite subject
He had a secretary brief him on each guest at the door
questions.explain: Whenever Roosevelt expected a visitor, he read late into the previous night on the subject he knew the guest cared about most. The point is preparation on the guest’s interest, not simply inviting the guest to talk.

questions.unitTitle: How to Interest People
questions.q: In How to Interest People, what did William Lyon Phelps’s aunt reveal about the visitor who had talked to the eight-year-old Phelps about boats?
options: He was a New York lawyer who cared nothing about boats
He was a sea captain who loved talking to children
He was a boat builder hoping to sell to the family
He was a Yale professor who later taught Phelps
questions.explain: The aunt explained he was a New York lawyer with not the slightest interest in boats; he talked about them because he saw the boy was interested. “He made himself agreeable.”

questions.unitTitle: How to Interest People
questions.q: In How to Interest People, what was the first thing Edward L. Chalif asked for when he entered the corporation president’s office?
options: Money for one Scout’s trip to the European jamboree
A tour of the company’s headquarters
A letter of introduction to the branch presidents
To see the framed check for a million dollars
questions.explain: Chalif had heard the president had framed a cancelled million-dollar check, so he asked to see it and to hear how it came to be drawn. He did not raise the trip until the president asked why he had come.

questions.unitTitle: How to Interest People
questions.section: Principle: Talk in terms of the other person’s interests
questions.q: In How to Interest People, what turned out to be the passion of the hotel manager whom Henry G. Duvernoy had been trying to sell bread to?
options: Collecting rare cookbooks
The Hotel Greeters of America
Yachting on Long Island Sound
Raising money for the Boy Scouts
questions.explain: The manager was president of the Hotel Greeters of America and of the International Greeters, and attended every convention. Duvernoy saw “this society was not only his hobby, it was the passion of his life.”

questions.unitTitle: How to Interest People
questions.section: Principle: Talk in terms of the other person’s interests
questions.q: In How to Interest People, before he could meet R. J. Funkhouser, whose interests did Edward E. Harriman study first?
options: Funkhouser’s stern, long-serving secretary
Funkhouser’s business partners
Funkhouser’s grown children
The mayor of Hagerstown
questions.explain: Funkhouser shielded himself from job seekers with a dedicated secretary, so Harriman studied her interests and goals and talked about her part in Funkhouser’s success; she then arranged the meeting.

questions.unitTitle: How to Interest People
questions.q: Where does How to Interest People (Principle 5) sit within Part Two, Six Ways to Make People Like You?
options: It opens Part Two, before the principle about smiling
It follows the chapter on being a good listener and precedes the one on making the other person feel important
It closes Part Two, after the chapter on making the other person feel important
It comes between the chapters on smiling and on remembering names
questions.explain: Part Two runs from becoming genuinely interested in others, through smiling, names and listening, to talking in terms of the other person’s interests, and ends with making the other person feel important. Principle 5 builds on listening by choosing what to talk about.

questions.unitTitle: How to Interest People
questions.section: Principle: Talk in terms of the other person’s interests
questions.q: True or false: In How to Interest People, Henry G. Duvernoy called on the hotel manager every week for four years without getting the business.
questions.explain: Duvernoy called weekly for four years, went to the manager’s social affairs and even lived in the hotel, but failed until he found out what interested the man.
