questions.unitTitle: How to Interest People
questions.q: True or false: In How to Interest People, Edward L. Chalif asked the corporation president to pay for five Scouts to go to the European jamboree.
questions.explain: Chalif asked for only one boy. The president, warmed up by talk of his framed check, sent five boys and Chalif himself, and added much more.

questions.unitTitle: How to Interest People
questions.q: Carnegie says Roosevelt knew, as all leaders know, that the royal road to a person’s heart is to talk about the things he or she ____ most.
questions.explain: The line comes right after the Roosevelt story: “the royal road to a person’s heart is to talk about the things he or she treasures most.”

questions.unitTitle: How to Interest People
questions.q: In How to Interest People, Phelps’s aunt said the visitor talked about boats all evening because he is a ____.
questions.explain: The aunt answered that he was a gentleman: he saw the boy liked boats and talked about what would interest and please him. Phelps said he never forgot the remark.

questions.unitTitle: How to Interest People
questions.section: Principle: Talk in terms of the other person’s interests
questions.q: In How to Interest People, the hotel manager Duvernoy courted was president of a society called the Hotel ____ of America.
questions.explain: The manager headed the Hotel Greeters of America and the International Greeters. Talking about the Greeters won Duvernoy a half-hour of enthusiasm and, days later, the order.

questions.unitTitle: How to Interest People
questions.section: Principle: Talk in terms of the other person’s interests
questions.q: Principle 5 of Part Two reads: Talk in terms of the other person’s ____.
questions.explain: The chapter closes with Principle 5: talk in terms of the other person’s interests. Every story in the chapter shows someone succeeding by doing just that.

questions.unitTitle: How to Interest People
questions.section: Principle: Talk in terms of the other person’s interests
questions.q: Which of these did Henry G. Duvernoy do during his four years of failing to sell bread to the hotel manager, before he changed his tactics?
options: Called on the manager every week
Went to the social affairs the manager attended
Took rooms in the hotel and lived there
Talked to the manager about the Hotel Greeters
Joined the manager’s society as a member
questions.explain: Weekly calls, attending the same social events and living in the hotel were his old tactics, and all failed. Talking about the Greeters and being sold a membership came only after he decided to find out what interested the man.

questions.unitTitle: How to Interest People
questions.q: Which of these did the corporation president give Edward L. Chalif beyond the single Scout’s trip he asked for?
options: A trip for five boys and Chalif himself
A copy of the framed million-dollar check
A letter of credit for a thousand dollars
Letters of introduction to his branch presidents
A seat on the company’s board
questions.explain: The president sent five boys and Chalif, gave a thousand-dollar letter of credit for seven weeks in Europe and letters to his branch presidents; he even met them in Paris. Nothing was given to Chalif from the check itself.

questions.unitTitle: How to Interest People
questions.q: Put the events of Edward L. Chalif’s story in How to Interest People in the order they happened.
items: Chalif hears the president has framed a million-dollar check
Chalif asks to see the check and hear how it was drawn
The president asks what Chalif came to see him about
The president sends five boys and Chalif to Europe
questions.explain: Chalif learned of the check first, opened by admiring it, and stated his request only when the president asked. The result was far more than he had asked for.

questions.unitTitle: How to Interest People
questions.q: Put the six principles of Part Two, Six Ways to Make People Like You, in the order Carnegie presents them.
items: Become genuinely interested in other people
Smile
Remember a person’s name
Be a good listener
Talk in terms of the other person’s interests
Make the other person feel important
questions.explain: How to Interest People gives Principle 5, after listening and before the closing principle on making the other person feel important, sincerely.

questions.unitTitle: How to Interest People
questions.section: Principle: Talk in terms of the other person’s interests
questions.q: In How to Interest People, match each person to how they used someone else’s interests.
pairs: Read late the night before on a guest’s favourite subject
Talked about boats to an eight-year-old who loved them
Studied a stern secretary’s goals to reach her employer
questions.explain: Each example shows the same move: find out what the other person cares about and talk about that first. The requests, if any, came afterward.

questions.unitTitle: How to Interest People
questions.section: Principle: Talk in terms of the other person’s interests
questions.q: In How to Interest People, match each person to the result of talking in terms of another’s interests.
pairs: The hotel steward phoned asking for samples and prices
Hired at once and prospered for over twenty years
Five boys sent to Europe for seven weeks
An enlargement of his life with each conversation
questions.explain: The results range from sales and jobs to Herzig’s personal reward. Carnegie concludes that this principle “pays off for both parties.”

questions.unitTitle: How to Interest People
questions.section: Principle: Talk in terms of the other person’s interests
questions.q: In How to Interest People, sort Henry G. Duvernoy’s actions by whether they came before or after he resolved to change his tactics.

items.t: Calling on the manager every week
Attending the manager’s social affairs
Living in the hotel to get the business
Finding out what caught the manager’s enthusiasm
Talking about the Hotel Greeters
Being sold a membership in the Greeters

questions.explain: The old tactics were persistence aimed at his own goal; after studying human relations he turned to the manager’s passion and said nothing about bread.

questions.unitTitle: How to Interest People
questions.q: In How to Interest People, sort these topics by whether Edward L. Chalif opened his meeting with them or held them back until asked.

items.t: The framed million-dollar check
How the check came to be drawn
The Boy Scouts
The jamboree in Europe
The favour he wanted

questions.explain: Carnegie stresses that Chalif did not begin with the Scouts, the jamboree or his request: “He talked in terms of what interested the other man.”

questions.unitTitle: How to Interest People
questions.q: In How to Interest People, what lesson did William Lyon Phelps take from his aunt’s explanation of the visitor who talked about boats?
questions.a: The visitor, a New York lawyer, cared nothing about boats but talked about them because he saw the boy was interested; his aunt called this the mark of a gentleman who “made himself agreeable.” Phelps learned that you please people by talking about what interests them, not you, and he never forgot the remark.

questions.unitTitle: How to Interest People
questions.q: In How to Interest People, why does Carnegie point out what Edward L. Chalif did not talk about at the start of his meeting with the corporation president?
questions.a: Chalif did not begin with the Boy Scouts, the jamboree or his request; he began with the president’s framed million-dollar check. Carnegie highlights this to show he talked in terms of the other man’s interests, and Chalif himself said that without warming the man up first he would not have found him one-tenth as easy to approach. The president then gave far more than was asked.

questions.unitTitle: How to Interest People
questions.section: Principle: Talk in terms of the other person’s interests
questions.q: In How to Interest People, how did Edward E. Harriman use other people’s interests to get a job with R. J. Funkhouser?
questions.a: Harriman found that Funkhouser’s main interest was power and money, and that a stern secretary guarded him, so he studied her interests too and talked with her about her part in his success; she arranged a meeting. With Funkhouser he did not ask for a job but said he could make money for him and explained how his ideas would serve Funkhouser’s success. He was hired at once and both prospered for over twenty years.

questions.unitTitle: How to Interest People
questions.section: Principle: Talk in terms of the other person’s interests
questions.q: In How to Interest People, what does the example of Howard Z. Herzig add to Carnegie’s case for talking in terms of the other person’s interests?
questions.a: Herzig shows that the principle benefits the one who practises it, not only the listener. Asked about his reward, he said each person gave a different reward, but in general it was “an enlargement of his life each time he spoke to someone.” Carnegie uses this to conclude that the principle pays off for both parties.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: In the post office story in How to Make People Like You Instantly, what did Carnegie praise about the bored clerk?
options: His head of hair
His speed at weighing envelopes
His neat handwriting on receipts
His patience with the long queue
questions.explain: Carnegie looked for something he could honestly admire and told the clerk, “I certainly wish I had your head of hair.” He praised nothing about the clerk's work.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: In the post office story, what question did Carnegie ask himself before speaking to the clerk?
options: What does this clerk want from his job?
How can I get served faster today?
What is there about him that I can honestly admire?
What do we have in common that we could talk about?
questions.explain: To make the clerk like him, Carnegie knew he must say something nice about the clerk, not about himself, so he asked what he could honestly admire. He admits this is sometimes hard with strangers.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: When a listener asked Carnegie what he wanted to get out of the post office clerk, what did Carnegie say he actually got?
options: Faster service whenever he came back
A friend who later did him a favour
A good story to use in his lectures
The feeling of having done something for him with nothing possible in return
questions.explain: Carnegie says he wanted something priceless and got it: the feeling that he had done something for the clerk without the clerk being able to do anything in return. He scorns the idea of praising people only to get something.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.section: Principle: Make the other person feel important—and do it sincerely
questions.q: In How to Make People Like You Instantly, what does Carnegie call the one all-important law of human conduct?
options: Never criticize anyone in public
Always let the other person do most of the talking
Always make the other person feel important
Always remember the other person's name
questions.explain: The law is “Always make the other person feel important.” Carnegie claims that obeying it brings countless friends and constant happiness, while breaking it brings endless trouble.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.section: Principle: Make the other person feel important—and do it sincerely
questions.q: In How to Make People Like You Instantly, who is quoted as saying that the deepest principle in human nature is the craving to be appreciated?
options: John Dewey
William James
Charles Schwab
Ralph Waldo Emerson
questions.explain: William James spoke of the craving to be appreciated. John Dewey is the one who called the desire to be important the deepest urge in human nature.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.section: Principle: Make the other person feel important—and do it sincerely
questions.q: According to How to Make People Like You Instantly, how did Jesus sum up the one important precept that philosophers had arrived at?
options: Every man I meet is my superior in some way
Talk to people about themselves
Be hearty in your approbation and lavish in your praise
Do unto others as you would have others do unto you
questions.explain: Carnegie calls it probably the most important rule in the world: “Do unto others as you would have others do unto you.” He then urges readers to obey this Golden Rule.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: In the charity concert story, why did David G. Smith hand the cash box to Rose?
options: He saw the box as a symbol of authority and gave her a role that mattered
She was the only helper who knew how to count change
The committee member had told him she must handle the money
He wanted to keep his own hands free to serve drinks
questions.explain: Two elderly ladies each thought they were in charge, so Smith gave Rose the cash box, a symbol of authority of sorts, and put Jane in charge of the teenagers at the soda machine. Both felt important and the evening went happily.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: A diner is served tea when he ordered coffee. Following Carnegie's mashed potatoes example in How to Make People Like You Instantly, what should he say?
options: Point out the mistake firmly so it does not happen again
Drink the tea to avoid making a fuss
Say he is sorry to trouble the server but he would prefer coffee
Ask to speak to the manager about the error
questions.explain: Carnegie advises saying “I’m sorry to trouble you, but I prefer French fried.” because such courtesy shows respect for the server, who will then be glad to change the order.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: In How to Make People Like You Instantly, what was the turning point in Hall Caine's life?
options: Winning a scholarship that ended his blacksmith's apprenticeship
Writing a lecture praising Rossetti, who then made him his secretary
Selling his first novel, The Christian, to a London publisher
Meeting Rossetti by chance on the Isle of Man
questions.explain: Caine sent Rossetti a lecture praising his artistic achievement, and the delighted Rossetti invited him to London as his secretary. There Caine met the literary artists of the day, which launched his career.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: After the shy student Chris was invited into the advanced class, what did his teacher Ronald J. Rowland do to remember the lesson?
options: He opened the advanced class to every beginner
He wrote Chris a letter of thanks
He started praising one student at the start of each lesson
He hung a sign reading you are important at the front of the classroom
questions.explain: Rowland made a sign reading “you are important” to remind himself that each student he faced was equally important. Chris had taught him our deep desire to feel important.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.section: Principle: Make the other person feel important—and do it sincerely
questions.q: You are introduced to a new neighbour who is a retired bus driver. Which approach best follows Carnegie's point about Emerson's saying that every man is his superior in some way?
options: Tell him about your own career so he knows who you are
Find something he knows or does better than you and sincerely show you recognise it
Avoid personal topics until you know him well
Praise him warmly whether or not you mean it
questions.explain: Carnegie says almost everyone feels superior to you in some way, and a sure way to their hearts is to let them see, subtly and sincerely, that you recognise their importance. Insincere praise fails the sincerity he insists on.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.section: Principle: Make the other person feel important—and do it sincerely
questions.q: Why does Carnegie quote Shakespeare's lines about proud man dressed in a little brief authority in How to Make People Like You Instantly?
options: To show that those with least justification for feeling important often bolster their egos with conceit
To warn readers never to accept positions of authority
To prove that kings have always craved flattery
To show that the Golden Rule appears in English literature
questions.explain: Carnegie calls it pathetic that those with the least justification for a feeling of achievement often prop up their egos with a nauseating show of tumult and conceit. The quotation illustrates that craving, not a ban on authority.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: In the story of the Connecticut attorney Mr. R——, what did he first admire when talking with his wife's elderly aunt?
options: Her Packard car
Her paisley shawls
Her house, built about 1890
Her garden
questions.explain: He looked around for something he could honestly admire and asked whether the house was built about 1890, saying it reminded him of the house he was born in. The treasures and the Packard came later.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: According to Carnegie, why did the elderly aunt insist on giving Mr. R—— her cherished Packard?
options: She wanted to stop her relatives from selling it
She could no longer afford to keep it
She hoped he would give her legal advice for free
She was starving for recognition and he gave her genuine appreciation
questions.explain: Carnegie says the lonely lady was “starving for a little recognition” and no one gave her any. When Mr. R—— appreciated her home, her gratitude could express itself only through the gift of the car.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: In Donald M. McMahon's landscaping story, what did McMahon praise that led the judge to give him a puppy?
options: The judge's rhododendrons and azaleas
The judge's dogs and the blue ribbons they won
The judge's career on the bench
The judge's large estate
questions.explain: McMahon told the judge he had a lovely hobby and admired his prize-winning dogs. The judge spent over an hour showing him the kennel and then gave his son a puppy.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: Before James Adamson met George Eastman, what did the architect warn him about?
options: He would not stand a chance if he took more than five minutes of Eastman's time
Eastman disliked salesmen who praised his buildings
Eastman had already chosen another seating company
Eastman would only discuss prices in writing
questions.explain: The architect said Eastman was a strict, very busy disciplinarian, so Adamson should tell his story quickly and get out. Instead, by admiring the office, Adamson ended up talking for hours and lunching with him.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: How to Make People Like You Instantly is the last chapter of Part Two. Which chapter comes immediately after it?
options: How to Interest People
The Big Secret of Dealing with People
If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin
You Can't Win an Argument
questions.explain: Part Two, Six Ways to Make People Like You, ends with this chapter. Part Three, How to Win People to Your Way of Thinking, opens with You Can't Win an Argument.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: True or false: Carnegie admits that he did want something out of the post office clerk.
questions.explain: He says he wanted something priceless and got it: the feeling of having done something for the clerk that the clerk could not repay. What he did not want was any material return.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.section: Principle: Make the other person feel important—and do it sincerely
questions.q: True or false: In How to Make People Like You Instantly, Carnegie says Zoroaster taught the great precept of human relations in China.
questions.explain: Carnegie says Zoroaster taught it in Persia twenty-five hundred years ago. It was Confucius who preached it in China.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: True or false: The chairs that George Eastman proudly showed James Adamson were ones he had bought in Italy and painted himself.
questions.explain: Eastman bought the chairs in Japan and repainted them after the sun peeled the paint. They were worth only a few dollars, but he was proud because he had painted them himself.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: True or false: Hall Caine had no more than eight years' schooling, yet he died the richest literary man of his time.
questions.explain: Carnegie stresses that Caine was a blacksmith's son with little schooling. He suggests Caine might have died poor and unknown had he not written an essay admiring a famous man.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: True or false: Mr. R—— gladly accepted the aunt's Packard because he did not own a car.
questions.explain: Mr. R—— had a new car and tried to refuse, suggesting her relatives or a secondhand dealer. He accepted only because he could not refuse without hurting her feelings.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.section: Principle: Make the other person feel important—and do it sincerely
questions.q: True or false: In How to Make People Like You Instantly, Disraeli is quoted as saying that if you talk to people about themselves, they will listen for hours.
questions.explain: Carnegie closes the chapter with Disraeli, one of the shrewdest men who ever ruled the British Empire: “Talk to people about themselves,” and they will listen for hours.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: True or false: After the theater-seat story, George Eastman and James Adamson remained close friends until Eastman's death.
questions.explain: Carnegie leaves the reader to guess who got the $90,000 order, then adds that the two men were close friends from then until Eastman's death.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.section: Principle: Make the other person feel important—and do it sincerely
questions.q: Carnegie's all-important law of human conduct is: Always make the other person feel ____.
questions.explain: Carnegie claims this law, if obeyed, brings countless friends and constant happiness. It rests on the desire to be important that he calls the deepest urge in human nature.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.section: Principle: Make the other person feel important—and do it sincerely
questions.q: Principle 6 of Part Two reads: Make the other person feel important—and do it ____.
questions.explain: The word sincerely matters because Carnegie says people do not want cheap, insincere flattery but crave sincere appreciation.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.section: Principle: Make the other person feel important—and do it sincerely
questions.q: William James said that the deepest principle in human nature is the craving to be ____.
questions.explain: Carnegie pairs this with John Dewey's view that the desire to be important is the deepest urge in human nature.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.section: Principle: Make the other person feel important—and do it sincerely
questions.q: According to Carnegie, John Dewey said that the desire to be important is the deepest ____ in human nature.
questions.explain: Carnegie adds that this urge separates us from the animals and has been responsible for civilization itself.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.section: Principle: Make the other person feel important—and do it sincerely
questions.q: After quoting Do unto others as you would have others do unto you, Carnegie urges: So let's obey the ____, and give unto others what we would have others give unto us.
questions.explain: Carnegie says the precept is as old as history and was taught by Zoroaster, Confucius, Lao-tse, Buddha and Jesus. Asked when to apply it, he answers all the time, everywhere.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: In the charity concert story, David G. Smith gave Rose the ____ box, realising it was a symbol of authority.
questions.explain: By giving Rose the money to look after and putting Jane in charge of the soda machine, Smith made each lady feel important and ended the quarrel over who was in charge.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: Hall Caine became secretary to the poet Dante Gabriel ____ after praising his work in a lecture.
questions.explain: Rossetti, delighted by the praise, invited the blacksmith's son to London. Carnegie uses the story to show the stupendous power of sincere, heartfelt appreciation.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: The elderly aunt gave Mr. R—— a ____ car that her husband had bought for her shortly before he died.
questions.explain: She had never ridden in it since his death and would not let her waiting relatives or strangers have it. She gave it to him because he appreciated beautiful things.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: Rubbing a panel in George Eastman's office, James Adamson remarked that it was English ____, a little different in texture from the Italian kind.
questions.explain: Eastman confirmed it was imported English oak chosen by a friend who specialized in fine woods. Adamson's informed admiration of the office opened hours of conversation.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.section: Principle: Make the other person feel important—and do it sincerely
questions.q: In How to Make People Like You Instantly, Carnegie says you do not want to listen to cheap, insincere ____, but you do crave sincere appreciation.
questions.explain: This is why the principle ends with the words do it sincerely. In each story the speaker first looks for something he can honestly admire.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.section: Principle: Make the other person feel important—and do it sincerely
questions.q: Which of these does Carnegie name as having taught the one important precept of human relations?
options: Zoroaster
Socrates
Lao-tse
Marcus Aurelius
Confucius
questions.explain: Carnegie lists Zoroaster, Confucius, Lao-tse, Buddha, the sacred books of Hinduism and Jesus. Socrates and Marcus Aurelius are not in his list.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: Which of these little phrases does Carnegie list as courtesies that oil the cogs of everyday life?
options: “I’m sorry to trouble you”
“Would you mind?”
“As I told you before”
“Thank you”
“No problem”
questions.explain: Carnegie lists phrases such as I'm sorry to trouble you, Would you be so kind as to, Won't you please, Would you mind and Thank you, calling them the hallmark of good breeding.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: Which of these did James Adamson do during his visit to George Eastman?
options: Praised the beauty of Eastman's office
Presented his seat samples and prices within five minutes
Identified a wall panel as English oak
Drew Eastman out about his early struggles in business
Criticized the hand carving as old-fashioned
questions.explain: Adamson admired the office, recognised the English oak, and listened, absorbed, as Eastman told of his poverty and his experiments with dry plates. He never got to a quick sales pitch, and he praised rather than criticized.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: Which of these treasures did the elderly aunt show Mr. R—— in her house?
options: Paisley shawls
Chairs brought from Japan
Wedgwood china
An old English tea set
Persian rugs
questions.explain: Her treasures included paisley shawls, an old English tea set, Wedgwood china, French furniture, Italian paintings and silk draperies from a French chateau. The Japanese chairs belong to the Eastman story.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: Which of these did restaurant owner Claude Marais do when his key employee Paulette resigned?
options: Told her he could not accept her resignation because she was as important to the restaurant as he was
Offered her a large pay rise
Repeated his words in front of the entire staff
Invited her to his home and restated his confidence with his family present
Accepted the resignation and hired a replacement
questions.explain: Marais made Paulette feel important privately, before the staff and before his family, and she withdrew her resignation. Carnegie mentions no pay rise.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: Which of these did the judge give Donald M. McMahon after McMahon admired his dogs?
options: A puppy for his son
A typed pedigree and feeding instructions
A blue ribbon from Madison Square Garden
More than an hour of his valuable time
A contract to landscape another estate
questions.explain: McMahon says the judge gave him a puppy worth several hundred dollars and one hour and fifteen minutes of his time, and typed out the pedigree and feeding instructions himself.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: Which of these institutions did George Eastman point out to James Adamson as ways he was trying to help humanity?
options: The University of Rochester
The Eastman Photographic Museum
The Children’s Hospital
The General Hospital
The Rochester Public Library
questions.explain: Eastman named the University of Rochester, the General Hospital, the Homeopathic Hospital, the Friendly Home and the Children's Hospital. Adamson warmly congratulated him on using his wealth this way.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: Put the events of Carnegie's post office story in order, from first to last.
items: Carnegie notices the clerk looks bored with his job
Carnegie asks himself what he can honestly admire about the clerk
Carnegie says he wishes he had the clerk's head of hair
The clerk says many people have admired his hair
questions.explain: Carnegie first sees the monotonous grind of the clerk's day, then looks for something honest to admire, praises his hair, and leaves the clerk beaming and proud.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: Put the stages of Hall Caine's rise in order, from first to last.
items: He devoured Rossetti's poetry
He wrote a lecture praising Rossetti and sent him a copy
Rossetti invited him to London as his secretary
He met the literary artists of the day
He became the richest literary man of his time
questions.explain: Caine's love of sonnets and ballads led to his admiring lecture, which won him the secretary's post. Encouraged by the writers he met there, he launched a hugely successful career.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: Put the events of James Adamson's visit to George Eastman in order, from first to last.
items: The architect warns Adamson to take no more than five minutes
Adamson admires Eastman's office
Eastman tells of his poor childhood and early experiments
Eastman invites Adamson home to lunch to see his painted chairs
The two men stay close friends until Eastman's death
questions.explain: Praise of the office led Eastman to talk for hours about the room, his charities and his struggles, then to invite Adamson to lunch. The friendship lasted until Eastman died.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: Put the events of Mr. R——'s visit to his wife's aunt in order, from first to last.
items: He asks whether the house was built about 1890
She shows him the treasures from her travels
She takes him to the garage to see the Packard
She says she will give him the car
He suggests she sell it to a secondhand dealer
questions.explain: His honest admiration of the house led to a tour of her treasures and then the Packard. When he tried to decline, suggesting her relatives or a dealer, she insisted he take it.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: Put the six ways to make people like you in the order Carnegie numbers them in Part Two.
items: Become genuinely interested in other people
Smile
Remember a person's name
Be a good listener
Talk in terms of the other person's interests
Make the other person feel important
questions.explain: The In a Nutshell summary at the end of this chapter lists all six principles of Part Two. Making the other person feel important, done sincerely, is the sixth and last.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.section: Principle: Make the other person feel important—and do it sincerely
questions.q: In How to Make People Like You Instantly, match each person to the idea Carnegie quotes from them.
pairs: The desire to be important is the deepest urge in human nature
The deepest principle in human nature is the craving to be appreciated
Every man I meet is my superior in some way
Talk to people about themselves and they will listen for hours
Do unto others as you would have others do unto you
questions.explain: Carnegie gathers these voices to support one law: make the other person feel important. Dewey and James explain the craving; Emerson, Disraeli and Jesus show how to answer it.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: Match each person in How to Make People Like You Instantly to what was admired about them.
questions.explain: In each story the admirer chose something he could honestly praise that mattered to the other person. Carnegie stresses that the praise was sincere, not flattery.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: Match each story in How to Make People Like You Instantly to how it turned out.
pairs: The judge gave his son a puppy
questions.explain: Each result followed from making someone feel important. Carnegie presents them as proof of the stupendous power of sincere, heartfelt appreciation.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.section: Principle: Make the other person feel important—and do it sincerely
questions.q: Match each teacher Carnegie names to the place where he says the great precept was taught.
pairs: The bank of the Holy Ganges
questions.explain: Carnegie uses this list to show that the precept is as old as history. Out of thousands of years of speculation, he says, only this one important rule has evolved.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: Match each person who told a story in How to Make People Like You Instantly to his role.
pairs: Ran the refreshment booth at a charity concert
Taught arts and crafts in California
Superintendent of a nursery and landscape firm
President of the Superior Seating Company
questions.explain: Carnegie draws his examples from people in ordinary jobs to show that this philosophy of appreciation can work magic almost every day, not only for ambassadors.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: Sort these stories from How to Make People Like You Instantly by how they ended.
groups: Ended with a gift to the admirer
Ended with a job or a kept employee

items.t: Mr. R—— admires the aunt's house
McMahon admires the judge's dogs
Hall Caine praises Rossetti
Claude Marais tells Paulette she is important
Rowland invites Chris into the advanced class

questions.explain: The aunt gave a Packard and the judge a puppy. Caine won a secretary's post, Paulette stayed, and Chris won a place in the advanced class.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.section: Principle: Make the other person feel important—and do it sincerely
questions.q: Sort these names from How to Make People Like You Instantly by how Carnegie uses them.
groups: Quoted on the human craving for importance
Named as a teacher of the great precept

items.t: John Dewey
William James
Emerson
Zoroaster
Confucius
Lao-tse
Buddha

questions.explain: Dewey, James and Emerson describe how people want to feel important or superior. The religious teachers are listed as having taught the rule summed up as do unto others.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: Sort these principles by the part of the book in which they appear.
groups: Part One: Fundamental Techniques in Handling People
Part Two: Six Ways to Make People Like You

items.t: Don't criticize, condemn or complain
Give honest and sincere appreciation
Arouse in the other person an eager want
Smile
Be a good listener
Make the other person feel important—and do it sincerely

questions.explain: Part One gives three fundamental techniques. Part Two's six ways end with this chapter's principle, which builds on Part One's call for honest, sincere appreciation.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: Sort these details by the story in How to Make People Like You Instantly they belong to.
groups: Mr. R—— and the elderly aunt

items.t: English oak panelling
Chairs brought from Japan
The first camera he ever owned
A house built about 1890
Paisley shawls
A car jacked up on blocks

questions.explain: Eastman showed his office, his charities, his first camera and his repainted Japanese chairs. The aunt showed her house, her travel treasures and the Packard in the garage.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: Which life story in How to Make People Like You Instantly does each detail come from: the novelist Hall Caine or the shy crafts student Chris?

items.t: Son of a blacksmith
Greeba Castle on the Isle of Man
A lecture praising a famous poet
Fourteen years old
Invited into the advanced class
A sign in the classroom

questions.explain: Caine, a blacksmith's son, won fame after praising Rossetti and later lived at Greeba Castle. Chris was a shy fourteen-year-old whose invitation to the advanced class led his teacher to put up a sign.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: Why did Carnegie react so strongly when a listener asked what he wanted to get out of the post office clerk?
questions.a: Carnegie thought it contemptibly selfish to give a little happiness and honest appreciation only to get something back; people whose souls are no bigger than sour crab apples deserve to fail. He did want something, but it was priceless: the feeling of having done something for the clerk that the clerk could never repay, a feeling that stays in the memory long afterward.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.section: Principle: Make the other person feel important—and do it sincerely
questions.q: What is Carnegie's all-important law of human conduct, and what does he claim follows from obeying or breaking it?
questions.a: The law is always to make the other person feel important. Carnegie claims that if we obey it we will almost never get into trouble and will gain countless friends and constant happiness, but the instant we break it we get into endless trouble. He grounds it in Dewey's desire to be important and James's craving to be appreciated.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.section: Principle: Make the other person feel important—and do it sincerely
questions.q: How does Carnegie link his law of making others feel important to the teachings of philosophers and religious leaders?
questions.a: He says that out of thousands of years of speculation on human relationships only one important precept has evolved, taught by Zoroaster, Confucius, Lao-tse, Buddha, the books of Hinduism and Jesus. Jesus summed it up as do unto others as you would have others do unto you. Since we all want approval and sincere appreciation, we should give the same to others, all the time and everywhere.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: How did David G. Smith settle the quarrel between Rose and Jane at the charity concert, and why did it work?
questions.a: Each lady thought she was in charge, so Smith gave Rose the cash box, saying he would feel better if she looked after the money, and made Jane responsible for showing the teenagers how to run the soda machine. Each was given a role that made her feel important, so the tension vanished and Smith enjoyed the concert.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: A new team leader inherits two senior colleagues who each believe they should run the same project. Using Carnegie's charity concert example, what might the leader do?
questions.a: Like David G. Smith with Rose and Jane, the leader could give each colleague a distinct, visible responsibility that signals authority, such as one handling the budget and the other supervising the junior staff. Each then feels important and trusted, and the rivalry gives way to cooperation without anyone losing face.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: Why, according to Carnegie, did the elderly aunt give Mr. R—— her Packard?
questions.a: She lived alone in a big house with her treasures and memories, once young and sought after but now isolated in old age, and no one gave her any genuine appreciation. When Mr. R—— sincerely admired her house and things, it was like a spring in the desert. Her gratitude could express itself only through the gift of her cherished car.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: What does the story of George Eastman and James Adamson show about famous, successful people?
questions.a: Eastman had invented the film behind motion pictures and made a hundred million dollars, yet he craved little recognitions just as ordinary people do. When Adamson sincerely admired his office and listened to his story, a strict, busy man gave him hours, lunch and lifelong friendship, and was proud of cheap chairs simply because he had painted them himself.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.section: Principle: Make the other person feel important—and do it sincerely
questions.q: Recite Principle 6 of Part Two from memory.
questions.a: Make the other person feel important—and do it sincerely.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: Recite from memory the six ways to make people like you, as Carnegie summarises them at the end of Part Two.
questions.a: 1. Become genuinely interested in other people. 2. Smile. 3. Remember that a person’s name is to that person the sweetest and most important sound in any language. 4. Be a good listener. Encourage others to talk about themselves. 5. Talk in terms of the other person’s interests. 6. Make the other person feel important—and do it sincerely.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.section: Principle: Make the other person feel important—and do it sincerely
questions.q: Why does Carnegie insist that you make the other person feel important sincerely, rather than simply praising them?
questions.a: He says people do not want cheap, insincere flattery but crave sincere appreciation. In each of his stories the speaker first asks what he can honestly admire, as Carnegie did with the clerk's hair and Mr. R—— did with the aunt's house. Recognition of a person's importance must be real, though it can be shown subtly.

questions.unitTitle: How to Make People Like You Instantly
questions.q: How does How to Make People Like You Instantly link back to Part One, The Big Secret of Dealing with People?
questions.a: Carnegie notes that, as already noted, John Dewey called the desire to be important the deepest urge in human nature, and he repeats William James on the craving to be appreciated and Charles Schwab's being hearty in approbation and lavish in praise. The chapter turns that earlier secret into the last of the six ways to make people like you: make the other person feel important, sincerely.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.q: In You Can’t Win an Argument, where did the quotation about a divinity that shapes our ends actually come from, according to Carnegie?
options: The Bible, as the storyteller insisted
A speech by Abraham Lincoln
Shakespeare’s Hamlet, Act Five, Scene Two
The sayings of Ben Franklin
questions.explain: Carnegie knew the line was from Shakespeare, and Frank Gammond later confirmed it: “Hamlet, Act Five, Scene Two.” The storyteller’s claim that it came from the Bible was the mistake Carnegie rushed to correct.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.q: In You Can’t Win an Argument, why does Carnegie say he corrected the storyteller at the banquet for Sir Ross Smith?
options: To get a feeling of importance and display his superiority
Because the host had asked him to keep the facts straight
To protect his friend Frank Gammond’s reputation as a scholar
Because the storyteller had asked for his opinion on the line
questions.explain: Carnegie admits he acted “to get a feeling of importance and display my superiority.” Gammond later points out that the storyteller had not asked for his opinion at all.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.q: In You Can’t Win an Argument, what did Frank Gammond do when the disputed quotation was put to him at the banquet?
options: He declined to judge and changed the subject
He kicked Carnegie under the table and said the storyteller was right
He quietly told Carnegie he was right but said nothing aloud
He named the play and scene so both men could check it
questions.explain: Gammond kicked Carnegie under the table and declared that the line was from the Bible, even though he knew it was from Hamlet. He let the storyteller save face instead of proving him wrong.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.q: In You Can’t Win an Argument, how does Carnegie say an argument ends nine times out of ten?
options: With the weaker side quietly giving way
With both sides agreeing to differ politely
With the better-informed person changing the other’s mind
With each side more firmly convinced than ever that he is right
questions.explain: Carnegie says that nine times out of ten each contestant leaves more firmly convinced than ever that he is absolutely right. Arguments harden opinions rather than change them.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.q: In You Can’t Win an Argument, why does Carnegie say you lose even when you win an argument?
options: Because the facts usually turn out to be on the other side
Because the other person feels inferior, is hurt in his pride and resents your triumph
Because winning takes more time than the point is worth
Because onlookers side with the person who lost
questions.explain: If you shoot the other man’s argument full of holes, you feel fine but he feels inferior, his pride is hurt, and he resents your triumph. As the couplet says, a man convinced against his will keeps his opinion.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.q: In You Can’t Win an Argument, what did Carnegie discover was the real reason Patrick J. O’Haire was failing to sell trucks?
options: He knew too little about the trucks he was selling
He was too shy to approach prospective buyers
He was selling a truck that buyers thought inferior
He kept scrapping with and antagonizing the people he wanted to sell to
questions.explain: A little questioning showed that O’Haire was continually scrapping with and antagonizing his prospects. He won arguments but, as he put it, he hadn’t sold anything.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.q: A car salesperson’s customer says that the salesperson’s brand is junk and that they are buying the rival model instead. Following Patrick J. O’Haire’s method in You Can’t Win an Argument, what should the salesperson say first?
options: Agree that the rival model is a good car made by a fine company
Point out the rival model’s weaknesses with facts and figures
Ask the customer who told them such a thing
Offer a large discount to change the customer’s mind
questions.explain: O’Haire agreed that the Whose-It was a good truck, which left the buyer with nothing to argue against; only then did he turn to the good points of his own truck. Attacking the rival only made his prospects argue for it and sell themselves on it.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.q: In You Can’t Win an Argument, why does Ben Franklin call the victory won by arguing and contradicting an empty one?
options: Because the other person will soon forget the point
Because the facts may later prove you wrong
Because you will never get your opponent’s good will
Because no one important is there to witness it
questions.explain: Franklin says arguing may win a victory sometimes, but it is empty “because you will never get your opponent’s good will.” Carnegie adds that you can seldom have both the victory and the good will.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.q: In You Can’t Win an Argument, what point does Carnegie draw from the doggerel about William Jay, who died maintaining his right of way?
options: That you should always know your rights before you argue
That careless people deserve the trouble they get
That most people in an argument are in fact wrong
That being right in an argument is as futile for changing a mind as being wrong
questions.explain: William Jay was right, dead right, but just as dead as if he were wrong. Likewise, you may be right in an argument and still be as futile at changing another’s mind as if you were wrong.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.q: In You Can’t Win an Argument, what made the stubborn tax inspector turn friendly towards Frederick S. Parsons?
options: Parsons produced new records proving the debt was bad
Parsons stopped arguing and admitted the inspector’s importance
Parsons appealed to the inspector’s superior
Parsons offered to pay part of the disputed tax
questions.explain: The inspector wanted a feeling of importance and got it by asserting his authority while Parsons argued. Once the argument stopped and his importance was admitted, he became “a sympathetic and kindly human being.”

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.q: You Can’t Win an Argument is the first chapter of which part of the book?
options: Part One: Fundamental Techniques in Handling People
Part Two: Six Ways to Make People Like You
Part Three: How to Win People to Your Way of Thinking
Part Four: Be a Leader
questions.explain: The chapter opens Part Three, How to Win People to Your Way of Thinking. Its principle, avoiding argument, is the first step before any of the later ways of persuading.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.section: Principle: The only way to get the best of an argument is to avoid it
questions.q: In You Can’t Win an Argument, what does Lincoln mean by saying it is better to give your path to a dog than be bitten contesting for the right, since even killing the dog would not cure the bite?
options: Fighting for your rights can cost more than giving way, and winning does not undo the damage
You should never let others take what is clearly yours
Dangerous people should be avoided at all costs
Only fight battles where you are sure to win
questions.explain: Lincoln told a young officer to yield larger things where his rights were only equal and even lesser ones that were clearly his own. Personal contention costs temper and self-control, and victory does not repair that harm.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.q: True or false: In You Can’t Win an Argument, Carnegie admits that he once planned to write a book on argumentation.
questions.explain: He taught debating and argumentation in New York and says that once, “I am ashamed to admit, I planned to write a book on the subject.”

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.q: True or false: In You Can’t Win an Argument, Frank Gammond sided with the storyteller because Gammond himself believed the quotation came from the Bible.
questions.explain: Gammond knew the line was from Hamlet. He sided with the storyteller deliberately, so that a guest at a festive occasion could save face.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.q: True or false: In You Can’t Win an Argument, the tax inspector decided three days later to leave Frederick S. Parsons’s tax return exactly as it was filed.
questions.explain: After Parsons stopped arguing and gave him sincere appreciation, the inspector called three days later and left the return as filed, so the nine thousand dollars was not taxed.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.q: True or false: In You Can’t Win an Argument, Carnegie says his first task with Patrick J. O’Haire was to teach him to talk more persuasively.
questions.explain: Carnegie says his first problem was not to teach O’Haire to talk; his immediate task was to train him to refrain from talking and to avoid verbal fights.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.section: Principle: The only way to get the best of an argument is to avoid it
questions.q: True or false: In You Can’t Win an Argument, Jan Peerce’s pact with his wife was that when one of them yells, the other should leave the room.
questions.explain: The pact was that when one yells, the other should listen, “because when two people yell, there is no communication, just noise and bad vibrations.”

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.q: In You Can’t Win an Argument, Frank Gammond sums up his advice to Carnegie in four words: always avoid the ____.
questions.explain: Gammond’s point is that you should not push a quarrel to a sharp point: let the other man save face rather than prove him wrong.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.section: Principle: The only way to get the best of an argument is to avoid it
questions.q: The principle of You Can’t Win an Argument: the only way to get the best of an argument is to ____ it.
questions.explain: Carnegie concludes from thousands of arguments that the only way to get the best of one is to avoid it, as you would avoid rattlesnakes and earthquakes.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.q: In You Can’t Win an Argument, Carnegie quotes a couplet: a man convinced against his will is of the same opinion ____.
questions.explain: The couplet explains why winning an argument fails: the loser resents the defeat and keeps his opinion.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.section: Principle: The only way to get the best of an argument is to avoid it
questions.q: In You Can’t Win an Argument, Carnegie quotes Buddha: hatred is never ended by hatred but by ____.
questions.explain: Carnegie adds that a misunderstanding likewise is never ended by an argument but by tact, diplomacy, conciliation and a sympathetic desire to see the other person’s viewpoint.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.q: In You Can’t Win an Argument, Ben Franklin says that arguing and contradicting may win a victory, but it will be an ____ victory.
questions.explain: The victory is empty because you will never get your opponent’s good will.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.section: Principle: The only way to get the best of an argument is to avoid it
questions.q: In the Bits and Pieces suggestions quoted in You Can’t Win an Argument, you can measure the size of a person by what makes him or her ____.
questions.explain: This is the reason given under Control your temper: losing your temper shows how small you are.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.q: In You Can’t Win an Argument, the tax inspector was demonstrating a common human frailty: he wanted a feeling of ____.
questions.explain: While Parsons argued, the inspector got his feeling of importance by asserting his authority; once his importance was admitted, he became kindly.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.q: Which of these does Carnegie mention in You Can’t Win an Argument as part of his past as an inveterate arguer?
options: He argued with his brother about everything
He studied logic and argumentation and entered debating contests
He taught debating and argumentation in New York
He published a successful textbook on debating
He trained as a lawyer before teaching
questions.explain: Carnegie argued with his brother, studied logic and debating at college, and later taught debating in New York. He only planned a book on the subject and never says he trained in law.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.q: Which of these points does Frank Gammond make on the way home from the banquet in You Can’t Win an Argument?
options: They were guests at a festive occasion
Carnegie should let the man save his face
The man had not asked for Carnegie’s opinion
The storyteller was an important man who could harm Carnegie
Scholars still disagree about where the line comes from
questions.explain: Gammond asks why prove a man wrong at a festive occasion, why not let him save face, and notes that the man did not ask for Carnegie’s opinion. He gives no warning about the storyteller’s power and has no doubt the line is from Hamlet.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.q: Which of these did Frederick S. Parsons do to win over the tax inspector in You Can’t Win an Argument?
options: He stopped arguing and changed the subject
He told the inspector, sincerely, that he learned from experience while Parsons learned from books
He brought in more facts to prove the debt was bad
He threatened to take the case to a higher official
questions.explain: Parsons decided to avoid argument, change the subject and give appreciation, saying the inspector learned “from the firing line of experience.” More facts had already failed: reason and facts were wasted on the inspector.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.section: Principle: The only way to get the best of an argument is to avoid it
questions.q: Which of these are among the Bits and Pieces suggestions in You Can’t Win an Argument for keeping a disagreement from becoming an argument?
options: Welcome the disagreement
Listen first
Look for areas of agreement
Trust your first instinctive impression
Win the first point quickly to set the tone
questions.explain: The list includes welcoming the disagreement, listening first and looking for areas of agreement. It says the opposite of trusting your first impression: distrust it, since your first reaction may be you at your worst.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.section: Principle: The only way to get the best of an argument is to avoid it
questions.q: Which of these are among the hard questions the Bits and Pieces suggestions in You Can’t Win an Argument tell you to ask yourself before a postponed meeting?
options: Could my opponents be right?
What price will I have to pay if I win?
Will my reaction drive my opponents further away or draw them closer?
How can I prove at the meeting that they are wrong?
Who else can I bring in to back my side?
questions.explain: The questions ask whether your opponents could be right, what winning would cost, and whether your reaction would push them away or draw them closer. None is about proving them wrong or gathering allies.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.q: In You Can’t Win an Argument, put the events of the Sir Ross Smith banquet in order.
items: The storyteller says the quotation is from the Bible
Carnegie corrects him and says it is from Shakespeare
The two agree to put the question to Frank Gammond
Gammond kicks Carnegie and says the storyteller is right
On the way home Gammond names Hamlet and explains why he did it
questions.explain: Carnegie’s unasked-for correction led to the appeal to Gammond, who sided with the storyteller in public and explained his reasons only on the way home.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.q: In You Can’t Win an Argument, put the stages of Frederick S. Parsons’s dispute with the tax inspector in order.
items: Parsons argues for an hour that the item is a bad debt
Parsons decides to avoid argument and give appreciation
The inspector talks about his work, his frauds and his children
Three days later the inspector leaves the return as filed
questions.explain: Argument only made the inspector more stubborn; appreciation let him expand his ego, and he then decided in Parsons’s favour.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.section: Principle: The only way to get the best of an argument is to avoid it
questions.q: In You Can’t Win an Argument, put the first four Bits and Pieces suggestions in the order they are listed.
items: Welcome the disagreement
Distrust your first instinctive impression
Control your temper
Listen first
questions.explain: The list moves from welcoming disagreement, to guarding against your defensive first reaction and your temper, to letting your opponents talk first.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.q: Put these chapter titles in the order they appear in the book, around You Can’t Win an Argument.
items: How to Make People Like You Instantly
You Can’t Win an Argument
A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.explain: How to Make People Like You Instantly ends Part Two; You Can’t Win an Argument opens Part Three and is followed by A Sure Way of Making Enemies and then If You’re Wrong, Admit It.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.section: Principle: The only way to get the best of an argument is to avoid it
questions.q: Match each person in You Can’t Win an Argument to the advice they give.
pairs: Arguing wins only an empty victory without the opponent’s good will
Hatred is never ended by hatred but by love
Better give your path to a dog than be bitten by him
When one partner yells, the other should listen
questions.explain: Each saying makes the same case from a different angle: argument costs good will, temper and communication, while yielding preserves them.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.q: Match each person in You Can’t Win an Argument to who they were.
pairs: Australian flying ace whom Carnegie managed
Carnegie’s old friend who had studied Shakespeare for years
Former chauffeur who struggled to sell trucks
Income tax consultant disputing a nine-thousand-dollar item
Opera tenor married nearly fifty years
questions.explain: These are the people in the chapter’s main stories and sayings: the banquet, the truck salesman, the tax dispute and the marriage pact.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.section: Principle: The only way to get the best of an argument is to avoid it
questions.q: Match each Bits and Pieces suggestion in You Can’t Win an Argument to the reason given for it.
pairs: It may let you be corrected before a serious mistake
Your first reaction may be you at your worst
Admitting error disarms opponents and reduces defensiveness
Anyone who disagrees is interested in the same things you are
Both sides get time to think the problem through
questions.explain: Each suggestion comes with its own reason, and all aim to stop a disagreement from turning into an argument.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.q: Match each chapter to its principle, as summed up in the book.
pairs: How to Make People Like You Instantly
Make the other person feel important, and do it sincerely
The only way to get the best of an argument is to avoid it
A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
Show respect for the other person’s opinions
If you are wrong, admit it quickly and emphatically
questions.explain: Avoiding argument opens Part Three; the next chapters build on it by respecting the other person’s opinions and admitting your own errors.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.section: Principle: The only way to get the best of an argument is to avoid it
questions.q: Sort these responses to a disagreement by whether the Bits and Pieces suggestions in You Can’t Win an Argument recommend them.

items.t: Let your opponents finish before you speak
Dwell first on the points you agree on
Apologize for your mistakes
Suggest meeting again later to think it over
Defend and debate each point as it comes
Act on your first defensive reaction
Move rapidly ahead without considering their points

questions.explain: The list says listen first, look for agreement, be honest and postpone action. It warns against resisting, defending or debating, against trusting your first defensive reaction, and against rushing ahead.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.q: Sort these behaviours of Patrick J. O’Haire in You Can’t Win an Argument into his old way and his new way of selling.

items.t: Seeing red when a prospect criticized his trucks
Arguing against the competitor’s truck
Leaving pleased that he had told the buyer something
Agreeing that the Whose-It is a good truck
Keeping his mouth shut
Turning the talk to the good points of the White truck

questions.explain: In the old way, the more O’Haire argued against the competitor, the more the buyer sold himself on it. In the new way, agreeing left no room for argument and led to the White truck’s merits.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.q: Sort these features of the tax dispute in You Can’t Win an Argument by their effect on the inspector.

items.t: An hour of wrangling over the bad debt
Reason and facts pressed on him
A chance to assert his authority loudly
Sincere praise for his experience on the firing line
Being let to talk about his work and frauds he uncovered
Having his importance admitted

questions.explain: While Parsons argued, the inspector fed his sense of importance by asserting authority and grew more stubborn. Once his importance was admitted and he could expand his ego, he became kindly.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.q: In You Can’t Win an Argument, explain why Carnegie says you cannot win an argument.
questions.a: If you lose an argument you lose it, and if you win it you still lose. Shooting the other man’s argument full of holes makes him feel inferior, hurts his pride and makes him resent your triumph. As the couplet puts it, a man convinced against his will is of the same opinion still.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.q: In You Can’t Win an Argument, what lesson did Frank Gammond teach Carnegie at the Sir Ross Smith banquet, and why did Carnegie need it?
questions.a: Gammond knew the line was from Hamlet but sided with the storyteller, then explained that there was no point proving a guest wrong at a festive occasion: it would not make him like you, he had not asked for the correction, and he should be let to save face. “Always avoid the acute angle.” Carnegie needed it because he had been an inveterate arguer who had studied and even taught argumentation.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.q: In You Can’t Win an Argument, how did Patrick J. O’Haire’s changed approach to buyers who praised a rival truck end the arguments that had cost him sales?
questions.a: He agreed that the Whose-It was a good truck made by a fine company, which left the buyer speechless and with no room for argument. The talk then moved to the good points of the White truck. Before, the more he argued against the rival, the more the buyer argued for it and sold himself on it; now O’Haire keeps his mouth shut, and it pays.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.q: In You Can’t Win an Argument, what does Carnegie say the tax inspector’s change of attitude shows about human nature?
questions.a: The inspector showed one of the most common human frailties: he wanted a feeling of importance. While Parsons argued, he got it by loudly asserting his authority and grew more stubborn. Once Parsons stopped arguing and sincerely admitted his importance, he became a sympathetic and kindly human being and decided in Parsons’s favour.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.q: In You Can’t Win an Argument, what does the epitaph of William Jay teach about being right in an argument?
questions.a: William Jay died maintaining his right of way: he was right, dead right, but just as dead as if he had been wrong. In the same way, you may be right in an argument, but as far as changing the other person’s mind goes you will probably be as futile as if you were wrong. Being right is no use if it costs the outcome you wanted.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.section: Principle: The only way to get the best of an argument is to avoid it
questions.q: In You Can’t Win an Argument, what advice did Lincoln give the young officer who had quarrelled with an associate?
questions.a: Lincoln said no man resolved to make the most of himself can spare time for personal contention, still less afford its cost in temper and self-control. He advised yielding larger things where your rights are only equal, and lesser ones even when clearly your own. It is better to give your path to a dog than be bitten, because even killing the dog would not cure the bite.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.section: Principle: The only way to get the best of an argument is to avoid it
questions.q: At a family dinner, your uncle states a historical date you know is wrong and the table turns to you. Using the ideas in You Can’t Win an Argument, what would Carnegie advise and why?
questions.a: Carnegie would advise not correcting him: the only way to get the best of an argument is to avoid it. Like Frank Gammond at the banquet, you would let your uncle save face, since he did not ask for your opinion and proving him wrong would not make him like you. Winning would only make him feel inferior and resent you, and he would likely keep his opinion anyway.

questions.unitTitle: You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.q: Why does You Can’t Win an Argument come first in Part Three, How to Win People to Your Way of Thinking?
questions.a: Before trying to bring anyone round to your view, you must stop doing the thing that hardens their opposition: arguing. Carnegie shows that argument leaves each side more convinced than ever and costs the other person’s good will, so avoiding it clears the ground for the persuasion methods that follow, such as respecting the other person’s opinions and admitting your own mistakes. It also builds on Part Two’s point that people want to feel important.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: In A Sure Way of Making Enemies, what share of the time did Theodore Roosevelt say he would need to be right to reach the highest measure of his expectation?
options: 50 percent of the time
75 percent of the time
90 percent of the time
55 percent of the time
questions.explain: Roosevelt confessed that being right 75 percent of the time would satisfy his highest hopes. The 55 percent figure is Carnegie’s Wall Street line: be sure of that and you could make a million dollars a day.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: What does the title A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It point to as the sure way of making enemies?
options: Telling other people that they are wrong
Forgetting the names of people you meet
Complaining about people behind their backs
Refusing to admit your own mistakes
questions.explain: The whole chapter is about the damage done by telling people they are wrong and ends with the principle never to say it. Forgetting names and admitting your own mistakes belong to other chapters.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.section: Principle: Show respect for the other person’s opinions. Never say, “You’re wrong.”
questions.q: True or false: In A Sure Way of Making Enemies, Carnegie says you can tell people they are wrong by a look, an intonation or a gesture just as eloquently as you can in words.
questions.explain: Carnegie warns that the message does not need words: a look, a tone of voice or a gesture can say it just as clearly, and it does the same harm.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.section: Principle: Show respect for the other person’s opinions. Never say, “You’re wrong.”
questions.q: Which of these does Carnegie say you strike a direct blow at when you tell people they are wrong?
options: Their sense of humour
Their intelligence
Their pride
Their self-respect
Their physical comfort
questions.explain: Carnegie lists intelligence, judgment, pride and self-respect. The blow makes people want to strike back, not change their minds.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.section: Principle: Show respect for the other person’s opinions. Never say, “You’re wrong.”
questions.q: In A Sure Way of Making Enemies, why does Carnegie say that all the logic of a Plato or an Immanuel Kant will not alter the opinions of people you have told are wrong?
options: Because most people cannot follow philosophical reasoning
Because opinions on such matters are fixed in childhood
Because you have hurt their feelings
Because logic only works when it is written down
questions.explain: Once you have hurt someone’s feelings, argument no longer reaches them. The problem is wounded pride, not a lack of ability to follow logic.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.section: Principle: Show respect for the other person’s opinions. Never say, “You’re wrong.”
questions.q: Why does Carnegie say you should never begin by announcing “I am going to prove so-and-so to you”?
options: Because it wastes time that could be spent listening
Because it shows you have prepared too little
Because people forget an argument once it has been announced
Because it amounts to saying you are smarter than the listener, which is a challenge
questions.explain: Carnegie says such an opening is tantamount to saying “I’m smarter than you are.” It arouses opposition and makes the listener want to fight before you even start.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: In A Sure Way of Making Enemies, Carnegie quotes Galileo: You cannot teach a man anything; you can only help him to find it within ____.
questions.explain: Galileo’s saying supports Carnegie’s advice to prove things so subtly that no one feels you are doing it: the other person should seem to find the truth for himself.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: Carnegie quotes Lord Chesterfield’s advice to his son: Be ____ than other people if you can; but do not tell them so.
questions.explain: Chesterfield’s line sums up the advice: you may know better, but announcing it only arouses opposition.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: Carnegie quotes Socrates as saying repeatedly to his followers in Athens: One thing only I know, and that is that I know ____.
questions.explain: Carnegie says he cannot hope to be smarter than Socrates, so he has quit telling people they are wrong, and finds that it pays.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: Match each person Carnegie quotes in A Sure Way of Making Enemies to the saying he is quoted as giving.
pairs: Men must be taught as if you taught them not
You can only help a man find it within himself
Be wiser than other people if you can, but do not tell them so
One thing only I know, and that is that I know nothing
questions.explain: All four sayings back the same advice: if you are going to prove anything, do it so subtly that no one feels you are doing it.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.section: Principle: Show respect for the other person’s opinions. Never say, “You’re wrong.”
questions.q: Which of these sayings does Carnegie quote in A Sure Way of Making Enemies to support proving things so subtly that no one feels you are doing it?
options: If you want to gather honey, don’t kick over the beehive
Men must be taught as if you taught them not
You cannot teach a man anything; you can only help him find it within himself
Be wiser than other people if you can; but do not tell them so
The only way to get the best of an argument is to avoid it
questions.explain: Pope, Galileo and Chesterfield are quoted here. The beehive line and the advice to avoid arguments come from earlier chapters.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.section: Principle: Show respect for the other person’s opinions. Never say, “You’re wrong.”
questions.q: Carnegie says there is magic, positive magic, in the phrases: I may be wrong. I frequently am. Let’s examine the ____.
questions.explain: Carnegie says nobody anywhere will ever object to your saying “I may be wrong. Let’s examine the facts.”

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.section: Principle: Show respect for the other person’s opinions. Never say, “You’re wrong.”
questions.q: Your colleague insists the team meeting is on Thursday, and you are fairly sure it is on Wednesday. According to A Sure Way of Making Enemies, what is the best thing to say?
options: You are wrong, it is Wednesday, and I can prove it
Let me show you the email so you can see your mistake
Fine, have it your way, it is Thursday
I thought it was Wednesday, but I may be wrong; let us check the calendar
questions.explain: Carnegie advises beginning with “I thought otherwise, but I may be wrong” and then examining the facts. Proving the other person wrong wounds pride, while simply giving in gives up the facts.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: True or false: Harold Reinke, the class member who changed how he handled customers’ complaints, was a Ford dealer in Billings, Montana.
questions.explain: Reinke was a Dodge dealer in Billings, Montana. He told customers his dealership had made many mistakes and might have erred in their case.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: Which of these results did Harold Reinke report after he began telling complaining customers that his dealership might have erred in their case?
options: Customers became more reasonable about settling the matter
He was able to raise his prices
Several customers thanked him for his understanding attitude
Two customers brought in friends to buy new cars
He was promoted to regional manager
questions.explain: Reinke found the approach disarming: customers released their feelings, became more reasonable, thanked him, and two even brought in friends to buy cars.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: Match each class member in A Sure Way of Making Enemies to his or her job.
pairs: Industrial engineering supervisor at a yarn-processing plant
