Salesman for a lumber company in New York
Young New York attorney who argued before the Supreme Court
questions.explain: Carnegie draws on all four to show that telling people they are wrong fails in a courtroom or a business, while respect for their opinions succeeds.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: What did Harold Reinke change in his handling of customers’ complaints, and what does his story show?
questions.a: Reinke, a Dodge dealer, had been hard-boiled and callous with complaints, which caused flared tempers and lost business. He began saying that his dealership had made many mistakes, might have erred in the customer’s case, and asked to be told about it. Customers calmed down, settled more reasonably, thanked him and even brought in friends, showing that respect for others’ opinions wins people over where bluntness drives them away.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: In the story of Mr. S—— before the Supreme Court, what did he reply when a justice said the statute of limitations in admiralty law was six years?
options: That it was actually seven years
That there is no statute of limitations in admiralty
That the question was not relevant to the case
That he would check and report back to the court
questions.explain: Mr. S—— said bluntly: “Your Honor, there is no statute of limitations in admiralty.” He was right, but the correction chilled the court.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: True or false: Mr. S—— later concluded that the Supreme Court justice had been right about the statute of limitations in admiralty.
questions.explain: Mr. S—— still believed he had the law on his side. His point was that being right did not help: he failed to persuade because he told a learned and famous man he was wrong.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: Put the events of Mr. S——’s Supreme Court story in order.
items: A justice says the admiralty statute of limitations is six years
Mr. S—— stares, then says bluntly there is none
A hush falls on the court
Mr. S—— speaks well but fails to persuade
questions.explain: The justice’s remark came first, then the blunt correction, the chill in the room, and finally the realisation that he had not persuaded despite his best speech.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: What lesson does Mr. S——, the young New York attorney, draw from his argument before the Supreme Court?
questions.a: When a justice said the statute of limitations in admiralty was six years, Mr. S—— bluntly told him there was none. He was right and he spoke better than ever, but the court went cold and he did not persuade. He concluded that he had made “the enormous blunder of telling a very learned and famous man that he was wrong.”

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: Which of these does Carnegie list as things most citizens don’t want to change their minds about?
options: Their religion
Their favorite movie star
Their haircut
Their doctor’s advice
Their daily route to work
questions.explain: Carnegie lists religion, haircut, communism and favorite movie star to show that most of us are prejudiced and biased rather than logical.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: True or false: Carnegie advises anyone inclined to tell people they are wrong to read a paragraph from James Harvey Robinson every evening before going to bed.
questions.explain: He says to read it every morning before breakfast. The paragraph comes from Robinson’s book The Mind in the Making.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: Carnegie quotes a paragraph from James Harvey Robinson’s book The Mind in the ____.
questions.explain: Carnegie calls Robinson’s The Mind in the Making an enlightening book and quotes its passage on why we cling to our beliefs.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: According to the James Harvey Robinson passage Carnegie quotes, what is really dear to us when someone says one of our beliefs is wrong?
options: Our self-esteem, which feels threatened
The ideas themselves, which we reasoned out carefully
The people who first taught us the belief
The time and effort we spent forming the belief
questions.explain: Robinson says “It is obviously not the ideas themselves that are dear to us, but our self-esteem which is threatened.” He adds that we form our beliefs quite heedlessly.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: According to the James Harvey Robinson passage Carnegie quotes, the little word ____ is the most important one in human affairs.
questions.explain: Robinson says the word my has the same force whether it is my dinner, my dog, my country or my God, and properly reckoning with it is the beginning of wisdom.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: According to the James Harvey Robinson passage in A Sure Way of Making Enemies, why do people cling to their beliefs when told they are wrong?
questions.a: Robinson says we form our beliefs heedlessly, yet resent any suggestion that they are wrong and harden our hearts. What we defend is not the ideas but our self-esteem, because the belief has become ours, tied to the little word my. So most of our so-called reasoning “consists in finding arguments for going on believing as we already do.”

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: Carl Rogers wrote that he found it of enormous value when he could permit himself to ____ the other person.
questions.explain: Rogers says it is necessary to permit oneself to understand another, because our first reaction to what we hear is usually to judge it.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: According to the Carl Rogers passage in A Sure Way of Making Enemies, what is our first reaction to most of the statements we hear from other people?
options: Agreement, because we want to be liked
Silence, while we think of a reply
An evaluation or judgment rather than an understanding
Curiosity about where the speaker got the idea
questions.explain: Rogers says we almost immediately feel that’s right, that’s stupid or that’s unreasonable, and very rarely let ourselves understand what the statement means to the other person.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: Sort each idea by which writer Carnegie quotes for it in A Sure Way of Making Enemies.

items.t: We change our minds easily until told we are wrong
Our self-esteem, not the idea, is what feels threatened
Most reasoning is finding arguments to keep believing
Our first reaction to a statement is to judge it
We rarely understand what a statement means to the speaker
It is necessary to permit oneself to understand another

questions.explain: Robinson’s passage from The Mind in the Making is about why we defend our beliefs; Rogers’s passage from On Becoming a Person is about judging instead of understanding.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: Match each book quoted or recommended in A Sure Way of Making Enemies to its author.
pairs: An autobiography Carnegie calls a classic of American literature
questions.explain: Carnegie quotes Robinson and Rogers on how people judge and defend beliefs, and recommends Franklin’s autobiography for its advice on dealing with people.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: In Carnegie’s story of the expensive draperies, why did he admit he had paid too much to the second friend but not to the first?
options: The second friend knew more about interior decorating
He had had time to think the price over by then
The first friend was someone he disliked
The second friend admired the draperies instead of attacking his judgment
questions.explain: The first friend told the truth, but it reflected on his judgment, so he defended himself. The second admired the draperies, and with no attack to resist he freely confessed he had paid too much.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: Put the events of Carnegie’s draperies story in order.
items: The bill arrives and Carnegie is dismayed
A friend says the decorator put one over on him
Carnegie defends the price as buying quality
Another friend admires the draperies
Carnegie admits he paid too much
questions.explain: The blunt friend made him defend the purchase; the admiring friend the next day made him confess. The order shows that the same truth is admitted only when no one forces it on us.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: What does Carnegie’s story of the expensive draperies show about how people admit they are wrong?
questions.a: When one friend said the decorator had cheated him, Carnegie defended the price, even though she was right, because few people like truths that reflect on their judgment. When another friend admired the draperies, he admitted he had paid too much. We may admit our mistakes to ourselves, and to others if handled gently and tactfully, but not when someone tries to force the unpalatable fact on us.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: How did Horace Greeley try to make President Lincoln agree with him?
options: By a campaign of argument, ridicule and abuse
By private letters full of flattery
By organising public meetings against him
By offering his newspaper’s support in return
questions.explain: Greeley waged a bitter campaign of argument, ridicule and abuse for years, and Lincoln never came round. Carnegie’s verdict is that ridicule and abuse never work.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: In Ben Franklin’s story, what did the old Quaker friend warn would happen to young Franklin if he kept his opinionated ways?
options: He would lose his business to more polite rivals
He would never know any more than he did now, since no one would try to tell him anything
He would be voted out of every public office he held
He would end up quarrelling with his own family
questions.explain: The friend said Franklin knew so much that no one could tell him anything, and no one would try, so he was not likely to know more than he did now, which was very little.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: Which of these did the old Quaker friend say in rebuking young Ben Franklin?
options: His opinions had a slap in them for everyone who differed with him
He wrote too slowly to succeed as a printer
His friends enjoyed themselves better when he was not around
He spent far too much money on books
He knew so much that no man could tell him anything
questions.explain: The rebuke was about Franklin’s offensive, know-it-all manner, not about his work or his spending.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: Ben Franklin said he made it a rule to forbear all direct ____ to the sentiment of others, and all positive assertion of his own.
questions.explain: Franklin also forbade himself words that implied a fixed opinion, and began his replies by noting where the other person’s opinion would be right.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: Which of these expressions did Ben Franklin adopt in place of words that imported a fixed opinion?
options: It is certainly so
Undoubtedly this is the case
It so appears to me at present
I am sure you will agree
questions.explain: Franklin dropped words like certainly and undoubtedly and used phrases such as I conceive, I apprehend, I imagine, or it so appears to me at present.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: Sort each expression by whether Ben Franklin forbade it or adopted it.

items.t: certainly
undoubtedly
I conceive
I apprehend
I imagine
it so appears to me at present

questions.explain: Franklin forbade himself every word that imported a fixed opinion and adopted tentative expressions that left room for the other person.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: True or false: Ben Franklin said that for perhaps fifty years no one had heard a dogmatical expression escape him.
questions.explain: Franklin said the modest manner he first put on against his natural inclination became so habitual that for perhaps fifty years no dogmatical expression escaped him.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: To what does Ben Franklin chiefly credit his influence in public councils, after his character of integrity?
options: His eloquence as a public speaker
His wealth and family connections
His skill at winning debates
His habit of proposing his opinions modestly
questions.explain: Franklin says he was a bad speaker, never eloquent and hesitant in his words, yet he generally carried his points thanks to his modest, non-dogmatic habit.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: Put the stages of Ben Franklin’s change in order.
items: An old Quaker friend rebukes him
He realises the rebuke is true
He makes a rule against direct contradiction
The modest manner becomes habitual
He carries his points in public councils
questions.explain: Franklin accepted the rebuke, changed his ways by rule, found the manner became second nature, and credits it for his influence in public life.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: How did Ben Franklin change after the old Quaker friend’s rebuke, and what did he say the change gained him?
questions.a: Franklin accepted the rebuke and made it a rule to forbear all direct contradiction of others and all positive assertion of his own, avoiding words like certainly and using phrases like I conceive or I imagine. When he thought someone was in error, he first noted where their opinion would be right. His conversations went more pleasantly, his opinions met less contradiction, and though a bad speaker he generally carried his points in public councils.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: Why did Katherine A. Allred’s first meeting about her new incentive system fail?
options: She was so busy defending her system that she left management no opening to admit problems with the old one
Her system could not handle the twelve different varieties of yarn
Management had already chosen a system from another plant
She presented the system without any figures to support it
questions.explain: Allred told management in detail how they were wrong and left them no graceful way to admit the old system’s problems, so the issue was dead.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: Which of these did Katherine A. Allred do at her second meeting with management about the incentive system?
options: She asked where they felt their problems were
She told them in detail how they were wrong
She asked their opinions on the best way to proceed
She brought in an outside expert to support her
She let them develop her system themselves with low-keyed suggestions
questions.explain: The second time she asked questions and offered only occasional suggestions, so management built the system and then enthusiastically accepted it. Telling them they were wrong was what sank the first meeting.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: Put the events of Katherine A. Allred’s incentive-system story in order.
items: She tells management in detail how they are wrong
The meeting fails and the issue is dead
She takes several sessions of the course
She asks management where their problems are
Management enthusiastically accepts her system
questions.explain: The failure came from proving management wrong; after the course she drew out their views and let them reach her system themselves.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: To what does R. V. Crowley compare lumber inspectors, because once they make a decision they never change it?
options: Supreme Court justices
Baseball umpires
Army sergeants
Customs officers
questions.explain: Crowley said lumber inspectors “are like baseball umpires. Once they make a decision, they never change it.” Winning arguments with them had cost his firm thousands of dollars.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: In R. V. Crowley’s story, why was the customer’s inspector grading the white pine too strictly?
options: He had been told to reject the shipment whatever its quality
He was using an out-of-date set of grading rules
He was schooled in hard woods but not experienced in white pine
He disliked Crowley from an earlier argument
questions.explain: Crowley saw that the inspector knew hard woods but was not a competent inspector of white pine, which was Crowley’s own strong suit. He still raised no objection.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: Which of these did R. V. Crowley do at the customer’s plant when his lumber was rejected?
options: He asked them to keep unloading so he could see how things were going
He quoted the grading rules to show the lumber was up to grade
He asked friendly questions about why certain pieces were unsatisfactory
He told the inspector he was misinterpreting the rules
He insisted they were right to reject boards unsuitable for their purpose
questions.explain: Crowley deliberately did not quote rules or say the inspector was wrong. Friendly questions and agreement that they were right to reject unsuitable boards thawed the inspector.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: Sort each action by whether R. V. Crowley did it before or after he changed his tactics.

items.t: Told lumber inspectors they were wrong
Won arguments that did no good
Lost his firm thousands of dollars
Asked the inspector to keep laying out rejects
Asked friendly questions about rejected pieces
Agreed they need not take unsuitable boards

questions.explain: For years Crowley won arguments and lost money; after resolving to abandon arguments he watched, asked questions and never insinuated the inspector was wrong.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: True or false: In R. V. Crowley’s story, the inspector finally went through the entire carload again, accepted the whole lot, and Crowley’s firm received a check in full.
questions.explain: After Crowley left, the inspector reinspected the car and accepted all of it. Crowley says tact saved a substantial amount of cash and goodwill beyond price.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: Put the events of R. V. Crowley’s carload story in order.
items: A customer phones to say the lumber is below grade
Crowley asks them to continue unloading
Crowley asks friendly questions about rejects
The inspector admits he is inexperienced on white pine
The inspector accepts the whole carload
questions.explain: Crowley let the inspector keep working, questioned him in a friendly way, and gradually the inspector admitted his inexperience and accepted the lot.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: How did R. V. Crowley get the customer’s inspector to accept a carload he had rejected, and what did it save?
questions.a: Instead of quoting grading rules and proving the inspector wrong, Crowley asked him to keep laying out rejects and asked friendly questions about why pieces were unsatisfactory, insisting they were right to reject boards unsuitable for their purpose. The inspector warmed up, admitted he was inexperienced on white pine and realised his firm had not specified a good enough grade. He accepted the whole carload, saving Crowley’s company a substantial amount of cash and much goodwill.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.section: Principle: Show respect for the other person’s opinions. Never say, “You’re wrong.”
questions.q: Asked how a pacifist could admire General Daniel “Chappie” James, Martin Luther King replied: I judge people by their own ____—not by my own.
questions.explain: King’s answer shows respect for another person’s standards: he judged James by James’s principles, not his own.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.section: Principle: Show respect for the other person’s opinions. Never say, “You’re wrong.”
questions.q: Match each historical figure in A Sure Way of Making Enemies to what Carnegie reports about him.
pairs: Tried to drive Lincoln into agreement by ridicule and abuse
Praised an officer who missed no chance to malign him
Judged people by their own principles, not his
Told his son to be diplomatic to gain his point
questions.explain: Greeley is the warning example; Lee, King and Akhtoi show the respect and diplomacy that Carnegie recommends.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.section: Principle: Show respect for the other person’s opinions. Never say, “You’re wrong.”
questions.q: What do the examples of Robert E. Lee and Martin Luther King show about respecting other people’s opinions?
questions.a: King admired General James despite their differing views because, as he said, “I judge people by their own principles—not by my own.” Lee praised an officer who often maligned him, explaining that the president had asked his opinion of the officer, not the officer’s opinion of him. Both show fairness toward others and judging them on their own terms instead of attacking them for disagreeing.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.section: Principle: Show respect for the other person’s opinions. Never say, “You’re wrong.”
questions.q: True or false: Carnegie says King Akhtoi of Egypt advised his son to be diplomatic about 200 years before Christ was born.
questions.explain: Carnegie says it was 2,200 years before Christ, to show that the chapter’s idea is very old. He also cites Jesus: “Agree with thine adversary quickly.”

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.section: Principle: Show respect for the other person’s opinions. Never say, “You’re wrong.”
questions.q: Sort each approach by whether A Sure Way of Making Enemies says it makes people dig in or opens their minds.

items.t: Announcing that you will prove something to them
Bluntly telling them they are wrong
A campaign of ridicule and abuse
Saying you may be wrong and examining the facts
Asking questions in a friendly, cooperative spirit
Noting where their opinion would be right

questions.explain: Every attack on a person’s judgment arouses opposition; admitting you may be wrong, asking questions and noting where they are right lets them change their minds without losing face.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.section: Principle: Show respect for the other person’s opinions. Never say, “You’re wrong.”
questions.q: Principle 2 of Part Three of How to Win Friends and Influence People begins: Show ____ for the other person’s opinions.
questions.explain: The full principle is to show respect for the other person’s opinions and never say “You’re wrong.”

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.section: Principle: Show respect for the other person’s opinions. Never say, “You’re wrong.”
questions.q: Recite Principle 2 of Part Three from memory, and say briefly what it asks of the reader.
questions.a: Show respect for the other person’s opinions. Never say, “You’re wrong.” It asks us not to tell people bluntly that they are wrong, by word, look or gesture, since that wounds their pride and makes them resist. Instead we should admit we may be wrong, examine the facts together and use a little diplomacy.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.section: Principle: Show respect for the other person’s opinions. Never say, “You’re wrong.”
questions.q: Why does Carnegie say that telling people they are wrong never makes them want to agree with you?
questions.a: Telling people they are wrong strikes a direct blow at their intelligence, judgment, pride and self-respect. That makes them want to strike back, never to change their minds, and once their feelings are hurt even perfect logic will not alter their opinions. Since changing minds is hard enough already, Carnegie asks why we should handicap ourselves.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.section: Principle: Show respect for the other person’s opinions. Never say, “You’re wrong.”
questions.q: A manager hears a team member present a plan she is sure contains a serious mistake, in front of the whole team. Using A Sure Way of Making Enemies, how should she respond?
questions.a: She should not say the plan is wrong, by word or look, since that would strike at the team member’s pride and make him defend it. She could say “I thought otherwise, but I may be wrong,” suggest they examine the facts together, and ask questions that let him find the problem himself, as Allred and Crowley did. Noting first where his idea is right, as Franklin did, would make him more willing to change it.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: Which chapter follows A Sure Way of Making Enemies in Part Three and turns to the case where you are the one in the wrong?
options: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
A Drop of Honey
The Secret of Socrates
You Can’t Win an Argument
questions.explain: If You’re Wrong, Admit It comes next, so the book moves from not telling others they are wrong to admitting your own errors. You Can’t Win an Argument comes before this chapter.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: Match each early chapter of Part Three to its principle.
pairs: The only way to get the best of an argument is to avoid it
A Sure Way of Making Enemies
Show respect for others’ opinions; never say they are wrong
If you are wrong, admit it quickly and emphatically
questions.explain: These are Principles 1 to 4 of Part Three, How to Win People to Your Way of Thinking, which open by removing the habits that make people resist.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: Sort each principle into the part of How to Win Friends and Influence People where it appears.
groups: Part Two: Six Ways to Make People Like You
Part Three: How to Win People to Your Way of Thinking

items.t: Smile
Be a good listener
Remember a person’s name
Avoid arguments
Show respect for the other person’s opinions
Begin in a friendly way

questions.explain: Part Two is about being liked; Part Three, where this chapter sits, is about winning people to your way of thinking, starting with not arguing or telling them they are wrong.

questions.unitTitle: A Sure Way of Making Enemies—and How to Avoid It
questions.q: How does A Sure Way of Making Enemies follow from You Can’t Win an Argument and prepare for If You’re Wrong, Admit It?
questions.a: You Can’t Win an Argument says the only way to get the best of an argument is to avoid it. This chapter narrows that to the commonest spark of argument, telling someone they are wrong, and replaces it with respect and the phrase that you may be wrong. The next chapter turns the same idea around: when you really are wrong, admit it quickly and emphatically.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.q: In If You’re Wrong, Admit It, what rule was Carnegie breaking when he walked his dog Rex in Forest Park?
options: Letting the dog run without a muzzle or a leash
Walking the dog in the park after dark
Letting the dog chase the park’s squirrels
Riding a horse on the park’s footpaths
questions.explain: The mounted policeman reprimanded him for letting the dog run loose in the park without a muzzle and leash, which was against the law. Carnegie admitted he knew the law but thought Rex would do no harm.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.q: In If You’re Wrong, Admit It, why does Carnegie say the mounted policeman let him off when he condemned himself?
options: The officer had already forgotten his earlier warning
Showing mercy was the only way left to nourish his self-esteem
The officer feared Carnegie would complain to the judge
Carnegie promised to keep the dog at home in future
questions.explain: Being human, the policeman wanted a feeling of importance. Once Carnegie condemned himself, the officer could only feel important by taking the magnanimous attitude of showing mercy.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.q: In If You’re Wrong, Admit It, what did Carnegie do when the mounted policeman caught Rex loose a second time?
options: He argued that a small dog could do no real harm
He apologized and quickly put the muzzle on the dog
He spoke first and declared himself guilty with no excuses
He waited silently for the officer to write the fine
questions.explain: He did not wait for the officer to start talking: he said he had been caught red-handed and had no alibis or excuses. The argument that a little dog does no harm was later made by the policeman himself.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.q: In If You’re Wrong, Admit It, what did the commercial artist Ferdinand E. Warren say made him leave a fault-finding art director’s office in disgust?
options: The director’s refusal to pay him on time
The rush deadlines the director always set
The criticism itself, which was usually unfair
The director’s method of attack, not the criticism
questions.explain: Warren said he often left in disgust “not because of the criticism, but because of his method of attack.” He accepted that rush jobs can lead to slight errors.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.q: In If You’re Wrong, Admit It, how did Ferdinand E. Warren’s meeting with the hostile art director end?
options: The director took him to lunch and gave him a check and another commission
The director accepted his offer to redo the whole drawing for free
The director gave the next commission to a more careful artist
The director made him correct the error before paying him
questions.explain: Warren’s eagerness to criticize himself took all the fight out of the director, who refused to let him redo the drawing, took him to lunch and gave him a check and a new commission.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.q: In If You’re Wrong, Admit It, what mistake had Bruce Harvey of Albuquerque made?
options: He had fired an employee who was on sick leave
He had authorized full wages for an employee on sick leave
He had forgotten to pay an employee for overtime work
He had blamed the personnel department for a payroll error
questions.explain: Harvey had wrongly authorized full wages to an employee on sick leave. It was his boss, not Harvey, who blamed the personnel department.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.section: Principle: If you are wrong, admit it quickly and emphatically
questions.q: In If You’re Wrong, Admit It, whom did Robert E. Lee ask to appoint “a younger and abler man” after Pickett’s charge failed?
options: General George E. Pickett
General Lewis A. Armistead
Jefferson Davis, president of the Confederacy
The Confederate division commanders
questions.explain: Lee was so saddened and shocked that he sent in his resignation and asked Jefferson Davis, the president of the Confederacy, to appoint a younger and abler man.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.section: Principle: If you are wrong, admit it quickly and emphatically
questions.q: In If You’re Wrong, Admit It, why had Michael Cheung’s middle-aged class member in Hong Kong waited for his son to make the first move?
options: His son had refused an earlier apology
He was still recovering from opium addiction
He did not know where his son was living
In Chinese tradition an older person cannot take the first step
questions.explain: The father, now cured of opium addiction, felt bound by the tradition that an older person cannot take the first step, so he believed his son should seek reconciliation.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.section: Principle: If you are wrong, admit it quickly and emphatically
questions.q: In If You’re Wrong, Admit It, how did Elbert Hubbard typically answer a reader who wrote in angrily to disagree with an article?
options: He said he did not entirely agree with it himself and invited the reader to visit
He printed the letter and answered each of the reader’s points in turn
He thanked the reader but explained why the article was correct
He ignored the insults and simply sent a copy of his next article
questions.explain: Hubbard replied that, thinking it over, he did not entirely agree with the article himself, was glad to learn the reader’s view and invited him to visit. Carnegie asks what anyone could say to a man who treated them like that.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.section: Principle: If you are wrong, admit it quickly and emphatically
questions.q: At the close of If You’re Wrong, Admit It, what does Carnegie advise us to do when we are right?
options: Admit we may be wrong even when we are not
Hold firm until the other person concedes
Try to win people gently and tactfully to our way of thinking
Say nothing and let events prove us right
questions.explain: He pairs two rules: when we are right, win people gently and tactfully to our way of thinking; when we are wrong, admit it quickly and with enthusiasm.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.q: Which principle comes directly before If you are wrong, admit it quickly and emphatically in Part Three of How to Win Friends and Influence People?
options: The only way to get the best of an argument is to avoid it
Show respect for the other person’s opinions. Never say, “You’re wrong.”
Begin in a friendly way
Talk about your own mistakes before criticizing the other person
questions.explain: Chapter 3.2 teaches never to tell others they are wrong; Chapter 3.3 turns to the other case, when we ourselves are wrong. Avoiding argument is Principle 1 and beginning in a friendly way is Principle 4.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.q: True or false: In If You’re Wrong, Admit It, Bruce Harvey’s boss first blamed the personnel department for the payroll error.
questions.explain: The boss blamed the personnel department, then the accounting department, then two other people, while Harvey kept repeating that it was his own fault.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.q: True or false: In If You’re Wrong, Admit It, Carnegie says the chances are ten to one that criticizing yourself first will lead the other person to take a generous, forgiving attitude.
questions.explain: Carnegie puts the odds far higher: “The chances are a hundred to one that a generous, forgiving attitude will be taken”.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.section: Principle: If you are wrong, admit it quickly and emphatically
questions.q: True or false: At the close of If You’re Wrong, Admit It, Carnegie says that if we are honest with ourselves we will find we are wrong only rarely.
questions.explain: He says the opposite: we are wrong surprisingly often if we are honest with ourselves, which is why the habit of admitting it matters.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.q: True or false: If you are wrong, admit it quickly and emphatically is the third principle in Part Three, How to Win People to Your Way of Thinking.
questions.explain: It is Principle 3 of Part Three, after avoiding arguments and showing respect for the other person’s opinions, and before beginning in a friendly way.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.q: In If You’re Wrong, Admit It, Carnegie asks: isn’t it much easier to listen to ____ than to bear condemnation from alien lips?
questions.explain: If we are going to be rebuked anyway, he argues, it is far better to beat the other person to it and criticize ourselves.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.q: In If You’re Wrong, Admit It, Carnegie says there is a certain degree of satisfaction in having the ____ to admit one’s errors.
questions.explain: Admitting errors takes courage, and it clears the air of guilt and defensiveness and often helps solve the problem the error created.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.section: Principle: If you are wrong, admit it quickly and emphatically
questions.q: In If You’re Wrong, Admit It, Carnegie praises Robert E. Lee for blaming himself and only himself for the failure of ____’s charge at Gettysburg.
questions.explain: Lee rode out alone to meet the beaten troops returning from Pickett’s charge and told them the defeat was his fault.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.section: Principle: If you are wrong, admit it quickly and emphatically
questions.q: In If You’re Wrong, Admit It, the Hong Kong father said he may lose ____ by asking a younger person’s forgiveness, but it was his responsibility to admit his fault.
questions.explain: Losing face mattered in his tradition, but he decided the principle outweighed it, went to his son and was forgiven.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.section: Principle: If you are wrong, admit it quickly and emphatically
questions.q: If You’re Wrong, Admit It ends with an old proverb: by fighting you never get enough, but by ____ you get more than you expected.
questions.explain: The proverb sums up the chapter’s stories, in which giving way to the other person brought back more than any defense could have won.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.section: Principle: If you are wrong, admit it quickly and emphatically
questions.q: Complete the principle of If You’re Wrong, Admit It: If you are wrong, admit it quickly and ____.
questions.explain: The principle reads: If you are wrong, admit it quickly and emphatically. In the closing paragraph Carnegie also puts it as admitting our mistakes quickly and with enthusiasm.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.section: Principle: If you are wrong, admit it quickly and emphatically
questions.q: Which of these does Carnegie say about General George E. Pickett in If You’re Wrong, Admit It?
options: He refused to lead the attack himself
His auburn hair almost touched his shoulders
He wrote ardent love-letters almost daily on the battlefield
He blamed Lee publicly for the defeat
He rode off with his cap at a rakish angle over his right ear
questions.explain: Carnegie paints Pickett as picturesque: long auburn locks, daily love letters like Napoleon in Italy, and a jaunty ride toward the Union lines. Nothing in the chapter has him refusing to lead or blaming Lee.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.section: Principle: If you are wrong, admit it quickly and emphatically
questions.q: Which of these were true of the class member in Michael Cheung’s Hong Kong course, as told in If You’re Wrong, Admit It?
options: His son had turned down an earlier apology
He had been estranged from his son for many years
He had never seen his grandchildren
He admitted his fault quickly as soon as the course began
He had once been an opium addict
questions.explain: The father, a cured opium addict, had been estranged from his son for years and had never met his grandchildren. He said it was too late to admit his fault quickly, only emphatically.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.q: Which of these did the art director say after Ferdinand E. Warren criticized himself, in If You’re Wrong, Admit It?
options: He would give the next job to another artist
The error was not a serious mistake
The whole drawing would have to be redone
The slight error had not cost his firm any money
Warren should lower his fee for the job
questions.explain: The director switched to defending Warren, saying it was not a serious mistake and had cost the firm nothing. He refused Warren’s offer to redo the drawing.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.q: Which of these did the mounted policeman say after Carnegie confessed, in If You’re Wrong, Admit It?
options: That he would have to tell it to the judge
That it is a temptation to let a little dog run when nobody is around
That the dog might bite a child
That Carnegie was taking the matter a bit too seriously
questions.explain: After the confession the officer excused Carnegie and told him to let Rex run over the hill out of sight. The threats about the judge and a bitten child came in the first encounter, before Carnegie learned to condemn himself.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.q: Put the events of Carnegie’s encounters with the mounted policeman in Forest Park in order.
items: The officer reprimands Carnegie for the loose, unmuzzled dog
Carnegie meekly promises to obey the law
Carnegie and Rex decide to take a chance without the muzzle
Carnegie confesses before the officer can speak
The officer tells him to let Rex run over the hill out of sight
questions.explain: The first meeting brought threats; after Carnegie broke his promise and was caught, his quick confession turned the officer into a merciful ally.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.q: Put the events of Ferdinand E. Warren’s meeting with the fault-finding art director in order.
items: The director phones to say something is wrong with a rush job
Warren says he is at fault and ashamed of himself
The director starts to defend Warren
Warren offers to do the drawing all over
The director takes Warren to lunch and gives him another commission
questions.explain: Each time Warren criticized himself, the director moved further to his side, ending by refusing the redo and offering more work.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.section: Principle: If you are wrong, admit it quickly and emphatically
questions.q: Put these moments of Pickett’s charge at Gettysburg, as Carnegie tells them, in order.
items: Pickett’s troops cheer him as he rides toward the Union lines
Union infantry rise from behind the stone wall and fire
Armistead vaults over the stone wall
Southern battleflags are planted on Cemetery Ridge
Lee rides out alone to meet the returning troops
questions.explain: The charge reached Cemetery Ridge only for a moment, the high-water mark of the Confederacy, before Lee met the beaten troops and took all the blame.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.q: Put the first four principles of Part Three, How to Win People to Your Way of Thinking, in order.
items: The only way to get the best of an argument is to avoid it
Show respect for the other person’s opinions
If you are wrong, admit it quickly and emphatically
Begin in a friendly way
questions.explain: Part Three moves from avoiding argument, to never telling others they are wrong, to admitting our own errors, and then to beginning in a friendly way.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.section: Principle: If you are wrong, admit it quickly and emphatically
questions.q: Match each person in If You’re Wrong, Admit It to how they admitted a fault.
pairs: Offered to redo a drawing for a fault-finding art director
Kept telling his boss a payroll error was his own fault
Told his beaten troops he alone had lost the battle
Told angry readers he did not entirely agree with his article himself
Asked his estranged son for forgiveness
questions.explain: Each example shows a different setting, business, war, writing and family, where taking the blame turned conflict into goodwill.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.q: Match each figure named in If You’re Wrong, Admit It to the description Carnegie gives.
pairs: The standard of graciousness Carnegie compares the policeman to
Led the final plunge over the stone wall
President of the Confederacy who received Lee’s resignation
Taught Carnegie’s course in Hong Kong
questions.explain: Rex and Lord Chesterfield belong to the opening policeman story; Armistead and Davis to the Gettysburg story; Cheung to the Hong Kong reconciliation.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.section: Principle: If you are wrong, admit it quickly and emphatically
questions.q: Match each story in If You’re Wrong, Admit It to the lesson it best shows.
pairs: Self-condemnation lets the other person feel important by showing mercy
Refusing alibis can end a chain of blame and earn respect
Admitting fault can matter more than keeping an old tradition
Agreeing with a critic can turn an enemy into a friend
questions.explain: Carnegie uses each story to show a different payoff of admitting error: mercy, respect, reconciliation and friendship.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.q: Sort each remark from the second Forest Park encounter in If You’re Wrong, Admit It by who said it.

items.t: I’m guilty. I have no alibis, no excuses
Sure it’s a temptation, but it is against the law
No, but he may kill squirrels
A little dog like that isn’t going to harm anybody
I think you are taking this a bit too seriously
Let him run over the hill where I can’t see him

questions.explain: The two men swapped sides: Carnegie argued the case against himself, and the officer argued for leniency.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.section: Principle: If you are wrong, admit it quickly and emphatically
questions.q: Sort each item about Robert E. Lee after Pickett’s charge in If You’re Wrong, Admit It into alibis Lee could have used or what Lee actually did.

items.t: Some division commanders had failed him
The cavalry arrived too late to support the infantry
This had gone wrong and that had gone awry
Sent his resignation to Jefferson Davis
Rode out alone to meet the beaten troops
Said the defeat was all his own fault

questions.explain: Carnegie says Lee could have found a score of alibis but was far too noble to blame others, and few generals in history have had the courage to admit what he did.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.section: Principle: If you are wrong, admit it quickly and emphatically
questions.q: Sort each item from If You’re Wrong, Admit It into defending your mistakes or admitting your mistakes.

items.t: What any fool can do, and most fools do
Breaking lances with a policeman
Seeking alibis
Raises one above the herd
Clears the air of guilt and defensiveness
A lot more fun than trying to defend oneself

questions.explain: Carnegie says any fool can defend his mistakes, but admitting them gives a feeling of nobility and exultation, clears the air and is more fun.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.q: In If You’re Wrong, Admit It, why did the mounted policeman turn lenient when Carnegie condemned himself?
questions.a: The policeman, being human, wanted a feeling of importance. When Carnegie condemned himself first, there was nothing left to scold, so the only way the officer could nourish his self-esteem was to take the magnanimous attitude of showing mercy. Had Carnegie defended himself, he would have been arguing with a policeman.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.q: In If You’re Wrong, Admit It, what does Carnegie advise doing when you know you are going to be rebuked anyway, and what result does he expect?
questions.a: Beat the other person to it: say about yourself all the derogatory things you know the other person is thinking or intends to say, before they get the chance. Carnegie says the chances are a hundred to one that the other person will then take a generous, forgiving attitude and minimize your mistakes, as the mounted policeman did.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.q: In If You’re Wrong, Admit It, how did Ferdinand E. Warren’s self-criticism change the art director’s behavior?
questions.a: The director had been hostile and gloating, eager to criticize. When Warren said he was at fault, had no excuse and was ashamed, the director began defending him, calling it a minor detail that had cost nothing. Warren’s eagerness to criticize himself took all the fight out of the director, who took him to lunch and gave him a check and another commission.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.q: In If You’re Wrong, Admit It, what did Bruce Harvey gain by refusing to seek alibis for his payroll error?
questions.a: Each time his boss exploded and blamed someone else, Harvey repeated that the mistake was his. The boss finally accepted it and told him to straighten it out, so the error was corrected and nobody got into trouble. Harvey felt great for handling a tense situation, and his boss respected him more ever since.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.section: Principle: If you are wrong, admit it quickly and emphatically
questions.q: In If You’re Wrong, Admit It, why does Carnegie hold up Robert E. Lee’s conduct after Pickett’s charge as an example?
questions.a: Lee could have blamed the defeat on division commanders, late cavalry or other things that went wrong, but he was too noble to blame others. He rode out alone to meet the beaten troops and said, “All this has been my fault,” then offered his resignation. Carnegie says few generals in history have had the courage and character to admit that.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.section: Principle: If you are wrong, admit it quickly and emphatically
questions.q: In If You’re Wrong, Admit It, what does the story from Michael Cheung’s Hong Kong class show about applying the principle?
questions.a: It shows that the benefit of applying the principle can outweigh an old tradition. The father believed an older person cannot take the first step, so he waited for his estranged son. Deciding it was too late to admit his fault quickly but not too late to admit it emphatically, he asked his son’s forgiveness, received it and met his grandchildren at last.

questions.unitTitle: If You’re Wrong, Admit It
questions.q: How does If You’re Wrong, Admit It fit with the chapter before it on never telling people they are wrong?
questions.a: Chapter 3.2 deals with the case where the other person is wrong: show respect for their opinions and never say they are wrong. Chapter 3.3 covers the other case, when we are wrong, which Carnegie says is surprisingly often. He sums up both: when right, win people gently and tactfully; when wrong, admit it quickly and with enthusiasm.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.q: In A Drop of Honey, what does Woodrow Wilson say will happen if someone comes at him with fists doubled?
options: He will step back and let the other man cool off
His own fists will double just as fast
He will ask the man to sit down and take counsel
He will give way so long as the man is sincere
questions.explain: Wilson promised that his fists would double “as fast as yours.” Sitting down to take counsel is the alternative he recommends, not his reaction to hostility.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.q: In A Drop of Honey, why was John D. Rockefeller, Jr., the most fiercely despised man in Colorado in 1915?
options: He had bought up the state’s farmland at strike-breaking prices
He had publicly called the striking miners lawless agitators
He controlled the Colorado Fuel and Iron Company during a bloody miners’ strike
He had closed the coal camps and evicted miners’ families
questions.explain: Miners were striking for higher wages against the Colorado Fuel and Iron Company, which Rockefeller controlled. The strike had lasted two years, with property destroyed and strikers shot.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.q: In A Drop of Honey, what had Rockefeller done in the weeks before he addressed the strikers’ representatives?
options: Visited the coal camps, talked with the representatives and met their families
Prepared detailed figures proving the company could not raise wages
Arranged for troops to keep order at the meeting
Sent written offers of a small wage increase to each camp
questions.explain: Carnegie stresses that Rockefeller spent weeks making friends: he visited the southern coal field camps, spoke with nearly every representative, and met many wives and children in their homes.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.q: In A Drop of Honey, what was the outcome of Rockefeller’s friendly speech to the strikers’ representatives?
options: The company granted the full wage increase the strikers wanted
The miners agreed to arbitration by an outside board
The strike ended only after a further year of negotiation
The strikers went back to work without another word about the wage increase
questions.explain: The speech presented facts so amicably that the strikers returned to work without saying another word about the raise they had fought for so violently. It also won Rockefeller a host of admirers.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.q: A manager has watertight figures proving that a resentful employee is wrong about a decision. According to A Drop of Honey, what is likely to happen if the manager simply lays out the proof?
options: The employee will accept the figures because logic settles the matter
The employee will become more hostile, because ill feeling is not overcome by logic
The employee will agree outwardly and then quietly comply
The employee will ask for time and then come round on his own
questions.explain: Carnegie argues that when a man’s heart is full of ill feeling toward you, you cannot win him “with all the logic in Christendom.” Proving people wrong stirs up more anger, as he says would have happened had Rockefeller argued with the miners.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.section: Principle: Begin in a friendly way
questions.q: In A Drop of Honey, what did Robert F. Black of the White Motor Company do for the idle strike pickets?
options: Paid them half wages for as long as the strike lasted
Invited them to a dinner with the company’s directors
Bought them baseball bats and gloves and rented a bowling alley
Offered them temporary jobs in another of the company’s plants
questions.explain: Instead of condemning the strikers, Black praised them in the Cleveland papers, bought baseball equipment so they could play on vacant lots, and rented a bowling alley for those who preferred it.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.section: Principle: Begin in a friendly way
questions.q: A lawyer wants to persuade a sceptical committee. Which opening best follows the method that A Drop of Honey credits to Daniel Webster?
options: This may be worth thinking about, and with your experience you will see why
Any reasonable person must admit that my case is unanswerable
Let me show you exactly where your earlier view went wrong
I will now prove beyond doubt that you have been misled
questions.explain: Webster introduced his strongest arguments with mild remarks such as “This may, perhaps, be worth thinking of,” with no bulldozing or high-pressure methods. The other openings force an opinion or tell the listener he is wrong.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.section: Principle: Begin in a friendly way
questions.q: In A Drop of Honey, what did O. L. Straub talk about first when his hard-boiled landlord came to see him?
options: How high the rent was compared with other buildings
The failures of other tenants to get a reduction
His plan to move out when the lease expired
How much he liked the apartment house and how well it was run
questions.explain: Straub deliberately did not begin with the high rent. He greeted the landlord warmly and praised the building and its management before mentioning that he could not afford to stay.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.section: Principle: Begin in a friendly way
questions.q: In A Drop of Honey, what did the photographer think the scene of Dean Woodcock’s pole repair proved?
options: That the utility’s equipment was unsafe and badly maintained
That companies like the utility were full of waste motion
That the repair crew had not been properly trained
That the company was hiding an accident from the public
questions.explain: Seeing dozens of people watching two men on a pole, the photographer believed it showed waste and planned to tell his stockholder mother and perhaps the newspapers.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.section: Principle: Begin in a friendly way
questions.q: In A Drop of Honey, how did Gerald H. Winn open his meeting with the subdivision owner about his flooded basement?
options: By listing the repair bills for the furnace and water heater
By pointing out that the owner had neglected to put in a storm drain
By talking about the owner’s recent vacation to the West Indies
By mentioning that he had consulted a lawyer about the damage
questions.explain: Winn stayed calm and began with the owner’s West Indies vacation, raising the “little” water problem only when the timing felt right.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.q: Why is the chapter titled A Drop of Honey?
options: It recalls the beehive image from the book’s first chapter about criticism
It refers to Rockefeller’s description of his speech to the miners
It names a fable of Aesop that Carnegie read as a boy
It comes from Lincoln’s maxim that friendliness wins more than bitterness
questions.explain: The title comes from the maxim Lincoln quoted: “a drop of honey catches more flies than a gallon of gall.” Carnegie returns to it at the chapter’s end; the boyhood fable is the sun and the wind, not the honey saying.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.q: How does A Drop of Honey fit with the three chapters before it in Part Three, How to Win People to Your Way of Thinking?
options: They warn against arguing, saying you’re wrong and defending your own errors; this one shows how to open positively
They deal with making people like you; this one begins the advice on leadership
They teach how to criticise without offence; this one teaches how to praise
They are about listening; this one is about talking in terms of the other person’s interests
questions.explain: Principles 1 to 3 of Part Three tell the reader to avoid arguments, respect others’ opinions and admit mistakes. Principle 4, “Begin in a friendly way,” turns to how to start the conversation in the first place.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.q: True or false: In A Drop of Honey, Carnegie says that a person whose heart is rankling with ill feeling toward you can still be won over if your logic is strong enough.
questions.explain: Carnegie says the opposite: you cannot win such a person “with all the logic in Christendom.” People may be led, not forced, if you are gentle and friendly.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.q: True or false: In A Drop of Honey, Lincoln advises that if you would win a man to your cause, you should first convince him that you are his sincere friend.
questions.explain: Lincoln said that such friendship is the drop of honey that catches a man’s heart, which is “the great high road to reason.”

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.section: Principle: Begin in a friendly way
questions.q: True or false: In A Drop of Honey, the White Motor Company strike dragged on for months and ended with lasting bitterness on both sides.
questions.explain: Carnegie reports that the strike ended with a compromise settlement within a week, without any ill feeling or rancor.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.section: Principle: Begin in a friendly way
questions.q: True or false: A tenant who opens a rent negotiation by listing everything wrong with the building is following the approach that worked for O. L. Straub in A Drop of Honey.
questions.explain: Straub did the reverse: he praised the building and its management first. He says it was the friendly, sympathetic, appreciative approach that won, while the complaining methods of other tenants had failed.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.section: Principle: Begin in a friendly way
questions.q: True or false: In A Drop of Honey, F. Gale Connor got his car problem dealt with by going past the service department to the dealership owner and speaking warmly of his reputation.
questions.explain: Connor saw that shouting at or reasoning with the service manager would not work. He told the owner, Mr. White, that friends had recommended the dealership, and the owner got personally involved and even lent him his car.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.q: In A Drop of Honey, Lincoln quotes the old maxim that a drop of honey catches more flies than a gallon of ____.
questions.explain: The maxim contrasts a little sweetness with a great deal of bitterness. Carnegie closes the chapter by repeating it.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.q: In A Drop of Honey, Lincoln says that the drop of honey catches a man’s heart, which is the great high road to ____.
questions.explain: For Lincoln, winning the heart through sincere friendship comes before any appeal to reason, because the heart is the road to it.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.q: In A Drop of Honey, Carnegie says people cannot be forced or driven to agree with us, but they may possibly be ____ to, if we are gentle and friendly.
questions.explain: Carnegie contrasts forcing and driving with leading: people “may possibly be led to” agree when we are gentle and friendly.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.section: Principle: Begin in a friendly way
questions.q: In A Drop of Honey, Carnegie says Robert F. Black’s friendliness toward the strikers did what friendliness always does: it begot ____.
questions.explain: The strikers answered Black’s kindness by borrowing brooms and carts and tidying up the factory grounds while still on strike.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.section: Principle: Begin in a friendly way
questions.q: In A Drop of Honey, O. L. Straub says that with his landlord he was hearty in his approbation and lavish in his ____.
questions.explain: Straub echoes the book’s earlier phrase “hearty in my approbation and lavish in my praise,” and praised the building before mentioning money.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.section: Principle: Begin in a friendly way
questions.q: In the fable told in A Drop of Honey, the sun tells the wind that gentleness and friendliness are always stronger than fury and ____.
questions.explain: The wind’s fury only made the old man clutch his coat tighter, while the sun’s warmth made him take it off.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.section: Principle: Begin in a friendly way
questions.q: The principle of A Drop of Honey is: Begin in a ____ way.
questions.explain: Principle 4 of Part Three is “Begin in a friendly way.” Every example in the chapter opens with friendliness before the problem is raised.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.q: Which of these ideas appeared in Rockefeller’s speech to the strikers’ representatives, as quoted in A Drop of Honey?
options: That they met not as strangers but as friends
That he was there only by their courtesy
That outside agitators had misled the miners
That he was glad to discuss their common interests
That the company could not afford higher wages
questions.explain: The speech glowed with friendship: meeting as friends, being present by their courtesy, and discussing common interests. It contained no accusations and no argument about wages.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.q: Which of these people does Carnegie, in A Drop of Honey, say ought to realize that people don’t want to change their minds?
options: Scolding parents
Domineering bosses
Nagging wives
Patient teachers
Generous employers
questions.explain: Carnegie names scolding parents, domineering bosses, husbands and nagging wives, people who try to force agreement. Patient or generous people are not the ones he warns.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.section: Principle: Begin in a friendly way
questions.q: Which of these did Robert F. Black do during the White Motor Company strike, according to A Drop of Honey?
options: Praised the strikers in an advertisement in the Cleveland papers
Bought the pickets baseball bats and gloves
Rented a bowling alley for strikers who preferred bowling
Threatened to replace the strikers with new workers
Warned the public about tyranny and Communists
questions.explain: Black did not lose his temper or talk of tyranny and Communists. He complimented the strikers on “the peaceful way in which they laid down their tools” and gave them ways to pass the time.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.section: Principle: Begin in a friendly way
questions.q: Which of these did O. L. Straub’s landlord do after Straub’s friendly reception, according to A Drop of Honey?
options: Told Straub his troubles with complaining tenants
Offered to reduce the rent without being asked
Asked what decorating he could do for Straub
Insisted that Straub sign a two-year lease
Raised the rent of the other tenants instead
questions.explain: Relieved to have a satisfied tenant, the landlord shared his troubles, offered a reduction, accepted Straub’s figure, and on leaving asked what decorating he could do.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.section: Principle: Begin in a friendly way
questions.q: Which of these did the subdivision owner agree to do for Gerald H. Winn, according to A Drop of Honey?
options: Pay for the water damage
Put in a storm drain to prevent it happening again
Buy back the house at its full price
Pay for Winn’s insurance in future years
questions.explain: A few days after the friendly meeting, the owner called to say he would pay for the damage and install a storm drain. Winn believes that without the friendly start he would have struggled to get the owner to accept full liability.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.q: Put these events of Rockefeller’s handling of the Colorado strike, as told in A Drop of Honey, in the order they happened.
items: A bloody strike rages for two years
Rockefeller spends weeks making friends in the camps
Rockefeller gives his friendly speech to the representatives
The strikers go back to work without more talk of wages
questions.explain: Carnegie stresses that the friendship-building came first: weeks of visits to camps and homes made it possible for the speech to win over men who had wanted to hang him.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.section: Principle: Begin in a friendly way
questions.q: Put the stages of O. L. Straub’s dealings with his landlord, as told in A Drop of Honey, in order.
items: Straub writes that he will vacate when his lease expires
Straub greets the landlord warmly and praises the building
The landlord tells of his troubles with complaining tenants
The landlord offers to reduce the rent
The landlord asks what decorating he can do
questions.explain: The friendly opening came before any mention of money. The landlord then opened up about his troubles, offered a reduction unprompted, and finally offered decorating as he left.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.section: Principle: Begin in a friendly way
questions.q: Put the events of the fable of the sun and the wind, as told in A Drop of Honey, in order.
items: The wind bets it can get the old man’s coat off first
The wind blows until it is almost a tornado
The old man clutches his coat tighter
The sun comes out and smiles kindly on the old man
The old man mops his brow and takes off his coat
questions.explain: The harder the wind blew, the tighter the man held his coat; only the sun’s warmth made him remove it. The sun then told the wind that gentleness and friendliness are stronger than fury and force.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.q: Put the first five principles of Part Three, How to Win People to Your Way of Thinking, in the book’s order.
items: Avoid arguments
Show respect for the other person’s opinions
If you are wrong, admit it quickly
Begin in a friendly way
Get the other person saying yes, yes
questions.explain: A Drop of Honey gives Principle 4, coming after the chapter on admitting your own mistakes and before The Secret of Socrates, which teaches getting the other person saying “yes, yes” immediately.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.q: In A Drop of Honey, match each speaker to what he said.
pairs: Come at me with fists doubled and mine will double as fast
First convince a man you are his sincere friend
This is a red-letter day in my life
People don’t want to change their minds and can’t be forced
questions.explain: Wilson, Lincoln and Carnegie each make the case that hostility breeds hostility and friendliness wins; Rockefeller’s speech is the chapter’s first demonstration.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.section: Principle: Begin in a friendly way
questions.q: In A Drop of Honey, match each person to the situation in which he used a friendly approach.
pairs: A bloody strike of Colorado coal miners
A strike at the White Motor Company plant
Trying to get his rent reduced
questions.explain: Carnegie moves from strikes and courtrooms to an everyday matter like rent, to show the friendly approach works far beyond big public conflicts.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.section: Principle: Begin in a friendly way
questions.q: In A Drop of Honey, match each class member to the problem he faced.
pairs: A hard-boiled landlord and high rent
A photographer who saw waste in a repair job
A flooded basement caused by a missing storm drain
A new car back at the service department a third time
questions.explain: Each class member faced someone who could easily have become an opponent, and each solved the problem by beginning in a friendly way.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.section: Principle: Begin in a friendly way
questions.q: In A Drop of Honey, four class members each opened a difficult conversation with goodwill. Match each to what he actually said or did first.
pairs: Praised the apartment house and how it was run
Agreed with a critical photographer that the scene looked wasteful before explaining it
Chatted about a recent vacation to the West Indies
Said friends had recommended the dealership
questions.explain: Each man led with goodwill, praise or agreement instead of anger. Straub, Winn and Connor raised their complaint only after that. Woodcock calmed a photographer who was ready to show the company as wasteful.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.q: In A Drop of Honey, sort these into what Rockefeller actually did with the miners and what Carnegie imagines he might have done instead.

items.t: Visited the camps and talked with the representatives
Met many of the miners’ wives and children
Spoke of mutual friendship and common interests
Hurled devastating facts in their faces
Told them by his tones that they were wrong
Proved by the rules of logic that they were wrong

questions.explain: Carnegie imagines the argumentative alternative to show what it would have produced: more anger, more hatred, more revolt.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.section: Principle: Begin in a friendly way
questions.q: In A Drop of Honey, sort these actions during the White Motor Company strike by who did them.
groups: Robert F. Black, the company president

items.t: Praised the peaceful way the tools were laid down
Bought baseball bats and gloves
Rented a bowling alley
Borrowed brooms, shovels and rubbish carts
Picked up cigarette stubs and cigar butts
Tidied the factory grounds

questions.explain: Black’s friendliness came first and the strikers answered in kind, something Carnegie says had never been heard of in American labor wars.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.section: Principle: Begin in a friendly way
questions.q: Sort these approaches by whether A Drop of Honey presents them as the friendly approach or as fury and force.

items.t: Webster’s soft-spoken remarks to the jury
Woodcock agreeing the scene looked wasteful
Connor’s appeal to the owner’s fine reputation
The wind blowing almost like a tornado
Shouting at the service manager
Condemning strikers and talking of tyranny

questions.explain: Carnegie concludes that kindliness, friendliness and appreciation change minds more readily than “all the bluster and storming in the world.”

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.q: In A Drop of Honey, why does Carnegie say that logic cannot win over someone who feels ill will toward you, and what does he say works instead?
questions.a: When a man’s heart is full of discord and ill feeling toward you, no amount of logic will win him to your way of thinking; people don’t want to change their minds and cannot be forced or driven to agree. They may, however, be led to agree if we are gentle and friendly, ever so gentle and ever so friendly. Lincoln said the same: first convince a man you are his sincere friend.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.q: In A Drop of Honey, explain the point of Woodrow Wilson’s statement about doubled fists and taking counsel together.
questions.a: Wilson says hostility is met with hostility: come at him with fists doubled and his will double as fast. But if people sit down to understand why they differ and what the points at issue are, they will find the differences are few and the agreements many. With patience, candor and the desire to get together, they will get together, which is the chapter’s case for beginning in a friendly way.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.q: In A Drop of Honey, what made Rockefeller’s speech to the strikers’ representatives so remarkable, and what did it achieve?
questions.a: Rockefeller spoke to men who days earlier had wanted to hang him, yet he was as gracious as if addressing medical missionaries. After weeks of visiting camps and homes, he said they met not as strangers but as friends, spoke of mutual friendship and common interests, and said he was there only by their courtesy. The speech calmed the hatred, won him admirers, and the strikers returned to work without another word about the wage increase.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.section: Principle: Begin in a friendly way
questions.q: In A Drop of Honey, how does the White Motor Company strike illustrate the idea that friendliness begets friendliness?
questions.a: Instead of condemning the 2,500 strikers, president Robert F. Black praised them in the Cleveland papers for laying down their tools peacefully, bought baseball gear for idle pickets and rented a bowling alley. The strikers responded by borrowing brooms and carts and cleaning up the factory grounds, something unheard of in American labor wars. The strike ended within a week in a compromise, without ill feeling or rancor.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.section: Principle: Begin in a friendly way
questions.q: A customer posts a photo suggesting your shop wastes money and says the local paper might like it. Using Dean Woodcock’s story in A Drop of Honey, how should you respond, and why?
questions.a: Like Woodcock, you should approach the person in a friendly way, first agree that it does look bad and that you would think the same in their position, and then calmly explain the unusual circumstances. Woodcock did this with a photographer who thought a pole repair showed waste; the man put away his camera, shook his hand and thanked him. The friendly approach saved the company embarrassment and bad publicity, where arguing would have hardened the man’s view.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.section: Principle: Begin in a friendly way
questions.q: Your neighbour’s blocked drain has flooded your garden and you plan to ask them to pay. Using Gerald H. Winn’s story in A Drop of Honey, how would Carnegie advise you to begin, and why?
questions.a: Winn, whose basement flooded because the subdivision owner had neglected to install a storm drain, decided that showing anger would serve no worthwhile purpose. He stayed calm, opened by talking about the owner’s recent vacation, and raised the problem only when the timing felt right; the owner agreed to pay for the damage and add a drain. So you should begin in a friendly way, since Winn says that without it getting the other person to accept full liability would have been very difficult.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.section: Principle: Begin in a friendly way
questions.q: In A Drop of Honey, what lesson does Carnegie draw from Aesop’s fable of the sun and the wind, and why does he say it still applies?
questions.a: The wind’s fury only made the old man clutch his coat tighter, while the sun’s kindly warmth made him take it off; gentleness and friendliness are stronger than fury and force. Carnegie notes that Aesop lived some twenty-six centuries ago, yet his truths about human nature hold just as well today. Kindliness, a friendly approach and appreciation change minds more readily than all the bluster and storming in the world.

questions.unitTitle: A Drop of Honey
questions.q: How does A Drop of Honey build on the earlier chapters of Part Three, and why does it make sense for it to come before The Secret of Socrates?
questions.a: The earlier chapters of Part Three warn against arguing, against telling people they are wrong, and urge admitting your own mistakes, all ways of not stirring up opposition. A Drop of Honey adds a positive first move: begin in a friendly way, since a person full of ill feeling cannot be won by logic. Having opened in friendship, the next chapter shows how to keep agreement going by getting the other person saying “yes, yes” immediately.

questions.unitTitle: The Secret of Socrates
questions.q: In The Secret of Socrates, why does Professor Overstreet say a “No” response is such a difficult handicap to overcome?
options: Once people say “No,” their pride demands they stay consistent with it
A “No” usually means the listener lacks the facts needed to agree
A “No” is a sign of anger that must cool before any talk can go on
Most people learn to say “No” in childhood and cannot unlearn it
questions.explain: Overstreet’s point is about pride: even if the “No” later seems ill-advised, the person feels bound to it. “Once having said a thing, you feel you must stick to it.”

questions.unitTitle: The Secret of Socrates
questions.q: In The Secret of Socrates, what does the comparison with a billiard ball illustrate about early “Yes” responses?
options: A listener rolls wherever the strongest speaker pushes
Once moving in the affirmative direction, a listener takes force to deflect and far more to reverse
Each “Yes” loses force, so a speaker must keep pushing harder
A listener bounces back to “No” as soon as the pressure stops
