questions.explain: A ball propelled one way takes some force to deflect and far more to send back the opposite way; early “Yes” responses set the listener’s mind moving in the affirmative direction in the same way.

questions.unitTitle: The Secret of Socrates
questions.q: In The Secret of Socrates, what question gave bank teller James Eberson his first “yes” from the customer who refused to fill in parts of the form?
options: Whether he wanted the highest interest rate the bank could offer
Whether he understood the bank’s rules could not be broken
Whether he would like the bank to pass his money to his next of kin if he died
Whether he had banked at the Greenwich Savings Bank before
questions.explain: Eberson asked whether, if the man died with money in the bank, he would want it transferred to his lawful next of kin. This framed the missing information as serving the customer, not the bank.

questions.unitTitle: The Secret of Socrates
questions.q: In The Secret of Socrates, why did the chief engineer tell Westinghouse representative Joseph Allison he could not buy the rest of the motors?
options: The price was higher than a competitor’s offer
The first motors had broken down within three weeks
The engineer’s budget for the year had been spent
The motors ran too hot for him to put his hand on them
questions.explain: The engineer said the motors were too hot to touch. Allison did not argue; he led him through questions about the association’s temperature standard and the mill room’s heat.

questions.unitTitle: The Secret of Socrates
questions.q: In The Secret of Socrates, how many years of calls had Allison’s company made on the customer before it finally sold him a few motors?
options: Thirteen years
Three years
Ten years
Twenty years
questions.explain: Allison’s predecessor had called for ten years without a sale and Allison called for three more, so the first order came after thirteen years. Three and ten are each only part of the total.

questions.unitTitle: The Secret of Socrates
questions.q: In The Secret of Socrates, what did the pleasant gentleman at the second bow store offer Eddie Snow after explaining they no longer rented bows?
options: A free loan of a bow for his visiting brother
A complete bow set on sale for only $4.95 more than a rental
A discount on his next rental at a partner store
A refund on the equipment he had bought elsewhere
questions.explain: After a string of “yes” answers about past rentals and saving money, the man explained complete bow sets were on sale for $34.95, just $4.95 more than renting. Snow bought one and became a regular customer.

questions.unitTitle: The Secret of Socrates
questions.q: In The Secret of Socrates, how does Carnegie describe the method Socrates used to persuade his opponents?
options: He told them bluntly where their reasoning was wrong
He let them talk until they contradicted themselves
He asked questions they had to agree with, gathering admissions until they accepted his conclusion
He quoted respected authorities until they gave way
questions.explain: Socrates never told people they were wrong; he asked questions his opponent had to agree with, winning one admission after another until the opponent embraced a conclusion he would have bitterly denied minutes before.

questions.unitTitle: The Secret of Socrates
questions.section: Principle: Get the other person saying “yes, yes” immediately
questions.q: A manager wants a reluctant team to adopt a new weekly check-in. Which opening best follows the principle “Get the other person saying ‘yes, yes’ immediately” from The Secret of Socrates?
options: Announce that the check-in starts Monday and is not up for debate
Begin by listing the problems the team has caused by poor communication
Ask the team to vote on the idea before any discussion
Ask whether they want fewer surprises late in projects, and whether a quick shared update might help
questions.explain: Carnegie advises starting with points of agreement and questions the other person will answer “Yes” to, so they move in the affirmative direction. An ultimatum or opening with faults invites an early “No.”

questions.unitTitle: The Secret of Socrates
questions.q: In Part Three of How to Win Friends and Influence People, which principle comes immediately before “Get the other person saying ‘yes, yes’ immediately”?
options: Begin in a friendly way
Let the other person do a great deal of the talking
If you are wrong, admit it quickly and emphatically
Appeal to the nobler motives
questions.explain: Principle 4, in A Drop of Honey, is to begin in a friendly way; The Secret of Socrates follows as Principle 5. Letting the other person do the talking comes next, as Principle 6.

questions.unitTitle: The Secret of Socrates
questions.q: True or false: In The Secret of Socrates, Carnegie advises beginning a talk by discussing the things on which you differ, so the disagreements are out of the way.
questions.explain: He says the opposite: don’t begin with differences but keep emphasizing what you agree on, ideally that “your only difference is one of method and not of purpose.”

questions.unitTitle: The Secret of Socrates
questions.q: True or false: In The Secret of Socrates, James Eberson admits that before studying human relations he would have told the customer the bank must refuse his account if he withheld the information.
questions.explain: Eberson says he had done exactly that in the past and is ashamed of it; the ultimatum made him feel like the boss but gave the customer no sense of welcome.

questions.unitTitle: The Secret of Socrates
questions.q: True or false: In The Secret of Socrates, the young man at Eberson’s bank ended up opening a trust account naming his mother as beneficiary.
questions.explain: Once he saw the questions were for his sake, he gave full information, opened a trust account at Eberson’s suggestion with his mother as beneficiary, and gladly answered questions about her too.

questions.unitTitle: The Secret of Socrates
questions.section: Principle: Get the other person saying “yes, yes” immediately
questions.q: True or false: According to The Secret of Socrates, a salesperson who opens by telling a hesitant buyer that the buyer’s doubts are wrong is applying the secret of Socrates.
questions.explain: Socrates never told people they were wrong. Carnegie urges that when tempted to say someone is wrong, we ask a gentle question that will get the “yes, yes” response.

questions.unitTitle: The Secret of Socrates
questions.q: In The Secret of Socrates, Carnegie says that when a person says “No” and really means it, the entire organism gathers itself together into a condition of ____.
questions.explain: Glandular, nervous and muscular systems all gather into a condition of rejection, with a physical withdrawal or readiness for withdrawal.

questions.unitTitle: The Secret of Socrates
questions.q: In The Secret of Socrates, the technique of Socrates, based on getting a “yes, yes” response, is now called the ____.
questions.explain: Carnegie says Socrates’ whole technique, now known by his name, rested on asking questions his opponent would have to agree with until he had an armful of yeses.

questions.unitTitle: The Secret of Socrates
questions.q: In The Secret of Socrates, Carnegie gives Socrates the nickname the ____ of Athens.
questions.explain: Carnegie introduces Socrates as “the gadfly of Athens,” a philosopher who sharply changed the course of human thought.

questions.unitTitle: The Secret of Socrates
questions.q: The Secret of Socrates closes with a Chinese proverb saying that he who treads ____ goes far.
questions.explain: Carnegie quotes the proverb twice, “He who treads softly goes far.”, as age-old wisdom about gentle persuasion.

questions.unitTitle: The Secret of Socrates
questions.section: Principle: Get the other person saying “yes, yes” immediately
questions.q: Principle 5 in The Secret of Socrates reads: Get the other person saying “yes, yes” ____.
questions.explain: The principle stresses timing: the yeses must come at once, before a “No” is spoken and pride makes the person stick to it.

questions.unitTitle: The Secret of Socrates
questions.q: Which of these does Carnegie name, in The Secret of Socrates, as parts of the organism that gather into a condition of rejection when a person really means “No”?
options: Circulatory
Glandular
Skeletal
Nervous
Muscular
questions.explain: The text lists the whole organism as “glandular, nervous, muscular” gathering itself into rejection; circulatory and skeletal systems are not mentioned.

questions.unitTitle: The Secret of Socrates
questions.q: Which of these did Joseph Allison do, in The Secret of Socrates, to win back the chief engineer who said the motors were too hot?
options: Agreed fully that motors running too hot should not be bought
Argued that the engineer had tested the motors wrongly
Asked how hot the mill room was
Asked whether water at 147 degrees would scald his hand
Offered a discount on the remaining motors
questions.explain: Allison refused to argue; he agreed, then asked questions about the association’s standard, the mill room’s temperature and the scalding water, each drawing a “yes.” No discount was offered.

questions.unitTitle: The Secret of Socrates
questions.q: Which of these did James Eberson resolve to do, in The Secret of Socrates, the morning he served the man who refused to answer some questions?
options: Talk about what the customer wanted rather than what the bank wanted
Make clear that the bank’s rules could not be flouted
Get the customer saying “yes, yes” from the very start
Hand the customer over to the bank manager
questions.explain: Eberson resolved to use “a little horse sense”: talk about the customer’s wants and get him saying “yes, yes” from the start. Insisting on the rules was his old habit, which he regretted.

questions.unitTitle: The Secret of Socrates
questions.q: Which of these people does Carnegie mention, in The Secret of Socrates, as hard to turn once they say “No” at the beginning?
options: A student
A customer
An employer
A child
A neighbor
questions.explain: Carnegie lists a student, customer, child, husband or wife: once they say “No,” it takes “the wisdom and the patience of angels” to turn that negative around. Employers and neighbors are not named.

questions.unitTitle: The Secret of Socrates
questions.q: In The Secret of Socrates, put Joseph Allison’s steps with the chief engineer in the order they happened.
items: Gets agreement that motors must meet the association’s standards
Gets agreement that the standard allows 72 degrees above room temperature
Learns the mill room is about 75 degrees
Gets agreement that 147-degree water would scald a hand
Suggests the engineer keep his hands off the motors
questions.explain: Allison built yes upon yes: the standard, the 72-degree allowance, the mill-room heat, the 147-degree total and finally the suggestion to keep hands off, after which $35,000 of business followed.

questions.unitTitle: The Secret of Socrates
questions.q: In The Secret of Socrates, put the steps of Eddie Snow’s phone call with the second bow store in order.
items: Snow asks about renting a bow
The man says they no longer rent bows
The man asks whether Snow has rented before
The man asks whether Snow likes to save money
The man explains complete sets are on sale for $34.95
Snow buys a set and becomes a regular customer
questions.explain: The gentleman collected a series of “yes” answers about past rentals, their cost and saving money before presenting the sale price, so buying felt like the reasonable choice.

questions.unitTitle: The Secret of Socrates
questions.q: In The Secret of Socrates, put these illustrations in the order Carnegie presents them.
items: James Eberson and the bank customer
Joseph Allison and the hot motors
Eddie Snow and the bow store
Socrates and his questions
The Chinese proverb about treading softly
questions.explain: Carnegie gives three modern cases first, then turns to Socrates as the classic master of the method, and closes with the Chinese proverb.

questions.unitTitle: The Secret of Socrates
questions.q: In The Secret of Socrates, match each person to their part in the chapter.
pairs: Explains why a “No” is hard to overcome
Bank teller who won over a reluctant new depositor
Westinghouse representative accused of selling hot motors
Became a regular at a bow store that no longer rented
Won one admission after another with questions
questions.explain: Overstreet supplies the psychology; Eberson, Allison and Snow give modern cases; Socrates is the classic example the chapter is named after.

questions.unitTitle: The Secret of Socrates
questions.q: In The Secret of Socrates, match each figure to what it stood for.
pairs: Heat a motor may run above room temperature
Total motor temperature in the mill room
Business the engineer lined up for the next month
Sale price of a complete bow set
Extra cost of buying a bow set over renting
questions.explain: Allison added the 72-degree allowance to the 75-degree mill room to get 147 degrees and won $35,000 in orders; the bow store priced sets at $34.95, only $4.95 above a rental.

questions.unitTitle: The Secret of Socrates
questions.q: Match each chapter of Part Three of How to Win Friends and Influence People to its principle.
pairs: Admit you are wrong quickly and emphatically
Get the other person saying “yes, yes” immediately
The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints
Let the other person do a great deal of the talking
questions.explain: The Secret of Socrates sits between beginning in a friendly way and letting the other person talk: each principle shapes how a conversation opens so the other person moves toward agreement.

questions.unitTitle: The Secret of Socrates
questions.q: In The Secret of Socrates, sort each reaction by whether it goes with saying “No” and meaning it, or with saying “Yes.”

items.t: Physical withdrawal or readiness for withdrawal
Neuromuscular system on guard against acceptance
Pride demands staying consistent
A forward-moving attitude
An accepting, open attitude
Attention easier to capture for the final proposal

questions.explain: A real “No” sets the whole organism against acceptance and engages pride; a “Yes” brings none of the withdrawal, leaving the person open and more likely to accept the ultimate proposal.

questions.unitTitle: The Secret of Socrates
questions.q: In The Secret of Socrates, sort each action by whether it belongs to James Eberson’s old way with customers or to his “yes, yes” approach.

items.t: Threatening to refuse the account
Showing who was boss
Insisting the rules could not be flouted
Saying the information was not absolutely necessary
Asking about passing money to next of kin
Talking about what the customer wanted

questions.explain: The old ultimatum made Eberson feel important but left the customer unwelcome; the new approach agreed first and framed the questions as serving the customer.

questions.unitTitle: The Secret of Socrates
questions.q: In The Secret of Socrates, explain, using Professor Overstreet’s account, why it matters so much to start a person in the affirmative direction.
questions.a: Once a person says “No,” pride of personality demands that they stay consistent with it, even if they later feel it was ill-advised. A real “No” also sets the whole organism, glandular, nervous and muscular, into a condition of rejection and withdrawal. A “Yes” brings none of this, leaving the person open and forward-moving, so the more yeses we induce at the outset, the more likely we are to win attention for our ultimate proposal.

questions.unitTitle: The Secret of Socrates
questions.q: In The Secret of Socrates, what lesson did Joseph Allison say had cost him years and countless thousands of dollars to learn, and how did he apply it with the chief engineer?
questions.a: He learned that “it doesn’t pay to argue,” and that it is more profitable to see things from the other person’s viewpoint and get them saying “yes, yes.” Instead of disputing the claim that the motors were too hot, he agreed, then asked questions about the National Electrical Manufacturers Association standard allowing 72 degrees Fahrenheit above room temperature, and the 75-degree mill room (147 degrees in all). The engineer admitted 147-degree motors would scald a hand anyway, and he then lined up about $35,000 of business.

questions.unitTitle: The Secret of Socrates
questions.q: In The Secret of Socrates, how and why did the attitude of the young man at James Eberson’s bank change?
questions.a: Eberson agreed that the withheld information was not absolutely necessary, then asked whether the man would want his money passed to his next of kin if he died, and whether it would help to name that person. The man said “yes” each time and softened when he realized the information was for his sake, not the bank’s. He gave complete information and opened a trust account naming his mother as beneficiary, forgetting the original issue.

questions.unitTitle: The Secret of Socrates
questions.section: Principle: Get the other person saying “yes, yes” immediately
questions.q: In The Secret of Socrates, what does Carnegie say Socrates did instead of telling people they were wrong, and what does he urge us to do the next time we are tempted to tell someone they are wrong?
questions.a: Socrates asked questions his opponent would have to agree with, winning one admission after another until the opponent, almost without realizing it, embraced a conclusion he would earlier have bitterly denied. This is the Socratic method, based on the “yes, yes” response. Carnegie urges us to remember old Socrates and ask a gentle question that will get the “yes, yes” response.

questions.unitTitle: The Secret of Socrates
questions.q: How does The Secret of Socrates fit the earlier chapters of Part Three of How to Win Friends and Influence People, and why does its principle belong at this point?
questions.a: Part Three is about winning people to your way of thinking, and its first chapters say to avoid arguments, never tell people they are wrong, admit your own errors and begin in a friendly way. The Secret of Socrates gives a positive technique for the next moment of a conversation: once you have begun in a friendly way, steer at once toward points of agreement so the other person says “Yes” rather than a “No” that pride will defend. It replaces telling someone they are wrong with a gentle question.

questions.unitTitle: The Secret of Socrates
questions.section: Principle: Get the other person saying “yes, yes” immediately
questions.q: Using the principle of The Secret of Socrates, describe how you might talk with a neighbor who angrily objects to your plan to plant a tall hedge on your shared boundary.
questions.a: Begin not with the disagreement but with what you both want, such as privacy, a pleasant garden and good relations, so that your only difference is one of method and not of purpose. Ask gentle questions the neighbor will answer “Yes” to, such as whether they would also like less noise from the road or a shield from passersby, before raising the hedge’s height or position. Avoid telling them they are wrong, since an early “No” makes pride insist on sticking to it.

questions.unitTitle: The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints
questions.q: In The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints, why does Carnegie say it is dangerous to interrupt someone you disagree with?
options: They will not pay attention to you while they still have many ideas of their own wanting expression
They will lose their train of thought and become confused about their own position
They will take the interruption as an admission that you have lost the argument
They will feel obliged to agree with you out of politeness and later resent it
questions.explain: Carnegie warns that people will not listen to you while they still have a lot of ideas of their own “crying for expression.” So you should listen patiently and encourage them to speak fully.

questions.unitTitle: The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints
questions.q: In The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints, what did the motor company’s president do after G.B.R. wrote that he had lost his voice?
options: He postponed the meeting until G.B.R. could speak again
He asked the purchasing agent to read G.B.R.’s written proposal aloud
He offered to speak for G.B.R., showed the samples and praised their good points
He handed G.B.R. a list of questions to answer in writing
questions.explain: The president said he would do the talking, exhibited the samples and praised them, and so took the side G.B.R. would have taken. G.B.R. contributed only smiles, nods and a few gestures.

questions.unitTitle: The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints
questions.q: In The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints, how did Charles T. Cubellis prepare before his interview with the founder of a Wall Street business?
options: He rehearsed a detailed account of his own experience and achievements
He wrote to former employees asking about the firm’s weaknesses
He prepared a list of improvements he could make to the business
He spent hours on Wall Street finding out everything he could about the founder
questions.explain: Before calling, Cubellis spent hours finding out about the person who had founded the business. That research let him open with a question about the founder’s early start, which got the founder talking.

questions.unitTitle: The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints
questions.q: In The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints, why does Carnegie say La Rochefoucauld’s advice about friends is true?
options: Because friends who excel us will eventually help us to excel as well
Because when friends excel us they feel important, but when we excel them some feel inferior and envious
Because people only respect those who are more successful than they are
Because boasting about our own success makes us appear dishonest
questions.explain: Carnegie explains that our friends feel important when they excel us, while some of them feel inferior and envious when we excel them. That is why we should let them talk about their achievements rather than boast about ours.

questions.unitTitle: The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints
questions.q: In The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints, what was unusual about Roy G. Bradley’s story compared with that of Charles Cubellis?
options: Bradley was the candidate, and he won the job by asking about the founder’s past
Bradley lost a good candidate because he talked too much in the interview
Bradley used a written questionnaire instead of a spoken interview
Bradley was the employer, and by listening he let a candidate talk himself into the job
questions.explain: Carnegie says Bradley had “the opposite problem”: he was the one hiring, and by letting Richard Pryor do most of the talking, Pryor convinced himself to join the firm.

questions.unitTitle: The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints
questions.q: True or false: G.B.R. believed he would have lost the upholstery contract if he had not lost his voice.
questions.explain: G.B.R. said he would have lost the contract had he not lost his voice, because he had the wrong idea about the whole proposition. He found by accident how well it pays to let the other person talk.

questions.unitTitle: The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints
questions.q: True or false: The founder interviewed by Charles T. Cubellis said he had started his business with $45,000 in cash and an original idea.
questions.explain: The founder said he started with only $450 in cash and an original idea, with nothing but desk room and one stenographer. The tiny sum is what made his story of struggle so proud.

questions.unitTitle: The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints
questions.q: True or false: According to Carnegie, our friends would much rather listen to us boast about our achievements than talk about their own.
questions.explain: Carnegie says the reverse: even our friends would much rather talk to us about their achievements than listen to us boast about ours.

questions.unitTitle: The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints
questions.section: Principle: Let the other person do a great deal of the talking
questions.q: Principle 6 of Part Three reads: Let the other person do a great deal of the ____.
questions.explain: The principle is to let the other person do a great deal of the talking. It sums up every story in the chapter, from the speechless salesman to the listening mother.

questions.unitTitle: The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints
questions.q: In The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints, G.B.R. lost his voice through a severe attack of ____.
questions.explain: G.B.R. arrived in town with a severe attack of laryngitis and could hardly whisper. His illness forced him to let the president talk for him.

questions.unitTitle: The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints
questions.q: In The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints, Laurie told her mother she needed her not as a bossy mother but as a ____, an outlet for her confusion about growing up.
questions.explain: Mrs. Wilson realised Laurie needed her as a confidante, someone to listen, not someone giving more orders.

questions.unitTitle: The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints
questions.q: In The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints, Carnegie quotes the French philosopher La ____: “If you want enemies, excel your friends; but if you want friends, let your friends excel you.”
questions.explain: The saying comes from La Rochefoucauld, whom Carnegie calls the French philosopher. Carnegie uses it to show why friends prefer to talk about their own achievements.

questions.unitTitle: The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints
questions.q: In The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints, Roy G. Bradley said that because he had been a good ____ and let Dick do most of the talking, Dick was able to weigh both sides fairly.
questions.explain: Bradley credited his success to being a good listener. By resisting the urge to add to Dick’s thoughts, he let Dick reach a positive conclusion on his own.

questions.unitTitle: The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints
questions.q: Which of these does Carnegie advise in the opening of The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints for someone trying to win others to their way of thinking?
options: Ask the other people questions
Interrupt quickly when you disagree so errors do not stand
Listen patiently and with an open mind
Encourage them to express their ideas fully
Explain your own case thoroughly before they reply
questions.explain: Carnegie says to ask questions, listen patiently with an open mind, and encourage people to express their ideas fully. He calls interrupting dangerous and warns that most people already talk too much themselves.

questions.unitTitle: The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints
questions.q: Which of these were present when G.B.R. met the motor company’s executives in conference?
options: The textile engineer
The purchasing agent
The chairman of the board
The president of the company
The company’s chief lawyer
questions.explain: G.B.R. faced the textile engineer, the purchasing agent, the director of sales and the president. No chairman or lawyer is mentioned.

questions.unitTitle: The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints
questions.q: Which of these did the founder tell Charles T. Cubellis about his early struggles?
options: He fought against discouragement and battled ridicule
He worked Sundays and holidays, twelve to sixteen hours a day
He inherited a small firm from his father
He was rescued by a wealthy partner after nearly going bankrupt
questions.explain: The founder described battling discouragement and ridicule and working Sundays and holidays for long hours. He started with $450 and an idea; there was no inheritance or rescuing partner.

questions.unitTitle: The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints
questions.q: Put the events of G.B.R.’s upholstery story in the order they happened.
items: G.B.R. arrives in town with laryngitis
He writes on a pad that he has lost his voice
The president offers to do the talking for him
The president shows the samples and praises them
G.B.R. is awarded the contract
questions.explain: G.B.R. lost his voice, wrote a note, and the president then spoke for him and praised the samples. The lively discussion that followed ended with G.B.R. winning the biggest order he had ever received.

questions.unitTitle: The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints
questions.q: Put the events of Barbara Wilson’s story about her daughter Laurie in the order they happened.
items: Mrs. Wilson lectures, threatens and punishes Laurie without success
Laurie leaves the house before finishing her chores
Too tired to scream, Mrs. Wilson sadly asks why
Laurie asks whether her mother really wants to know
Mrs. Wilson lets Laurie do all the talking she wants
questions.explain: After her failed lectures and punishments, Mrs. Wilson simply asked why when Laurie disobeyed again. Laurie poured out her feelings, and from then on her mother listened and the relationship improved.

questions.unitTitle: The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints
questions.q: In The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints, match each person to their story.
pairs: Lost his voice and won a fabric contract while the president spoke for him
Repaired her relationship with her teenage daughter by listening
Got a job by asking a founder about his early struggles
Let a sales candidate talk himself into joining a small brokerage
Won colleagues as friends by boasting less and listening more
questions.explain: Each story shows the same principle in a different setting: business sales, family, job hunting, hiring and the workplace.

questions.unitTitle: The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints
questions.q: Match each detail from The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints to the story it belongs to.
pairs: Value of the upholstery fabric order
Sum the Wall Street founder started his business with
When the founder began with desk room and one stenographer
Drawbacks of working for Bradley’s small brokerage firm
questions.explain: The fabric order was worth $1,600,000; the founder started with $450 twenty-eight years earlier; and Bradley’s firm offered no benefits or prospect leads, only independence.

questions.unitTitle: The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints
questions.q: In The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints, sort each behaviour into what failed and what worked.

items.t: Mrs. Wilson lecturing and punishing Laurie
Henrietta bragging daily about her placements
Mrs. Wilson asking Laurie why and then listening
Henrietta asking colleagues to share their joys
Cubellis asking the founder about his early start
Mrs. Wilson interrupting Laurie with more orders

questions.explain: In each story, talking at people, boasting and giving orders drove them away, while asking and listening won them over.

questions.unitTitle: The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints
questions.q: In The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints, sort each person by their role in the business stories.

items.t: G.B.R., the fabric representative
Charles T. Cubellis
Richard Pryor, the sales candidate
The motor company’s president
The Wall Street founder
Roy G. Bradley

questions.explain: G.B.R., Cubellis and Pryor were trying to win a contract or job; the president, the founder and Bradley held the power to give it. In each case the deal went well because the other side was allowed to do most of the talking.

questions.unitTitle: The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints
questions.section: Principle: Let the other person do a great deal of the talking
questions.q: Which situation best applies Carnegie’s principle of letting the other person do a great deal of the talking?
options: A shop manager lets an angry customer explain the whole complaint before saying anything
A shop manager quickly lists the store’s return policy as soon as the customer starts
A shop manager corrects each wrong detail as the customer tells the story
A shop manager tells the customer about similar complaints solved last week
questions.explain: Carnegie advises letting people talk themselves out without interrupting, since they will not listen while their own ideas still need expression. Correcting or lecturing first is exactly the interruption he calls dangerous.

questions.unitTitle: The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints
questions.section: Principle: Let the other person do a great deal of the talking
questions.q: Recite Principle 6 of Part Three of How to Win Friends and Influence People from memory.
questions.a: Let the other person do a great deal of the talking.

questions.unitTitle: The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints
questions.q: In The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints, explain why G.B.R. said he would have lost the contract had he not lost his voice.
questions.a: G.B.R. had the wrong idea about the whole proposition and would have done all the talking himself. Because he could not speak, the president spoke for him, praised his samples and took his side in the discussion. He discovered by accident how richly it can pay to let the other person do the talking.

questions.unitTitle: The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints
questions.q: In The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints, what did Barbara Wilson realise about why her relationship with Laurie had broken down, and what changed it?
questions.a: She realised she had never listened to Laurie: she was always giving orders and interrupted whenever Laurie wanted to share her thoughts and feelings. Laurie needed a confidante, not a bossy mother. Once Mrs. Wilson let her do all the talking she wanted, their relationship improved greatly and Laurie became cooperative again.

questions.unitTitle: The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints
questions.q: In The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints, how did Charles T. Cubellis make a favourable impression on his prospective employer?
questions.a: He researched the founder beforehand and opened by asking about the firm’s humble beginnings. Since almost every successful person likes to reminisce about early struggles, the founder talked at length and enjoyed it. Cubellis showed interest in the other person and his problems and let him do most of the talking, and he was hired after only brief questions about his own experience.

questions.unitTitle: The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints
questions.q: How does The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints extend the advice of Chapter 2.4, An Easy Way to Become a Good Conversationalist?
questions.a: Chapter 2.4 taught being a good listener and encouraging others to talk about themselves as a way to make people like you. Chapter 3.6 applies the same habit to winning people to your way of thinking: let them talk themselves out, especially when you disagree. Several of its stories, such as Bradley’s and Cubellis’s, show listening winning business as well as liking.

questions.unitTitle: The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints
questions.q: The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints sits between The Secret of Socrates and How to Get Cooperation. Which link best describes this order?
options: It moves from winning arguments to admitting mistakes and then to criticising tactfully
It moves from getting early yes answers, to letting the other person talk, to letting them feel the idea is theirs
It moves from flattering people, to remembering names, to smiling
It moves from setting a high standard, to dramatising ideas, to throwing down a challenge
questions.explain: Principle 5 is getting the other person saying yes immediately, Principle 6 is letting them do most of the talking, and Principle 7 is letting them feel the idea is theirs. Each step keeps the other person active in reaching agreement.

questions.unitTitle: The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints
questions.q: What does the title The Safety Valve in Handling Complaints suggest about letting the other person talk?
options: It is a way of avoiding complaints by refusing to discuss them
It is a last resort to use only when every other method has failed
It lets the other person release pent-up ideas and feelings so they can then listen to you
It protects you from blame by making the other person speak first
questions.explain: A safety valve releases pressure. Carnegie says people will not attend to you while their own ideas are still crying for expression, so letting them talk themselves out releases that pressure.

questions.unitTitle: How to Get Cooperation
questions.q: In How to Get Cooperation, what did sales manager Adolph Seltz first ask his discouraged salespeople to tell him at the sales meeting?
options: Which of their colleagues was working hardest
Why their sales figures had fallen so far
Exactly what they expected from him
How many hours a day they were willing to work
questions.explain: Seltz first asked what they expected from him and wrote their ideas on the blackboard; only after promising to give them those qualities did he ask what he had a right to expect from them.

questions.unitTitle: How to Get Cooperation
questions.q: In How to Get Cooperation, after how many failed calls on the New York stylist did Eugene Wesson decide he must be in a mental rut?
questions.explain: After 150 failures over three years of weekly calls, Wesson resolved to spend one evening a week studying how to influence human behavior.

questions.unitTitle: How to Get Cooperation
questions.q: In How to Get Cooperation, what did the skillful X-ray manufacturer’s letter to Dr. L—— say about the new machines?
options: They were the finest equipment in America and priced below every rival
They had already been installed in several leading hospitals
They came with a guarantee that the hospital could return them at no cost
They were not perfect, and the firm wanted his ideas on improving them
questions.explain: Instead of praising the equipment like the other sales representatives, the letter admitted the machines were not perfect and asked for the doctor’s advice, which made him feel important.

questions.unitTitle: How to Get Cooperation
questions.q: A manager wants her team to adopt a new weekly planning meeting. According to the principle in How to Get Cooperation, which approach is most likely to win their cooperation?
options: Announce the meeting firmly and explain the penalties for missing it
Describe the problem, ask the team how they would solve it, and build on their suggestions
Circulate a detailed memo showing why her plan is clearly the best one
Ask a senior executive to order the team to attend
questions.explain: Carnegie argues that people resist feeling sold or told and prefer acting on their own ideas, so consulting the team and letting the idea grow from their suggestions follows the Seltz and Wesson pattern.

questions.unitTitle: How to Get Cooperation
questions.section: Principle: Let the other person feel that the idea is his or hers
questions.q: In How to Get Cooperation, what did Colonel Edward M. House do when Woodrow Wilson presented House’s own suggestion as his idea at the dinner table?
options: He politely reminded Wilson where the suggestion had come from
He wrote to The Saturday Evening Post to set the record straight
He let Wilson keep feeling the idea was his and even gave him public credit
He dropped the policy because Wilson had first seemed to disapprove of it
questions.explain: House cared about results, not credit, so he never said the idea was his. He went further and gave Wilson public credit for such ideas.

questions.unitTitle: How to Get Cooperation
questions.section: Principle: Let the other person feel that the idea is his or hers
questions.q: In How to Get Cooperation, how did the New Brunswick camp owner win Carnegie’s business when other camps had flooded him with booklets and testimonials?
options: He sent names and telephone numbers of New York people who had stayed at his camp and invited Carnegie to call them
He offered Carnegie a free first week of fishing and canoeing
He telephoned Carnegie personally to describe the camp’s best features
He sent more printed testimonials than any other camp
questions.explain: The camp owner let Carnegie discover for himself what the camp offered; Carnegie knew one of the men on the list, phoned him and booked. The others tried to sell, but one let him sell himself.

questions.unitTitle: How to Get Cooperation
questions.section: Principle: Let the other person feel that the idea is his or hers
questions.q: In How to Get Cooperation, according to the Lao-tse passage Carnegie quotes, why do rivers and seas receive the homage of a hundred mountain streams?
options: Because they are larger and stronger than the streams
Because they keep below the streams
Because they flow before the streams and lead them
Because the streams have nowhere else to go
questions.explain: Lao-tse says rivers and seas reign over the mountain streams because they keep below them; likewise the sage who wishes to be above people puts himself below them.

questions.unitTitle: How to Get Cooperation
questions.section: Principle: Let the other person feel that the idea is his or hers
questions.q: In How to Get Cooperation, Carnegie quotes Emerson’s essay Self-Reliance. What does Emerson say we recognize in every work of genius?
options: The hard work of a lonely mind
A truth no one else had imagined
The voice of an earlier master
Our own rejected thoughts
questions.explain: Emerson wrote: “In every work of genius we recognize our own rejected thoughts; they come back to us with a certain alienated majesty.”

questions.unitTitle: How to Get Cooperation
questions.section: Principle: Let the other person feel that the idea is his or hers
questions.q: Principle 7 of Part Three reads: Let the other person feel that the ____ is his or hers.
questions.explain: The chapter’s principle is to let the other person feel the idea is his or hers, because people have more faith in ideas they discover for themselves.

questions.unitTitle: How to Get Cooperation
questions.section: Principle: Let the other person feel that the idea is his or hers
questions.q: In How to Get Cooperation, Carnegie quotes Emerson: in every work of genius we recognize our own rejected thoughts; they come back to us with a certain alienated ____.
questions.explain: Emerson’s line in Self-Reliance ends “with a certain alienated majesty”: our own ideas impress us when they return to us.

questions.unitTitle: How to Get Cooperation
questions.q: In How to Get Cooperation, Adolph Seltz said his salespeople had made a sort of ____ bargain with him, which they were determined to keep as long as he kept his part.
questions.explain: Seltz said “The people had made a sort of moral bargain with me,” and consulting them about their wishes was the shot in the arm they needed.

questions.unitTitle: How to Get Cooperation
questions.q: In How to Get Cooperation, Eugene Wesson summed up his changed approach to the stylist: I didn’t have to sell him. He ____.
questions.explain: Once Wesson asked the buyer for his ideas, the buyer felt he was creating the designs, so Wesson no longer had to sell: the buyer bought.

questions.unitTitle: How to Get Cooperation
questions.section: Principle: Let the other person feel that the idea is his or hers
questions.q: In How to Get Cooperation, Colonel House said the best way to convert Woodrow Wilson to an idea was to plant it in his mind ____, but so as to interest him in it.
questions.explain: House learned to plant ideas casually so that Wilson would think about them on his own account, rather than urging policies on him.

questions.unitTitle: How to Get Cooperation
questions.q: True or false: In How to Get Cooperation, Eugene Wesson called on the leading New York stylist once a week for five years before he changed his approach.
questions.explain: Wesson called once a week, every week, for three years. The stylist always looked at the sketches but never bought.

questions.unitTitle: How to Get Cooperation
questions.section: Principle: Let the other person feel that the idea is his or hers
questions.q: True or false: In How to Get Cooperation, Colonel House said that the first time his method of planting an idea in Wilson’s mind worked, it was part of a deliberate plan.
questions.explain: House said the first time it worked it was an accident: Wilson seemed to disapprove of a policy House urged, then days later presented it as his own.

questions.unitTitle: How to Get Cooperation
questions.q: True or false: In Part Three, the principle Let the other person feel that the idea is his or hers comes directly after Let the other person do a great deal of the talking.
questions.explain: Principle 6 of Part Three is to let the other person do a great deal of the talking, and Principle 7, the subject of How to Get Cooperation, follows it.

questions.unitTitle: How to Get Cooperation
questions.q: Which of these did Adolph Seltz’s salespeople say he had a right to expect from them?
options: Loyalty
A larger share of the commissions
Initiative
Fewer sales meetings
Teamwork
questions.explain: Their replies included loyalty, honesty, initiative, optimism, teamwork and eight hours a day of enthusiastic work; they asked for nothing in return at that point.

questions.unitTitle: How to Get Cooperation
questions.q: Which of these does Dr. L—— give as reasons he ordered the X-ray equipment described in How to Get Cooperation?
options: He felt important because a manufacturer had sought his advice
The manufacturer offered the lowest price
He felt the idea of buying the equipment was his own
The sales representative praised the machines more convincingly than rivals
The letter promised the machines were perfect
questions.explain: Dr. L—— said the letter made him feel important and that nobody had tried to sell to him: he felt the idea was his own and sold himself. The letter actually admitted the machines were not perfect.

questions.unitTitle: How to Get Cooperation
questions.section: Principle: Let the other person feel that the idea is his or hers
questions.q: Which of these does Carnegie say about Colonel House’s handling of Woodrow Wilson in How to Get Cooperation?
options: He did not care about credit
He wanted results
He interrupted Wilson to claim the idea as his own
He gave Wilson public credit for the ideas
He was a member of Wilson’s cabinet
questions.explain: House was too adroit to claim credit; he wanted results and gave Wilson public credit. He was a secret adviser whom Wilson leaned on even more than members of his cabinet.

questions.unitTitle: How to Get Cooperation
questions.q: In How to Get Cooperation, put the stages of Eugene Wesson’s dealings with the New York stylist in order.
items: Calls weekly for three years without a sale
Resolves to study influencing human behavior one evening a week
Brings unfinished sketches and asks how to finish them
Returns three days later to collect the buyer’s suggestions
Has the sketches finished to the buyer’s ideas and all are accepted
questions.explain: Wesson’s years of failure led him to study human behavior; his new approach of asking for the buyer’s ideas led to every sketch being accepted and scores of later orders.

questions.unitTitle: How to Get Cooperation
questions.q: Put these principles from Part Three, How to Win People to Your Way of Thinking, in the order Carnegie presents them.
items: Get the other person saying yes, yes immediately
Let the other person do a great deal of the talking
Let the other person feel that the idea is his or hers
Try honestly to see things from the other person’s point of view
questions.explain: These are Principles 5 to 8 of Part Three. How to Get Cooperation (Principle 7) sits between letting the other person talk and seeing things from the other person’s point of view.

questions.unitTitle: How to Get Cooperation
questions.q: In How to Get Cooperation, match each person to how they let someone else own the idea.
pairs: Asked his salespeople what they expected from him and what he could expect from them
Asked a buyer how unfinished sketches could be completed so he could use them
Asked his daughter if she would like to visit the places from her history course
Invited a hospital doctor to look over new machines and suggest improvements
questions.explain: Each person consulted the other side instead of pressing a conclusion, so the salespeople, the buyer, the family and the doctor all felt the decision was their own.

questions.unitTitle: How to Get Cooperation
questions.section: Principle: Let the other person feel that the idea is his or hers
questions.q: In How to Get Cooperation, match each source to the idea Carnegie takes from it.
pairs: We recognize our own rejected thoughts in every work of genius
The sage who wishes to be above people puts himself below them
Plant an idea casually so the other person thinks about it on his own account
Let the customer phone past guests and discover the value for himself
questions.explain: All four point the same way: influence works best when the other person feels the idea or decision came from within.

questions.unitTitle: How to Get Cooperation
questions.section: Principle: Let the other person feel that the idea is his or hers
questions.q: In How to Get Cooperation, sort these actions by whether they try to sell or tell, or let the other person own the idea.
groups: Letting the other person own the idea

items.t: Wesson urging the buyer to buy what Wesson thought he ought to have
Rival X-ray sales representatives praising their own equipment
Camps mailing Carnegie booklets and printed testimonials
Wesson asking the buyer how to finish the sketches
A camp owner inviting Carnegie to phone his former guests
House planting an idea casually in Wilson’s mind

questions.explain: Carnegie contrasts those who pushed their wares with those who let the other person discover the idea; in his words about the camps, “The others had been trying to sell me on their service, but one let me sell myself.”

questions.unitTitle: How to Get Cooperation
questions.q: In How to Get Cooperation, sort these destinations by whose vacation idea they belonged to in Paul M. Davis’s family.

items.t: Gettysburg battlefield
Independence Hall
Williamsburg
New Mexico
Arizona
Nevada

questions.explain: Davis wanted historic eastern sites, while Nancy wanted a western tour. By interesting their daughter Anne in the eastern sites, Davis let Nancy herself propose the eastern trip.

questions.unitTitle: How to Get Cooperation
questions.q: In How to Get Cooperation, why did Eugene Wesson fail for years to sell sketches to the New York stylist, and what changed?
questions.a: Wesson had urged the buyer to buy what Wesson thought he ought to have, so after three years and 150 calls he had made no sales. He then took unfinished sketches and asked the buyer how they could be finished so he could use them. The buyer felt he was creating the designs, accepted all of them and ordered scores more; as Wesson put it, he didn’t have to sell him: he bought.

questions.unitTitle: How to Get Cooperation
questions.q: In How to Get Cooperation, how did Paul M. Davis get his family to choose an eastern historic vacation without arguing for it?
questions.a: Davis wanted to see eastern historic sites, while his wife Nancy wanted a western tour. Instead of pressing his case, he asked their daughter Anne, fresh from a U.S. history course, whether she would like to visit the places she had studied. Two evenings later Nancy herself proposed the eastern trip as great for Anne, and everyone agreed, because the idea now felt like hers.

questions.unitTitle: How to Get Cooperation
questions.section: Principle: Let the other person feel that the idea is his or hers
questions.q: In How to Get Cooperation, what lesson does Carnegie draw from Lao-tse’s saying about rivers, seas and mountain streams?
questions.a: Lao-tse says rivers and seas reign over the mountain streams because they keep below them, and so the sage who wishes to be above people puts himself below them and behind them. Then people do not feel his weight or resent his lead. Carnegie offers it as advice for readers: lead by staying in the background and letting others feel the ideas are their own.

questions.unitTitle: How to Get Cooperation
questions.q: Why is Principle 7, Let the other person feel that the idea is his or hers, a fitting chapter in Part Three, How to Win People to Your Way of Thinking, and what does its title How to Get Cooperation signal?
questions.a: Part Three is about winning people to your way of thinking without force, and this chapter builds on the previous principle of letting the other person do most of the talking by taking the next step: letting them reach the conclusion themselves. The title signals that the goal is willing cooperation rather than reluctant compliance, since people dislike feeling sold or told and prefer acting on their own ideas. It leads naturally into the next principle, seeing things honestly from the other person’s point of view.

questions.unitTitle: How to Get Cooperation
questions.section: Principle: Let the other person feel that the idea is his or hers
questions.q: A parent wants a teenager to follow a regular study timetable. Using Colonel House’s technique from How to Get Cooperation, how might the parent go about it?
questions.a: Rather than handing down a timetable, the parent could raise the idea casually in a way that interests the teenager, for example by asking how they would like to fit study around the things they enjoy, so the teenager thinks about it on their own account. When the teenager later proposes a plan, the parent should not say it was really the parent’s idea but let the teenager keep the credit. Like House with Wilson, the parent cares about results, not credit.

questions.unitTitle: A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You
questions.q: In A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You, what does Carnegie say any fool can do when other people are totally wrong?
options: Condemn them
Try to understand them
Put yourself in their place
Find the reason for their actions
questions.explain: Carnegie writes “Don’t condemn them. Any fool can do that.” Trying to understand them is the harder course he says only wise, tolerant, exceptional people attempt.

questions.unitTitle: A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You
questions.q: In A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You, Carnegie says there is a reason why the other person thinks and acts as he does, and that if you ferret out that reason you have the ____ to his actions, perhaps to his personality.
questions.explain: Carnegie says finding the reason behind someone’s behaviour gives you “the key to his actions, perhaps to his personality.”

questions.unitTitle: A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You
questions.q: True or false: In A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You, Carnegie says that only wise, tolerant, exceptional people even try to understand people who are wrong.
questions.explain: After saying any fool can condemn, Carnegie adds “Only wise, tolerant, exceptional people even try to do that,” meaning try to understand them.

questions.unitTitle: A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You
questions.q: In A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You, what does Carnegie say you gain by asking yourself how you would feel and react if you were in the other person’s shoes?
options: You will win every argument you enter
You will save yourself time and irritation and increase your skill in human relationships
You will never again be taken advantage of by others
You will find it easier to prove the other person wrong
questions.explain: Carnegie promises that this question saves time and irritation and will sharply increase your skill in human relationships; the aim is understanding, not winning or proving anyone wrong.

questions.unitTitle: A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You
questions.q: In A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You, Carnegie quotes the saying that by becoming interested in the ____, we are less likely to dislike the effect.
questions.explain: The quoted saying is “by becoming interested in the cause, we are less likely to dislike the effect.” Understanding why someone acts lessens irritation at what they do.

questions.unitTitle: A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You
questions.q: In A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You, what exercise does Kenneth M. Goode suggest in How to Turn People Into Gold, and what conclusion does it lead to?
questions.a: Goode asks you to stop a minute and contrast your keen interest in your own affairs with your mild concern about anything else, then realise that everybody else feels exactly the same way. Grasping this gives you, as it gave Lincoln and Roosevelt, the only solid foundation for dealing with people: “success in dealing with people depends on a sympathetic grasp of the other person’s viewpoint.”

questions.unitTitle: A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You
questions.q: Which of these did Sam Douglas do after he learned to see the lawn from his wife’s point of view?
options: Went out and helped her pull weeds
Complimented her on how fine the lawn looked
Hired someone to cut the grass so she could rest
Persuaded her to cut the grass only once a week
Bought better soil to replace the concrete-like ground
questions.explain: Douglas joined his wife in the weeding and afterwards often helped and praised the fine job she was doing with soil like concrete. He did not try to change her routine or take the work away from her.

questions.unitTitle: A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You
questions.q: True or false: In the Sam Douglas story, it was Mr. Douglas who first suggested that he and his wife spend an evening pulling weeds together.
questions.explain: It was his wife who said she wanted to pull weeds and invited him to keep her company; he first declined, then thought better of it and joined her.

questions.unitTitle: A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You
questions.q: Put the events of the Sam Douglas story in the order they happened.
items: He tells his wife she spends too much time on the lawn
After the course, he realises she enjoys the work
His wife invites him to keep her company while she weeds
He helps her and they spend an hour in pleasant conversation
He often helps and compliments her on how fine the lawn looks
questions.explain: Years of critical remarks came first; the course changed his view, and accepting her invitation to weed led to regular help and praise and a happier life for both.

questions.unitTitle: A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You
questions.q: Priya keeps telling her flatmate that he wastes every Sunday tinkering with his old bicycle, and each time their evening is spoiled. Following the lesson Carnegie draws from Sam Douglas in A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You, what should she do?
options: Explain once more, calmly, why the bicycle is not worth the effort
Say nothing and let him find out for himself
Consider that he may enjoy the work, take an interest in it and praise his effort
Suggest a more useful hobby he could take up instead
questions.explain: Douglas had never considered that his wife enjoyed her gardening and would appreciate a compliment; once he saw it her way, helping and praising her brought a happier life for both.

questions.unitTitle: A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You
questions.q: Which of these does Dr. Gerald S. Nirenberg, quoted in A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You, recommend for encouraging a listener to be open to your ideas?
options: Begin by giving the other person the purpose or direction of your conversation
Govern what you say by what you would want to hear if you were the listener
Accept his or her viewpoint
Open with your strongest argument before the listener can object
Keep your purpose hidden until the listener has agreed to something
questions.explain: Nirenberg lists starting with the purpose or direction of the conversation, speaking as you would want to be spoken to as a listener, and accepting the other’s viewpoint. Leading with your strongest argument or hiding your purpose are not part of his advice.

questions.unitTitle: A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You
questions.q: In A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You, Dr. Gerald S. Nirenberg says cooperativeness in conversation is achieved when you show that you consider the other person’s ideas and feelings as ____ as your own.
questions.explain: Nirenberg writes that cooperativeness comes when you treat the other person’s ideas and feelings “as important as your own.”

questions.unitTitle: A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You
questions.section: Principle: Try honestly to see things from the other person’s point of view
questions.q: In A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You, match each person to what the chapter says about them.
pairs: Success with people depends on a sympathetic grasp of their viewpoint
Treat the other’s ideas and feelings as important as your own
Would rather walk the sidewalk for two hours than enter an interview unprepared
Apologized to the man handling her overdue car payment
Learned to help with and praise his wife’s gardening
questions.explain: Goode and Nirenberg are authors Carnegie quotes, Donham is the Harvard Business School dean, and Novak and Douglas are course members whose stories illustrate the principle.

questions.unitTitle: A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You
questions.section: Principle: Try honestly to see things from the other person’s point of view
questions.q: In A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You, who does Carnegie say caused almost all the fires that killed young trees in the park near his home?
options: Careless smokers walking through the park
Campers who ignored the warning sign
The mounted policeman’s lack of patrols
Youngsters cooking a frankfurter or an egg under the trees
questions.explain: Carnegie stresses that the fires were not caused by careless smokers but almost all by boys who went to the park to go native and cook under the trees.

questions.unitTitle: A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You
questions.section: Principle: Try honestly to see things from the other person’s point of view
questions.q: True or false: In A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You, when Carnegie reported a spreading park fire, the mounted policeman said it was none of his business because he was off duty.
questions.explain: The policeman said it was none of his business because the fire was not in his precinct, not because he was off duty.

questions.unitTitle: A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You
questions.section: Principle: Try honestly to see things from the other person’s point of view
questions.q: In A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You, how did the boys respond when Carnegie first ordered them to put out their fires and threatened them with arrest?
options: They obeyed, but sullenly and with resentment
They refused and he had them arrested
They thanked him and moved to the sandpit
They ran off and left the fire burning
questions.explain: Carnegie says “They obeyed—obeyed sullenly and with resentment,” and he suspects they rebuilt the fire once he had ridden over the hill. The sandpit came only with his later, friendlier approach.

questions.unitTitle: A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You
questions.section: Principle: Try honestly to see things from the other person’s point of view
questions.q: In A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You, why does Carnegie say that in his early efforts to stop park fires he was so eager to do the right thing that he did the wrong thing?
questions.a: He was so unhappy about the fires that he rode up, warned the boys they could be jailed, ordered them with a tone of authority to put the fire out, and threatened arrest. He was merely unloading his own feelings without thinking of the boys’ point of view. The result was sullen, resentful obedience, and he suspects they rebuilt the fire after he left.

questions.unitTitle: A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You
questions.section: Principle: Try honestly to see things from the other person’s point of view
questions.q: In A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You, put the parts of Carnegie’s later, friendlier talk to the boys at a park fire in the order he gave them.
items: Asks if they are having a good time and what they will cook
Says he loved to build fires as a boy and still does
Explains how careless boys’ fires spread and kill the trees
Asks them to rake the leaves away and cover the fire with dirt
Suggests next time they build their fire in the sandpit over the hill
questions.explain: He opened with friendly interest and shared enthusiasm, then explained the danger, made polite requests, and finally offered a harmless place for future fires.

questions.unitTitle: A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You
questions.section: Principle: Try honestly to see things from the other person’s point of view
questions.q: In A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You, sort each item by which of Carnegie’s two ways of handling the boys at the park fires it belongs to.

items.t: Ordering the fire put out with a tone of authority
Threatening to have them arrested if they refused
The boys obeyed sullenly
The boys probably rebuilt the fire later
Asking what they were going to cook for supper
Admitting he loved building fires as a boy
Suggesting the sandpit for their next fire
The boys saved their faces

questions.explain: The first approach only unloaded Carnegie’s feelings and won resentful obedience; the second showed consideration for the boys’ point of view and won willing cooperation.

questions.unitTitle: A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You
questions.section: Principle: Try honestly to see things from the other person’s point of view
questions.q: Which of these does Carnegie say resulted from his friendlier way of speaking to the boys at the park fires?
options: The boys wanted to cooperate
The boys saved their faces
Both the boys and Carnegie felt better
The boys promised never to build a fire again
The policeman began to patrol the park properly
questions.explain: Carnegie says the talk made the boys want to cooperate, with no sullenness or resentment; they saved their faces, and both sides felt better. He reports no promise to stop building fires and no change in the policeman.

questions.unitTitle: A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You
questions.section: Principle: Try honestly to see things from the other person’s point of view
questions.q: In A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You, Carnegie says his considerate talk worked because the boys had not been forced to obey orders; instead they had saved their ____.
questions.explain: Carnegie writes “They hadn’t been forced to obey orders. They had saved their faces.” Respecting their dignity removed the resentment.

questions.unitTitle: A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You
questions.section: Principle: Try honestly to see things from the other person’s point of view
questions.q: In A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You, what did Elizabeth Novak say when the man handling her overdue car payment called on Monday morning?
options: She explained that the company’s Friday call had been rude and unfair
She apologised for the inconvenience and said she must be his most troublesome customer
She asked for a meeting with his manager to arrange new terms
She promised to borrow the $122 from a friend by the evening
questions.explain: Instead of becoming upset, Novak looked at things from his side, apologised sincerely and called herself his most troublesome customer. She did not complain or promise money she could not raise.

questions.unitTitle: A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You
questions.section: Principle: Try honestly to see things from the other person’s point of view
questions.q: Put the events of Elizabeth Novak’s car-payment story in the order they happened.
items: On Friday she gets a nasty call demanding $122 by Monday
On Monday she apologises and calls herself his most troublesome customer
His tone changes and he tells her about rude customers
She listens silently while he pours out his troubles
He says she can pay $20 by the end of the month
questions.explain: Her apology from his point of view changed his tone; her silent listening let him unburden himself, and then, without any suggestion from her, he offered easier terms.

questions.unitTitle: A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You
questions.section: Principle: Try honestly to see things from the other person’s point of view
questions.q: True or false: In the Elizabeth Novak story, the man handling her account agreed she could pay $20 by the end of the month and make up the balance whenever it was convenient.
questions.explain: Without any suggestion from her, he said it did not matter if she could not pay at once and offered exactly those terms.

questions.unitTitle: A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You
questions.section: Principle: Try honestly to see things from the other person’s point of view
questions.q: In A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You, how did looking at the situation from the account manager’s point of view change the outcome for Elizabeth Novak?
questions.a: Novak, six weeks late with a car payment and unable to raise $122 by Monday, expected the worst. Instead of getting upset she apologised for the trouble she caused him and called herself his most troublesome customer; his tone changed at once and he told her how rude his other customers were while she listened. Then, unasked, he let her pay $20 by the end of the month and the rest when convenient.

questions.unitTitle: A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You
questions.section: Principle: Try honestly to see things from the other person’s point of view
questions.q: In A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You, what question does Carnegie suggest you ask yourself before asking anyone to put out a fire, buy your product or contribute to your favourite charity?
options: How can I make the strongest case for what I want?
What will happen if he or she refuses?
Why should he or she want to do it?
What have I done for this person lately?
questions.explain: Carnegie advises pausing to think the whole thing through from the other person’s point of view and asking “Why should he or she want to do it?”

questions.unitTitle: A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You
questions.section: Principle: Try honestly to see things from the other person’s point of view
questions.q: Which of these benefits does Carnegie claim for thinking a request through from the other person’s point of view before you make it?
options: It will avoid making enemies
It will get better results
It means less friction and less shoe leather
It takes no extra time at all
It makes the other person feel obliged to you
questions.explain: Carnegie admits “True, this will take time,” but says it avoids making enemies and gets better results with less friction and less shoe leather.

questions.unitTitle: A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You
questions.section: Principle: Try honestly to see things from the other person’s point of view
questions.q: In A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You, Carnegie quotes Dean Donham of the Harvard ____ School on preparing for an interview.
questions.explain: Donham was dean of the Harvard Business School, whose words on preparing for interviews Carnegie repeats in italics for emphasis.

questions.unitTitle: A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You
questions.section: Principle: Try honestly to see things from the other person’s point of view
questions.q: In A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You, what did Dean Donham say about preparing for an interview, and why does Carnegie repeat it?
questions.a: Donham said he would rather walk the sidewalk in front of a person’s office for two hours than step inside without a perfectly clear idea of what he would say and what that person, from his knowledge of the person’s interests and motives, was likely to answer. Carnegie thought it so important that he repeated it in italics for emphasis, because it captures thinking a meeting through from the other person’s point of view.

questions.unitTitle: A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You
questions.section: Principle: Try honestly to see things from the other person’s point of view
questions.q: In A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You, what does Carnegie say about the one thing he hopes a reader gets from the whole book?
questions.a: He says that if the reader gets only one thing from the book, an increased tendency to think always in terms of the other person’s point of view and to see things from that person’s angle as well as their own, it may easily prove to be one of the stepping-stones of the reader’s career.

questions.unitTitle: A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You
questions.section: Principle: Try honestly to see things from the other person’s point of view
questions.q: In A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You, match each situation to its outcome as Carnegie reports it.
pairs: Sam Douglas begins helping with the weeding
A happier life for both him and his wife
Carnegie orders the boys to put out a fire
Carnegie asks the boys what they are cooking
Elizabeth Novak apologises to the account manager
Permission to pay $20 by the end of the month
questions.explain: Each success came from seeing things from the other person’s point of view; the one failure, Carnegie’s early commands, came from ignoring it.

questions.unitTitle: A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You
questions.section: Principle: Try honestly to see things from the other person’s point of view
questions.q: In A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You, sort each item by whether Carnegie recommends it or warns against it.

items.t: Trying to understand people who are wrong
Asking how you would feel in the other person’s shoes
Asking why the other person should want to do it
Knowing the other person’s interests and motives before an interview
Condemning people who are wrong
Unloading your feelings without thinking of the other’s view
Giving orders with a tone of authority
Threatening people with arrest to get obedience

questions.explain: Every recommended habit starts from the other person’s point of view; every warned-against habit, including Carnegie’s own early behaviour in the park, starts only from your own.

questions.unitTitle: A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You
questions.section: Principle: Try honestly to see things from the other person’s point of view
questions.q: Tom wants a colleague to swap weekend shifts with him. Following A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You, what should he do before asking?
options: Remind the colleague of the favours Tom has done in the past
Ask the manager to arrange the swap for him
Prepare a firm request so the colleague cannot easily refuse
Think the request through from the colleague’s side and ask why he would want to do it
questions.explain: Carnegie advises pausing before any request to think it through from the other person’s point of view and ask why he or she should want to do it, which avoids friction and gets better results.

questions.unitTitle: A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You
questions.q: What does the title A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You signal about Chapter 3.8, and what is the formula?
questions.a: The title promises a simple, repeatable method that can be applied anywhere. The formula is to try honestly to see things from the other person’s point of view: ask how you would feel in their shoes, and why they should want to do what you ask. Carnegie shows it working on matters as small as weeds and as tense as an overdue car payment.

questions.unitTitle: A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You
questions.q: The closing wish of A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You, that readers learn to see things from the other person’s angle as well as their own, echoes advice Carnegie quoted earlier in Part One from whom?
options: Henry Ford
Charles Schwab
John D. Rockefeller
Andrew Carnegie
questions.explain: In Part One Carnegie quotes Henry Ford: “If there is any one secret of success,” it lies in the ability to get the other person’s point of view and see things from that person’s angle as well as your own; Chapter 3.8 builds a whole principle on it.

questions.unitTitle: A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You
questions.q: Match each Part Three principle number to its wording, placing A Formula That Will Work Wonders for You among its neighbours.
pairs: Let the other person feel that the idea is his or hers
Try honestly to see things from the other person’s point of view
Be sympathetic with the other person’s ideas and desires
questions.explain: Chapter 3.8 gives Principle 8; it follows How to Get Cooperation (Principle 7) and leads into What Everybody Wants (Principle 9), which moves from seeing another’s view to sympathising with it.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.q: In What Everybody Wants, what does Carnegie say you can tell an irritated person and still be 100 percent sincere?
options: That they are entirely right and you were wrong
That you would feel just as they do if you were them
That their feelings will pass in a day or two
That most reasonable people would agree with them
questions.explain: Carnegie’s magic phrase is sincere because, if you were the other person, you would of course feel just as he does. It does not concede that the other person is right on the facts.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.q: In What Everybody Wants, what point does Carnegie make with the example of Al Capone?
options: That even hardened criminals respond to sincere praise
That criminals almost never blame themselves for anything
That firm punishment is the only answer to bad behaviour
That his body, mind and experiences alone made him what he was
questions.explain: Carnegie says that with Capone’s body, temperament, mind, environment and experiences you would be exactly what he was, for those things alone made him. So people deserve little credit or discredit for being what they are.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.q: In What Everybody Wants, what mistake did Carnegie make in his radio broadcast about Louisa May Alcott?
options: He said twice that she had lived in Concord, New Hampshire
He said she had written Little Women in Philadelphia
He gave the wrong title for her best-known book
He confused her with another Massachusetts author
questions.explain: Alcott lived and wrote in Concord, Massachusetts, but Carnegie spoke of visiting her home in Concord, New Hampshire, and said it twice. Letters and telegrams poured in.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.q: In What Everybody Wants, what did Carnegie do about the Colonial Dame’s angry letter the next time he was in Philadelphia?
options: He wrote her a sharp reply about her poor manners
He spoke to her society about Alcott’s life in Concord
He telephoned her, thanked her for the letter and apologized
He called at her home with a signed copy of his book
questions.explain: He phoned her, thanked her for writing, and called his slip a stupid blunder. The sharp reply about courtesy was what he felt like writing but chose not to.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.q: In What Everybody Wants, what did President Taft say a wise person does with the first severe reply to an offensive letter?
options: Sends it at once while the facts are fresh
Shows it to a trusted adviser before mailing it
Locks it in a drawer for two days and then does not send it
Rewrites it in milder words and posts it next morning
questions.explain: Taft advised locking the letter in a drawer, because “such communications will always bear two days’ delay in answering”, and then not sending it. He then wrote a polite letter instead.
