questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.q: In What Everybody Wants, why did President Taft not give the lobbying mother’s son the position she wanted?
options: The post needed technical qualifications and he followed the Bureau head’s advice
The senators who backed her had turned against the son
Her son was thought too young for so senior a post
He had already promised the post to a political friend
questions.explain: The place required technical qualification, so Taft followed the recommendation of the head of the Bureau and appointed somebody else. The senators had in fact spoken for her son.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.section: Principle: Be sympathetic with the other person’s ideas and desires
questions.q: A customer storms into a shop angry that a delivery came three days late. Which reply best follows the principle of What Everybody Wants?
options: Explain in detail that the courier, not the shop, was at fault
Point out that most deliveries arrive on time
Tell the customer that shouting will not get things done faster
Say you don’t blame them at all, and in their place you would feel the same
questions.explain: Principle 9 is to be sympathetic with the other person’s ideas and desires, as in the magic phrase about feeling just as they do. Explaining whose fault it was is an argument, not sympathy.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.q: In What Everybody Wants, what did Jay Mangum say to the hotel manager to get an eight-hour escalator shutdown?
options: That the maintenance contract required a full repair
That he understood the wish to keep shutdowns short, but a full job now would avoid a shutdown of days
That he would reduce the bill if the manager agreed to close the escalator
That the mechanic would not be available again for months
questions.explain: Instead of arguing, Mangum first sympathized with the manager’s desire not to inconvenience guests, then showed that a complete repair now would spare them a shutdown of several days.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.q: In What Everybody Wants, what did Babette’s mother tell Joyce Norris when thanked for getting Babette to trim her nails?
options: She had nothing to do with it; Babette decided on her own
She had insisted on it after the first lesson
She had promised Babette a reward for doing it
She had told Babette the teacher would refuse to teach her
questions.explain: The mother said Babette chose to do it herself, and that it was the first time she had ever trimmed her nails for anyone. Mrs. Norris had praised the nails rather than threatening.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.q: In What Everybody Wants, what did Sol Hurok do when Chaliapin phoned at noon to say he could not sing that night?
options: He reminded the singer of his contract with the Metropolitan
He sent a throat doctor to the singer’s hotel
He told the singer that the audience would be bitterly disappointed
He rushed over full of sympathy and offered to cancel the engagement
questions.explain: Hurok knew an entrepreneur could not argue with artists, so he hurried over, agreed the singer could not sing, and offered to cancel, saying the cost was nothing next to his reputation.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.q: What Everybody Wants comes right after the Part Three chapter whose principle is to try honestly to see things from the other person’s point of view. How does Principle 9 build on that?
options: It replaces understanding the other person with flattering them
It sets the other person’s feelings aside to focus on the facts
It moves from seeing the other person’s view to openly sympathizing with it
It turns to appealing to the other person’s nobler motives
questions.explain: Carnegie told himself, “After all, if I were she, I would probably feel just as she does,” and then decided to sympathize with her viewpoint. Appealing to nobler motives is the next chapter’s principle.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.q: True or false: In What Everybody Wants, Carnegie says three-fourths of the people you will ever meet are hungering and thirsting for sympathy.
questions.explain: He says “Three-fourths of the people you will ever meet are hungering and thirsting for sympathy,” and that if you give it to them they will love you.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.q: True or false: In What Everybody Wants, after Carnegie’s phone call the Colonial Dame insisted she had been right to write the letter she sent.
questions.explain: She apologized, said she had lost her temper and was ashamed of the letter, and ended by saying she would like to know him better.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.q: True or false: In What Everybody Wants, Dr. Arthur I. Gates is quoted as saying that craving sympathy is a childish trait adults outgrow.
questions.explain: Gates says the human species universally craves sympathy: children display their injuries, and adults show bruises and relate accidents and operations for the same purpose.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.q: True or false: What Everybody Wants gives Principle 9 of Part Three, How to Win People to Your Way of Thinking.
questions.explain: The chapter ends with Principle 9, be sympathetic with the other person’s ideas and desires, one of the Part Three principles for winning people to your way of thinking.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.q: In What Everybody Wants, Carnegie says the only reason you are not a ____ is that your mother and father weren’t.
questions.explain: The joke makes the Al Capone point: what we are comes from what we inherited and experienced, so we deserve little credit for it.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.q: In What Everybody Wants, Carnegie advises saying to yourself about irritated, unreasoning people: There, but for the grace of ____, go I.
questions.explain: Because such people deserve little discredit for what they are, Carnegie tells the reader to pity and sympathize with them and repeat this saying.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.q: In What Everybody Wants, President Taft is said to have learned the enormous chemical value of ____ in neutralizing the acid of hard feelings.
questions.explain: Carnegie introduces Taft’s story of the disappointed mother as an example of sympathy softening hard feelings.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.q: In What Everybody Wants, Sol Hurok said an early lesson with temperamental stars was the need for sympathy, sympathy and more sympathy with their ____.
questions.explain: Hurok, who handled artists such as Chaliapin, Isadora Duncan and Pavlova, learned to sympathize with their quirks rather than fight them.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.section: Principle: Be sympathetic with the other person’s ideas and desires
questions.q: Principle 9 in What Everybody Wants is: Be sympathetic with the other person’s ideas and ____.
questions.explain: The principle asks for sympathy with both what the other person thinks and what they want.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.q: In What Everybody Wants, Carnegie held back his reply to the Colonial Dame because he realized any ____ fool could tell her off.
questions.explain: He saw that “any hotheaded fool could do that—and that most fools would do just that,” and he wanted to be above fools.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.q: Which of these does Carnegie say he gained by answering the Colonial Dame with sympathy in What Everybody Wants?
options: A written apology printed in a Philadelphia paper
The satisfaction of controlling his temper
The satisfaction of returning kindness for an insult
An invitation to speak to her society in Concord
More real fun than telling her off would have given
questions.explain: He names the satisfaction of controlling his temper and of returning kindness for an insult, and says making her like him was more fun than telling her to jump in the Schuylkill River. No printed apology or invitation is mentioned.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.q: Which of these were in President Taft’s polite reply to the disappointed mother in What Everybody Wants?
options: A promise of the next suitable vacancy for her son
His understanding of a mother’s disappointment
The fact that a technical post meant following the Bureau head’s advice
An admission that he owed her for the votes she had gathered
A hope that her son would do well in the position he already had
questions.explain: Taft said he realized a mother’s disappointment, explained that the post needed technical qualifications, and hoped her son would succeed where he was. He promised nothing and conceded no debt.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.q: Which of these does Dr. Arthur I. Gates, quoted in What Everybody Wants, say adults do to gain sympathy?
options: Show their bruises
Boast about their successes
Relate their accidents
Give details of surgical operations
Hide their illnesses from others
questions.explain: Gates says adults show their bruises and relate their accidents and illnesses, “especially details of surgical operations.” Boasting and hiding illness are the opposite of seeking sympathy.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.section: Principle: Be sympathetic with the other person’s ideas and desires
questions.q: Which of these replies to an upset friend apply the principle of What Everybody Wants?
options: I can see why you’re upset; I would be too
You’re overreacting to a very small thing
If I were in your position, I’d feel exactly the same
Let me show you exactly where you went wrong
questions.explain: Both chosen replies sympathize with the friend’s feelings, echoing the magic phrase. Calling the reaction excessive or listing errors invites argument and ill feeling.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.q: Put the events of Carnegie’s Louisa May Alcott story in What Everybody Wants in the order they happened.
items: Carnegie says Concord, New Hampshire twice on the air
A Colonial Dame sends him a scorching letter
He resolves to sympathize with her viewpoint
He telephones her in Philadelphia and apologizes
She says she would like to know him better
questions.explain: His anger came first, then the decision to treat it as a game of turning hostility into friendliness. Because he sympathized, she began sympathizing with him.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.q: Put the events of President Taft’s story of the disappointed mother in What Everybody Wants in the order they happened.
items: The mother lobbies Taft for six weeks with senators
Taft appoints someone else on the Bureau head’s advice
She writes calling him ungrateful
He writes her a polite, sympathetic reply
A letter in her handwriting reports her serious illness
The couple are first to greet the Tafts at a musicale
questions.explain: Taft’s polite reply first mollified her; after the second letter he again sympathized but held firm, and the couple soon appeared at the White House.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.q: Put the stages of Chaliapin’s performance day in What Everybody Wants in order.
items: At noon he phones saying he cannot sing
Hurok rushes over and offers to cancel
At five he asks Hurok to come back later
At seven-thirty he agrees to sing if a cold is announced
questions.explain: Each time, Hurok sympathized and offered to cancel rather than arguing, until the singer agreed to perform on condition that his bad cold was announced.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.q: Put these Part Three principles in the order Carnegie presents them, ending with the one that follows What Everybody Wants.
items: Let the other person do a great deal of the talking
Let the other person feel that the idea is his or hers
Try honestly to see things from the other person’s point of view
Be sympathetic with the other person’s ideas and desires
Appeal to the nobler motives
questions.explain: Principle 9, the subject of What Everybody Wants, comes after the principle of seeing the other person’s point of view and before the appeal to nobler motives in the next chapter.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.q: In What Everybody Wants, match each person to how they showed sympathy.
pairs: Phoned an angry listener to thank her and apologize
Wrote that he realized a mother’s disappointment
Acknowledged a manager’s wish to keep shutdowns short
Praised a pupil’s nails while suggesting she trim them
Agreed his star could not sing and offered to cancel
questions.explain: Each story shows sympathy with the other person’s feelings or wishes coming before, or instead of, any argument.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.q: In What Everybody Wants, match each book to the person Carnegie connects with it.
pairs: Dr. Arthur I. Gates, its author
Louisa May Alcott, subject of Carnegie’s broadcast
questions.explain: Taft’s story comes from his book Ethics in Service, Gates’s remark on sympathy from Educational Psychology, and Carnegie’s geography slip from a broadcast about the author of Little Women.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.q: In What Everybody Wants, match each person to the outcome of being treated with sympathy.
pairs: Said she would like to know Carnegie better
Agreed an eight-hour shutdown beat several days
Trimmed her nails on her own
questions.explain: In every case sympathy won cooperation without a fight, often with the other person changing their mind of their own accord.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.q: Sort these actions from What Everybody Wants into sympathetic responses and unsympathetic responses.

items.t: Mangum saying he understood the manager’s concern
Norris calling Babette’s nails beautiful
Hurok offering to cancel Chaliapin’s concert
Carnegie phoning to thank and apologize
Carnegie’s planned reply about her poor courtesy
Taft’s first severe draft, locked in a drawer
Refusing to teach a pupil with long nails
Arguing with a singer who says he cannot sing

questions.explain: The chapter contrasts what people felt like doing, or could have done, with the sympathetic course they actually took. Norris did not threaten, and Hurok knew artists could not be handled by argument.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.section: Principle: Be sympathetic with the other person’s ideas and desires
questions.q: Sort these everyday responses by whether they apply or ignore the principle of What Everybody Wants.

items.t: Telling an angry customer you would feel the same in their place
Saying you understand a colleague’s worry before explaining a deadline
Admiring a neighbour’s prized tree before asking to trim it
Telling a complainer that others have it far worse
Firing back a list of errors in a rude email at once
Telling a nervous patient their fear is silly

questions.explain: Principle 9 means sympathizing with the other person’s ideas and desires first, as Norris did with Babette’s nails. Dismissing feelings or answering in anger does the opposite.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.q: Sort these statements by whether they match Carnegie’s view in What Everybody Wants.

items.t: You deserve very little credit for being what you are
Irritated, bigoted people deserve little discredit for what they are
We should pity and sympathize with unreasoning people
Bad-tempered people choose their temper and should be told so
Sympathy should be kept for those who have earned it
Telling off a rude critic is what wise people do

questions.explain: Carnegie argues that inheritance and experience make people what they are, so we should feel sorry for difficult people. He says any hotheaded fool could tell a critic off.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.q: In What Everybody Wants, why does Carnegie say you can tell an irritated person you would feel just as they do and be completely sincere?
questions.a: Because if you had inherited the other person’s body, temperament and mind and had their environment and experiences, you would be exactly what they are and feel as they feel. Carnegie illustrates this with Al Capone, and jokes that you are not a rattlesnake only because your parents weren’t. So you deserve little credit for what you are, and difficult people deserve little discredit.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.q: In What Everybody Wants, why did Carnegie hold back the stinging reply he wanted to send the Colonial Dame, and what did he do instead?
questions.a: He realized any hotheaded fool could tell her off and most fools would, and he wanted to be above fools, so he made a game of turning her hostility into friendliness. Telling himself that in her place he would feel as she did, he phoned her, thanked her, and apologized for his blunder. She then apologized, sympathized with his point of view, and said she would like to know him better.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.q: In What Everybody Wants, what does President Taft’s handling of the disappointed mother teach about answering an angry letter?
questions.a: Taft’s first impulse was to be severe, but he advised locking such a reply in a drawer for two days and then not sending it. Instead he wrote as polite a letter as he could, showing he understood a mother’s disappointment while explaining why he had to follow the Bureau head’s advice. Sympathy mollified her without his giving way on the appointment.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.q: In What Everybody Wants, how did Joyce Norris get Babette to cut her long fingernails without demanding it?
questions.a: She did not threaten Babette or refuse to teach her; she told her she had attractive hands and beautiful nails, and that playing would be quicker and easier if she trimmed them. By treating the nails as a thing of beauty and cutting them as a real sacrifice, she showed sympathy with what Babette cared about. Babette chose to trim them herself, for the first time for anyone.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.q: In What Everybody Wants, why did Sol Hurok meet Chaliapin’s claims that he could not sing with sympathy instead of argument?
questions.a: Hurok had learned that temperamental stars needed sympathy, sympathy and more sympathy with their idiosyncrasies, and that an entrepreneur could not handle artists by arguing. So he agreed the singer could not sing and offered to cancel, which let Chaliapin come round by himself. By evening the singer agreed to go on, provided his bad cold was announced.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.section: Principle: Be sympathetic with the other person’s ideas and desires
questions.q: In What Everybody Wants, what does Dr. Arthur I. Gates’s quotation add to Carnegie’s argument, and what principle does Carnegie draw from it?
questions.a: Gates says the human species universally craves sympathy: children display or even inflict injuries to get it, and adults show bruises and tell of accidents and operations. This supports Carnegie’s claim that most people are hungry for sympathy. So if you want to win people to your way of thinking, be sympathetic with the other person’s ideas and desires.

questions.unitTitle: What Everybody Wants
questions.q: What does the title What Everybody Wants signal about the chapter’s argument?
questions.a: The thing everybody wants is sympathy. Carnegie claims that three-fourths of the people you meet are hungering and thirsting for it, and Gates calls it something “the human species universally craves.” Giving people this universal want, by sympathizing with their ideas and desires, is offered as a way to win them to your way of thinking.

questions.unitTitle: An Appeal That Everybody Likes
questions.q: In An Appeal That Everybody Likes, what two reasons does J. Pierpont Morgan say a person usually has for doing a thing?
options: One that sounds good and a real one
One selfish reason and one generous one
One he admits and one hidden even from himself
One for his own sake and one for his family
questions.explain: Morgan observed that a person has a reason that sounds good and a real one. The real reason is not hidden from the person: Carnegie says the person himself will think of it.

questions.unitTitle: An Appeal That Everybody Likes
questions.q: True or false: In An Appeal That Everybody Likes, Carnegie advises stressing the other person’s real reason for acting, because otherwise he will lose sight of it.
questions.explain: Carnegie says the opposite: “The person himself will think of the real reason. You don’t need to emphasize that.” What you should stress is the motive that sounds good.

questions.unitTitle: An Appeal That Everybody Likes
questions.q: In An Appeal That Everybody Likes, Carnegie says all of us, being ____ at heart, like to think of motives that sound good.
questions.explain: Because we are idealists at heart and like motives that sound good, Carnegie concludes that to change people we should appeal to the nobler motives.

questions.unitTitle: An Appeal That Everybody Likes
questions.q: In An Appeal That Everybody Likes, what stories did the wife of Jesse James’s son tell Carnegie at the James farm in Kearney, Missouri?
options: Jesse gave stolen money to the local churches to rebuild them
Jesse robbed trains and banks, then gave neighboring farmers money to pay off their mortgages
Jesse robbed only the banks that had foreclosed on poor farmers
Jesse returned the money he took from widows on the trains he robbed
questions.explain: She told how Jesse robbed trains and held up banks and then gave money to neighboring farmers to pay off their mortgages, which lets Carnegie suggest that even an outlaw saw himself as an idealist.

questions.unitTitle: An Appeal That Everybody Likes
questions.q: In An Appeal That Everybody Likes, why does Carnegie mention Jesse James and crime bosses such as Al Capone?
options: To show that generosity buys loyalty even among criminals
To warn that appeals to nobler motives fail with hardened people
To show that even such men likely saw themselves as idealists, fine and unselfish in their own eyes
To argue that crime grows when people lack a sense of honor
questions.explain: Carnegie says these men probably regarded themselves as idealists at heart, and that all people have a high regard for themselves. That self-image is what an appeal to nobler motives speaks to.

questions.unitTitle: An Appeal That Everybody Likes
questions.q: In An Appeal That Everybody Likes, explain the reasoning that leads Carnegie from J. Pierpont Morgan’s remark about two reasons to the rule of appealing to the nobler motives.
questions.a: Morgan observed that a person usually has two reasons for doing a thing: one that sounds good and a real one. The person will think of the real reason himself, so there is no need to emphasize it. But all of us, being idealists at heart, like to think of motives that sound good, so to change people Carnegie says we should appeal to the nobler motives.

questions.unitTitle: An Appeal That Everybody Likes
questions.q: Which of these people does Carnegie, in An Appeal That Everybody Likes, suggest probably regarded themselves as idealists at heart?
options: Jesse James
Dutch Schultz
Al Capone
J. Pierpont Morgan
Lord Northcliffe
questions.explain: Carnegie groups Jesse James with organized crime figures such as Dutch Schultz and Al Capone as men who saw themselves as idealists. Morgan is quoted for his remark about two reasons, and Northcliffe is an example of someone using the appeal.

questions.unitTitle: An Appeal That Everybody Likes
questions.q: True or false: In An Appeal That Everybody Likes, Carnegie states that all people you meet have a high regard for themselves and like to be fine and unselfish in their own estimation.
questions.explain: Carnegie draws this general point from the Jesse James story: everyone likes to think well of himself, which is why the nobler motive appeals.

questions.unitTitle: An Appeal That Everybody Likes
questions.section: Principle: Appeal to the nobler motives
questions.q: In An Appeal That Everybody Likes, Hamilton J. Farrell’s disgruntled tenant served notice to move out at once, even though his lease still had ____ months to run.
questions.explain: The lease had four months to run, and the tenant had lived there through the winter, the most expensive part of the year, so Farrell expected to lose the rent until fall.

questions.unitTitle: An Appeal That Everybody Likes
questions.section: Principle: Appeal to the nobler motives
questions.q: In An Appeal That Everybody Likes, what does Hamilton J. Farrell say he would ordinarily have done with the tenant who wanted to leave?
options: Offered him a lower rent for the rest of the lease
Found a new tenant quickly and let him go without a fuss
Had a lawyer write him a formal letter of warning
Told him to reread his lease and that the full balance of rent would fall due at once
questions.explain: Farrell says he would normally have waded into the tenant, told him to read his lease again and warned that the whole balance would fall due and he would move to collect. Instead he tried another tactic.

questions.unitTitle: An Appeal That Everybody Likes
questions.section: Principle: Appeal to the nobler motives
questions.q: In An Appeal That Everybody Likes, put the events of Hamilton J. Farrell’s dealings with his tenant in order.
items: The tenant gives notice that he is leaving at once
Farrell says he sized him up as a man of his word
Farrell asks him to think it over for a few days
The tenant and his wife talk it over
The tenant pays his rent in person and stays
questions.explain: Farrell answered the notice by praising the tenant’s honor and asking him to think it over; the couple then decided the only honorable thing was to live up to the lease.

questions.unitTitle: An Appeal That Everybody Likes
questions.section: Principle: Appeal to the nobler motives
questions.q: In An Appeal That Everybody Likes, Hamilton J. Farrell told his tenant that he had sized him up from the first as being a man of his ____.
questions.explain: By calling the tenant a man of his word, Farrell appealed to the nobler motive of keeping a promise, and the tenant chose to honor his lease.

questions.unitTitle: An Appeal That Everybody Likes
questions.section: Principle: Appeal to the nobler motives
questions.q: In An Appeal That Everybody Likes, what did Hamilton J. Farrell promise his tenant if he came back before the first of the month still intending to move?
options: He would accept the decision as final and admit he had been wrong in his judgment
He would let him go but keep his deposit to cover the lost rent
He would collect only half of the remaining rent
He would help him find a cheaper apartment elsewhere
questions.explain: Farrell gave his word that he would accept the decision as final and admit to himself he had misjudged the man, while repeating that he still believed the tenant would live up to his contract.

questions.unitTitle: An Appeal That Everybody Likes
questions.section: Principle: Appeal to the nobler motives
questions.q: In An Appeal That Everybody Likes, match each person to what he did.
pairs: Asked an editor to drop a picture of him because his mother disliked it
Told photographers too much publicity is not good for youngsters
Offered a check to an author’s favorite charity instead of to her
Told a tenant he believed him to be a man of his word
Left it to customers to adjust their own disputed bills
questions.explain: Each man got what he wanted by appealing to a nobler motive rather than to his own wishes or to money.

questions.unitTitle: An Appeal That Everybody Likes
questions.section: Principle: Appeal to the nobler motives
questions.q: In An Appeal That Everybody Likes, match each example to the nobler motive that was appealed to.
pairs: Lord Northcliffe’s letter about his picture
The desire not to harm children
Being a man of one’s word
Thomas’s visits to the car customers
questions.explain: Carnegie names motherhood for Northcliffe and the wish to refrain from harming children for Rockefeller; Farrell stressed keeping one’s word, and Thomas put the bill up to the customer’s sense of fair play.

questions.unitTitle: An Appeal That Everybody Likes
questions.section: Principle: Appeal to the nobler motives
questions.q: In An Appeal That Everybody Likes, Lord Northcliffe asked an editor to stop publishing a picture of him, giving as his reason that his ____ did not like it.
questions.explain: Instead of saying he disliked the picture, Northcliffe appealed to the respect and love that all of us have for motherhood.

questions.unitTitle: An Appeal That Everybody Likes
questions.section: Principle: Appeal to the nobler motives
questions.q: In An Appeal That Everybody Likes, how did Cyrus H. K. Curtis get Louisa May Alcott to write for him?
options: He offered her double the usual rate for a single story
He offered to send a hundred-dollar check to her favorite charity
He promised her the cover of The Saturday Evening Post
He appealed to her loyalty as a fellow New Englander
questions.explain: Curtis could not afford the prices other magazines paid, so he offered a check for a hundred dollars, not to her, but to her favorite charity, appealing to her nobler motives.

questions.unitTitle: An Appeal That Everybody Likes
questions.section: Principle: Appeal to the nobler motives
questions.q: True or false: In An Appeal That Everybody Likes, John D. Rockefeller, Jr. told newspaper photographers plainly that he did not want his children’s pictures published.
questions.explain: Carnegie stresses that Rockefeller did not say that. He reminded the photographers that some of them had children too and that too much publicity is not good for youngsters.

questions.unitTitle: An Appeal That Everybody Likes
questions.section: Principle: Appeal to the nobler motives
questions.q: In An Appeal That Everybody Likes, how does Carnegie answer the skeptic who says the approach will not work with the tough people he has to collect bills from?
options: He insists the method works with everyone if it is applied sincerely
He says tough cases should be handed straight to lawyers
He grants nothing works in all cases, but says that if you are not satisfied with your results, why not experiment
He says such people should be appealed to through their self-interest instead
questions.explain: Carnegie concedes the skeptic may be right, since nothing will work in all cases or with all people, then invites the reader to experiment and tells the James L. Thomas story.

questions.unitTitle: An Appeal That Everybody Likes
questions.section: Principle: Appeal to the nobler motives
questions.q: In An Appeal That Everybody Likes, sort each step by who took it in trying to collect the disputed car-service bills.

items.t: Told the customer bluntly they had come to collect an overdue bill
Insisted the company was absolutely and unconditionally right
Implied the company knew more about cars than the customer
Ended up arguing with the customer
Said he came to find out what the company had done or failed to do
Called the customer the authority on his own car
Listened with all the interest and sympathy the customer wanted
Left it to the customer to adjust the bill

questions.explain: The credit men claimed to be right and know more, and so they argued. Thomas withheld judgment, made the customer the authority, listened, and then appealed to his sense of fair play.

questions.unitTitle: An Appeal That Everybody Likes
questions.section: Principle: Appeal to the nobler motives
questions.q: In An Appeal That Everybody Likes, put the steps James L. Thomas took with each customer in order.
items: Says he came to find out what the company did or failed to do
Says he has no opinion until he hears the customer’s story
Tells the customer he knows more about his car than anyone
Lets the customer talk and listens with sympathy
Appeals to his fair play and leaves the bill up to him
questions.explain: Thomas only appealed to the nobler motives at the end, once the customer had been heard and was in a reasonable mood.

questions.unitTitle: An Appeal That Everybody Likes
questions.section: Principle: Appeal to the nobler motives
questions.q: Which of these were results of James L. Thomas’s approach to the six customers in An Appeal That Everybody Likes?
options: One customer refused to pay any of the disputed charge
Five customers gave the company the best of it
The company delivered new cars to all six within two years
The company took legal action against one customer
All six paid the full bill on the day of his visit
questions.explain: One customer paid none of the disputed charge, but the other five gave the company the best of it, and all six bought new cars within two years. The legal action was only threatened before Thomas was called in.

questions.unitTitle: An Appeal That Everybody Likes
questions.section: Principle: Appeal to the nobler motives
questions.q: In An Appeal That Everybody Likes, once the customer was in a reasonable mood, James L. Thomas put the whole thing up to his sense of fair ____.
questions.explain: Thomas told the customer he was impressed by his fairness and patience and then asked him to adjust the bill himself, which is the appeal to nobler motives.

questions.unitTitle: An Appeal That Everybody Likes
questions.section: Principle: Appeal to the nobler motives
questions.q: In An Appeal That Everybody Likes, why did the credit department fail to collect the six disputed car-service bills?
questions.a: The customers had signed for the work, so the company knew it was right and said so, which Carnegie calls the first mistake. The credit men told each customer bluntly that they had come to collect, made it plain the company was absolutely right and he was wrong, and implied they knew more about cars than he ever could. The result was that they argued, and no account was settled.

questions.unitTitle: An Appeal That Everybody Likes
questions.section: Principle: Appeal to the nobler motives
questions.q: In An Appeal That Everybody Likes, what general lesson did James L. Thomas draw from his experience of collecting bills?
questions.a: When nothing is known about a customer, the only sound basis is to assume he is sincere, honest, truthful and willing to pay once convinced the charges are correct. People are honest and want to discharge their obligations, and the exceptions are few. Even those inclined to chisel will usually react well if you make them feel you consider them honest, upright and fair.

questions.unitTitle: An Appeal That Everybody Likes
questions.section: Principle: Appeal to the nobler motives
questions.q: Your flatmate refuses to pay a share of the electricity bill, claiming one charge on it is wrong. Using the ideas in An Appeal That Everybody Likes, how might you handle it?
questions.a: Rather than insisting you are right, as the credit department did, ask what went wrong and listen to the whole story without offering an opinion. Once your flatmate is in a reasonable mood, appeal to the nobler motives: say you can see they are fair-minded and leave it to them to decide what is fair. Carnegie’s point is that people want to see themselves as honest and fair, and most will live up to that.

questions.unitTitle: An Appeal That Everybody Likes
questions.section: Principle: Appeal to the nobler motives
questions.q: In An Appeal That Everybody Likes, sort these remarks by whether they appeal to a nobler motive.

items.t: My mother doesn’t like that picture
I don’t like that picture
You have children yourselves, and too much publicity is bad for youngsters
I don’t want my children’s pictures published
I sized you up as a man of your word
Read your lease again
I will send a check to your favorite charity
If you move, the full balance of rent falls due at once

questions.explain: The nobler appeals speak to motherhood, care for children, keeping one’s word and charity; the others voice only the speaker’s wishes or legal rights.

questions.unitTitle: An Appeal That Everybody Likes
questions.q: Which principle does Carnegie present in Part Three immediately before Appeal to the nobler motives?
options: Dramatize your ideas
Throw down a challenge
Let the other person feel that the idea is his or hers
Be sympathetic with the other person’s ideas and desires
questions.explain: Principle 9, from What Everybody Wants, is to be sympathetic with the other person’s ideas and desires. Dramatizing your ideas and throwing down a challenge come after Principle 10.

questions.unitTitle: An Appeal That Everybody Likes
questions.q: Which of these statements about where An Appeal That Everybody Likes sits in the book are correct?
options: It gives Principle 10 of Part Three
Part Three is How to Win People to Your Way of Thinking
The chapter after it gives the principle Dramatize your ideas
It is the last chapter of Part Three
It opens Part Four, Be a Leader
questions.explain: The chapter is Principle 10 of Part Three, How to Win People to Your Way of Thinking, and is followed by the chapter on dramatizing your ideas. Part Three ends with Throw down a challenge, not with this chapter.

questions.unitTitle: An Appeal That Everybody Likes
questions.q: What does the title An Appeal That Everybody Likes signal about the chapter’s principle?
questions.a: The appeal is to the nobler motives, and everybody likes it because all people are idealists at heart who like to be fine and unselfish in their own estimation. Asking someone to act from a motive that sounds good flatters that self-image instead of attacking it. The title promises a way of winning people that works with this universal desire rather than against it.

questions.unitTitle: The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?
questions.q: In The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?, what rumor was being spread about the Philadelphia Evening Bulletin?
options: That it carried too much advertising and too little news
That its owners were about to sell it to a rival paper
That its reporters printed gossip instead of checked facts
That its price had risen too high for ordinary readers
questions.explain: Advertisers were being told the paper was no longer attractive to readers because it had too much advertising and too little news. The rumor was about content, not price, ownership or accuracy.

questions.unitTitle: The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?
questions.q: In The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?, how did the Philadelphia Evening Bulletin answer the whispering campaign against it?
options: It ran a series of front-page denials signed by the editor
It published survey figures showing how many people read it
It gathered all the reading matter from one average day into a book
It cut its advertising pages for a month to prove its point
questions.explain: The paper clipped all the reading matter from one ordinary day, classified it and published it as a book called One Day. Carnegie says this conveyed the facts more vividly than pages of figures and mere talk could have done.

questions.unitTitle: The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?
questions.q: In The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?, the book the Philadelphia Evening Bulletin made from a single day’s reading matter was titled ____.
questions.explain: The book was called One Day and ran to 307 pages, as many as a hardcover book, yet it had been sold for a few cents as one day’s paper.

questions.unitTitle: The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?
questions.q: True or false: In The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?, the Bulletin’s book of one day’s reading matter ran to 307 pages.
questions.explain: It contained 307 pages, as many as a hardcover book, which made the amount of reading matter the paper carried impossible to ignore.

questions.unitTitle: The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?
questions.q: In The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?, why does Carnegie say merely telling people a fact is no longer enough?
questions.a: Carnegie calls this the day of dramatization: “Merely stating a truth isn’t enough.” The truth has to be made vivid, interesting and dramatic through showmanship. The movies and television do it, and anyone who wants attention has to do it too.

questions.unitTitle: The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?
questions.q: In The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?, what happened when makers of a new rat poison gave dealers a window display with two live rats?
options: Customers complained and the display was removed early
Sales rose to five times their normal rate that week
Rival makers copied the display in other shop windows
Dealers doubled their orders before the display began
questions.explain: The week the live rats were shown, sales zoomed to five times their normal rate. Carnegie uses it to show that window display experts know the power of dramatization.

questions.unitTitle: The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?
questions.q: Which of these television commercial techniques does Carnegie describe in The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It? as dramatizing a product’s advantages?
options: An antacid changing the color of acid in a test tube while a competitor does not
A detergent getting a greasy shirt clean while another brand leaves it gray
A celebrity reading out a list of the product’s ingredients
A car maneuvering around a series of turns and curves
A price table comparing the product with three rivals
questions.explain: Carnegie lists the antacid in the test tube, the soap or detergent on the greasy shirt and the car taking turns and curves, plus happy faces. Lists of ingredients or prices are the kind of mere statement he says is not enough.

questions.unitTitle: The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?
questions.q: In The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?, what did NCR salesman Jim Yeamans do to get a grocer’s attention about his old cash registers?
options: He timed the grocer’s check-out line with a stopwatch
He showed the grocer a chart of his yearly losses
He brought a new register and rang up a sale on it
He threw a handful of pennies on the floor
questions.explain: After saying the grocer was literally throwing away pennies with every customer, he threw pennies on the floor. He said “the sound of pennies hitting the floor really stopped him,” and he won an order to replace all the old machines.

questions.unitTitle: The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?
questions.q: In The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?, Jim Yeamans told a grocer he was literally throwing away ____ every time a customer went through his line.
questions.explain: He said the grocer was throwing away pennies, then threw a handful of pennies on the floor to make the words real.

questions.unitTitle: The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?
questions.q: True or false: In The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?, Carnegie says modern suitors still propose on their knees to show they mean what they say.
questions.explain: He says the old-time lover went down on his knees, but we don’t propose on our knees any more. Many suitors still set up a romantic atmosphere before they pop the question.

questions.unitTitle: The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?
questions.q: In The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?, how did Joe B. Fant, Jr. get his two young children to pick up their toys?
questions.a: He invented a train game: his son Joey was the engineer, Captain Casey Jones, on his tricycle, and his daughter Janet’s wagon was hitched on as the caboose. Janet loaded the toys as coal and rode while her brother drove her around the room. The room got cleaned up “without lectures, arguments or threats.”

questions.unitTitle: The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?
questions.q: In The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?, match each person to the way they dramatized an idea.
pairs: Threw pennies on a grocer’s floor
Turned toy pick-up into a train game
Sent her boss a fill-in form to book a meeting
Dumped tagged jars of cold cream on a desk
questions.explain: Each story applies the same principle in a different setting: selling, home life with children, getting time at work, and presenting a market report.

questions.unitTitle: The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?
questions.q: In The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?, put the steps of Mary Catherine Wolf’s effort to see her boss in order.
items: She asked for an appointment and was sent to the secretary
She heard nothing definite all week
She left a formal letter with a form and return envelope in his in-basket
The boss filled in the form himself and gave her a time that afternoon
They talked for over an hour and resolved her problems
questions.explain: A week of waiting through the secretary produced nothing; the dramatized letter on Friday got a reply within three hours and a meeting that ran far past the ten minutes offered.

questions.unitTitle: The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?
questions.q: In The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?, how much time did Mary Catherine Wolf’s boss offer her on the returned form, and how long did they actually talk?
options: Thirty minutes offered; they talked for two hours
Ten minutes offered; they talked for over an hour
Five minutes offered; they talked for half an hour
Fifteen minutes offered; they talked all afternoon
questions.explain: He wrote that he could give her ten minutes that afternoon, and they talked for over an hour and resolved her problems.

questions.unitTitle: The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?
questions.q: In The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?, Mary Catherine Wolf enclosed a form letter and a self-addressed ____ so her boss could reply easily.
questions.explain: She asked him to fill out the form, or have his secretary do it, and return it in the self-addressed envelope; it came back the same day.

questions.unitTitle: The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?
questions.q: In The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?, why did James B. Boynton’s first meeting with the advertising man fail?
questions.a: He got sidetracked into a futile argument about the methods used in the investigation, with each side insisting the other was wrong. He won his point to his own satisfaction, but his time ran out and he still had produced no results. Winning the argument did not get his facts across.

questions.unitTitle: The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?
questions.q: Which of these happened on James B. Boynton’s second visit to the advertising man in Carnegie’s cold cream market report story?
options: He dumped thirty-two jars of competing cold cream on the desk
Each jar carried a tag giving the results of the trade investigation
He began by explaining the methods used in the study
The man read the tags and a friendly conversation developed
He left a printed report and asked for a reply by letter
questions.explain: He skipped the tabulations, emptied a suitcase of tagged rival jars on the desk, and the man picked them up one by one and became intensely interested. Defending his methods was what had sunk the first visit.

questions.unitTitle: The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?
questions.q: In The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?, sort these details of James B. Boynton’s market report story into his first visit and his second visit.

items.t: A futile discussion of investigation methods
He was told he was wrong and tried to prove he was right
His time was up with no results
Jars of rival cold cream with tags
A friendly conversation with more questions
Still talking at the end of an hour

questions.explain: The first time he argued and ran out of time; the second time he dramatized the same facts and the ten minutes he was given stretched past an hour.

questions.unitTitle: The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?
questions.q: In The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?, what does Boynton say was different between his failed visit and his successful one?
options: He had gathered new and stronger facts the second time
He brought a senior partner along the second time
He presented the same facts but used dramatization
He agreed with the man’s criticism of his methods
questions.explain: He says: “I was presenting the same facts this time that I had presented previously.” The only change was showmanship, which is the chapter’s whole point.

questions.unitTitle: The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?
questions.q: In The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?, Carnegie’s Principle 11 is: ____ your ideas.
questions.explain: The chapter closes with Principle 11, Dramatize your ideas: make a truth vivid, interesting and dramatic rather than merely stating it.

questions.unitTitle: The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?
questions.q: In The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?, sort these approaches into what Carnegie calls merely stating a truth and what he calls dramatizing it.

items.t: Pages of figures about a newspaper’s content
Tabulations of market data
Asking the secretary again for a meeting
A 307-page book of one day’s news
Two live rats in a shop window
Pennies thrown on a grocer’s floor

questions.explain: Carnegie contrasts figures, data and repeated requests with vivid acts that people can see or hear. Only the vivid acts got attention and results.

questions.unitTitle: The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?
questions.q: In The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?, apply Principle 11: a parent wants a teenager to see how much the family wastes on lights left on. How might the parent use Carnegie’s idea?
questions.a: Rather than lecturing again, the parent could make the waste vivid, for example by laying out on the table the coins equal to a month of wasted electricity. Like Yeamans’s pennies, something the teenager can see or hear grabs attention that words alone do not. Carnegie’s rule is to dramatize your ideas, because merely stating a truth isn’t enough.

questions.unitTitle: The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?
questions.q: Match each Part Three principle to its number, to place The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It? in its sequence.
pairs: Avoid arguments to get the best of them
questions.explain: Dramatize your ideas is the eleventh of the twelve ways to win people to your way of thinking, between appealing to nobler motives and the final chapter, When Nothing Else Works, Try This.

questions.unitTitle: The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?
questions.q: Put these chapters of Part Three, How to Win People to Your Way of Thinking, in the order they appear.
items: You Can’t Win an Argument
An Appeal That Everybody Likes
The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?
When Nothing Else Works, Try This
questions.explain: Part Three opens with the chapter on arguments and ends with throwing down a challenge; the dramatization chapter is the eleventh, just before the last.

questions.unitTitle: When Nothing Else Works, Try This
questions.q: In When Nothing Else Works, Try This, what did Charles Schwab do after a day-shift worker told him the shift had made six heats?
options: He promised the crew a bonus if the next shift beat six
He chalked a big figure six on the floor and walked away without a word
He told the manager to post the figure on the notice board
He praised the day crew loudly in front of the night shift
questions.explain: Schwab said nothing more: he simply chalked a six on the floor and left, letting the night shift discover it and ask what it meant. No bonus or speech was involved; the bare number did the work.

questions.unitTitle: When Nothing Else Works, Try This
questions.q: In When Nothing Else Works, Try This, what had Schwab’s mill manager already tried before Schwab stepped in?
options: Raising the men’s pay and adding fringe benefits
Asking the men for their own ideas on output
Praising the best workers in front of the rest
Coaxing, pushing, swearing at and threatening the men
questions.explain: The manager said he had coaxed the men, pushed them, sworn and cussed, and threatened them with damnation and being fired, yet nothing worked. That failure is what sets up the challenge as the thing to try when nothing else works.

questions.unitTitle: When Nothing Else Works, Try This
questions.q: In When Nothing Else Works, Try This, how did Charles Schwab, in his own words, say things get done?
options: By stimulating competition, not for money but in the desire to excel
By paying people more than any rival company would pay
By letting people feel that the idea is their own
By setting firm quotas and checking them every day
questions.explain: Schwab said the way to get things done is to stimulate competition, not in a sordid, money-getting way, but “in the desire to excel.” Paying more is exactly the money-getting kind he set aside.

questions.unitTitle: When Nothing Else Works, Try This
questions.q: In When Nothing Else Works, Try This, why did Theodore Roosevelt, newly picked for governor of New York, want to withdraw?
options: He had lost the backing of his own party leaders
He felt worn out after returning from the war in Cuba
The opposition found he was no longer a legal resident of the state
He feared the scandals then sweeping through Sing Sing
questions.explain: The opposition discovered he was no longer a legal resident of New York, and Roosevelt, frightened, wished to withdraw. Senator Platt’s challenge kept him in the fight.

questions.unitTitle: When Nothing Else Works, Try This
questions.q: In When Nothing Else Works, Try This, what did Frederic Herzberg find to be the one major factor that motivated people at work?
options: The pay the job offered
Good working conditions
Generous fringe benefits
The work itself
questions.explain: Herzberg studied the work attitudes of thousands of people and found that not money, conditions or benefits but the work itself was the major motivator: if it was exciting and interesting, people wanted to do a good job.

questions.unitTitle: When Nothing Else Works, Try This
questions.q: A club secretary cannot get any member to take on organising the difficult annual dinner. Following When Nothing Else Works, Try This, which approach would Carnegie recommend?
options: Tell a capable member frankly that it is a tough job that will take a big person to pull off
Remind members firmly that they agreed to do their share of club work
Offer the organiser a cash payment taken from the dinner’s profits
Choose the organiser by drawing names so that nobody can complain
questions.explain: This mirrors Al Smith with Lewis Lawes: admitting the job is tough and saying it will take a big person to do it throws down a challenge to the desire to excel. A cash payment appeals to money, which Schwab and Firestone say is not what moves good people.

questions.unitTitle: When Nothing Else Works, Try This
questions.q: True or false: In When Nothing Else Works, Try This, after seeing the night shift’s 7, the day shift left behind an enormous 10 when they quit that night.
questions.explain: The day crew, stung that the night shift thought itself better, pitched in with enthusiasm and left a swaggering 10 on the floor. Soon the lagging mill was out-producing every other mill in the plant.

questions.unitTitle: When Nothing Else Works, Try This
questions.q: True or false: In When Nothing Else Works, Try This, Al Smith persuaded Lewis Lawes to take charge of Sing Sing by offering him a much higher salary.
questions.explain: Smith offered no extra pay; he challenged Lawes, saying “It’ll take a big person to go up there and stay.” Lawes liked the idea of a job that called for someone big.

questions.unitTitle: When Nothing Else Works, Try This
questions.q: In When Nothing Else Works, Try This, Schwab asked the worker nearest him how many ____ his shift had made that day.
questions.explain: Schwab asked how many heats the shift had made, was told six, and chalked that number on the floor for the night shift to see.

questions.unitTitle: When Nothing Else Works, Try This
questions.q: In When Nothing Else Works, Try This, the motto of the King’s Guard in ancient Greece says that the brave put down their fears and go forward, sometimes to death, but always to ____.
questions.explain: Carnegie quotes the motto to ask what greater challenge there can be than the chance to overcome one’s fears, which is what Platt’s question offered Roosevelt.

questions.unitTitle: When Nothing Else Works, Try This
questions.q: In When Nothing Else Works, Try This, Harvey S. Firestone said that pay alone would never bring together or hold good people; he thought it was the ____ itself.
questions.explain: Firestone said, “I think it was the game itself.” Carnegie returns to the word at the end: the game is what every successful person loves.

questions.unitTitle: When Nothing Else Works, Try This
questions.q: The principle stated at the end of When Nothing Else Works, Try This, Principle 12 of Part Three, is: Throw down a ____.
questions.explain: Principle 12 reads Throw down a challenge. Carnegie also calls it throwing down the gauntlet, an appeal to the desire to excel.

questions.unitTitle: When Nothing Else Works, Try This
questions.q: Which of these are cases in When Nothing Else Works, Try This of someone being moved to act by a challenge?
options: Roosevelt staying in the race for governor after Platt asked if the hero of San Juan Hill was a coward
Lewis Lawes taking the Sing Sing job after being told it would take a big person to stay
The night shift rubbing out the 6 and chalking a 7
The mill workers responding to their manager’s threats of being fired
Firestone holding good people together by raising their pay
questions.explain: Roosevelt, Lawes and the night shift all rose to a challenge. The manager’s threats produced nothing, and Firestone said pay alone never held good people.

questions.unitTitle: When Nothing Else Works, Try This
questions.q: Which of these does Carnegie name, at the close of When Nothing Else Works, Try This, as things every successful person loves?
options: The chance for self-expression
The chance to prove his or her worth
A salary that rises every year
Freedom from comparison with others
Generous fringe benefits
questions.explain: He says every successful person loves the game: the chance for self-expression and the chance to prove one’s worth, to excel, to win. Freedom from comparison is the opposite of a challenge, and pay and benefits are what Herzberg found were not the main motivators.

questions.unitTitle: When Nothing Else Works, Try This
questions.q: Put these events from Schwab’s mill in When Nothing Else Works, Try This in the order they happened.
items: Schwab asks the manager for a piece of chalk
Schwab chalks a 6 on the floor
The night shift replaces it with a 7
The day shift leaves an enormous 10
The mill out-produces every other mill in the plant
questions.explain: The figure climbed shift by shift as each crew tried to beat the other, and the once-lagging mill soon led the plant.

questions.unitTitle: When Nothing Else Works, Try This
questions.q: Put these steps in the Sing Sing story in When Nothing Else Works, Try This in the order they happened.
items: Al Smith sends for Lewis E. Lawes
Smith asks Lawes to take charge of Sing Sing
Lawes hesitates over the dangers and his career
Smith says it will take a big person to go up there and stay
Lawes goes, stays and becomes the most famous warden of his time
questions.explain: Smith saw Lawes hesitate and only then threw down the challenge; Lawes liked the idea of a job that called for someone big, so he went and stayed.

questions.unitTitle: When Nothing Else Works, Try This
questions.q: In When Nothing Else Works, Try This, match each person to what he said or did.
pairs: Chalked the day shift’s output on the mill floor
Asked whether the hero of San Juan Hill was a coward
Told Lawes it would take a big person to run Sing Sing and stay
Said pay alone would never bring together or hold good people
Found that the work itself was the major motivator
questions.explain: Each figure supplies one piece of the case for the challenge: Schwab’s chalk, Platt’s taunt, Smith’s dare, Firestone’s view of the game and Herzberg’s study of motivation.

questions.unitTitle: When Nothing Else Works, Try This
questions.q: Match each chapter of Part Three, How to Win People to Your Way of Thinking, to the principle it ends with.
pairs: The Movies Do It. TV Does It. Why Don’t You Do It?
When Nothing Else Works, Try This
questions.explain: The nutshell at the end of When Nothing Else Works, Try This lists all twelve principles of Part Three; the challenge is the twelfth and last, following dramatizing your ideas.

questions.unitTitle: When Nothing Else Works, Try This
questions.q: In When Nothing Else Works, Try This, sort each action by who used it at the mill.

items.t: Coaxing the men
Swearing and cussing at them
Threatening them with being fired
Asking how many heats the shift made
Chalking the figure on the floor
Walking away without another word

questions.explain: The manager’s pressure got nothing; Schwab’s silent chalk figure turned the two shifts into rivals and output rose.

questions.unitTitle: When Nothing Else Works, Try This
questions.q: In When Nothing Else Works, Try This, sort each item by whether the chapter credits it as what truly moves people or says it is not the main motivator.

items.t: The desire to excel
The game itself
The desire for a feeling of importance
Pay alone
Good working conditions
Fringe benefits

questions.explain: Schwab, Firestone and Herzberg all point away from money, conditions and benefits toward the work, the game and the desire to excel, which Carnegie ties to the desire for a feeling of importance.

questions.unitTitle: When Nothing Else Works, Try This
questions.q: In When Nothing Else Works, Try This, explain how Charles Schwab raised the output of a lagging mill without giving the workers a single order.
questions.a: He asked the day shift how many heats they had made, chalked the answer, six, on the floor and walked away. The night shift saw it, took it as a mark to beat and left a 7; the day shift answered with a 10. The rivalry between shifts soon made the mill the most productive in the plant, where the manager’s coaxing and threats had failed.

questions.unitTitle: When Nothing Else Works, Try This
questions.q: In When Nothing Else Works, Try This, how does Carnegie use Theodore Roosevelt to show the power of a challenge?
questions.a: Roosevelt, picked to run for governor of New York, was frightened and wanted to withdraw when the opposition found he was no longer a legal resident. Senator Platt turned on him and asked, “Is the hero of San Juan Hill a coward?” Roosevelt stayed in the fight, so Carnegie says a challenge changed not only his life but the future of his nation; without it he would never have become President.

questions.unitTitle: When Nothing Else Works, Try This
questions.q: In When Nothing Else Works, Try This, how do Harvey Firestone and Frederic Herzberg support the case for throwing down a challenge?
questions.a: Firestone said pay alone never brought together or held good people; it was the game itself. Herzberg, studying thousands of workers from the factory floor to senior executives, found the major motivator was not money, conditions or benefits but the work itself. Carnegie concludes that what successful people love is the game: the chance for self-expression, to prove their worth, to excel and win.

questions.unitTitle: When Nothing Else Works, Try This
questions.q: Why does the title When Nothing Else Works, Try This suit the chapter’s place at the end of Part Three, How to Win People to Your Way of Thinking?
questions.a: It is the twelfth and last principle of Part Three, and the title presents the challenge as the method to reach for once the gentler approaches have been tried. The chapter opens with a manager who had coaxed, pushed and threatened without result, and Schwab’s chalk figure succeeds where all that failed. The chapter then closes with the nutshell list of all twelve principles before Part Four on leadership begins.

questions.unitTitle: If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin
questions.q: Chapter 4.1, If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin, opens Part Four (Be a Leader). What does its title signal about the chapter's job?
options: It tells the reader how to avoid ever criticizing anyone again
It gives the first step to take when correcting someone cannot be avoided
It explains how to win an argument with a stubborn opponent
It shows how to make a good first impression on strangers
questions.explain: The title assumes fault-finding is sometimes necessary and promises the right way to start it. That fits Part Four's aim of changing people without giving offense, rather than avoiding correction altogether.

questions.unitTitle: If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin
questions.q: True or false: If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin is the first chapter of Part Four, Be a Leader: How to Change People Without Giving Offense or Arousing Resentment.
questions.explain: The table of contents lists it as Chapter 4.1, the opening chapter of Part Four, right after Part Three ends with When Nothing Else Works, Try This.

questions.unitTitle: If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin
questions.q: How does the principle of If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin build on Part One's chapter The Big Secret of Dealing with People?
questions.a: The Big Secret of Dealing with People taught readers to give honest and sincere appreciation in all their dealings. Chapter 4.1 applies that same appreciation to the hardest moment of leadership, when a fault must be corrected: begin with praise and honest appreciation, so the person can hear the correction without resentment. The word honest keeps it tied to Part One's line between appreciation and flattery.

questions.unitTitle: If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin
questions.q: Put these first chapters of Part Four (Be a Leader) in the order they appear in the book.
items: If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin
How to Criticize—and Not Be Hated for It
Talk About Your Own Mistakes First
No One Likes to Take Orders
questions.explain: Part Four opens with how to begin when finding fault, then moves to how to criticize, to admitting your own mistakes first, and to asking questions instead of giving orders.

questions.unitTitle: If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin
questions.q: In the Calvin Coolidge story that opens If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin, after praising his secretary's dress, Coolidge asked her to be more careful with her ____.
questions.explain: Coolidge complimented her dress and looks, told her not to get stuck up, and then asked her to take more care with her punctuation.

questions.unitTitle: If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin
questions.q: In If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin, why does Carnegie call Calvin Coolidge's method with his secretary obvious but say its psychology was superb?
questions.a: Coolidge's praise of the dress was clumsy and he even admitted he said it to make her feel good, so the method was transparent. But the psychology was sound, because “It is always easier to listen to unpleasant things after we have heard some praise of our good points.” The praise prepared her to accept the request about her punctuation.

questions.unitTitle: If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin
questions.q: In If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin, what comparison does Carnegie use to introduce how William McKinley handled a party member's campaign speech in 1896?
options: A dentist giving Novocain before drilling
A gardener watering before pruning
A barber lathering a man before shaving him
A doctor warming his hands before an examination
questions.explain: Carnegie says a barber lathers a man before he shaves him, and that is exactly what McKinley did. The dentist and Novocain image comes at the end of the chapter, not with McKinley.

questions.unitTitle: If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin
questions.q: In If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin, how did McKinley turn down the prominent Republican's unsuitable campaign speech?
options: He called it splendid, asked whether it suited this particular occasion, and invited a new draft along his lines
He told the man the speech would raise a tornado of criticism and dropped him as a speaker
He accepted the speech but quietly gave it to another speaker to rewrite
He sent the speech to party leaders so they could deliver the refusal for him
questions.explain: McKinley praised it as magnificent, then questioned only its fit for the occasion and the party's standpoint, and asked for a new speech along lines he indicated. The tornado of criticism was Carnegie's judgment, which McKinley never said aloud.

questions.unitTitle: If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin
questions.q: Put the steps of the McKinley campaign speech story in If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin in order.
items: The man reads his speech aloud with great glee
McKinley calls it a splendid, magnificent speech
McKinley asks if it suits this occasion from the party's standpoint
The man writes a second speech along McKinley's lines
McKinley blue-pencils it and helps rewrite it
The man becomes an effective campaign speaker
questions.explain: McKinley praised first, then raised the problem of the occasion, then guided a rewrite, which turned the man into one of the campaign's effective speakers.

questions.unitTitle: If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin
questions.q: True or false: In If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin, the Republican whose speech McKinley turned down went on to become one of the effective speakers of the campaign.
questions.explain: After McKinley blue-penciled and helped rewrite his second speech, the man became one of the effective speakers of the campaign, his enthusiasm intact.

questions.unitTitle: If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin
questions.q: Which of these were McKinley's aims, according to Carnegie, when he dealt with the unsuitable campaign speech in If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin?
options: Not to hurt the man's feelings
Not to kill the man's splendid enthusiasm
Still to say no to the speech
To have the speech printed in party newspapers
To find a replacement speaker for the campaign
questions.explain: Carnegie says McKinley did not want to hurt the man's feelings or kill his enthusiasm, yet he had to say no. He kept the man as a speaker rather than replacing him.

questions.unitTitle: If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin
questions.q: In If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin, to whom did Abraham Lincoln write the letter Carnegie calls his second most famous?
options: General Burnside
Mrs. Bixby
Napoleon's biographer
General Joseph Hooker
questions.explain: The letter went to General Joseph Hooker on April 26, 1863, when Lincoln put him at the head of the Army of the Potomac. Lincoln's most famous letter was the one to Mrs. Bixby; Burnside is the earlier commander Hooker thwarted.

questions.unitTitle: If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin
questions.q: In If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin, Carnegie says Lincoln's most famous letter was written to Mrs. ____, expressing sorrow for the five sons she had lost in battle.
questions.explain: Carnegie ranks the letter to Mrs. Bixby first and the letter to General Hooker second among Lincoln's most famous letters.

questions.unitTitle: If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin
questions.q: True or false: In If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin, Carnegie says Lincoln's letter to General Hooker sold at public auction in 1926 for five thousand dollars.
questions.explain: It sold for twelve thousand dollars, which Carnegie notes was more than Lincoln managed to save in half a century of hard work.

questions.unitTitle: If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin
questions.q: In If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin, how did Lincoln word General Hooker's grave faults in his letter, which Carnegie praises for tact?
options: He listed them as serious failures that endangered the nation
He wrote that there were some things about which he was not quite satisfied with Hooker
He left them out entirely and praised Hooker only
He asked other generals to tell Hooker about them
questions.explain: Carnegie notes Lincoln never called them grave faults; he wrote: “There are some things in regard to which I am not quite satisfied with you.” He did still name the faults later in the letter.

questions.unitTitle: If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin
questions.q: Which of these did Lincoln praise in General Hooker before turning to his faults, in the letter printed in If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin?
options: Being a brave and skillful soldier
Not mixing politics with his profession
Having confidence in himself
Loyally supporting General Burnside
Calling for a dictator to lead the army
questions.explain: Lincoln opened with Hooker's bravery and skill, his keeping politics out of his profession, and his self-confidence. Thwarting Burnside and talk of a dictator were among the faults, not the praise.

questions.unitTitle: If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin
questions.q: In Lincoln's letter to General Hooker, printed in If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin, Lincoln writes that what he now asks of Hooker is military success, and that he will risk the ____.
questions.explain: Lincoln answers Hooker's remark that the country needed a dictator by saying only successful generals can set up as dictators, so he asks for victories and will risk that.

questions.unitTitle: If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin
questions.q: Match each point in Lincoln's letter to General Hooker, printed in If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin, to Lincoln's comment on it.
pairs: Within reasonable bounds, does good rather than harm
A valuable if not an indispensable quality
Hooker saying the country needed a dictator
Command was given in spite of it, not for it
Beware of rashness, but go forward with energy
questions.explain: Lincoln paired each judgment with fairness: he credited ambition and confidence, rejected the dictator talk, and ended by warning against rashness while urging victories.

questions.unitTitle: If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin
questions.q: Sort these items from Lincoln's letter to General Hooker, printed in If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin, into praise and faults.

items.t: A brave and skillful soldier
Does not mix politics with his profession
Has confidence in himself
Thwarted General Burnside as much as he could
Said the army and Government needed a dictator
Helped spread a spirit of criticizing the commander

questions.explain: Carnegie points out that even in this sharp letter Lincoln praised Hooker's real strengths before setting out his grave faults.

questions.unitTitle: If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin
questions.q: In If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin, why does Carnegie stress the dark state of the Civil War when he prints Lincoln's letter to General Hooker?
questions.a: The letter came after eighteen months of defeats, mass desertions and a Senate revolt, when Lincoln felt the nation was on the brink of destruction. The fate of the nation could depend on how this obstreperous general acted. Carnegie shows that even under that pressure, and in perhaps his sharpest letter as President, Lincoln praised Hooker before speaking of his faults.

questions.unitTitle: If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin
questions.q: In If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin, what problem sent W.P. Gaw of the Wark Company to New York?
options: A union strike had halted work on the office building
The building's architect wanted to change the design
A bank had refused to fund the final stage of building
The subcontractor making the ornamental bronze work said he could not deliver on time
questions.explain: The Philadelphia office building was almost finished when the bronze-work subcontractor declared he could not deliver on schedule, threatening heavy penalties. Phone calls and arguments had failed, so Gaw went in person.

questions.unitTitle: If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin
questions.q: Put the events of W.P. Gaw's visit to the bronze subcontractor in If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin in order.
items: Gaw remarks that the man's name is unique in the Brooklyn phone book
The man talks proudly about his family from Holland
Gaw praises the plant as one of the cleanest he has seen
The man shows Gaw around the factory and his machines
The man insists on taking Gaw to lunch
The man promises the material will be shipped on time
questions.explain: Gaw began with the man's name, family and factory, toured the plant and had lunch, and only then did the subcontractor himself raise business and promise delivery.

questions.unitTitle: If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin
questions.q: True or false: In If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin, W.P. Gaw raised the late bronze work before lunch, right after praising the subcontractor's factory.
questions.explain: Carnegie stresses that not a word was said about the real purpose of the visit until after lunch, and then it was the subcontractor who brought it up.

questions.unitTitle: If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin
questions.q: Which of these did W.P. Gaw compliment during his visit to the bronze subcontractor in If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin?
options: How large the plant was
How clean and neat the factory was
His system of fabrication
His low prices
His record of fast deliveries
questions.explain: Gaw praised the plant's size, called it one of the cleanest and neatest bronze factories he had seen, and explained why its fabrication system beat competitors'. Prices and delivery record never came up, and delivery was the very problem.

questions.unitTitle: If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin
questions.q: In If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin, Carnegie asks whether Mr. Gaw would have succeeded with the ____ method generally used on such occasions.
questions.explain: Carnegie contrasts Gaw's warm, appreciative approach with the forceful hammer-and-dynamite method, implying it would not have won the same result.

questions.unitTitle: If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin
questions.q: In If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin, how did W.P. Gaw get the bronze work delivered on time, and what does the result show?
questions.a: Instead of more heated arguments, Gaw met the subcontractor and sincerely admired his unusual name, his large clean plant, his fabrication system and the machines he had invented.
