The subcontractor enjoyed the meeting so much that after lunch he raised the subject himself and promised shipment even if other orders were delayed. “Mr. Gaw got everything that he wanted without even asking for it.” It shows the principle works in everyday business, not only for presidents.

questions.unitTitle: If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin
questions.q: In If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin, what was the teller trainee's problem in Dorothy Wrublewski's credit union?
options: She was rude to customers at the counter
She made errors in individual transactions
She was too slow in balancing out at the end of the day
She often arrived late for her shift
questions.explain: The trainee was pleasant, accurate and efficient with customers; only balancing out at the end of the day held everyone up. That is why the head teller wanted her fired.

questions.unitTitle: If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin
questions.q: In If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin, how did Dorothy Wrublewski handle the teller trainee the head teller wanted fired, and why did it work?
questions.a: She first watched the trainee and saw she was quick, accurate and friendly with customers. After closing, she praised her for exactly those strengths and only then suggested they review the procedure for balancing the cash drawer. Once the nervous trainee realized her manager had confidence in her, she followed the suggestions and soon mastered balancing out.

questions.unitTitle: If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin
questions.q: Match each person in If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin to their role in the chapter.
pairs: Praised a secretary's dress before mentioning her punctuation
Praised a campaign speech before asking for a rewrite
Praised a subcontractor's factory before any talk of business
Praised a trainee's work with customers before reviewing balancing
questions.explain: Each example follows the same pattern: genuine praise of good points first, and the correction or request afterward.

questions.unitTitle: If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin
questions.q: Match each story in If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin to its outcome.
pairs: The secretary blushed in confusion at such unusual praise
The writer became an effective speaker of the campaign
The building was finished on the date the contract specified
The trainee soon mastered balancing out
questions.explain: Carnegie's examples move from a quick White House scene to business and office life, and in each the praise opened the way to a good result.

questions.unitTitle: If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin
questions.section: Principle: Begin with praise and honest appreciation
questions.q: The principle of If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin is: Begin with praise and honest ____.
questions.explain: Principle 1 of Part Four reads: Begin with praise and honest appreciation.

questions.unitTitle: If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin
questions.section: Principle: Begin with praise and honest appreciation
questions.q: In Carnegie's comparison of beginning with praise to a dentist who starts with Novocain, in If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin, what does the drilling stand for?
options: The correction, which still has to be given
The praise, which can feel uncomfortable
The resentment the person feels afterward
The punishment for repeated mistakes
questions.explain: Carnegie says the patient still gets a drilling, but the Novocain is painkilling. The praise does not replace the correction; it makes the correction easier to take.

questions.unitTitle: If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin
questions.section: Principle: Begin with praise and honest appreciation
questions.q: Sort these examples from If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin into the praise given first and the correction or request that followed.

items.t: A compliment on a pretty dress
Be more careful with punctuation
A splendid, magnificent speech
Write a new speech along the lines indicated
Friendly and outgoing with the customers
Review the procedure for balancing the cash drawer

questions.explain: In the Coolidge, McKinley and Wrublewski stories the praise always came first, and the correction followed once the person felt valued.

questions.unitTitle: If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin
questions.section: Principle: Begin with praise and honest appreciation
questions.q: A restaurant manager must tell a waiter who keeps getting orders wrong. Following the principle of If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin, which opening is best?
options: List every wrong order first, then end with a quick compliment
Say nothing about the orders and hope he improves on his own
Praise him lavishly for things he knows he does badly
Sincerely praise his warmth with customers, then go over the orders together
questions.explain: Carnegie's principle is to begin with praise and honest appreciation of real good points, then correct, as Wrublewski did with her trainee. Ending with praise reverses the order, and praise the waiter knows is false is not honest appreciation.

questions.unitTitle: If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin
questions.section: Principle: Begin with praise and honest appreciation
questions.q: Which of these openings follow the principle of If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin for a manager about to raise a late report?
options: You have handled the client calls really well this month; now, about the report
Your figures are always accurate, so let's look at the timing together
This report is late again, and I am tired of it
Before you say anything, I want to talk about your lateness
questions.explain: The first two begin with honest appreciation of real strengths before turning to the problem. The others lead with the fault, which is exactly what Carnegie says to avoid.

questions.unitTitle: If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin
questions.section: Principle: Begin with praise and honest appreciation
questions.q: A teacher must tell a hardworking student that her essay missed the question. Using the principle of If You Must Find Fault, This Is the Way to Begin, how should the teacher start, and why?
questions.a: The teacher should begin with praise and honest appreciation of what is truly good, such as the student's effort or clear writing, and then turn to the essay missing the question. Carnegie argues it is always easier to hear unpleasant things after hearing praise of our good points. Like the dentist's Novocain, the praise does not remove the correction, but it takes away the sting so the student stays willing to improve.

questions.unitTitle: How to Criticize—and Not Be Hated for It
questions.q: When Charles Schwab found employees smoking beneath a No Smoking sign in his steel mill, what did he do?
options: Pointed to the sign and asked whether they could read
Handed each man a cigar and asked them to smoke outside
Said nothing and later had the foreman warn them
Put out his own cigar to set them an example
questions.explain: Schwab gave each man a cigar and said he would appreciate it if they smoked them outside. Carnegie stresses that he did not point to the sign and ask “Can’t you read?”

questions.unitTitle: How to Criticize—and Not Be Hated for It
questions.q: When John Wanamaker saw a customer being ignored while his salespeople chatted at the far end of the counter, how did he respond?
options: He waited on the woman himself and handed the purchase to the clerks to wrap
He called the salespeople over and reminded them of their duties
He apologized to the customer and reported the clerks to their manager
He stood beside the counter until the salespeople noticed him
questions.explain: Wanamaker said nothing, slipped behind the counter, served the woman himself and passed the purchase to the salespeople to be wrapped. The lesson reached them without a word of reproach.

questions.unitTitle: How to Criticize—and Not Be Hated for It
questions.q: How did Mayor Carl Langford of Orlando finally make his staff honor his open-door policy?
options: He moved his desk into the public lobby
He replaced his secretaries and administrators
He held weekly open meetings in city hall
He removed the door from his office
questions.explain: After repeated reminders failed, Langford took the door off his office, and his aides got the message. The symbolic act made the point indirectly where direct admonishing had not.

questions.unitTitle: How to Criticize—and Not Be Hated for It
questions.section: Principle: Call attention to people’s mistakes indirectly
questions.q: According to Carnegie, why might praise followed by the word but fail to change Johnnie’s attitude toward his studies?
options: Johnnie may doubt the praise was sincere and see it as a lead-in to criticism
Johnnie may feel the praise was too small for the effort he made
Johnnie may decide that his grades are already good enough
Johnnie may resent being compared with the other students
questions.explain: On hearing “but,” Johnnie might question the sincerity of the praise, which now seems a contrived lead-in to an inference of failure. Credibility is strained, so the objective is not reached.

questions.unitTitle: How to Criticize—and Not Be Hated for It
questions.section: Principle: Call attention to people’s mistakes indirectly
questions.q: What did Marge Jacob say to the foreman the morning after she and her children tidied the lumber debris in her yard?
options: That she would expect the yard to be kept tidy from now on
That the neighbors had complained about the mess of cut lumber
That she was pleased the front lawn was left nice and clean the night before
That she would pay extra if the workers cleaned up each evening
questions.explain: She told the foreman she was really pleased with how clean the lawn had been left, implying the standard without accusing anyone. The neighbors appear only as people the clean lawn would not offend.

questions.unitTitle: How to Criticize—and Not Be Hated for It
questions.section: Principle: Call attention to people’s mistakes indirectly
questions.q: When Lyman Abbott read his carefully polished sermon to his wife, what did she say about it?
options: That it would read better if he cut it in half
That it was as fine as anything Henry Ward Beecher had preached
That he should practice reading it aloud a few more times
That it would make an excellent article for the North American Review
questions.explain: She remarked that it would make an excellent article for the North American Review, praising it while subtly suggesting it would not do as a speech. Abbott saw the point and preached without notes.

questions.unitTitle: How to Criticize—and Not Be Hated for It
questions.section: Principle: Call attention to people’s mistakes indirectly
questions.q: True or false: Master Sergeant Harley Kaiser got reservists to cut their hair by threatening them with army regulations.
questions.explain: Although an old-time regular-army sergeant might have been expected to yell and threaten, Kaiser made his point indirectly. He appealed to them as leaders who should set an example and said he was getting his own hair cut.

questions.unitTitle: How to Criticize—and Not Be Hated for It
questions.q: True or false: Carnegie says Schwab’s employees admired him because, although they knew he knew they had broken a rule, he said nothing about it and gave them a little present.
questions.explain: Carnegie writes that the men knew Schwab knew they had broken the rule, and admired him because he said nothing about it, gave them a gift and made them feel important.

questions.unitTitle: How to Criticize—and Not Be Hated for It
questions.section: Principle: Call attention to people’s mistakes indirectly
questions.q: Carnegie says that simply changing one three-letter word, replacing but with ____, can spell the difference between failure and success in changing people.
questions.explain: Changing “but” to “and” removes the inference of failure, so the praise is accepted and the desired change is suggested indirectly.

questions.unitTitle: How to Criticize—and Not Be Hated for It
questions.section: Principle: Call attention to people’s mistakes indirectly
questions.q: The principle of the chapter How to Criticize—and Not Be Hated for It is: Call attention to people’s mistakes ____.
questions.explain: Principle 2 of Part Four reads “Call attention to people’s mistakes indirectly.” Every story in the chapter shows a fault corrected without a direct rebuke.

questions.unitTitle: How to Criticize—and Not Be Hated for It
questions.section: Principle: Call attention to people’s mistakes indirectly
questions.q: Carnegie says calling attention to mistakes indirectly works wonders with ____ people, who may resent bitterly any direct criticism.
questions.explain: He introduces the Marge Jacob story by noting that indirect correction “works wonders with sensitive people who may resent bitterly any direct criticism.”

questions.unitTitle: How to Criticize—and Not Be Hated for It
questions.section: Principle: Call attention to people’s mistakes indirectly
questions.q: Harley Kaiser told the reserve noncommissioned officers that they would be most effective when they lead by ____.
questions.explain: Kaiser framed the haircut issue as leadership: they should be the example for their men to follow, and he was getting his own hair cut.

questions.unitTitle: How to Criticize—and Not Be Hated for It
questions.q: In How to Criticize—and Not Be Hated for It, which of these stories show a fault finally being corrected by an action rather than a rebuke?
options: Schwab handing cigars to men smoking under a No Smoking sign
Wanamaker serving an ignored customer himself
Langford removing the door from his office
Lincoln writing a letter to General Meade that he never sent
Wanamaker firing salespeople who ignored customers
questions.explain: Schwab, Wanamaker and Langford each corrected a fault by action rather than rebuke. The Lincoln letter belongs to an earlier chapter, and Carnegie says nothing about Wanamaker firing anyone.

questions.unitTitle: How to Criticize—and Not Be Hated for It
questions.section: Principle: Call attention to people’s mistakes indirectly
questions.q: Which of these results followed the indirect corrections described in How to Criticize—and Not Be Hated for It?
options: Several reservists went to the barbershop that same afternoon
Marge Jacob’s foreman came in daily seeking approval of the lawn
Lyman Abbott tore up his manuscript and preached without notes
Lyman Abbott published his sermon in the North American Review
Marge Jacob hired a different crew to finish her house
questions.explain: The reservists got regulation haircuts, the foreman began seeking approval, and Abbott preached without notes. Abbott’s wife only suggested the article idea; nothing says it was published, and Mrs. Jacob kept the builders because they did excellent work.

questions.unitTitle: How to Criticize—and Not Be Hated for It
questions.section: Principle: Call attention to people’s mistakes indirectly
questions.q: Put the steps of Marge Jacob’s approach to the untidy builders in the order they happened.
items: She notices cut lumber strewn across the yard
After the workers leave, she and her children pile the debris in a corner
Next morning she tells the foreman she is pleased the lawn was left clean
The workers start piling the debris themselves each day
questions.explain: She first saw the mess, quietly cleaned it herself, then praised the foreman for a clean lawn. From then on the workers cleaned up and the foreman sought her approval.

questions.unitTitle: How to Criticize—and Not Be Hated for It
questions.section: Principle: Call attention to people’s mistakes indirectly
questions.q: Put these moments from the Lyman Abbott story in the order they happened.
items: Henry Ward Beecher dies
Abbott is invited to speak in Beecher’s pulpit
Abbott writes and polishes his sermon
His wife suggests it would make an excellent magazine article
Abbott tears up the manuscript and preaches without notes
questions.explain: Beecher died on March 8, 1887, Abbott was invited to fill his pulpit, polished a written sermon, received his wife’s indirect hint, and then preached without notes.

questions.unitTitle: How to Criticize—and Not Be Hated for It
questions.q: Match each person with the indirect way they corrected a fault.
pairs: Gave smokers cigars and asked them to smoke outside
Removed the door from his office
Announced he was getting his own hair cut
questions.explain: Each acted or spoke in a way that let the others see their own fault: the smokers, the idle clerks, the gatekeeping aides and the long-haired reservists.

questions.unitTitle: How to Criticize—and Not Be Hated for It
questions.section: Principle: Call attention to people’s mistakes indirectly
questions.q: Match each person with the problem they set out to correct.
pairs: Builders leaving lumber debris in the yard
A sermon that read like an essay
Aides blocking citizens from seeing the mayor
questions.explain: Each problem was solved without direct criticism: praise for a clean lawn, an appeal to leadership, a suggestion to publish, and a missing door.

questions.unitTitle: How to Criticize—and Not Be Hated for It
questions.section: Principle: Call attention to people’s mistakes indirectly
questions.q: Sort these remarks to Johnnie into the version that strains credibility and the version Carnegie recommends.

items.t: We are proud of you for raising your grades, but you should have worked harder on algebra
We are proud of you, and by continuing the same efforts your algebra can catch up
Johnnie may doubt the original praise was sincere
Johnnie accepts the praise with no inference of failure
The praise seems a contrived lead-in to criticism
Johnnie will likely try to live up to our expectations

questions.explain: Following praise with “but” makes the praise look like a set-up for criticism. Using “and” lets the praise stand and points to the desired change indirectly.

questions.unitTitle: How to Criticize—and Not Be Hated for It
questions.section: Principle: Call attention to people’s mistakes indirectly
questions.q: Sort these into what Carnegie says Abbott’s wife might have said with less judgment and what she actually did.

items.t: Told him it reads like an encyclopedia
Warned that he would put people to sleep
Asked why he did not talk like a human being
Praised the sermon as a fine magazine article
Subtly suggested it would not do as a speech

questions.explain: Carnegie lists the blunt criticism she could have offered, then shows that she instead praised the piece as an article, which hinted it would not work as a speech.

questions.unitTitle: How to Criticize—and Not Be Hated for It
questions.section: Principle: Call attention to people’s mistakes indirectly
questions.q: Explain why Carnegie recommends replacing but with and when following praise with a request for change. Use the Johnnie example.
questions.a: If we praise Johnnie for raising his grades and then say “but” he should have worked harder at algebra, he may doubt the praise and see it as a contrived lead-in to criticism, so credibility is strained. Saying instead that by continuing the same efforts his algebra can catch up lets him accept the praise with no inference of failure. The change is suggested indirectly, and he will likely try to live up to our expectations.

questions.unitTitle: How to Criticize—and Not Be Hated for It
questions.section: Principle: Call attention to people’s mistakes indirectly
questions.q: How did Master Sergeant Harley Kaiser get reserve noncommissioned officers to accept regulation haircuts, and why did it work?
questions.a: Instead of yelling and threatening, he told them they were leaders who are most effective when they lead by example. He said he was getting his own hair cut though it was shorter than theirs, and invited them to look in the mirror and decide whether they needed one. Several went to the barbershop that afternoon, because the point was made indirectly and appealed to their pride as leaders rather than attacking them.

questions.unitTitle: How to Criticize—and Not Be Hated for It
questions.q: How does Principle 2, Call attention to people’s mistakes indirectly, build on Principle 1 of Part Four, and which principle follows it?
questions.a: Principle 1 says to begin with praise and honest appreciation; Principle 2 shows how to keep that praise from being undone, by avoiding a critical “but” and letting people see their own mistakes indirectly. It continues Part Four’s aim of changing people without giving offense or arousing resentment. It is followed by Principle 3, talk about your own mistakes before criticizing the other person.

questions.unitTitle: How to Criticize—and Not Be Hated for It
questions.q: What does the chapter title How to Criticize—and Not Be Hated for It signal about Carnegie’s view of criticism, and how do the chapter’s stories deliver on it?
questions.a: The title admits that correcting people is sometimes necessary but warns that direct criticism breeds resentment. The stories of Schwab, Wanamaker, Langford, Marge Jacob, Kaiser and Abbott’s wife all show faults corrected through actions, praise or suggestion rather than rebuke. The chapter closes on the principle “Call attention to people’s mistakes indirectly.”

questions.unitTitle: Talk About Your Own Mistakes First
questions.q: In Talk About Your Own Mistakes First, what did Carnegie conclude after honestly comparing his niece Josephine at nineteen with himself at the same age?
options: That she had made far more blunders than he ever had
That she lacked judgment she should have been born with
That her batting average was better than his had been
That they had both been equally poor at the work
questions.explain: Thinking it over honestly and impartially, he decided Josephine’s batting average at nineteen was better than his own had been, adding wryly that this was not much of a compliment to her.

questions.unitTitle: Talk About Your Own Mistakes First
questions.q: In Talk About Your Own Mistakes First, what did engineer E. G. Dillistone show his secretary to help her stop making spelling mistakes?
options: A dictionary he left open on her desk every morning
His little black thumb-index book of words he found hard to spell
A page of her letters marked up in red ink
A spelling course he had taken as a young engineer
questions.explain: He sat down with her, said the word was one he always had trouble with, and opened the spelling book he kept for such words. Merely pointing out errors had not worked.

questions.unitTitle: Talk About Your Own Mistakes First
questions.section: Principle: Talk about your own mistakes before criticizing the other person
questions.q: In Talk About Your Own Mistakes First, after the uproar over his published remarks, what did Kaiser Wilhelm II ask Prince von Bülow to do?
options: Resign as Imperial Chancellor to calm England
Travel to London and apologize on his behalf
Stop the newspaper from printing any further remarks
Announce that he had advised the Kaiser to say those things
questions.explain: The panicky Kaiser wanted von Bülow to take the blame by announcing it was all his responsibility, that he had advised his monarch to make the remarks.

questions.unitTitle: Talk About Your Own Mistakes First
questions.section: Principle: Talk about your own mistakes before criticizing the other person
questions.q: In Talk About Your Own Mistakes First, what does Carnegie say was von Bülow’s one error in handling the Kaiser?
options: He began by hinting the Kaiser was a half-wit instead of talking about his own shortcomings
He refused outright to take any of the blame for the remarks
He praised the Kaiser so much that the praise sounded insincere
He let the Kaiser’s remarks be printed in the first place
questions.explain: Carnegie says von Bülow should have begun by talking about his own shortcomings and Wilhelm’s superiority, “not by intimating that the Kaiser was a half-wit in need of a guardian.”

questions.unitTitle: Talk About Your Own Mistakes First
questions.section: Principle: Talk about your own mistakes before criticizing the other person
questions.q: In Talk About Your Own Mistakes First, how did Clarence Zerhusen handle discovering that his fifteen-year-old son was experimenting with cigarettes?
options: He warned his son in detail about the dangers of smoking
He threatened to punish his son if he smoked again
He told his son how he had started at about the same age and got hooked
He forbade anyone in the family to smoke at home
questions.explain: He did not exhort, threaten or warn; he simply explained how he had started smoking at about his son’s age and how the nicotine had gotten the best of him.

questions.unitTitle: Talk About Your Own Mistakes First
questions.q: In Part Four of How to Win Friends and Influence People, which principle comes immediately before Talk about your own mistakes before criticizing the other person?
options: Begin with praise and honest appreciation
Call attention to people’s mistakes indirectly
Ask questions instead of giving direct orders
If you are wrong, admit it quickly and emphatically
questions.explain: This is Principle 3 of Part Four; Principle 2, from How to Criticize—and Not Be Hated for It, is to call attention to mistakes indirectly. Praise comes first as Principle 1, and asking questions follows as Principle 4.

questions.unitTitle: Talk About Your Own Mistakes First
questions.section: Principle: Talk about your own mistakes before criticizing the other person
questions.q: A manager must tell a junior analyst that her first report contains several errors. Which opening best follows the principle of Talk About Your Own Mistakes First?
options: Here is a full list of the errors so you never repeat them.
You really should have caught these; they are basic.
Next time, check with me before you send anything out.
I made this exact kind of slip in my first year, so I know how easy it is.
questions.explain: Carnegie’s principle is to talk about your own mistakes before criticizing the other person, so the manager should begin by humbly admitting a similar error. The other openings go straight to the fault.

questions.unitTitle: Talk About Your Own Mistakes First
questions.q: According to Talk About Your Own Mistakes First, what makes it much less difficult to listen to a recital of your own faults?
options: The critic first humbly admits that he, too, is far from impeccable
The critic writes the faults down rather than saying them aloud
The critic points out the faults only in private
The critic promises a reward once the faults are corrected
questions.explain: Carnegie says it is not nearly so difficult to hear about your faults “if the person criticizing begins by humbly admitting that he, too, is far from impeccable.”

questions.unitTitle: Talk About Your Own Mistakes First
questions.section: Principle: Talk about your own mistakes before criticizing the other person
questions.q: True or false: In Talk About Your Own Mistakes First, Clarence Zerhusen discovered that his fifteen-year-old son was experimenting with cigarettes.
questions.explain: Zerhusen of Timonium, Maryland, found his fifteen-year-old son David trying cigarettes and dealt with it by admitting his own addiction.

questions.unitTitle: Talk About Your Own Mistakes First
questions.section: Principle: Talk about your own mistakes before criticizing the other person
questions.q: True or false: In Talk About Your Own Mistakes First, Kaiser Wilhelm II made his notorious boastful announcements while he was a guest in France.
questions.explain: He made them while he was a guest in England, which made matters infinitely worse, and allowed them to be printed in the Daily Telegraph.

questions.unitTitle: Talk About Your Own Mistakes First
questions.section: Principle: Talk about your own mistakes before criticizing the other person
questions.q: True or false: In Talk About Your Own Mistakes First, von Bülow won back the Kaiser by praising him before he made any criticism.
questions.explain: Von Bülow knew he ought to have praised before condemning, but it was too late, so he did the next best thing: he praised after he had criticized, and it worked.

questions.unitTitle: Talk About Your Own Mistakes First
questions.section: Principle: Talk about your own mistakes before criticizing the other person
questions.q: In Talk About Your Own Mistakes First, the Kaiser gave his royal permission to have his remarks printed in the newspaper called the ____.
questions.explain: His silly, egotistical announcements, made while a guest in England, were printed in the Daily Telegraph and set the whole continent buzzing.

questions.unitTitle: Talk About Your Own Mistakes First
questions.section: Principle: Talk about your own mistakes before criticizing the other person
questions.q: Principle 3 of Part Four, from Talk About Your Own Mistakes First, is: Talk about your own ____ before criticizing the other person.
questions.explain: The chapter closes with the principle a good leader follows: talk about your own mistakes before criticizing the other person.

questions.unitTitle: Talk About Your Own Mistakes First
questions.q: In Talk About Your Own Mistakes First, Carnegie told Josephine that she was not born with ____, which comes only with experience.
questions.explain: He reminded her that judgment comes only with experience and that she was better than he had been at her age, before suggesting what would have been wiser.

questions.unitTitle: Talk About Your Own Mistakes First
questions.section: Principle: Talk about your own mistakes before criticizing the other person
questions.q: In Talk About Your Own Mistakes First, the furious Kaiser shouted that von Bülow considered him a ____, capable of blunders von Bülow could never commit.
questions.explain: Von Bülow’s protest that no one could think he had advised such remarks implied the Kaiser alone was the fool, so the Kaiser exploded: “You consider me a donkey.”

questions.unitTitle: Talk About Your Own Mistakes First
questions.section: Principle: Talk about your own mistakes before criticizing the other person
questions.q: In Talk About Your Own Mistakes First, after the von Bülow story, Carnegie asks us to imagine what humility and ____ can do for you and me in our daily contacts.
questions.explain: Von Bülow humbled himself and exalted the Kaiser, and Carnegie asks us to imagine “what humility and praise can do for you and me in our daily contacts.”

questions.unitTitle: Talk About Your Own Mistakes First
questions.section: Principle: Talk about your own mistakes before criticizing the other person
questions.q: Which of these claims did Kaiser Wilhelm II make in the remarks printed in the Daily Telegraph, as described in Talk About Your Own Mistakes First?
options: He was the only German who felt friendly toward the English
He intended to give up the throne to keep the peace
He was building a navy against the menace of Japan
His campaign plan had enabled Lord Roberts to defeat the Boers
Germany would join Russia and France against England
questions.explain: Among his boasts were that he alone of Germans felt friendly to England, that his navy was aimed at Japan, and that his plan won the Boer War for Lord Roberts. He said nothing about abdicating or joining Russia and France; he claimed to have saved England from them.

questions.unitTitle: Talk About Your Own Mistakes First
questions.section: Principle: Talk about your own mistakes before criticizing the other person
questions.q: Which of these did von Bülow credit the Kaiser with surpassing him in, when he recovered from his blunder in Talk About Your Own Mistakes First?
options: Historical knowledge
Naval and military knowledge
Diplomacy
Natural science
Public speaking
questions.explain: He praised the Kaiser’s naval and military knowledge and, above all, his natural science. Historical knowledge and diplomacy were the qualities von Bülow modestly claimed for himself.

questions.unitTitle: Talk About Your Own Mistakes First
questions.section: Principle: Talk about your own mistakes before criticizing the other person
questions.q: Which of these did Clarence Zerhusen say he did NOT do when talking to his son about smoking, in Talk About Your Own Mistakes First?
options: Exhort him to stop
Explain how he had started smoking at about his son’s age
Make threats
Remind him of his own irritating cough
Warn him about the dangers of cigarettes
questions.explain: He says he did not exhort, threaten or warn about dangers; all he did was point out how he was hooked and what it had meant to him, including his irritating cough.

questions.unitTitle: Talk About Your Own Mistakes First
questions.section: Principle: Talk about your own mistakes before criticizing the other person
questions.q: Put these events of the von Bülow and Kaiser episode in Talk About Your Own Mistakes First in the order they happened.
items: The Kaiser’s boastful remarks are printed in the Daily Telegraph
The panicky Kaiser asks von Bülow to take the blame
Von Bülow protests that nobody would believe he gave such advice
The Kaiser shouts that von Bülow thinks him a donkey
Von Bülow praises the Kaiser and humbles himself
The Kaiser shakes his hand several times
questions.explain: The remarks caused uproar, the Kaiser sought a scapegoat, von Bülow’s protest insulted him, and only praise after the criticism turned the Kaiser into an enthusiastic friend.

questions.unitTitle: Talk About Your Own Mistakes First
questions.q: Put the examples in Talk About Your Own Mistakes First in the order Carnegie presents them.
items: Carnegie and his niece Josephine
E. G. Dillistone and his secretary’s spelling
Von Bülow and Kaiser Wilhelm II
Clarence Zerhusen and his son’s smoking
questions.explain: Carnegie opens with his own experience, adds an engineer’s office example, gives the dramatic historical case of the Kaiser, and ends with a father admitting a mistake he had not yet corrected.

questions.unitTitle: Talk About Your Own Mistakes First
questions.q: In Talk About Your Own Mistakes First, match each person to their situation.
pairs: A nineteen-year-old secretary with almost no business experience
An engineer whose secretary’s letters had spelling mistakes
An Imperial Chancellor asked to take the blame for his monarch
A father whose teenage son was trying cigarettes
questions.explain: Each example shows a different setting, from office to court to family, where admitting one’s own faults first made correction acceptable.

questions.unitTitle: Talk About Your Own Mistakes First
questions.section: Principle: Talk about your own mistakes before criticizing the other person
questions.q: In Talk About Your Own Mistakes First, match each person to the way they admitted their own shortcomings.
pairs: Recalled the blunders he made at nineteen
Showed the book of words he had trouble spelling
Called himself shamefully ignorant of natural science
Told how nicotine had gotten the best of him
questions.explain: All four lowered themselves first: Carnegie through his past blunders, Dillistone through his spelling book, von Bülow through his ignorance of science, and Zerhusen through his addiction.

questions.unitTitle: Talk About Your Own Mistakes First
questions.section: Principle: Talk about your own mistakes before criticizing the other person
questions.q: Sort these openings by whether they follow the principle of Talk About Your Own Mistakes First.

items.t: A coach mentions dropping the same catch himself before correcting a player
An editor recalls her own early typos before pointing out errors
A parent admits his own procrastination before asking about late homework
A manager opens by calling the work careless
A teacher lists a student’s errors in front of the class
A supervisor warns of penalties without mentioning himself

questions.explain: The principle is to talk about your own mistakes before criticizing, so the openings that begin with the critic’s own faults follow it; those that go straight to the other person’s faults do not.

questions.unitTitle: Talk About Your Own Mistakes First
questions.section: Principle: Talk about your own mistakes before criticizing the other person
questions.q: In Talk About Your Own Mistakes First, sort these into von Bülow’s first reply to the Kaiser and his later recovery.

items.t: Said nobody could suppose he had advised such remarks
Implied the Kaiser was a half-wit in need of a guardian
Praised the Kaiser’s naval and military knowledge
Admired the Kaiser’s explanations of the barometer and Roentgen rays
Admitted having no notion of chemistry or physics
Claimed only some historical knowledge and skill in diplomacy

questions.explain: His first protest insulted the Kaiser by implying the blunder was beneath him; his recovery exalted the Kaiser and humbled himself, which made the Kaiser beam.

questions.unitTitle: Talk About Your Own Mistakes First
questions.q: In Talk About Your Own Mistakes First, what stopped Carnegie from simply criticizing his niece Josephine, and how did he change the way he pointed out her mistakes?
questions.a: When he started to criticize her he stopped himself, remembering he was twice her age with far more experience, and recalling the blunders he had made at nineteen. He concluded her record was better than his had been. Afterwards he began by saying her mistake was no worse than many of his own, that judgment comes only with experience, and only then asked whether another way would have been wiser.

questions.unitTitle: Talk About Your Own Mistakes First
questions.q: In Talk About Your Own Mistakes First, how did E. G. Dillistone reduce his secretary’s spelling errors, and why did his approach work where pointing out errors had not?
questions.a: Merely pointing out errors had not made her proofread more, so he sat down with her, said a word did not look right and that it was one he always had trouble with, and showed her the thumb-index spelling book he kept. By admitting his own weakness he made the correction feel shared rather than an attack, and her spelling errors were significantly reduced.

questions.unitTitle: Talk About Your Own Mistakes First
questions.section: Principle: Talk about your own mistakes before criticizing the other person
questions.q: A team lead must tell a colleague that his presentation to a client went badly. Using the von Bülow story from Talk About Your Own Mistakes First, how should she begin, and why?
questions.a: She should begin by talking about her own shortcomings and the colleague’s strengths, not by implying he is incompetent. Von Bülow insulted the Kaiser by suggesting the blunder was beneath him, and only won him back by humbling himself and praising the Kaiser. Carnegie concludes that a few sentences humbling oneself and praising the other party can turn an insulted person into a staunch friend.

questions.unitTitle: Talk About Your Own Mistakes First
questions.section: Principle: Talk about your own mistakes before criticizing the other person
questions.q: What does the Clarence Zerhusen story in Talk About Your Own Mistakes First show about admitting mistakes you have not yet corrected?
questions.a: Carnegie says admitting your own mistakes, even when you haven’t corrected them, can help convince someone to change. Zerhusen, still a smoker, did not lecture or threaten his son but told him how he had started young and was now hooked. His son decided not to smoke, and the conversation also led Zerhusen himself to quit with his family’s support.

questions.unitTitle: Talk About Your Own Mistakes First
questions.q: How does Talk About Your Own Mistakes First fit into Part Four’s sequence on changing people without giving offense?
questions.a: Part Four teaches how to correct people without arousing resentment. After Principle 1, begin with praise and honest appreciation, and Principle 2, call attention to mistakes indirectly, this chapter adds Principle 3: humble yourself by admitting your own mistakes before criticizing. It echoes the Part Three advice to admit when you are wrong, now used as a way to soften criticism, and leads on to asking questions instead of giving direct orders.

questions.unitTitle: No One Likes to Take Orders
questions.q: In No One Likes to Take Orders, who told Carnegie about a man who had never heard Owen D. Young give a direct order?
options: Lowell Thomas, while helping Carnegie plan his lecture tours
Ida Tarbell, the dean of American biographers, over dinner
Owen D. Young’s own secretary, in a letter to Carnegie
A student in one of Carnegie’s classes in Wyoming, Pennsylvania
questions.explain: Ida Tarbell told Carnegie at dinner that, while writing her biography of Owen D. Young, she interviewed a man who had shared Young’s office for three years.

questions.unitTitle: No One Likes to Take Orders
questions.q: True or false: In No One Likes to Take Orders, the man who sat in the same office as Owen D. Young for three years said he never once heard Young give a direct order to anyone.
questions.explain: He declared that in all that time Young never gave a direct order; Young always gave suggestions instead.

questions.unitTitle: No One Likes to Take Orders
questions.q: In No One Likes to Take Orders, Carnegie sums up Owen D. Young’s style by saying he always gave ____, not orders.
questions.explain: Young said things like asking whether something would work or inviting people to consider an idea, so he offered suggestions rather than commands.

questions.unitTitle: No One Likes to Take Orders
questions.q: In No One Likes to Take Orders, sort these phrasings by whether Owen D. Young used them or never said them.

items.t: You might consider this
Do you think that would work?
What do you think of this?
Maybe if we were to phrase it this way it would be better
Do this or do that
Don’t do this or don’t do that

questions.explain: Young framed everything as a question or a gentle proposal, even when reviewing an assistant’s letter; he never issued flat commands or prohibitions.

questions.unitTitle: No One Likes to Take Orders
questions.q: Which of these does Carnegie, in No One Likes to Take Orders, say a technique like Owen D. Young’s does for the person being directed?
options: Makes it easy for the person to correct errors
Saves the person’s pride and gives a feeling of importance
Encourages cooperation instead of rebellion
Gets the job done faster than a direct order would
Removes the need for the leader to check the work
questions.explain: Carnegie lists three effects: easy correction of errors, saved pride with a feeling of importance, and cooperation instead of rebellion. He makes no claim about speed or about leaders no longer checking work.

questions.unitTitle: No One Likes to Take Orders
questions.q: In No One Likes to Take Orders, what did the angry instructor in Dan Santarelli’s story threaten to do if the student did not move his car?
options: Report the student to the school’s director that very day
Have the car towed away at the student’s own expense
Bar the student from using the school’s shops
Wrap a chain around the car and drag it out of there
questions.explain: The instructor screamed that he would put a chain around the car and drag it out, a brash order that bred lasting resentment.

questions.unitTitle: No One Likes to Take Orders
questions.q: True or false: In No One Likes to Take Orders, after the instructor shouted at him to move his car, only the student who owned the car went on to resent the instructor.
questions.explain: Not only that student but all the students in the class did whatever they could to give the instructor a hard time and make his job unpleasant.

questions.unitTitle: No One Likes to Take Orders
questions.q: In No One Likes to Take Orders, why does Carnegie say the instructor’s order about the parked car backfired even though the student was in the wrong, and how could it have been handled instead?
questions.a: Carnegie notes that resentment caused by a brash order may last a long time, even when the order corrects an obviously bad situation. The student was wrong to block the driveway, yet the arrogant demand made him and his whole class resent the instructor and make his job unpleasant. Had the instructor asked in a friendly way whose car was in the driveway and suggested that moving it would let other cars in and out, the student would gladly have moved it and nobody would have been upset.

questions.unitTitle: No One Likes to Take Orders
questions.q: In No One Likes to Take Orders, match each person to who they were.
pairs: The dean of American biographers, who dined with Carnegie
A man whose office-mate never heard him give a direct order
A teacher at a vocational school in Wyoming, Pennsylvania
General manager of a precision machine-parts plant in Johannesburg
questions.explain: Tarbell passed on the Young story from her biography research; Santarelli told the parked-car story in one of Carnegie’s classes; Macdonald ran the small South African manufacturing plant.

questions.unitTitle: No One Likes to Take Orders
questions.q: In No One Likes to Take Orders, put the events of Ian Macdonald’s large order in the order they happened.
items: He doubted the plant could meet the delivery date
He called everybody together and explained the situation
He said how much the order would mean to the company and to them
He asked questions about ways to handle the order
The employees offered ideas and insisted he take the order
The order was accepted, produced and delivered on time
questions.explain: Instead of pushing his people to rush the work, Macdonald first explained and appealed to what the order meant, then asked questions; the workers’ own ideas led them to insist on taking it.

questions.unitTitle: No One Likes to Take Orders
questions.q: Which of these questions did Ian Macdonald, in No One Likes to Take Orders, put to his employees about the large order?
options: Is there anything we can do to handle this order?
Can anyone think of different ways to process it through the shop?
Is there any way to adjust our hours or personnel assignments that would help?
Who is willing to work weekends without extra pay?
Why is the shop always behind on its schedule?
questions.explain: Macdonald asked whether anything could be done, whether anyone could find a different way through the shop, and whether hours or assignments could be adjusted. He did not demand sacrifices or blame the shop.

questions.unitTitle: No One Likes to Take Orders
questions.section: Principle: Ask questions instead of giving direct orders
questions.q: In No One Likes to Take Orders, Carnegie says asking questions not only makes an order more palatable; it often stimulates the ____ of the persons whom you ask.
questions.explain: Macdonald’s workers show this: once asked, they came up with many ideas for getting the order through the shop.

questions.unitTitle: No One Likes to Take Orders
questions.section: Principle: Ask questions instead of giving direct orders
questions.q: In No One Likes to Take Orders, according to Carnegie, when are people more likely to accept an order?
options: When the order comes from someone with clear authority
When the order is explained in writing with reasons
When they have had a part in the decision that caused it
When the order is paired with praise for past work
questions.explain: Carnegie writes that people are more likely to accept an order if they have had a part in the decision behind it, which is why asking questions works.

questions.unitTitle: No One Likes to Take Orders
questions.section: Principle: Ask questions instead of giving direct orders
questions.q: In No One Likes to Take Orders, Principle 4 of Part Four reads: Ask questions instead of giving direct ____.
questions.explain: The chapter closes with the principle “Ask questions instead of giving direct orders.”

questions.unitTitle: No One Likes to Take Orders
questions.section: Principle: Ask questions instead of giving direct orders
questions.q: A hospital ward is suddenly asked to take in extra patients when the staff rota is already full. Which response by the head nurse best follows the approach of No One Likes to Take Orders?
options: Gathering the staff, explaining what it means, and asking how they could adjust shifts to manage
Posting a new rota with longer shifts and telling staff it is not open to discussion
Refusing the extra patients because the schedule cannot possibly be changed
Telling each nurse privately to work faster so the extra patients can be absorbed
questions.explain: This mirrors Ian Macdonald, who, rather than pushing his people to rush, explained the situation and asked questions such as whether hours or assignments could be adjusted.

questions.unitTitle: No One Likes to Take Orders
questions.section: Principle: Ask questions instead of giving direct orders
questions.q: In No One Likes to Take Orders, what does Ian Macdonald’s handling of the large order show about the benefits of asking questions instead of giving orders?
questions.a: Macdonald thought the order impossible, but instead of pushing his people he explained the situation and asked them how it might be handled. Asking questions stimulated their creativity: they came up with many ideas and insisted he take the order. Because they had a part in the decision, they accepted the work with a “We can do it” attitude, and the order was delivered on time.

questions.unitTitle: No One Likes to Take Orders
questions.q: No One Likes to Take Orders belongs to Part Four of the book. What is the aim of that part, which its principle serves?
options: Winning people to your way of thinking in an argument
Changing people without giving offense or arousing resentment
Making people like you the moment you meet them
Handling complaints by letting people talk themselves out
questions.explain: Part Four is titled Be a Leader: How to Change People Without Giving Offense or Arousing Resentment, and asking instead of ordering avoids the resentment a brash order causes.

questions.unitTitle: No One Likes to Take Orders
questions.q: How does No One Likes to Take Orders fit with the chapters around it in Part Four and with the earlier advice in Part Three?
questions.a: It is the fourth of Part Four’s leadership principles, following beginning with praise, calling attention to mistakes indirectly and talking about your own mistakes first, and preceding letting the other person save face. Like them, it changes behavior while protecting the other person’s pride. It also echoes Part Three’s principle to let the other person feel that the idea is his or hers, since questions let people take part in the decision.

questions.unitTitle: Let the Other Person Save Face
questions.q: In Let the Other Person Save Face, what did General Electric do about Charles Steinmetz, who was failing as head of the calculating department?
options: Gave him a new title for work he already did and let someone else run the department
Moved him to lead a new research laboratory in a different city
Kept him as head but appointed a deputy to make all the decisions
Praised him publicly at a dinner and then asked him to resign quietly
questions.explain: GE made him Consulting Engineer of the General Electric Company, a new title for work he was already doing, and gave the department to someone else. He was not moved, sidelined by a deputy, or eased out.

questions.unitTitle: Let the Other Person Save Face
questions.q: In Let the Other Person Save Face, why did Marshall A. Granger’s accounting firm have to let many people go each year?
options: It lost clients every spring to larger accounting firms
Its business was seasonal, so staff went after the income tax rush
It hired trainees who rarely passed their professional exams
It cut staff after each annual review of its budget
questions.explain: Granger wrote that the firm’s business was mostly seasonal, so many people had to be let go once the income tax rush was over. Nothing about the dismissals reflected poor work or lost clients.

questions.unitTitle: Let the Other Person Save Face
questions.q: In Fred Clark’s story in Let the Other Person Save Face, why was the production supervisor evasive when the vice president questioned him?
options: He did not understand the production process being discussed
He was protecting a colleague who had caused the fault
He did not want to be embarrassed in front of his peers
He was already planning to leave for a competitor
questions.explain: The vice president’s tone was aggressive and aimed at exposing faulty performance, and the supervisor, not wanting to be embarrassed before his peers, dodged the questions. His leaving for a competitor came months later, as a result of the encounter.

questions.unitTitle: Let the Other Person Save Face
questions.q: In Anna Mazzone’s story in Let the Other Person Save Face, what reason did her boss give the meeting for the failed test-marketing?
options: A fault in the test design that he himself had approved
Poor data supplied to her by the sales department
Unrealistic deadlines set by senior management
Her lack of experience, not her lack of ability
questions.explain: In front of her colleagues the boss said her lack of experience, not her lack of ability, was the reason for the failure, and that errors on a new project are not unusual. He did not shift the blame onto anyone else.

questions.unitTitle: Let the Other Person Save Face
questions.section: Principle: Let the other person save face
questions.q: In Let the Other Person Save Face, what does the quotation from Antoine de Saint-Exupéry say really matters?
options: What other people say about a man behind his back
What a man thinks of himself, not what I think of him
Whether a man is right or wrong in the dispute
How quickly a man admits his mistakes to others
questions.explain: Saint-Exupéry wrote that he had no right to diminish a man in his own eyes, because what matters is the man’s view of himself, not the speaker’s view of him. Carnegie uses this to say that being right does not justify making someone lose face.

questions.unitTitle: Let the Other Person Save Face
questions.section: Principle: Let the other person save face
questions.q: A team leader discovers that a new analyst’s first report contains a serious error, just before a group meeting. Which response best follows the principle of Let the Other Person Save Face?
options: Correct the report in the meeting so everyone can learn from the mistake
Say nothing and quietly give the analyst’s next project to someone else
Note that errors on a first project are not unusual and voice confidence in the analyst
Ask the analyst pointed questions in the meeting to find out what went wrong
questions.explain: Like Anna Mazzone’s boss, the leader should treat the error as normal for a new project and show faith in the person, protecting their pride. Pointed public questioning is what wrecked the supervisor in Fred Clark’s story.

questions.unitTitle: Let the Other Person Save Face
questions.section: Principle: Let the other person save face
questions.q: True or false: Carnegie says that even when we are right and the other person is definitely wrong, causing that person to lose face only destroys ego.
questions.explain: Carnegie states that even if we are right and the other is definitely wrong, we only destroy ego by causing someone to lose face. Being right is no licence to humiliate.

questions.unitTitle: Let the Other Person Save Face
questions.q: True or false: After being berated at the production meeting in Fred Clark’s story, the supervisor became a more careful worker and stayed with the company for years.
questions.explain: The supervisor, basically a good worker, was useless to the company from then on and left a few months later for a competitor, where he was reportedly doing a fine job. The public attack destroyed the working relationship.

questions.unitTitle: Let the Other Person Save Face
questions.q: In Let the Other Person Save Face, General Electric moved Charles Steinmetz out of his department by making him ____ Engineer of the General Electric Company.
questions.explain: The new title, Consulting Engineer, described work Steinmetz was already doing, so he kept his pride while someone else headed the department.

questions.unitTitle: Let the Other Person Save Face
questions.q: In Let the Other Person Save Face, Marshall A. Granger says his firm’s old, hasty way of firing seasonal staff left them with disappointment and a feeling of being ____.
questions.explain: Granger wrote that the casual dismissals left people disappointed and feeling ‘let down,’ with no love for the firm. After he changed his approach, they no longer felt let down.

questions.unitTitle: Let the Other Person Save Face
questions.section: Principle: Let the other person save face
questions.q: Carnegie’s Principle 5 in Part Four reads: Let the other person ____.
questions.explain: The chapter closes with Principle 5: “Let the other person save face.”

questions.unitTitle: Let the Other Person Save Face
questions.section: Principle: Let the other person save face
questions.q: In the Saint-Exupéry quotation that ends Let the Other Person Save Face, hurting a man in his ____ is called a crime.
questions.explain: Saint-Exupéry wrote: “Hurting a man in his dignity is a crime.”

questions.unitTitle: Let the Other Person Save Face
questions.q: Which of these does Carnegie list in Let the Other Person Save Face as ways we ride roughshod over the feelings of others?
options: Finding fault
Issuing threats
Criticizing a child or an employee in front of others
Asking questions instead of giving direct orders
Calling attention to mistakes indirectly
questions.explain: Carnegie names getting our own way, finding fault, issuing threats and criticizing a child or employee in front of others. Asking questions and indirect correction are gentler methods from other Part Four chapters, not examples of hurting pride.

questions.unitTitle: Let the Other Person Save Face
questions.q: Which of these did Marshall A. Granger say to departing seasonal employees under his new, more considerate approach?
options: That on the tough Newark assignment they came through with flying colors
That they had always understood they were only hired for the busy season
That they were going a long way, wherever they worked
That the firm believed in them and was rooting for them
That they would be the first rehired the next season
questions.explain: Granger praised the Newark assignment, told the person he was going a long way, and said the firm believed in him and was rooting for him. The reminder about being hired only for the busy season belonged to the old, casual method, and he made no rehiring promise.

questions.unitTitle: Let the Other Person Save Face
questions.q: Put these events from Anna Mazzone’s story in Let the Other Person Save Face in the order they happened.
items: The test results revealed a serious error in her planning
She found she had no time to talk to her boss before the meeting
She reported briefly and said she would repeat the study
Her boss thanked her and voiced his confidence in front of colleagues
She left resolved never to let her boss down again
questions.explain: The error came first, then the lack of time to warn her boss, then her short report, then the boss’s public support, which left her determined not to let him down.

questions.unitTitle: Let the Other Person Save Face
questions.q: Put these examples in the order Carnegie presents them in Let the Other Person Save Face.
items: General Electric’s new title for Charles Steinmetz
Marshall A. Granger’s letter about firing seasonal staff
Fred Clark’s account of a vice president berating a supervisor
Anna Mazzone’s account of her boss’s response to her error
Antoine de Saint-Exupéry’s words on a man’s dignity
questions.explain: The chapter opens with Steinmetz, moves to Granger’s letter, sets the two class members’ contrasting stories side by side, and ends with Saint-Exupéry before stating the principle.

questions.unitTitle: Let the Other Person Save Face
questions.q: In Let the Other Person Save Face, match each person to how Carnegie describes them.
pairs: Electrical genius who failed as a department head
Certified public accountant who wrote about firing seasonal staff
Marketing specialist for a food packer
questions.explain: These are the descriptions the chapter gives each figure. Steinmetz was a genius with electricity but a failure at running the calculating department.

questions.unitTitle: Let the Other Person Save Face
questions.q: In Let the Other Person Save Face, match each story to its outcome.
pairs: Steinmetz given a new title at G.E.
He was happy and there was no storm
Staff returned with keen personal affection when needed
The vice president’s public attack in Fred Clark’s story
The supervisor left for a competitor
Anna Mazzone’s boss backing her after her error
She resolved never to let him down again
questions.explain: Each face-saving approach kept goodwill, while the one public humiliation cost the company a good worker.

questions.unitTitle: Let the Other Person Save Face
questions.section: Principle: Let the other person save face
questions.q: Sort these actions from Let the Other Person Save Face by whether they cause someone to lose face or let them save face.

items.t: Berating a supervisor in a meeting and accusing him of lying
Telling a worker he was only hired for the busy season anyway
Criticizing an employee in front of others
Giving a new title for work already being done
Blaming a failure on inexperience rather than lack of ability
Recalling a departing worker’s success on a tough assignment

questions.explain: The public berating, the casual dismissal and criticism before others hurt pride. The new title, the boss’s kind explanation and Granger’s praise let people keep their dignity.

questions.unitTitle: Let the Other Person Save Face
questions.q: Sort these details by which class member’s story in Let the Other Person Save Face they belong to.

items.t: A vice president asked aggressive, pointed questions
The employee was accused of lying
A good worker later joined a competitor
The test-marketing of a new product
A planning error meant the test had to be redone
The speaker resolved not to cry in front of the men

questions.explain: Clark described a supervisor humiliated at a production meeting, who then left. Mazzone described her own test-marketing error and her boss’s supportive response.

questions.unitTitle: Let the Other Person Save Face
questions.q: In Let the Other Person Save Face, how did General Electric deal with Charles Steinmetz, and why does Carnegie tell the story?
questions.a: Steinmetz was a genius with electricity but a failure as head of the calculating department, and he was both indispensable and highly sensitive. GE made him Consulting Engineer, a new title for work he was already doing, and let someone else head the department. Steinmetz was happy and the company avoided a storm, which shows the power of letting a person save face.

questions.unitTitle: Let the Other Person Save Face
questions.q: In Let the Other Person Save Face, how did Marshall A. Granger change the way he let seasonal staff go, and what difference did it make?
questions.a: At first the firm fired people quickly and casually, reminding them they were only hired for the busy season, which left them disappointed, feeling let down and with no love for the firm. Granger began calling each person in only after thinking over their work, praising what they had done well and saying the firm believed in them. They left feeling much better, knew they would have been kept if there were work, and came back with keen personal affection when needed.

questions.unitTitle: Let the Other Person Save Face
questions.section: Principle: Let the other person save face
questions.q: What contrast do the stories of Fred Clark and Anna Mazzone draw in Let the Other Person Save Face?
questions.a: Both involve an employee whose work is questioned in a meeting before colleagues. In Clark’s company a vice president aggressively exposed a supervisor’s faults and accused him of lying, destroying the relationship, and the good worker became useless and left for a competitor. Mazzone’s boss instead thanked her, called the error normal on a new project and expressed faith in her, so she left determined never to let him down. Faultfinding loses people; letting them save face wins their loyalty.

questions.unitTitle: Let the Other Person Save Face
questions.q: How does Let the Other Person Save Face fit the purpose of Part Four, Be a Leader: How to Change People Without Giving Offense or Arousing Resentment?
questions.a: Part Four is about correcting and changing people without offending them or stirring resentment. This chapter applies that aim to the hardest moments, such as discharging or reprimanding someone, where a few minutes’ thought and a considerate word can ease the sting. Protecting the other person’s pride, even when we are right, keeps their goodwill, which is the leader’s goal throughout Part Four.

questions.unitTitle: How to Spur People On to Success
questions.q: In How to Spur People On to Success, what did Pete Barlow do the moment a new dog in his act showed the slightest improvement?
options: He patted, praised and fed it meat, making a great to-do
He ignored the dog until it had mastered the whole trick
He moved the dog straight on to a harder trick
He scolded the other dogs so the new one would notice
questions.explain: Barlow rewarded even the smallest progress with pats, praise and meat. Carnegie notes animal trainers have used this technique for centuries and asks why we do not use the same common sense with people.

questions.unitTitle: How to Spur People On to Success
questions.q: In How to Spur People On to Success, what did Enrico Caruso’s mother do after his first teacher said he could not sing?
options: She found him a better-known teacher in Rome
She praised him, said she saw improvement and went barefoot to pay for lessons
She made him keep working in the factory until he was older
She asked the teacher to give him a second audition
questions.explain: The poor peasant mother hugged him, told him she knew he could sing and could already see improvement, and saved money for lessons by going barefoot. Carnegie says her praise and encouragement changed his life.

questions.unitTitle: How to Spur People On to Success
questions.q: In How to Spur People On to Success, what job did the young Charles Dickens have while trying to become a writer?
options: Sweeping out a dry-goods store for fourteen hours a day
Working as a clerk in a London debtors’ prison
Pasting labels on bottles of blacking in a rat-infested warehouse
Selling newspapers on the streets of London
questions.explain: Dickens pasted labels on bottles of blacking in a rat-infested warehouse and slept in a dismal attic. The fourteen-hour days in a dry-goods store belong to the H. G. Wells story.

questions.unitTitle: How to Spur People On to Success
questions.q: In How to Spur People On to Success, how did H. G. Wells’s old schoolmaster respond to his despairing letter?
options: He urged Wells to stay at the shop and endure it
He sent Wells money to leave the shop and travel
He told Wells to write stories about his hardship
He praised his intelligence and offered him a teaching job
questions.explain: The schoolmaster gave him a little praise, assured him he was very intelligent and fitted for finer things, and offered him a job as a teacher. Carnegie says that praise changed Wells’s future and left its mark on English literature.

questions.unitTitle: How to Spur People On to Success
questions.q: A supervisor wants to praise a new employee’s first report in the way Keith Roper praised the young printer in How to Spur People On to Success. Which remark fits best?
options: “Laying out the figures this way made this the clearest report we have had.”
“You’re good, keep up the great work on everything you do.”
“Everyone here thinks you are a wonderful person to work with.”
“Not bad for a beginner, but the next report should be better.”
questions.explain: Roper pointed out exactly why the work was superior and how it mattered to the company. Carnegie says specific praise comes across as sincere, while a general “You’re good” can sound like mere flattery.

questions.unitTitle: How to Spur People On to Success
questions.q: In How to Spur People On to Success, what does Carnegie say B. F. Skinner showed by experiments with animals and humans?
options: That criticism given privately works as well as praise
That praise reinforces good behaviour while poorer behaviour atrophies
That rewards only work on animals and not on adult humans
That praise must be given at least once a day to have any effect
questions.explain: Carnegie calls praise instead of criticism the basic concept of Skinner’s teachings: the good things people do are reinforced and the poorer things wither for lack of attention.

questions.unitTitle: How to Spur People On to Success
questions.q: A team member who usually misses deadlines hands in one task a day early. According to How to Spur People On to Success, what should the team leader do?
options: Say nothing, since one early task is not yet a real change
Point out that the other deadlines are still being missed
Praise this improvement now, even though it is small
Wait until the improvement has lasted a full month before mentioning it
questions.explain: Carnegie urges us to praise even the slightest improvement, because that inspires the other person to keep on improving. Waiting for a big change is exactly what the dog trainer did not do.

questions.unitTitle: How to Spur People On to Success
questions.section: Principle: Praise the slightest improvement and praise every improvement
questions.q: In How to Spur People On to Success, why does Carnegie quote William James near the end of the chapter?
options: To show that criticism is sometimes needed to wake people up
To prove that praise works better on children than on adults
To explain how B. F. Skinner designed his experiments
To answer the charge of exaggeration about people’s unused powers
questions.explain: Carnegie claims praise can literally transform people, then anticipates the objection “Exaggeration?” James’s words that we are only half awake and live far within our limits support the claim.

questions.unitTitle: How to Spur People On to Success
questions.q: The principle of How to Spur People On to Success tells us to be “hearty in your approbation and lavish in your praise.” Whose words were these first presented as, earlier in the book?
options: Abraham Lincoln’s
Charles Schwab’s
William James’s
Jess Lair’s
questions.explain: In The Big Secret of Dealing with People, Schwab says he is anxious to praise but loath to find fault, and hearty in his approbation and lavish in his praise. Chapter 4.6 turns his words into a leadership principle.

questions.unitTitle: How to Spur People On to Success
questions.q: True or false: In How to Spur People On to Success, Charles Dickens was not paid a shilling for the first story he had accepted, yet the editor’s praise changed his life.
questions.explain: He was paid nothing, but one editor had praised him and given him recognition. He was so thrilled he wandered the streets in tears, and Carnegie says that encouragement changed his whole life.

questions.unitTitle: How to Spur People On to Success
questions.q: True or false: In How to Spur People On to Success, John Ringelspaugh reports that once his family switched to praise, the children’s improved behaviour lasted forever without ever levelling off.
questions.explain: Ringelspaugh admits it did not last forever, but the norm reached after things levelled off was much better, with the children doing far more right things than wrong ones.

questions.unitTitle: How to Spur People On to Success
questions.section: Principle: Praise the slightest improvement and praise every improvement
questions.q: True or false: In How to Spur People On to Success, Principle 6 advises saving praise for large improvements so that it keeps its value.
questions.explain: The principle says the opposite: praise the slightest improvement and praise every improvement, being lavish in your praise.

questions.unitTitle: How to Spur People On to Success
questions.section: Principle: Praise the slightest improvement and praise every improvement
questions.q: True or false: In How to Spur People On to Success, Carnegie says the principles of the book will work only when they come from the heart.
questions.explain: He repeats that the principles work only when sincere: “I am not advocating a bag of tricks.” He calls it a new way of life.

questions.unitTitle: How to Spur People On to Success
questions.q: In How to Spur People On to Success, Carnegie asks why we don’t use meat instead of a ____ when trying to change people.
questions.explain: Animal trainers reward progress with meat, and Carnegie asks why we don’t use the same common sense with people: praise instead of condemnation.

questions.unitTitle: How to Spur People On to Success
questions.q: In How to Spur People On to Success, Jess Lair writes that praise is like ____ to the warm human spirit.
questions.explain: Lair writes that “we cannot flower and grow without it,” yet most of us give the cold wind of criticism far more readily than the warm sunshine of praise.

questions.unitTitle: How to Spur People On to Success
questions.section: Principle: Praise the slightest improvement and praise every improvement
questions.q: In How to Spur People On to Success, Carnegie sums up: abilities wither under criticism; they blossom under ____.
questions.explain: This line comes just before the principle and contrasts the effect of criticism with that of encouragement on a person’s abilities.

questions.unitTitle: How to Spur People On to Success
questions.section: Principle: Praise the slightest improvement and praise every improvement
questions.q: In How to Spur People On to Success, William James is quoted as saying that compared with what we ought to be, we are only half ____.
questions.explain: James argues we use only a small part of our physical and mental resources. Carnegie adds that one unused power is our ability to praise people and inspire them.

questions.unitTitle: How to Spur People On to Success
questions.section: Principle: Praise the slightest improvement and praise every improvement
questions.q: In How to Spur People On to Success, Carnegie says that when praise is ____, it comes across as sincere rather than as something said just to make one feel good.
questions.explain: Roper singled out a specific accomplishment instead of making general flattering remarks, so his praise meant much more to the young printer.

questions.unitTitle: How to Spur People On to Success
questions.q: Which of these people does How to Spur People On to Success present as having had their lives changed by a few words of praise?
options: Enrico Caruso
Charles Dickens
H. G. Wells
Abraham Lincoln
Charles Schwab
questions.explain: Carnegie tells how praise from a mother, an editor and a schoolmaster changed the lives of Caruso, Dickens and Wells. Lincoln and Schwab are not used as examples of this in the chapter.

questions.unitTitle: How to Spur People On to Success
questions.q: Which of these hardships of the young Charles Dickens does How to Spur People On to Success describe?
options: He had attended school for no more than four years
His father had been jailed for debt
He slept in an attic room with two other boys from the slums
He had lost his mother as a small child
He was dismissed from his first job for poor work
questions.explain: Carnegie lists his short schooling, his father’s jailing for debt, hunger, warehouse work and a dismal shared attic. He says nothing about losing his mother or being dismissed.

questions.unitTitle: How to Spur People On to Success
questions.q: Which of these did Keith Roper do when he talked with the young printer in How to Spur People On to Success?
options: Told him how pleased he was with the work
Pointed out exactly why the work was superior
Explained how important his contribution was to the company
Offered him a pay rise on the spot
Moved him away from the supervisor who disliked him
questions.explain: Roper praised the work as the best from that shop for some time, said exactly why, and stressed its importance to the company. No pay rise or transfer is mentioned; the praise alone turned the printer around.

questions.unitTitle: How to Spur People On to Success
questions.q: Which of these did John Ringelspaugh report after his family began praising their children instead of harping on their faults, in How to Spur People On to Success?
options: Some of the really upsetting behaviour stopped within the first day or two
The children began going out of their way to do things right
The parents found it easy from the start to find things to praise
The children never misbehaved again
questions.explain: Upsetting behaviour stopped quickly and the children began capitalizing on the praise. But he says finding things to praise was really tough at first, and the improvement did not last forever.

questions.unitTitle: How to Spur People On to Success
questions.q: In How to Spur People On to Success, put the three stories of famous lives changed by praise in the order Carnegie tells them.
items: Enrico Caruso and his mother
Charles Dickens and the editor
H. G. Wells and his schoolmaster
questions.explain: Carnegie moves from the Naples factory boy Caruso, to Dickens in the London warehouse, to Wells in the London dry-goods store.

questions.unitTitle: How to Spur People On to Success
questions.q: In How to Spur People On to Success, put the events of H. G. Wells’s story in order.
items: Works two years as a clerk in a dry-goods store
Tramps fifteen miles to see his mother
Writes a despairing letter to his old schoolmaster
Receives praise and the offer of a teaching job
Writes many bestselling books
questions.explain: After two years of drudgery he walked to his mother, then wrote to his old schoolmaster, whose praise and job offer set him on the path to becoming a bestselling author.

questions.unitTitle: How to Spur People On to Success
questions.q: Put these parts of How to Spur People On to Success in the order Carnegie presents them.
items: Pete Barlow training his dogs
Caruso, Dickens and Wells
B. F. Skinner’s experiments
Ringelspaugh’s children and Roper’s printer
William James on unused powers
questions.explain: The chapter starts from animal training, gives famous lives changed by praise, adds Skinner’s experimental support, then everyday cases at home and at work, and ends with James on our latent powers before the principle.

questions.unitTitle: How to Spur People On to Success
questions.q: In How to Spur People On to Success, match each person to the one whose praise changed their course.
pairs: His mother, a poor peasant woman
An editor who accepted one of his stories
Keith Roper, who came to the print shop
questions.explain: Each story shows praise from one person at a turning point: a mother, an editor, a schoolmaster and a company manager.

questions.unitTitle: How to Spur People On to Success
questions.q: In How to Spur People On to Success, match each example to the point Carnegie uses it to make.
