pairs: Praise reinforces good behaviour and lets poorer behaviour wither
Praise instead of yelling improves children at home
Specific praise comes across as sincere
questions.explain: The dogs give the basic idea, Skinner gives experimental support, the Ringelspaughs show it at home, and Roper shows it at work and why specific praise is believed.

questions.unitTitle: How to Spur People On to Success
questions.q: In How to Spur People On to Success, match each writer quoted or cited to how Carnegie describes or uses them.
pairs: Psychologist who compares praise to sunlight
Great contemporary psychologist whose basic concept is praise over criticism
Psychologist and philosopher who says we are only half awake
questions.explain: Lair supplies the sunlight image, Skinner the experimental basis, and James the idea of unused powers that praise can awaken.

questions.unitTitle: How to Spur People On to Success
questions.q: In How to Spur People On to Success, sort these images by whether Carnegie links them to praise or to criticism.

items.t: Meat for the dog
Warm sunshine
Abilities blossoming
Flowering and growing
The whip
The cold wind
Abilities withering
Condemnation

questions.explain: Carnegie and Lair pair meat, sunshine and blossoming with praise, and the whip, cold wind and withering with criticism and condemnation.

questions.unitTitle: How to Spur People On to Success
questions.section: Principle: Praise the slightest improvement and praise every improvement
questions.q: In How to Spur People On to Success, sort these remarks by whether they are specific, sincere praise or mere flattery.

items.t: Pointing out exactly why the work was superior
Explaining how the work matters to the company
Singling out one particular accomplishment
Simply saying you’re good
Making general flattering remarks
Saying nice things just to make someone feel good

questions.explain: Carnegie says nobody wants insincerity or flattery. Praise tied to a specific accomplishment comes across as sincere; general compliments do not.

questions.unitTitle: How to Spur People On to Success
questions.q: In How to Spur People On to Success, why does Carnegie begin with Pete Barlow training dogs, and what question does it lead him to ask?
questions.a: Barlow praised, patted and fed a dog the moment it showed the slightest improvement, a technique animal trainers have used for centuries. Carnegie asks why we don’t use the same common sense with people: meat instead of a whip, praise instead of condemnation. Praising even the slightest improvement inspires the other person to keep on improving.

questions.unitTitle: How to Spur People On to Success
questions.q: In How to Spur People On to Success, explain how the story of Charles Dickens shows the power of praise.
questions.a: Dickens had little schooling, a father jailed for debt, and a job pasting labels in a rat-infested warehouse; he was so unsure of himself that he mailed his first manuscript at night. Story after story was refused until one was accepted, unpaid, but with an editor’s praise. That recognition thrilled him and changed his whole life; without it he might have stayed in factory work.

questions.unitTitle: How to Spur People On to Success
questions.q: A youth coach has a new player who keeps making mistakes, and the coach has been shouting at every error. Using How to Spur People On to Success, explain what the coach should do instead and why.
questions.a: The coach should look hard for something the player does right and praise it, even the slightest improvement, rather than harping on faults. As with the Ringelspaugh children, praise makes good behaviour grow and lets poorer habits wither for lack of attention, as Skinner’s experiments showed. The praise should name exactly what was done well so it comes across as sincere.

questions.unitTitle: How to Spur People On to Success
questions.section: Principle: Praise the slightest improvement and praise every improvement
questions.q: In How to Spur People On to Success, why was Keith Roper’s praise of the young printer effective, and how does Carnegie distinguish it from flattery?
questions.a: Roper did not just say “You’re good”; he pointed out exactly why the work was superior and how important it was to the company. Because the praise singled out a specific accomplishment, it was meaningful and believed, and the printer became loyal and dedicated. Carnegie says we all crave appreciation, but nobody wants insincerity or flattery.

questions.unitTitle: How to Spur People On to Success
questions.section: Principle: Praise the slightest improvement and praise every improvement
questions.q: In How to Spur People On to Success, how does Carnegie use William James to argue that praise can transform people, not just change them?
questions.a: James says that compared with what we ought to be we are only half awake and live far within our limits, with powers we habitually fail to use. Carnegie applies this to the reader: one unused power is the ability to praise people and inspire them with a realization of their latent possibilities. By awakening the hidden treasures people possess, praise can literally transform them.

questions.unitTitle: How to Spur People On to Success
questions.q: How does How to Spur People On to Success fit the aim of Part Four, and how does it connect to the advice of Part One?
questions.a: Part Four is about how to change people without giving offense or arousing resentment, and this chapter offers praise of every improvement in place of criticism as a way to do it. It builds on Part One’s Big Secret of Dealing with People, where Schwab says he is anxious to praise but loath to find fault. The principle even repeats his phrase: be “hearty in your approbation and lavish in your praise.”

questions.unitTitle: Give a Dog a Good Name
questions.q: In Give a Dog a Good Name, what did service manager Henry Henke do when his once-good mechanic Bill began turning in unsatisfactory work?
options: Warned Bill that his job was at risk unless his speed improved
Assigned Bill easier jobs until his old standards returned
Had a heart-to-heart talk recalling Bill’s fine record before raising the decline
Posted the customers’ complaints where the whole shop could see them
questions.explain: Instead of bawling him out or threatening him, Henke reminded Bill he was a fine mechanic with many satisfied customers, then said his recent work fell short of his own old standards. Threats are exactly what Henke avoided.

questions.unitTitle: Give a Dog a Good Name
questions.section: Principle: Give the other person a fine reputation to live up to
questions.q: In Give a Dog a Good Name, Samuel Vauclain says the average person can be led readily if you have their respect and show that you respect them for what?
options: Their loyalty to the company
Some kind of ability
Their honesty in admitting mistakes
Their years of long service
questions.explain: Vauclain, then president of the Baldwin Locomotive Works, said people can be led if you show that you respect that person “for some kind of ability.”

questions.unitTitle: Give a Dog a Good Name
questions.q: In Georgette Leblanc’s story in Give a Dog a Good Name, what did she say to Marie the Dishwasher that changed Marie’s life?
options: That she did not know what treasures were within her
That she would one day marry well and become a lady
That she was the hardest worker in the whole hotel
That her cooking was better than the chef’s own
questions.explain: Leblanc told her point-blank, “Marie, you do not know what treasures are within you.” The talk of becoming a lady was Marie’s own words two months later, not Leblanc’s.

questions.unitTitle: Give a Dog a Good Name
questions.q: In Give a Dog a Good Name, after Dr. Martin Fitzhugh’s note to his charwoman Bridgit, how much additional time did she spend to make his office shine?
options: The extra half hour he offered
An extra hour on each visit
A whole extra day that week
None at all
questions.explain: Though he offered to pay for an extra half hour, Fitzhugh reports she outperformed all her past efforts and spent no extra time: “That’s right—none at all.”

questions.unitTitle: Give a Dog a Good Name
questions.section: Principle: Give the other person a fine reputation to live up to
questions.q: A coach wants a careless player to start passing the ball more. Following Give a Dog a Good Name, which approach would Carnegie recommend?
options: Bench the player for a game so he feels the cost of holding the ball
Tell the player, in front of the team, that he is known as a generous team player and you are counting on that
List every match where his selfishness cost the team a goal
Praise the other players’ passing loudly so he notices the contrast
questions.explain: Carnegie advises acting as though the trait you want were already one of the person’s outstanding characteristics and stating it openly. Punishment and pointed comparison are the fault-finding the chapter sets aside.

questions.unitTitle: Give a Dog a Good Name
questions.q: Give a Dog a Good Name is Principle 7 of which part of How to Win Friends and Influence People?
options: Fundamental Techniques in Handling People
How to Win People to Your Way of Thinking
Be a Leader: How to Change People Without Giving Offense or Arousing Resentment
Six Ways to Make People Like You
questions.explain: It sits in Part Four, on changing people without giving offense, and the chapter ends by calling this the difficult leadership role of changing the attitude or behavior of others. Part Three also has a Principle 7, but it is about letting the other person feel the idea is theirs.

questions.unitTitle: Give a Dog a Good Name
questions.q: True or false: In Give a Dog a Good Name, sales representative Bill Parker told the store manager Jack that he respected Jack for always being willing to listen and big enough to change his mind when the facts warrant it.
questions.explain: Returning after Jack turned down the new product line, Parker praised exactly these qualities, and with that reputation to live up to Jack could hardly refuse another hearing.

questions.unitTitle: Give a Dog a Good Name
questions.q: True or false: In Give a Dog a Good Name, two months after Georgette Leblanc’s remark, Marie the Dishwasher announced her coming marriage to the nephew of the hotel’s owner.
questions.explain: Marie announced her marriage to the nephew of the chef, not the owner, and said she was going to be a lady.

questions.unitTitle: Give a Dog a Good Name
questions.section: Principle: Give the other person a fine reputation to live up to
questions.q: Carnegie’s Principle 7 in Give a Dog a Good Name is: Give the other person a fine ____ to live up to.
questions.explain: The principle asks you to credit people with the quality you want, so they will make great efforts rather than see you disillusioned.

questions.unitTitle: Give a Dog a Good Name
questions.section: Principle: Give the other person a fine reputation to live up to
questions.q: In Give a Dog a Good Name, Carnegie quotes Shakespeare: Assume a ____, if you have it not.
questions.explain: Carnegie quotes “Assume a virtue, if you have it not.” and adds that it may be well to assume and state openly that others have the virtue you want them to develop.

questions.unitTitle: Give a Dog a Good Name
questions.q: The old saying behind the title Give a Dog a Good Name runs: Give a dog a bad ____ and you may as well hang him.
questions.explain: Carnegie turns the saying around: give the dog a good name and see what happens.

questions.unitTitle: Give a Dog a Good Name
questions.q: In Give a Dog a Good Name, teacher Ruth Hopkins told the notorious bad boy Tommy that she understood he was a natural ____.
questions.explain: She told Tommy she would depend on him to help make the class the best in the fourth grade, giving him a leader’s reputation to live up to.

questions.unitTitle: Give a Dog a Good Name
questions.q: Which of these did fourth-grade teacher Ruth Hopkins do to handle the Tommy problem in Give a Dog a Good Name?
options: Made a small friendly comment to each new student as she greeted them
Told Tommy she would depend on him to help make the class the best in the fourth grade
Complimented Tommy on everything he did over the first few days
Warned Tommy that she had heard all about him from his third-grade teacher
Seated Tommy apart from the boys he used to fight with
questions.explain: She greeted every student with a small comment, called Tommy a natural leader she would depend on, and reinforced it with compliments over the first days. She never confronted him with his bad record.

questions.unitTitle: Give a Dog a Good Name
questions.q: Which of these responses to a good worker who begins turning in shoddy work does Carnegie say fall short in Give a Dog a Good Name?
options: Firing the worker
Berating the worker
Reminding the worker of a fine past record
Giving the worker a fine reputation to live up to
questions.explain: Firing really doesn’t solve anything, and berating usually causes resentment. Recalling the worker’s fine record and reputation is the approach Henke used successfully.

questions.unitTitle: Give a Dog a Good Name
questions.q: Put the parts of Henry Henke’s talk with his mechanic Bill in Give a Dog a Good Name in the order he said them.
items: You are a fine mechanic with many years in the trade
We have had a number of compliments about your work
Lately your jobs take longer and fall short of your old standards
Perhaps jointly we could find a way to correct the problem
questions.explain: Henke opened with Bill’s skill and customer praise, only then named the slowdown, and closed by proposing they solve it together.

questions.unitTitle: Give a Dog a Good Name
questions.q: Put the events of Marie the Dishwasher’s story in Give a Dog a Good Name in order.
items: Leblanc tells Marie she does not know the treasures within her
Marie goes back to the kitchen and repeats the remark
The staff begin to give Marie a certain consideration
Marie starts taking care of her face and body
Marie announces her coming marriage to the chef’s nephew
questions.explain: The remark was repeated in the kitchen, others treated her with new respect, she began caring for herself, and two months later she announced her marriage.

questions.unitTitle: Give a Dog a Good Name
questions.q: In Give a Dog a Good Name, match each person to who they were.
pairs: Service manager for a truck dealership in Lowell, Indiana
President of the Baldwin Locomotive Works
Author of Souvenirs, My Life with Maeterlinck
Fourth-grade teacher in Brooklyn, New York
questions.explain: Each gave someone a fine reputation to live up to, except Vauclain, whose remark on respect states the idea behind the principle.

questions.unitTitle: Give a Dog a Good Name
questions.section: Principle: Give the other person a fine reputation to live up to
questions.q: In Give a Dog a Good Name, match each person to the reputation they were given to live up to.
pairs: A fine mechanic whose work drew customer compliments
Always willing to listen and big enough to change his mind
Someone who had been doing a fine job of cleaning
A natural leader who could help make the best class
A person with treasures within her
questions.explain: In every case the speaker credited the person with the very quality they wanted to see, and the person lived up to it.

questions.unitTitle: Give a Dog a Good Name
questions.section: Principle: Give the other person a fine reputation to live up to
questions.q: Sort these ways of improving someone into those that follow Give a Dog a Good Name and those the chapter warns against.
groups: Gives a fine reputation to live up to

items.t: Act as though the wanted trait is already outstanding in them
State openly that they have the virtue you want
Show that you respect them for some ability
Fire the worker whose work has slipped
Berate the worker for shoddy work
Bawl the worker out or threaten him

questions.explain: Carnegie says firing solves nothing and berating breeds resentment, while crediting people with the trait makes them work hard rather than see you disillusioned.

questions.unitTitle: Give a Dog a Good Name
questions.q: In Give a Dog a Good Name, sort these details into the story they belong to.

items.t: Had started her career as a scullery assistant
Repeated the remark in the kitchen and no one made fun of her
Began to take careful care of her face and body
Picked fights with the boys and teased the girls
Could learn rapidly and master school work easily
Was told he would help make the best class in the fourth grade

questions.explain: Marie’s story comes from Georgette Leblanc’s memoir; Tommy’s comes from teacher Ruth Hopkins in Brooklyn.

questions.unitTitle: Give a Dog a Good Name
questions.section: Principle: Give the other person a fine reputation to live up to
questions.q: State Principle 7 from Give a Dog a Good Name and explain what Carnegie means by it.
questions.a: Give the other person a fine reputation to live up to. If you want to improve a person in some respect, act as though that trait were already one of their outstanding characteristics, and say so openly. People will then make prodigious efforts rather than see you disillusioned.

questions.unitTitle: Give a Dog a Good Name
questions.q: In Give a Dog a Good Name, why did Henry Henke’s talk with his slipping mechanic Bill work better than firing or scolding him?
questions.a: Firing would not solve anything and berating would only cause resentment. Henke instead reminded Bill that he was a fine mechanic whose work had drawn compliments, and framed the slowdown as falling below Bill’s own old standards. With that reputation to live up to, Bill again became a fast and thorough mechanic.

questions.unitTitle: Give a Dog a Good Name
questions.q: How does the story of Marie the Dishwasher in Give a Dog a Good Name illustrate the power of a good reputation?
questions.a: Marie was a plain, downtrodden scullery worker until Georgette Leblanc told her she did not know the treasures within her. Believing it, Marie was treated with new consideration by others and began caring for herself, and within two months announced her marriage. As Leblanc put it, “A small phrase had changed her entire life.”

questions.unitTitle: Give a Dog a Good Name
questions.q: How does Give a Dog a Good Name fit between the chapters on praising every improvement and making the fault seem easy to correct in Part Four?
questions.a: Part Four is about changing people without giving offense or arousing resentment. The chapter before it asks the leader to praise the slightest improvement, and this one goes a step further by crediting people in advance with the trait you want them to develop. The next chapter keeps the same encouraging spirit by making the fault seem easy to correct.

questions.unitTitle: Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct
questions.q: In Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct, what did the bachelor friend’s first dancing teacher tell him?
options: That he was all wrong and would have to forget everything and begin all over again
That his dancing was old-fashioned but his fundamentals were all right
That he had a natural sense of rhythm and was a natural-born dancer
That he would learn faster in a group class than in private lessons
questions.explain: She told him he was all wrong and must start over; he says “that took the heart out of me” and he quit. The kinder verdict about sound fundamentals came from the second teacher.

questions.unitTitle: Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct
questions.q: In Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct, why did Lowell Thomas tell Carnegie that bridge would be a cinch for him?
options: Because Carnegie had played cards often as a young man in Missouri
Because bridge is only memory and judgment, and Carnegie had written articles on memory
Because Mrs. Thomas would be his partner and guide him through each hand
Because the game that night was friendly and nobody would keep score
questions.explain: Thomas said there was nothing to bridge except memory and judgment, and since Carnegie had written articles on memory, it was right up his alley. The game was made to seem easy and Carnegie was told he had a flair for it.

questions.unitTitle: Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct
questions.q: In Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct, what did Ely Culbertson say caused him to make a profession of bridge?
options: Failing at every other job he tried after arriving in America in 1922
The huge sales of his first book, translated into a dozen languages
Josephine Dillon persuading him that he was a potential genius at the card table
Winning at a friendly game despite his habit of post-mortem examinations
questions.explain: Culbertson told Carnegie it was that encouragement and that alone that made bridge his profession. His failures at teaching, coal and coffee came before, but they did not point him to bridge.

questions.unitTitle: Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct
questions.q: In Clarence M. Jones’s story in Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct, what goal did he set for his son David with the flash cards?
options: To finish the cards in under 52 minutes by the end of the first week
To get through the repeat stack once every night without help
To bring home a B in math on his next report card
To get all the cards correct in eight minutes with no incorrect answers
questions.explain: Jones promised they would stop the nightly drill once David could do all the cards correctly in eight minutes, a goal that seemed impossible to David. Fifty-two minutes was his time on the first night.

questions.unitTitle: Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct
questions.section: Principle: Use encouragement. Make the fault seem easy to correct
questions.q: A new cashier keeps miscounting change and says she is hopeless with numbers. Which response best follows Carnegie’s principle in Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct?
options: Tell her plainly she is doing it all wrong so she knows exactly where she stands
Tell her it is just a matter of a simple counting habit and that she clearly has the knack for it
Move her to stocking shelves where her weakness with numbers will not matter
List every mistake she made this week so she can study them one by one
questions.explain: Carnegie says to be liberal with encouragement, make the thing seem easy to do and show faith in the person’s ability. Telling someone they are doing it all wrong, he warns, destroys almost every incentive to improve.

questions.unitTitle: Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct
questions.q: In the In a Nutshell list for Part Four, Be a Leader, which principle comes right after Use encouragement. Make the fault seem easy to correct?
options: Give the other person a fine reputation to live up to
Let the other person save face
Make the other person happy about doing the thing you suggest
Ask questions instead of giving direct orders
questions.explain: Principle 8 is followed by the ninth and last leadership principle, making the other person happy about doing the thing you suggest. A fine reputation to live up to is Principle 7, which comes just before.

questions.unitTitle: Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct
questions.q: True or false: In Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct, Ely Culbertson came to America in 1922 and first tried to get a job teaching philosophy and sociology.
questions.explain: Carnegie reports that Culbertson arrived in 1922 and tried to get a teaching job in philosophy and sociology but could not, before failing at selling coal and coffee.

questions.unitTitle: Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct
questions.q: True or false: In Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct, David Jones’s science fair exhibit on levers won first prize for the entire city of Cincinnati.
questions.explain: The exhibit took first prize at his school’s science fair and then won third prize for the entire city of Cincinnati, not first.

questions.unitTitle: Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct
questions.section: Principle: Use encouragement. Make the fault seem easy to correct
questions.q: Carnegie’s eighth leadership principle reads: Use ____. Make the fault seem easy to correct.
questions.explain: The principle pairs encouragement with making the fault seem easy to correct, the two things every story in the chapter shows.

questions.unitTitle: Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct
questions.q: In Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct, Lowell Thomas told Carnegie there is nothing to bridge except memory and ____.
questions.explain: Thomas said “There is nothing to bridge except memory and judgment,” and since Carnegie had written about memory, the game seemed easy.

questions.unitTitle: Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct
questions.q: In Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct, the second dancing teacher assured the bachelor friend that he had a natural sense of ____.
questions.explain: She told him he had a natural sense of rhythm, and he says that encouraged him, gave him hope and made him want to improve.

questions.unitTitle: Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct
questions.q: In Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct, Clarence M. Jones says his son David had been called ____ by his classmates.
questions.explain: Because of the scar from his car accident, classmates called David Frankenstein and said his brains must have leaked out of the cut on his head.

questions.unitTitle: Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct
questions.q: Which of these did the second dancing teacher do, in the story that opens Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct?
options: Kept praising the things he did right
Minimized his errors
Said his fundamentals were all right
Told him to forget everything he knew
Offered to cut her fee if he practised daily
questions.explain: She said his dancing was a bit old-fashioned but the fundamentals were all right, praised what he did right and minimized his errors. Telling him to forget everything was the first teacher’s approach.

questions.unitTitle: Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct
questions.q: Which of these did Ely Culbertson try, without success, after coming to America and before becoming a bridge professional, in Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct?
options: Getting a job teaching philosophy and sociology
Selling coal
Selling coffee
Selling insurance
Writing for a newspaper
questions.explain: Carnegie lists three failures in a row: he could not get a teaching job, then failed at selling coal and then at selling coffee. Insurance and newspaper work are not mentioned.

questions.unitTitle: Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct
questions.q: Put these events in Ely Culbertson’s story from Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct in the order they happened.
items: He came to America in 1922
He failed to get a job teaching philosophy and sociology
He failed at selling coal
He failed at selling coffee
He met and married the bridge teacher Josephine Dillon
He made a profession of bridge
questions.explain: Carnegie tells the failures in sequence, teaching, then coal, then coffee, before Culbertson met Josephine Dillon, whose encouragement alone led him to make bridge his profession.

questions.unitTitle: Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct
questions.q: Put these stages of David Jones’s story from Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct in the order they happened.
items: He moved to Cincinnati at fifteen to live with his father
He drilled flash cards every night against a stop watch
He did all the cards perfectly in under eight minutes
He brought home a B in math
His lever exhibit won prizes at the school and city science fairs
He made the honor roll all through high school
questions.explain: The flash card drill came first and took a month to reach the eight-minute goal; the B in math, the science fair prizes and the honor roll followed as he found that learning was easy.

questions.unitTitle: Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct
questions.q: In Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct, match each person to what they did.
pairs: Persuaded Carnegie that bridge would be a cinch for him
Persuaded Culbertson he was a potential genius at the card table
Drilled his son with flash cards and celebrated every gain
Said her pupil was all wrong and must begin all over again
questions.explain: Thomas, Dillon and Jones each encouraged someone and made the task seem easy; the first dancing teacher did the opposite and her pupil quit.

questions.unitTitle: Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct
questions.q: In Clarence M. Jones’s flash card method in Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct, match each element to its role.
pairs: Where cards David answered correctly went
Where missed cards went after he was given the right answer
The target time for ending the nightly drill
questions.explain: Missed cards were corrected and repeated until none were left, each night was timed, and reaching eight minutes with no errors would end the nightly drill.

questions.unitTitle: Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct
questions.section: Principle: Use encouragement. Make the fault seem easy to correct
questions.q: In Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct, sort these ways of treating someone by their effect according to Carnegie.
groups: Makes the person want to improve

items.t: Saying the person is stupid at the thing
Saying the person has no gift for it
Saying the person is doing it all wrong
Being liberal with encouragement
Making the thing seem easy to do
Showing faith in the person’s ability
Saying the person has an undeveloped flair for it

questions.explain: Carnegie says the first approach destroys almost every incentive to try to improve, while the opposite technique makes a person practise until dawn in order to excel.

questions.unitTitle: Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct
questions.q: In Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct, sort these facts about David Jones into before and after his flash card drills.

items.t: Spent years in special classes for slow learners
Was in seventh grade, two years behind his age group
Added on his fingers
Could barely read
Brought home a B in math
Began using his natural talent for drawing
Was elected to the national honor society

questions.explain: Before, school officials had judged him brain-injured; after he discovered that learning was easy, his math, reading and drawing improved and he made the honor roll.

questions.unitTitle: Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct
questions.q: In the dancing lessons story that opens Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct, why did the bachelor friend quit the first teacher but improve with the second?
questions.a: The first teacher may have told the truth, but by emphasizing his mistakes and saying he must start over she took the heart out of him and left him no incentive. The second praised what he did right, minimized his errors and said he had a natural sense of rhythm. Even though he suspects she was flattering him, it encouraged him, gave him hope and made him want to improve, so he became a better dancer than he would have been.

questions.unitTitle: Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct
questions.section: Principle: Use encouragement. Make the fault seem easy to correct
questions.q: In Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct, what does Carnegie say happens when you tell a child, spouse or employee they are stupid at something, and what does he recommend instead?
questions.a: Telling them they are stupid at it, have no gift for it and are doing it all wrong destroys almost every incentive to try to improve. Instead he recommends the opposite technique: be liberal with encouragement, make the thing seem easy to do, and let the person know you have faith in their ability and that they have an undeveloped flair for it. Then, he says, they will practise until dawn in order to excel.

questions.unitTitle: Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct
questions.q: In Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct, how did Clarence M. Jones’s flash card routine make his son David’s faults seem easy to correct, and what was the result?
questions.a: Each wrong answer was simply corrected and the card put in a repeat stack until none were left, while Jones made a big deal of every right answer and the family celebrated each drop in the nightly time. In a month David went from 52 minutes to under eight and made “the fantastic discovery that learning was easy and fun.” His math, reading and drawing improved, he won science fair prizes and made the honor roll all through high school.

questions.unitTitle: Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct
questions.q: How does Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct fit Part Four’s aim of changing people without giving offense or arousing resentment, and how does it echo the chapter before it?
questions.a: Part Four is about changing people’s behaviour without resentment, and this chapter shows a way to correct a fault without discouraging the person: encourage them and make the fault seem easy to fix. It echoes the previous principle, giving the other person a fine reputation to live up to, because telling someone they have a natural flair or are a potential genius, as Lowell Thomas and Josephine Dillon did, gives them a good opinion of themselves to live up to.

questions.unitTitle: Making People Glad to Do What You Want
questions.q: When Colonel House broke the news to Bryan that House, not Bryan, would go to Europe as peace emissary, what reason did he give?
options: The President wanted a man with no political ambitions to go
The President thought an official visit by Bryan would attract too much attention
The President needed Bryan to stay home and manage the Senate
The President feared Bryan’s pacifism would offend the warlords
questions.explain: House said Bryan’s going would attract a great deal of attention and make people wonder why he was there. Carnegie notes that House practically told Bryan he was too important for the job, and Bryan was satisfied.

questions.unitTitle: Making People Glad to Do What You Want
questions.q: According to McAdoo, how did Woodrow Wilson make him feel when inviting him to be Secretary of the Treasury?
options: That he was the only man in the party able to do the job
That refusing the post would be a betrayal of the country
That the cabinet place was a reward for his campaign work
That by accepting the honor he would be doing Wilson a favor
questions.explain: McAdoo said Wilson “created the impression that by accepting this great honor I would be doing him a favor.” So the highest honor Wilson could give also made McAdoo feel doubly important.

questions.unitTitle: Making People Glad to Do What You Want
questions.q: In Carnegie’s account of the League of Nations, what did Wilson do that failed to make the Senate and the Republican Party happy?
options: He left Republican leaders such as Root, Hughes and Lodge out of the peace conference
He refused to let the Senate vote on the peace treaty at all
He appointed Republicans to the conference but ignored their advice
He announced the League without consulting his own cabinet
questions.explain: Wilson took unknown men from his own party instead of prominent Republicans, and refused to let them feel the League was their idea too. Carnegie calls this crude handling of human relations.

questions.unitTitle: Making People Glad to Do What You Want
questions.q: What happened after Dale O. Ferrier offered his son Jeff a dollar per bushel basket of pears, minus a dollar for every pear left in the yard?
options: Jeff did the chore once but soon went back to doing it poorly
Jeff asked for a higher rate and the two settled on a new deal
Jeff picked up every pear and had to be watched so he did not pull pears off the trees
Jeff refused the deal because he feared losing more than he earned
questions.explain: Ferrier says Jeff not only picked up all the pears but had to be watched so he would not pull a few off the trees to fill baskets. The deal replaced an eyeball-to-eyeball confrontation.

questions.unitTitle: Making People Glad to Do What You Want
questions.q: How did the man Carnegie knew manage to refuse many speaking invitations while leaving the other person content?
options: He explained in detail how busy and overcommitted he was
He suggested a substitute speaker right after expressing regret
He promised to accept the next invitation instead
He sent a gift to the organizers along with his refusal
questions.explain: After thanking them and regretting he could not accept, he suggested another speaker, so the other person had no time to feel unhappy about the refusal. Carnegie stresses he did not merely talk about being too busy.

questions.unitTitle: Making People Glad to Do What You Want
questions.q: A club secretary keeps forgetting to keep the noticeboard up to date, and reminders have not helped. Following the Gunter Schmidt and Mrs. Gent examples, what should the club chair try?
options: Post a public list of the secretary’s missed duties
Quietly take over the noticeboard to avoid friction
Remind the secretary more often and more firmly
Give the secretary a title and charge of the noticeboard
questions.explain: Schmidt made a careless employee Supervisor of Price Tag Posting, and Mrs. Gent made the worst boy her lawn detective; in both cases a title and authority worked where reminders, criticism and coaxing had failed.

questions.unitTitle: Making People Glad to Do What You Want
questions.section: Principle: Make the other person happy about doing the thing you suggest
questions.q: In Carnegie’s first guideline for changing attitudes, what does being sincere involve?
options: Telling the other person frankly what you dislike about his work
Admitting your own mistakes before making any request
Not promising what you cannot deliver and focusing on the other person’s benefits
Praising the other person before you mention the task
questions.explain: The first guideline says not to promise anything you cannot deliver and to forget your own benefits and concentrate on the other person’s. Admitting your own mistakes is a different principle from earlier in Part Four.

questions.unitTitle: Making People Glad to Do What You Want
questions.section: Principle: Make the other person happy about doing the thing you suggest
questions.q: In the stockroom example, how happy does Carnegie expect John to be when the benefits of the job are pointed out to him?
options: Probably not very happy, but happier than if no benefits were pointed out
Delighted, because he has been given a chance to shine
Indifferent, because the task is the same either way
Resentful at first, but grateful once the customers arrive
questions.explain: Carnegie admits John will probably not be very happy, but happier than without the benefits, and more cooperative if he takes pride in his stockroom and the company image.

questions.unitTitle: Making People Glad to Do What You Want
questions.section: Principle: Make the other person happy about doing the thing you suggest
questions.q: What benefit does Carnegie promise the reader at the end of the chapter, even if these approaches do not always work?
options: People will like you more and argue with you less
You will never again have to give a direct order
Your people will eventually come to you with their own ideas
A 10 percent gain in successes makes you 10 percent more effective as a leader
questions.explain: He says it is naïve to expect a favorable reaction every time, but if you increase your successes by even 10 percent you are 10 percent more effective as a leader, and that is your benefit.

questions.unitTitle: Making People Glad to Do What You Want
questions.q: True or false: Carnegie says that Napoleon distributed 15,000 crosses and made fifty of his generals Marshals of France.
questions.explain: Napoleon distributed 15,000 crosses of the Legion of Honor, but he made eighteen of his generals Marshals of France, not fifty.

questions.unitTitle: Making People Glad to Do What You Want
questions.q: True or false: Carnegie claims that Wilson’s snubbing of the Republicans caused America to stay out of the League of Nations.
questions.explain: Carnegie lists keeping America out of the League among the results of Wilson’s crude handling, along with wrecking his career, ruining his health and shortening his life.

questions.unitTitle: Making People Glad to Do What You Want
questions.section: Principle: Make the other person happy about doing the thing you suggest
questions.q: True or false: Carnegie says you can count on a favorable reaction every time you make the other person happy about doing what you suggest.
questions.explain: He calls it naïve to believe you will always get a favorable reaction; he claims only that you are more likely to change attitudes this way than without these principles.

questions.unitTitle: Making People Glad to Do What You Want
questions.q: True or false: This chapter’s principle is the ninth and last in the In a Nutshell summary of Be a Leader.
questions.explain: The Be a Leader summary runs from beginning with praise to making the other person happy about doing the thing you suggest, which closes the list as Principle 9.

questions.unitTitle: Making People Glad to Do What You Want
questions.q: Answering critics who said he gave toys to war-hardened veterans, Napoleon replied that men are ruled by ____.
questions.explain: Carnegie uses Napoleon’s reply to answer the objection that giving titles is childish: titles and honors move even hardened soldiers.

questions.unitTitle: Making People Glad to Do What You Want
questions.q: Mrs. Ernest Gent stopped boys from running across her lawn by making the worst of them her ____ and putting him in charge of keeping trespassers off.
questions.explain: Criticism and coaxing had failed; the title and feeling of authority worked so well that her detective threatened to brand any boy who stepped on the lawn.

questions.unitTitle: Making People Glad to Do What You Want
questions.q: Napoleon was criticized for giving “toys” to his soldiers when he created the Legion of ____ and distributed 15,000 crosses.
questions.explain: The Legion of Honor crosses, the Marshals of France and the name Grand Army are Carnegie’s examples of titles that Napoleon used to rule men.

questions.unitTitle: Making People Glad to Do What You Want
questions.section: Principle: Make the other person happy about doing the thing you suggest
questions.q: Carnegie’s third guideline for the effective leader is: Be ____. Ask yourself what it is the other person really wants.
questions.explain: Being empathetic means asking what the other person really wants, which prepares for matching the benefits of the task to those wants.

questions.unitTitle: Making People Glad to Do What You Want
questions.section: Principle: Make the other person happy about doing the thing you suggest
questions.q: Principle 9 of Part Four reads: Make the other person ____ about doing the thing you suggest.
questions.explain: The principle, which Colonel House followed with Bryan, is to make the other person happy about doing the thing you suggest.

questions.unitTitle: Making People Glad to Do What You Want
questions.q: Which of these does Carnegie list as results of Wilson’s crude handling of the Republicans over the League of Nations?
options: Wilson wrecked his own career
Wilson ruined his health
Wilson lost his own party’s nomination
America stayed out of the League
The Senate censured Wilson
questions.explain: Carnegie says Wilson wrecked his career, ruined his health, shortened his life, kept America out of the League and altered world history. A lost nomination and a censure are not in his account.

questions.unitTitle: Making People Glad to Do What You Want
questions.q: Which of these did Mrs. Ernest Gent try, without success, before giving the worst boy a title?
options: Criticism
Calling the police
Coaxing
Putting up a fence
Paying the boys to stay off
questions.explain: She tried criticism and she tried coaxing, and neither worked. Only giving the ringleader a title and authority solved the problem.

questions.unitTitle: Making People Glad to Do What You Want
questions.q: Which of these titles and honors does Carnegie say Napoleon used with his soldiers?
options: Crosses of the Legion of Honor
The rank of Marshal of France for eighteen generals
Calling his troops the Grand Army
Knighthoods for his bravest sergeants
Gold medals for every veteran of ten campaigns
questions.explain: Napoleon distributed 15,000 crosses, made eighteen generals Marshals of France and called his troops the Grand Army. Knighthoods and gold medals are not mentioned.

questions.unitTitle: Making People Glad to Do What You Want
questions.section: Principle: Make the other person happy about doing the thing you suggest
questions.q: Which of these are among Carnegie’s guidelines for the effective leader who needs to change attitudes or behavior?
options: Know exactly what it is you want the other person to do
State clearly what you yourself will gain
Match the benefits to the other person’s wants
Give the request as a brief, firm order
Consider the benefits that person will receive
questions.explain: The guidelines include knowing what you want, considering the other person’s benefits and matching them to his wants. Carnegie says to forget your own benefits, and he contrasts the curt order with the benefits version.

questions.unitTitle: Making People Glad to Do What You Want
questions.section: Principle: Make the other person happy about doing the thing you suggest
questions.q: Put Carnegie’s six guidelines for changing attitudes or behavior in the order he lists them.
items: Be sincere
Know exactly what you want the other person to do
Be empathetic
Consider the benefits that person will receive
Match those benefits to the other person’s wants
Make the request so he sees he will personally benefit
questions.explain: The list moves from sincerity and a clear aim, through understanding the other person’s wants and benefits, to framing the request itself.

questions.unitTitle: Making People Glad to Do What You Want
questions.q: Put the events of the peace emissary story from 1915 in the order they happened.
items: Wilson decides to send a personal representative to Europe
Bryan longs to go and make his name immortal
Wilson appoints Colonel House instead
House tells Bryan his going would attract too much attention
Bryan is satisfied with the explanation
questions.explain: Wilson resolved to send an emissary, Bryan hoped to be chosen, House was appointed and then had to break the news without giving offense, which he did by implying Bryan was too important.

questions.unitTitle: Making People Glad to Do What You Want
questions.q: Put these examples in the order Carnegie presents them in Making People Glad to Do What You Want.
items: Colonel House and Bryan
Wilson inviting McAdoo into the cabinet
Wilson and the League of Nations
Dale Ferrier and the pears
Gunter Schmidt and the price tags
Mrs. Gent and her lawn detective
questions.explain: Carnegie opens with statesmen, including Wilson’s failure as a contrast, then turns to everyday people; Napoleon comes between Schmidt and Mrs. Gent to answer the charge that titles are childish.

questions.unitTitle: Making People Glad to Do What You Want
questions.q: Match each person in the chapter to how he made someone glad to go along.
pairs: Implied that Bryan was too important for the job
Made accepting a cabinet post seem a favor to himself
Paid per basket of pears and deducted per pear missed
Made a careless employee responsible for all price tags
questions.explain: Each turns a request or a disappointment into something the other person is happy about: importance, a deal, or a title with responsibility.

questions.unitTitle: Making People Glad to Do What You Want
questions.q: Match each person to how Carnegie identifies him or her.
pairs: A father from Fort Wayne, Indiana
A food store manager who took the course in West Germany
Carnegie’s friend from Scarsdale, New York
Invited to become Secretary of the Treasury
questions.explain: These are the people Carnegie names in his examples, from statesmen to a parent, a store manager and a homeowner.

questions.unitTitle: Making People Glad to Do What You Want
questions.section: Principle: Make the other person happy about doing the thing you suggest
questions.q: Match each guideline for the effective leader to what it asks of you.
pairs: Do not promise anything you cannot deliver
Ask yourself what the other person really wants
Fit what he will gain to what he wants
Convey the idea that he personally will benefit
questions.explain: Sincerity guards against empty promises, empathy finds the other person’s wants, and the last steps link the task’s benefits to those wants in how you ask.

questions.unitTitle: Making People Glad to Do What You Want
questions.q: In Making People Glad to Do What You Want, sort these approaches by how they turned out.

items.t: Schmidt giving the employee a supervisor title
Mrs. Gent making the ringleader her detective
Ferrier’s dollar-per-basket deal
Carnegie’s acquaintance suggesting a substitute speaker when declining an invitation
Schmidt’s reminders and admonitions
Mrs. Gent’s criticism and coaxing
Wilson snubbing the Republican leaders

questions.explain: Reminders, criticism, coaxing and snubs failed or backfired, while giving people something to be glad about, a title, a deal or a substitute, won cooperation.

questions.unitTitle: Making People Glad to Do What You Want
questions.section: Principle: Make the other person happy about doing the thing you suggest
questions.q: Sort these phrases from the stockroom example by which version of the request to John they belong to.

items.t: I need the stockroom cleaned out
So sweep it out
we won’t be faced with it later
it would make us look efficient
a good company image
a job that should be completed right away

questions.explain: The curt order states the speaker’s need and gives commands; the benefits version gives the same task but shows John that doing it now saves him later work and lets him contribute to the company image.

questions.unitTitle: Making People Glad to Do What You Want
questions.q: According to Carnegie, what went wrong with Wilson’s handling of the League of Nations, and why does he call it a turning point in history?
questions.a: Wilson refused to take prominent Republicans such as Root, Hughes or Lodge to the peace conference and took unknown men from his own party instead. He would not let the Republicans feel the League was partly their idea or let them have a finger in the pie. Carnegie says this crude handling wrecked Wilson’s career, ruined his health, shortened his life, kept America out of the League and altered the history of the world.

questions.unitTitle: Making People Glad to Do What You Want
questions.q: How did the man Carnegie knew turn down speaking invitations from friends and people he was obligated to without leaving them unhappy?
questions.a: He did not just explain that he was too busy. After expressing appreciation for the invitation and regret that he could not accept, he suggested a substitute speaker. That way the other person had no time to feel unhappy about the refusal, because his thoughts were turned at once to another speaker who could accept.

questions.unitTitle: Making People Glad to Do What You Want
questions.q: Why does Carnegie bring in Napoleon right after the story of Gunter Schmidt’s Supervisor of Price Tag Posting?
questions.a: He anticipates the objection that giving someone a title is childish. Napoleon faced the same criticism when he handed out Legion of Honor crosses, made generals Marshals of France and called his troops the Grand Army, and he answered, “Men are ruled by toys.” Carnegie concludes that giving titles and authority worked for Napoleon and will work for the reader too.

questions.unitTitle: Making People Glad to Do What You Want
questions.section: Principle: Make the other person happy about doing the thing you suggest
questions.q: Why is the benefits version of the request to John likely to work better than the curt order, and what does Carnegie assume about John?
questions.a: The curt order only states the speaker’s need and tells John what to do, while the benefits version shows what John gains: the job will not hang over him later, and he will have done his part to make the company look efficient and give it a good image. Carnegie assumes John takes pride in how his stockroom looks and cares about the company image. John will probably not be very happy, but he will be happier and more cooperative than if no benefits had been pointed out.

questions.unitTitle: Making People Glad to Do What You Want
questions.section: Principle: Make the other person happy about doing the thing you suggest
questions.q: A team leader needs someone to stay late on Friday to finish a report for a client. Using Carnegie’s guidelines, how should she make the request?
questions.a: She should first be sincere and promise nothing she cannot deliver, know exactly what she wants done, and ask herself what the team member really wants. Then she should consider the benefits he would get from the task, such as credit with the client or not facing the work on Monday, and match them to his wants. Finally she should put the request so that he sees he will personally benefit, rather than giving a curt order.

questions.unitTitle: Making People Glad to Do What You Want
questions.q: How does this final principle of Part Four echo ideas from earlier in the book, such as arousing an eager want and letting people feel an idea is theirs?
questions.a: Part One teaches that the way to move people is to arouse in the other person an eager want, and this chapter applies that to a leader’s requests by showing people what they will gain. Part Three teaches letting the other person feel the idea is his or hers, and Wilson’s failure to let the Republicans feel the League was their idea shows the cost of ignoring it. Closing the Be a Leader list, the principle sums up Part Four’s aim of changing people without giving offense or arousing resentment.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: In Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction, where did twenty-five hundred people gather on a cold January night in 1935 to hear the opening of the Carnegie course?
options: The grand ballroom of the Hotel Pennsylvania in New York
The main hall of the Y.M.C.A. on 125th Street in New York
The auditorium of the American Academy of Dramatic Arts
A lecture hall at the University of Chicago
questions.explain: Thomas opens with the crowd thronging into the grand ballroom of the Hotel Pennsylvania. The Y.M.C.A. is where Carnegie first taught years earlier, not the scene of this 1935 meeting.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: In Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction, what had drawn the crowd of twenty-five hundred to the 1935 meeting?
options: A cartoon by Believe-It-or-Not Ripley about Carnegie
A personal invitation letter from Dale Carnegie
A full-page announcement in the New York Sun
A radio broadcast by Lowell Thomas
questions.explain: The people had been lured by a newspaper ad: two evenings earlier they had seen a full-page announcement in the New York Sun urging them to learn to speak effectively and prepare for leadership.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: Why is Lowell Thomas’s biographical piece A Shortcut to Distinction given that title?
options: It names the shortest of Carnegie’s rules for handling people
It echoes Thomas’s claim that the ability to speak is a shortcut to distinction, the same thing young Carnegie sought in college
It refers to the quickest route Carnegie took from Missouri to New York
It is the title of the textbook Carnegie wrote for the Y.M.C.A. courses
questions.explain: Thomas states that “The ability to speak is a shortcut to distinction,” and later describes the insecure college student Carnegie looking for some shortcut to distinction and choosing speaking contests. Carnegie’s textbook was called Public Speaking and Influencing Men in Business.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: In Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction, what happened to the banker Godfrey Meyer after he spoke out at a Clifton, New Jersey, town meeting?
options: He was promoted to head of his bank’s Wall Street office
He was asked to teach a Carnegie course in New Jersey
He had his tax bill reduced by the town council
He was urged to run for the town council and led all ninety-six candidates
questions.explain: His angry talk about his tax bill led citizens to urge him to run for the council, and when the ballots were counted his name led all ninety-six candidates. He made far more friends in six weeks than in the previous twenty-five years.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: In Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction, what did the head of a national association of food manufacturers gain from learning to speak effectively?
options: More free publicity for his company in two years than a quarter of a million dollars of advertising had bought
A seat on the board of the Associated Press
A contract to supply food to the Y.M.C.A. schools
An invitation to address the royal family in London
questions.explain: Once he could think on his feet he became president of his association, his talks were carried on the Associated Press wires, and he received more free publicity than a quarter of a million dollars in direct advertising had brought.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: In Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction, why did the young Dale Carnegie decide to try to win a speaking contest at college?
options: His father insisted that he become a preacher
The college offered a cash prize that would pay for his board in town
He wanted influence and prestige, and saw that he had no flair for athletics
A teacher told him he was a natural orator
questions.explain: Ashamed of his poverty and developing an inferiority complex, he noticed that athletes and contest-winning speakers enjoyed influence and prestige. Lacking a flair for athletics, he chose speaking.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: In Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction, what did Carnegie achieve as a salesman for Armour and Company in western South Dakota?
options: He sold more shoes to railroad men than any other agent
He raised an unproductive territory from twenty-fifth place to first among twenty-nine car routes
He opened a new route from South Omaha to Wyoming
He became Armour’s youngest regional manager
questions.explain: Within two years he took a territory standing twenty-fifth and boosted it to first among all twenty-nine car routes out of South Omaha. He turned down the promotion Armour then offered.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: In Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction, how did Carnegie respond when the Y.M.C.A. schools refused to pay him two dollars a night to teach public speaking?
options: He gave up and returned to selling trucks
He hired a hall and taught the classes on his own
He offered to teach for free for one season
He agreed to teach on commission for a percentage of the net profits
questions.explain: He agreed to take a percentage of the net profits, if there were any. Within three years that arrangement was paying him thirty dollars a night instead of two.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: In Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction, what did Carnegie say is the way to develop self-confidence?
options: Do the thing you fear to do and get a record of successful experiences behind you
Study the great orators until their methods become second nature
Prepare every talk word for word and rehearse it alone
Speak only on subjects you already know thoroughly
questions.explain: He said the way is to do the thing you fear and build up a record of successes. That is why he made every class member talk at every session.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: In Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction, what did Carnegie say his main job really was?
options: Training people to give polished after-dinner speeches
Writing practical textbooks for adult schools
Helping people conquer their fears and develop courage
Teaching salesmanship to business executives
questions.explain: Carnegie would say teaching public speaking was incidental; his main job was to help people conquer their fears and develop courage.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: A new employee who speaks clearly and confidently in meetings is soon assumed by her managers to be more capable than her actual work shows. Which claim in Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction does this illustrate?
options: Knowledge alone is the open sesame to professional rewards
A person who can speak acceptably is credited with ability out of proportion to what he or she possesses
All people can talk when they get mad
The average person develops only a small part of his latent ability
questions.explain: Thomas says the ability to speak puts a person in the limelight, and that the acceptable speaker is usually credited with ability out of all proportion to what he or she really has. The idea that knowledge alone brings rewards is the belief he says business life disproves.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: Why does A Shortcut to Distinction by Lowell Thomas appear at the end of How to Win Friends and Influence People?
options: It is Carnegie’s own summary of the thirty principles
It is a set of exercises for practising the rules in Part Four
It answers critics of the first edition
It was written as an introduction to the original edition and is reprinted to give readers background on Carnegie
questions.explain: The note before the piece says it was written as an introduction to the original edition and is reprinted to give readers additional background on Dale Carnegie. It tells his life story rather than adding new principles.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: In Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction, why does Thomas call the ability to speak a shortcut to distinction?
questions.a: Thomas says that the ability to speak puts a person in the limelight and raises one head and shoulders above the crowd. The person who can speak acceptably is usually given credit for more ability than he or she really has. The stories of Godfrey Meyer and the food association president show leadership and prestige gravitating to the person who can talk.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: In Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction, what does Thomas think the crowd at the Hotel Pennsylvania reveals about education?
questions.a: He says adults returning ten or twenty years after school to take this training is a glaring commentary on the shocking deficiencies of the educational system. In school they believed knowledge alone was the open sesame to rewards, but business life showed them that personality and the ability to talk matter more than Latin verbs or a Harvard degree. Schools had taught Greek, Latin and higher mathematics but nothing on getting along with people.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: In Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction, describe how Patrick J. O’Haire changed through the Carnegie course and what his story shows.
questions.a: O’Haire, an Irish immigrant with four years of schooling, was a struggling truck salesman so crippled by an inferiority complex that he paced outside offices before daring to enter. At first he was dizzy with fear when speaking, but over the weeks he lost his fear of audiences, individuals and superiors, presented his ideas and was advanced into the sales department. At the Hotel Pennsylvania he held twenty-five hundred people with a rollicking story, showing that the course builds courage and confidence that carry into business life.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: In Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction, how did Carnegie’s experiences at the State Teachers’ College lead to his later career?
questions.a: Poor and ashamed of his clothes and of riding home to milk the cows, he developed an inferiority complex and looked for a shortcut to distinction. He practised speeches for months and, after many defeats, began winning every speaking contest, and other students he trained won too. Later he judged that this public-speaking training had given him more confidence, courage and poise in dealing with people than all his other courses together, so he proposed teaching public speaking to business people at the Y.M.C.A.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: In Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction, why was Carnegie forced to make his course swift and practical, and what kind of training resulted?
questions.a: His students were business men and women, many of whom had not been in a classroom for thirty years and were paying tuition on the installment plan. They wanted results quickly, usable the next day in business interviews and talks. So he developed a unique system combining public speaking, salesmanship, human relations and applied psychology, bound by no hard-and-fast rules.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: In Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction, why did Carnegie make every class member talk at every session?
questions.a: Carnegie believed almost anyone can speak acceptably with self-confidence and an idea boiling within, and that self-confidence comes from doing the thing you fear and building a record of successful experiences. Speaking at every session gave members that record. The audience was sympathetic because everyone was in the same boat, and the courage, confidence and enthusiasm gained carried over into their private speaking.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: How does Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction connect to Carnegie’s own introduction, How This Book Was Written—and Why?
questions.a: Both describe the survey by the University of Chicago and the United Y.M.C.A. Schools which found that adults’ second interest, after health, was getting along with and influencing people. Both report that no practical textbook on human relations existed. Thomas’s account of Carnegie’s courses and his practical, results-driven teaching supplies the background to the book that Carnegie says grew out of his classes, which is why it is reprinted for readers wanting background on him.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: A friend dreads speaking up in meetings and plans to wait until she feels confident before trying. Using Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction, what would Carnegie advise?
questions.a: Carnegie would tell her not to wait: the way to develop self-confidence is to do the thing you fear to do and get a record of successful experiences behind you. She should speak at every opportunity, ideally on something she feels strongly about, since he held that almost anyone can speak acceptably with self-confidence and an idea boiling within. As with the class members, repeated practice builds courage that carries over.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: In Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction, Thomas reports that a cartoon by Believe-It-or-Not Ripley said Carnegie had criticized ____ speeches.
questions.explain: Ripley’s cartoon put the figure at 150,000, which Thomas says is about one talk for almost every day since Columbus discovered America.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: In Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction, Thomas declares: The ability to speak is a ____ to distinction.
questions.explain: The line gives the piece its title: speaking ability puts a person in the limelight and raises one above the crowd.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: In Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction, because existing textbooks were too academic, Carnegie wrote his own book, Public Speaking and Influencing Men in ____.
questions.explain: It became the official text of all the Y.M.C.A.s and of the American Bankers’ Association and the National Credit Men’s Association.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: In Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction, after leaving Armour and Company, Carnegie went to New York and studied at the American Academy of ____ Arts.
questions.explain: He then toured playing Dr. Hartley in Polly of the Circus, but recognised he would never be a Booth or a Barrymore.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: In Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction, Thomas cites Professor William James of Harvard as saying the average person develops only ____ percent of his latent mental ability.
questions.explain: Thomas uses this to frame Carnegie’s achievement: by helping business people develop their latent possibilities he created a significant movement in adult education.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: In Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction, Carnegie claimed that all people can talk when they get ____.
questions.explain: He said even the most ignorant man, knocked down, would get up and talk with an eloquence rivalling William Jennings Bryan.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: In Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction, Carnegie’s family moved to a farm near the State ____ College at Warrensburg, Missouri, and he rode three miles to it on horseback each day.
questions.explain: Board in town cost a dollar a day, which he could not afford, so he lived on the farm and commuted on horseback.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: True or false: In Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction, Patrick J. O’Haire was born in Ireland and had attended school for only four years.
questions.explain: Thomas says O’Haire was born in Ireland, attended school for only four years, and worked as a mechanic and chauffeur before selling trucks.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: True or false: In Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction, the course had been playing to packed houses in New York City every season for the preceding ten years.
questions.explain: The course had run for the preceding twenty-four years, which is why Thomas rejects the idea that the crowd came from a sudden depression-era hunger for education.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: True or false: In Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction, Carnegie refused the promotion Armour and Company offered him and went to New York to study drama.
questions.explain: Armour told him he had achieved what seemed impossible and offered a promotion, but he resigned and studied at the American Academy of Dramatic Arts.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: True or false: In Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction, young Carnegie won the first speaking contest he entered at college.
questions.explain: Despite months of preparation he met defeat after defeat, grew so depressed he thought of suicide, and only then suddenly began winning every contest.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: Which of these organizations, according to Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction, had the Carnegie training conducted in their own offices?
options: The Westinghouse Electric Company
The McGraw-Hill Publishing Company
The New York Telephone Company
Armour and Company
The Packard Motor Car Company
questions.explain: Thomas lists Westinghouse, McGraw-Hill and the New York Telephone Company among skeptical, conservative firms that brought the training in-house. Armour and Packard were companies Carnegie himself worked for as a salesman.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: Which of these jobs did Carnegie hold before he began teaching at the Y.M.C.A., according to Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction?
options: Selling correspondence courses to ranchers in Nebraska and Wyoming
Selling bacon, soap and lard for Armour and Company
Touring as an actor in Polly of the Circus
Working as a bank clerk on Wall Street
Working as a mechanic in a machine shop
questions.explain: Carnegie sold correspondence courses, sold for Armour, and toured as Dr. Hartley before selling Packard cars. The Wall Street banker was Godfrey Meyer, and the machine shop belonged to Patrick O’Haire’s past.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: Which of these points appear both in Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction and in Carnegie’s introduction, How This Book Was Written—and Why?
options: A survey involving the University of Chicago and the United Y.M.C.A. Schools found health was adults’ first interest and human relations their second
No practical textbook on human relations could be found for adults
The survey interviewed every adult in Meriden, Connecticut, with 156 questions
Carnegie carried newborn pigs to their mother at three in the morning
questions.explain: Both pieces report the survey’s findings and the missing textbook. The Meriden details appear only in Carnegie’s introduction, and the story of the pigs only in Thomas’s biography.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: Which of these did Carnegie combine in the training system described in Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction?
options: Salesmanship
Human relations
Applied psychology
Latin and Greek grammar
Stage acting technique
Strict hard-and-fast rules
questions.explain: Thomas calls it a unique combination of public speaking, salesmanship, human relations and applied psychology. He stresses Carnegie was a slave to no hard-and-fast rules.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: Which of these hardships struck the Carnegie family farm in northwest Missouri, according to Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction?
options: The 102 River flooded the corn and swept away the hay
Fat hogs sickened and died from cholera
A drought dried up the wells for several years
A fire destroyed the barn and the livestock
questions.explain: Thomas describes floods from the 102 River, hogs dying of cholera, collapsing cattle and mule prices and the threat of foreclosure. Drought and fire are not mentioned.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: In Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction, put Carnegie’s working life in order, from first to last.
items: Selling correspondence courses to ranchers
Selling for Armour and Company in South Dakota
Studying at the American Academy of Dramatic Arts
Selling cars and trucks for Packard
Teaching public speaking at the Y.M.C.A.
questions.explain: After college he failed at correspondence courses, succeeded for Armour, tried acting, disliked selling Packard vehicles, and then turned to teaching public speaking at night.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: In Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction, put the first three speakers at the 1935 Hotel Pennsylvania meeting in the order they spoke.
items: Patrick J. O’Haire, the truck salesman
Godfrey Meyer, the banker
The head of a food manufacturers’ association
questions.explain: O’Haire spoke first, Meyer was the next speaker, and the food association president was the third.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: In Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction, put the events of Godfrey Meyer’s story in order.
items: He received a tax bill he thought unjust
He spoke out at the town meeting
Citizens urged him to run for the town council
His name led all ninety-six candidates
questions.explain: Instead of grumbling at home about his tax bill, he spoke at the town meeting; that talk led to his candidacy and his election win.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: In Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction, put the stages of Carnegie’s college speaking career in order.
items: He decided to win a speaking contest
He practised in the saddle and in the barn
He met defeat after defeat
He began winning every contest
Other students asked him to train them
questions.explain: Months of practice were followed by repeated defeats and despair, then a sudden run of wins, after which fellow students sought his training and won too.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: In Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction, match each speaker at the 1935 meeting to his story.
pairs: A shy truck salesman advanced into the sales department
A banker elected to the Clifton town council
Gained more free publicity than heavy advertising had bought
Came to prepare for one important three-minute speech
questions.explain: Each story shows speaking ability bringing promotion, office, prestige or preparation for a key moment.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: In Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction, match each place to what happened to Carnegie there.
pairs: He attended the State Teachers’ College
He wept in despair in a hotel room
He got a job selling for Armour and Company
He put on shows under royal patronage
questions.explain: These places trace his path from a poor student and failing salesman to a successful salesman and later an international lecturer.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: In Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction, match each number to what it counts.
pairs: People at the 1935 Hotel Pennsylvania meeting
Business people Carnegie trained over twenty-four years
Time each graduate had to speak at the meeting
Candidates in the Clifton council election
questions.explain: All four figures come from Thomas’s account of the 1935 meeting and the stories told there.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: In Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction, match each sum of money to what it refers to.
pairs: Carnegie’s pay for picking strawberries and cutting cockleburs
Board and room in Warrensburg he could not afford
The salary the Y.M.C.A. refused to pay him
What his commission earned within three years
questions.explain: The figures chart his rise from farm labourer to a teacher whose commission rose far above the salary first refused him.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: In Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction, sort these episodes of Carnegie’s life into setbacks and successes.

items.t: Losing contest after contest at college
Failing to sell correspondence courses
Being refused a salary by the Y.M.C.A.
Winning every speaking contest in college
Raising his Armour territory to first place
Seeing his textbook adopted by all the Y.M.C.A.s

questions.explain: Thomas presents Carnegie’s career as full of sharp contrasts, with each failure followed by a turn to success.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: In Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction, sort these into what the adult-education survey found adults wanted and what it found they did not want.

items.t: Knowledge about health
Skill in getting along with and influencing people
Suggestions they could use immediately at work and home
To become public speakers
High-sounding talk about psychology

questions.explain: The survey found health first and human relations second, and that adults wanted usable suggestions rather than becoming public speakers or hearing lofty psychology.

questions.unitTitle: A Shortcut to Distinction
questions.q: In Lowell Thomas’s A Shortcut to Distinction, sort these into features of Carnegie’s course and things it avoided.

items.t: Every member speaking at every session
A sympathetic audience all in the same boat
Results usable the next day in business
Hard-and-fast rules
Academic, impractical textbooks

questions.explain: Carnegie forced everyone to talk each session before a sympathetic audience and aimed at quick, practical results; he followed no rigid rules and wrote his own text because existing ones were too academic.
